Chapter 3Milnor §§4–5pp. 25–32Contents ↑

Chapter 3. Counting critical points: examples and the Morse inequalities

Milnor, “Morse Theory”, §4–§5, rewritten for a first-year graduate student who wants to know what the theorem is for. Every proof is complete; the outside facts used (standard properties of singular homology, Poincaré duality mod 2, Brown’s monotone union theorem) are stated precisely where they enter.

0. How many transition states must a flexible molecule have?

Take a molecule with two bonds about which parts of it can rotate. Its shape is described by two torsion angles \(\varphi\) and \(\psi\), each defined up to a full turn, so the configuration space is a torus and the potential energy is a smooth function \(V(\varphi, \psi)\) on it. The local minima of \(V\) are the conformers; to pass between them the molecule crosses a saddle point, a transition state; the maxima are the most crowded shapes. Is there a relation between the three numbers?

There is, and nothing about the chemistry enters. If the critical points are nondegenerate (the generic situation, Chapter 4), \[\#\{\text{saddles}\} = \#\{\text{minima}\} + \#\{\text{maxima}\}, \qquad \#\{\text{saddles}\} \ \ge\ \#\{\text{minima}\} + 1 .\] The same law holds for a double pendulum or a two-joint robot arm under any load. The constants come from the topology of the torus: its Betti numbers are \(1, 2, 1\).

This chapter proves such statements in general. The Morse inequalities bound the number \(C_\lambda\) of critical points of index \(\lambda\) of a Morse function on a compact manifold from below by its Betti numbers, and their alternating sum is an equality, the Euler characteristic. They are what survives of the cell decomposition of Chapter 2 when one only counts the cells.

First come Milnor’s examples of what the cell decomposition alone can do: two nondegenerate critical points force a sphere (Reeb), three force something like a projective plane, and complex projective space has a function with one critical point in each even index. In §7 the inequalities count the equilibria of a double pendulum and the conformers of a two-rotor molecule.

1. Reeb’s theorem: two critical points make a sphere (Milnor p. 25)

Conventions. In this chapter a manifold is smooth, Hausdorff, second countable and without boundary; \(f : M \to \mathbb{R}\) is smooth and \(M^a = f^{-1}(-\infty, a]\). A Morse function is one whose critical points are all nondegenerate. Earlier results are cited by Milnor’s numbers: the Morse lemma 2.2, Corollary 2.3 (nondegenerate critical points are isolated), Theorem 3.1 (if \(f^{-1}[a,b]\) is compact and free of critical points, the flow of a compactly supported multiple of \(\operatorname{grad} f\) carries \(M^a\) diffeomorphically onto \(M^b\), and \(M^a\) is a deformation retract of \(M^b\)), Theorem 3.2 with Remark 3.3 (quoted precisely in §5) and Theorem 3.5.

Two consequences of the Morse lemma are used repeatedly.

  1. A nondegenerate critical point that is a local minimum has index \(0\), and one that is a local maximum has index \(n\). Indeed if \(\lambda \ge 1\), then in Morse coordinates \(f(s e_1) = f(p) - s^2 < f(p)\) for small \(s \ne 0\), so \(p\) is not a local minimum; similarly for maxima.

  2. A Morse function on a compact manifold has finitely many critical points (Corollary 2.3 and compactness of the closed set of critical points).

Theorem 4.1 (Reeb). (checked by machine: V3.6, in a narrower form; V4.24, with its hypotheses made explicit)1 Let \(M\) be a compact \(n\)-manifold and \(f\) a smooth function on \(M\) with exactly two critical points, both nondegenerate. Then \(M\) is homeomorphic to \(S^n\).

Milnor’s figure on p. 25 shows the idea: a small sublevel set around the minimum is a disk, Theorem 3.1 stretches it until it covers everything except a small disk around the maximum, and two disks glued along their boundary spheres form a sphere.

Proof. If \(n = 0\), \(M\) is a finite set and every point is critical, so \(M\) has two points and is \(S^0\). Let \(n \ge 1\).

Step 1: the critical points are the minimum and the maximum. By compactness \(f\) attains its minimum at some \(p\) and its maximum at some \(q\), and both are critical (in a chart they are interior extrema). If \(f(p) = f(q)\) then \(f\) is constant and every point is critical, infinitely many since \(n \ge 1\). So \(p \ne q\) are the two critical points, and every other point \(x\) has \(f(p) < f(x) < f(q)\), since any point where an extreme value is attained is critical. Replacing \(f\) by \((f - f(p))/(f(q) - f(p))\), which has the same critical points and positively rescaled Hessians, we may assume \(f(p) = 0\), \(f(q) = 1\) and \(0 < f < 1\) on \(M \setminus \{p, q\}\).

Step 2: two small closed \(n\)-cells. By the Morse lemma and (i) there is a chart \(\phi\) from a neighbourhood \(U\) of \(p\) onto an open subset of \(\mathbb{R}^n\) with \(\phi(p) = 0\) and \(f \circ \phi^{-1}(x) = |x|^2\). Choose \(r > 0\) with \(\bar B_r \subset \phi(U)\) and put \(V = \phi^{-1}(B_r)\). The set \(M \setminus V\) is compact and does not contain \(p\), so \(f\) has a positive minimum \(m\) on it (put \(m = 1\) if \(M \setminus V\) is empty). For \(0 < \varepsilon < \min(m, r^2)\), every point with \(f \le \varepsilon\) lies in \(V\), where the condition reads \(|\phi|^2 \le \varepsilon\). Hence \(M^\varepsilon = \phi^{-1}(\bar B_{\sqrt\varepsilon})\), and \[h_0 : D^n \to M^\varepsilon, \qquad h_0(x) = \phi^{-1}(\sqrt{\varepsilon}\, x),\] is a homeomorphism (indeed a diffeomorphism) of the closed unit disk onto \(M^\varepsilon\) that carries the unit sphere \(S^{n-1}\) onto \(f^{-1}(\varepsilon)\). At \(q\) the Morse lemma and (i) give coordinates \(\psi\) with \(f \circ \psi^{-1}(y) = 1 - |y|^2\), and the same argument, after shrinking \(\varepsilon\) (keep \(\varepsilon < \tfrac12\)), shows that \(D_2 := f^{-1}[1-\varepsilon, 1]\) is the image of a homeomorphism \(h_2(y) = \psi^{-1}(\sqrt\varepsilon\, y)\) of \(D^n\), with \(h_2(S^{n-1}) = f^{-1}(1-\varepsilon)\).

Step 3: stretching the lower cell. The set \(f^{-1}[\varepsilon, 1-\varepsilon]\) is compact and free of critical points, so Theorem 3.1 gives a diffeomorphism \(\Phi\) of \(M\) with \(\Phi(M^\varepsilon) = M^{1-\varepsilon}\). Moreover \(\Phi(f^{-1}(\varepsilon)) = f^{-1}(1-\varepsilon)\): in the proof of Theorem 3.1, \(\Phi\) is the time-\((1-2\varepsilon)\) map of a flow along which \(f\) never decreases and increases with unit speed inside \(f^{-1}[\varepsilon, 1-\varepsilon]\). A point starting on the level \(\varepsilon\) is therefore on the level \(\varepsilon + t\) at every time \(t \le 1 - 2\varepsilon\), which gives \(\Phi(f^{-1}(\varepsilon)) \subset f^{-1}(1-\varepsilon)\), and running the flow backwards gives the reverse inclusion. Put \(D_1 := M^{1-\varepsilon}\) and \(h_1 := \Phi \circ h_0\), a homeomorphism \(D^n \to D_1\) with \(h_1(S^{n-1}) = f^{-1}(1-\varepsilon)\).

Step 4: gluing. Now \(M = D_1 \cup D_2\) and \(D_1 \cap D_2 = f^{-1}(1-\varepsilon) = h_1(S^{n-1}) = h_2(S^{n-1})\), so \(g := h_2^{-1} \circ h_1 : S^{n-1} \to S^{n-1}\) is a homeomorphism. Its cone \[G(x) = |x|\, g(x/|x|) \quad (x \ne 0), \qquad G(0) = 0,\] is a homeomorphism of \(D^n\) extending \(g\): it is continuous at \(0\) because \(|G(x)| = |x|\), and its inverse is the cone of \(g^{-1}\). (This is Alexander’s trick.) Write points of \(S^n \subset \mathbb{R}^n \times \mathbb{R}\) as \((x, s)\), so that \(x \in D^n\), and define \[H(x, s) = h_1(x) \ \text{ if } s \ge 0, \qquad H(x, s) = h_2(G(x)) \ \text{ if } s \le 0 .\] On the equator \(s = 0\) we have \(|x| = 1\) and \(h_2(G(x)) = h_2(g(x)) = h_1(x)\), so \(H\) is well defined, and it is continuous on each closed hemisphere (on each, \((x,s) \mapsto x\) is a homeomorphism onto \(D^n\)), hence continuous. \(H\) maps the upper hemisphere bijectively onto \(D_1\), the lower one onto \(D_2\), the equator onto \(D_1 \cap D_2\), and the open hemispheres into the disjoint sets \(D_1 \setminus D_2\) and \(D_2 \setminus D_1\); so \(H\) is a bijection \(S^n \to M\). A continuous bijection from a compact space to a Hausdorff space is a homeomorphism. \(\square\)

Milnor’s text skips the gluing. He ends by calling the construction of a homeomorphism between \(M\) and \(S^n\) “now easy”. What is needed is that Theorem 3.1 carries the boundary sphere of the lower cell onto that of the upper one (Step 3), and Alexander’s cone (Step 4). The cone is not differentiable at its vertex unless \(g\) is linear, and \(H\) need not be smooth along the equator; Remark 2 says “homeomorphic” cannot be improved.

Remark 1 (Milnor). (not checked by machine) Theorem 4.1 remains true when the two critical points are allowed to be degenerate.

Milnor cites his paper in Bull. Soc. Math. France 87 (1959), Theorem 1(3), and R. Rosen (Notices Amer. Math. Soc. 7, 1960). Here is a proof using one outside theorem.

Brown’s monotone union theorem (M. Brown, Proc. Amer. Math. Soc. 12 (1961), 812–814). If an \(n\)-manifold \(X\) is the union of open subsets \(W_1 \subset W_2 \subset \cdots\), each homeomorphic to \(\mathbb{R}^n\), then \(X\) is homeomorphic to \(\mathbb{R}^n\).

Proof of Remark 1. Step 1 above did not use nondegeneracy: \(f\) has exactly two critical points, the minimum \(p\) and the maximum \(q\), and we normalize \(f(p) = 0\), \(f(q) = 1\). Choose a chart \(\phi\) with \(\phi(p) = 0\) whose domain avoids \(q\) and whose image contains the closed unit ball, and let \(B = \phi^{-1}(\text{open unit ball})\); then \(B \cong \mathbb{R}^n\), the closure \(\bar B\) is compact and \(q \notin \bar B\). As in Step 2 choose \(\delta \in (0,1)\) with \(M^\delta \subset B\). For each \(b \in (\delta, 1)\), Theorem 3.1 gives a diffeomorphism \(\Phi_b\) of \(M\) with \(\Phi_b(M^\delta) = M^b\). It fixes \(q\): the vector field generating it vanishes outside a compact neighbourhood of \(f^{-1}[\delta, b]\), which may be taken inside \(f^{-1}(\delta/2, (1+b)/2)\). The open set \(W(b) := \Phi_b(B)\) is homeomorphic to \(\mathbb{R}^n\) and contains \(M^b\), and its closure \(\Phi_b(\bar B)\) is compact and does not contain \(q\), so \(\beta(b) := \max f(\Phi_b(\bar B)) < 1\). Choose \(b_1 \in (\delta, 1)\) and inductively \(b_{k+1} \in (\max(\beta(b_k), b_k, 1 - 1/k), 1)\), so that \(\delta < b_k < b_{k+1} < 1\). Then \[W(b_k) \subset \Phi_{b_k}(\bar B) \subset M^{\beta(b_k)} \subset M^{b_{k+1}} \subset W(b_{k+1}),\] and since \(b_k \to 1\) the union of the \(W(b_k)\) contains \(f^{-1}[0,1) = M \setminus \{q\}\), while each \(W(b_k)\) lies in \(M \setminus \{q\}\). By Brown’s theorem \(M \setminus \{q\} \cong \mathbb{R}^n\). Finally a homeomorphism \(\kappa : \mathbb{R}^n \to M \setminus \{q\}\) extends to a bijection \(S^n = \mathbb{R}^n \cup \{\infty\} \to M\) by \(\infty \mapsto q\). It is continuous at \(\infty\): for an open \(O \ni q\), the set \(\kappa^{-1}(M \setminus O)\) is compact, so its complement together with \(\infty\) is a neighbourhood of \(\infty\) mapped into \(O\). A continuous bijection from a compact space to a Hausdorff space is a homeomorphism. \(\square\)

Remark 2 (Milnor). (not checked by machine) \(M\) need not be diffeomorphic to \(S^n\) with its standard smooth structure. In On manifolds homeomorphic to the 7-sphere (Ann. of Math. 64 (1956), 399–405) Milnor found, on certain 3-sphere bundles over \(S^4\), functions with exactly two nondegenerate critical points, so that these 7-manifolds are homeomorphic to \(S^7\) by Theorem 4.1, and proved with characteristic classes that some of them are not diffeomorphic to \(S^7\). We quote this; it is not used later. The proof of Theorem 4.1 shows where smoothness is lost: \(M\) is two smooth disks glued by the diffeomorphism \(g\) of \(S^{n-1}\), and Alexander’s cone extends \(g\) over the disk only as a homeomorphism.

2. Three critical points (Milnor p. 26)

Milnor notes that if an \(n\)-manifold has a function with only three critical points, they have indices \(0\), \(n\) and \(n/2\) (“by Poincaré duality”), and the manifold has the homotopy type of an \((n/2)\)-sphere with an \(n\)-cell attached; implicitly \(M\) is compact and the critical points are nondegenerate. The proof uses the weak Morse inequalities of §6 with coefficients \(\mathbb{Z}/2\) (proved there independently of this section) and two facts.

Facts (mod 2 homology of closed manifolds). Let \(M\) be a compact connected \(n\)-manifold and \(b_i = \dim H_i(M; \mathbb{Z}/2)\). Then (a) \(b_n = 1\), and (b) \(b_i = b_{n-i}\) for all \(i\). Statement (a) is Hatcher, Algebraic Topology, Theorem 3.26 (every closed manifold is \(\mathbb{Z}/2\)-orientable); (b) is Poincaré duality with \(\mathbb{Z}/2\) coefficients (Hatcher, Theorem 3.30) combined with \(H^i(M;\mathbb{Z}/2) \cong \operatorname{Hom}(H_i(M;\mathbb{Z}/2), \mathbb{Z}/2)\) (universal coefficients over a field).

Proposition A (three critical points). Let \(M\) be a compact \(n\)-manifold, \(n \ge 1\), and \(f\) a smooth function on \(M\) with exactly three critical points, all nondegenerate. Then \(n\) is even, the indices are \(0\), \(n/2\), \(n\), and \(M\) has the homotopy type of a CW complex \(S^{n/2} \cup e^n\).

Proof. \(M\) is connected: on each component \(M'\) (compact and open in \(M\)), \(f\) attains its maximum and minimum at two distinct critical points, as in Step 1 of §1, so a disconnected \(M\) would have at least four. The minimum \(p_0\) has index \(0\) and the maximum \(p_2\) index \(n\), by (i) of §1. Let \(\lambda\) be the index of the third critical point \(p_1\), and \(c_i\) the number of critical points of index \(i\).

By Theorem 5.2 of §6 with \(F = \mathbb{Z}/2\): \(b_i \le c_i\) for all \(i\), and \(\sum (-1)^i b_i = \sum (-1)^i c_i\). Reducing the second relation mod 2, \(\sum b_i \equiv \sum c_i = 3\). Also \(b_0 = 1\) (\(M\) is connected), \(b_n = 1\) by (a), and \(0 \ne n\); so \(2 \le \sum b_i \le \sum c_i = 3\) with \(\sum b_i\) odd. Hence \(\sum b_i = 3\), which together with \(b_i \le c_i\) forces \(b_i = c_i\) for every \(i\). If \(\lambda = 0\) then \(c_0 = 2 \ne b_0\); if \(\lambda = n\) then \(c_n = 2 \ne b_n\). So \(0 < \lambda < n\), \(b_\lambda = 1\), and \(b_i = 0\) for \(i \notin \{0, \lambda, n\}\). By (b), \(b_{n-\lambda} = b_\lambda = 1\), so \(n - \lambda \in \{0, \lambda, n\}\), and \(0 < \lambda < n\) leaves \(n - \lambda = \lambda\).

Finally \(f(p_0) < f(p_1) < f(p_2)\): by (i), \(p_1\), whose index is neither \(0\) nor \(n\), is neither a local minimum nor a local maximum, so the extreme values are attained only at \(p_0\) and \(p_2\). The proof of Theorem 3.5 builds a CW complex homotopy equivalent to \(M\) by attaching cells in the order of the critical values: a \(0\)-cell; then an \((n/2)\)-cell attached to it, which gives \(S^{n/2}\) (a disk with its boundary collapsed to a point); then an \(n\)-cell. \(\square\)

A hidden hypothesis. “By Poincaré duality” must be read with coefficients \(\mathbb{Z}/2\): over \(\mathbb{Z}\) or \(\mathbb{Q}\) duality needs orientability, and Milnor’s own example \(\mathbb{R}P^2\) is not orientable (its rational Betti numbers are \(1, 0, 0\)). Duality alone is also not enough: the parity argument giving \(b_i = c_i\) is what makes the third critical point visible in homology.

Examples. On \(\mathbb{C}P^2\) the function \(\sum c_j |z_j|^2\) of §3 has indices \(0, 2, 4\); on \(\mathbb{R}P^2 = S^2/\pm 1\) the same formula has indices \(0, 1, 2\) (the computation of §3 with \(x_j\) real, each coordinate contributing \(1\) instead of \(2\)). The “forthcoming papers” of Eells and Kuiper (Manifolds which are like projective planes, Publ. Math. IHÉS 14, 1962) showed, using Adams’ theorem on Hopf invariant one, that \(n \in \{2, 4, 8, 16\}\).

3. Complex projective space (Milnor pp. 26–27)

Let \(\mathbb{C}P^n\) be the set of classes \((z_0 : z_1 : \dots : z_n)\) of \((n+1)\)-tuples of complex numbers with \(\sum |z_j|^2 = 1\), two tuples being identified when they differ by a factor of absolute value \(1\). Its smooth structure is given by the affine charts \((z_j/z_k)_{j \ne k}\) on \(U_k = \{z_k \ne 0\}\). Fix distinct real numbers \(c_0, \dots, c_n\) and put \[f(z_0 : \dots : z_n) = \sum_{j=0}^n c_j |z_j|^2 ,\] which is well defined because \(|\omega z_j| = |z_j|\) when \(|\omega| = 1\). (The scan of p. 26 drops the summation sign and the exponent; the formula in coordinates below shows what is meant.)

Coordinates. On \(U_0\) put \(x_j + i y_j := (|z_0|/z_0)\, z_j\) for \(j = 1, \dots, n\). This does not depend on the representative (multiplying all \(z_j\) by \(\omega\) multiplies \(|z_0|/z_0\) by \(\bar\omega\)). In terms of the affine coordinates \(u_j = z_j/z_0\), the normalization \(\sum|z_j|^2 = 1\) gives \(|z_0|^2(1 + |u|^2) = 1\), hence \(w := (x_j + iy_j)_j = u/\sqrt{1 + |u|^2}\). The map \(u \mapsto u/\sqrt{1+|u|^2}\) is a diffeomorphism of \(\mathbb{C}^n\) onto the open unit ball, with inverse \(w \mapsto w/\sqrt{1 - |w|^2}\). So \(x_1, y_1, \dots, x_n, y_n\) are coordinates mapping \(U_0\) diffeomorphically onto the open unit ball of \(\mathbb{R}^{2n}\), centred at \(p_0 = (1:0:\dots:0)\). Since \(|x_j + i y_j| = |z_j|\) for \(j \ge 1\) and \(|z_0|^2 = 1 - \sum_{j \ge 1} |z_j|^2\), \[f = c_0 + \sum_{j=1}^n (c_j - c_0)\,(x_j^2 + y_j^2) \qquad \text{on } U_0 .\]

Proposition B. \(f\) is a Morse function on \(\mathbb{C}P^n\) whose critical points are exactly \(p_k = (0 : \dots : 1 : \dots : 0)\) (\(1\) in position \(k\)), \(k = 0, \dots, n\), and the index at \(p_k\) is \(2\,\#\{j : c_j < c_k\}\). Consequently \(C_\lambda = 1\) for \(\lambda = 0, 2, 4, \dots, 2n\) and \(C_\lambda = 0\) otherwise.

Proof. On \(U_0\), \(\partial f/\partial x_j = 2(c_j - c_0) x_j\) and \(\partial f/\partial y_j = 2(c_j - c_0) y_j\) vanish together only at \(x = y = 0\), since \(c_j \ne c_0\); so \(p_0\) is the only critical point in \(U_0\). The Hessian there is diagonal with entries \(2(c_j - c_0)\), each twice, so \(p_0\) is nondegenerate of index \(2\,\#\{j : c_j < c_0\}\). The same computation in the analogous coordinates \((|z_k|/z_k)\, z_j\), \(j \ne k\), on \(U_k\) handles \(p_k\). The sets \(U_0, \dots, U_n\) cover \(\mathbb{C}P^n\), so there are no other critical points. As the \(c_j\) are distinct, \(k \mapsto \#\{j : c_j < c_k\}\) is a bijection of \(\{0, \dots, n\}\) onto itself (the rank of \(c_k\) in increasing order). \(\square\)

Corollary C (Milnor p. 27). \(\mathbb{C}P^n\) has the homotopy type of a CW complex \(e^0 \cup e^2 \cup \dots \cup e^{2n}\), and \(H_i(\mathbb{C}P^n; \mathbb{Z}) \cong \mathbb{Z}\) for \(i = 0, 2, \dots, 2n\) and \(0\) for all other \(i\).

Proof. \(\mathbb{C}P^n\) is compact (an image of \(S^{2n+1}\)), so Theorem 3.5 applies with Proposition B. In cellular homology (Hatcher, Theorem 2.35) the chain group is \(\mathbb{Z}\) in each even degree \(\le 2n\) and \(0\) in odd degrees, so every boundary map has zero source or target. \(\square\)

Proposition G in §6 gives a second proof that avoids Theorem 3.5 and cellular homology.

4. Subadditive functions (Milnor p. 28)

Morse, without Theorem 3.5, expressed the topology through inequalities between numbers. Fix a field \(F\). A pair \((X, Y)\) is a space \(X\) with a subspace \(Y\), possibly empty; \(H_\lambda(X,Y)\) is singular homology with coefficients in \(F\), and \(H_\lambda(X) = H_\lambda(X, \emptyset)\). Call \((X,Y)\) of finite type if \(\sum_\lambda \dim_F H_\lambda(X,Y) < \infty\). (Milnor says only “for any pair \((X,Y)\) such that this rank is finite”; we need one class of pairs on which all functions below are defined, closed under the operation of Lemma D.)

Facts from homology (Hatcher, Algebraic Topology, §§2.1–2.3), for any coefficient group:

  • (H1) For \(X \supset Y \supset Z\) the sequence of the triple \[\cdots \to H_\lambda(Y,Z) \to H_\lambda(X,Z) \to H_\lambda(X,Y) \xrightarrow{\ \partial\ } H_{\lambda-1}(Y,Z) \to \cdots \to H_0(X,Y) \to 0\] is exact and natural for maps of triples; \(Z = \emptyset\) gives the sequence of a pair.
  • (H2) Homotopic maps of pairs induce equal maps. Hence, by (H1) and the five lemma, if the inclusion \(Y \subset X\) is a homotopy equivalence then \(H_*(X,Y) = 0\), and a map of pairs that is the identity on the subspaces and a homotopy equivalence of the total spaces induces isomorphisms on relative homology.
  • (H3) Excision: if \(Z \subset A \subset X\) and the closure of \(Z\) lies in the interior of \(A\), the inclusion \((X \setminus Z, A \setminus Z) \to (X, A)\) induces isomorphisms.
  • (H4) \(H_\lambda(D^m, S^{m-1})\) is the coefficient group for \(\lambda = m\) and \(0\) otherwise (\(S^{-1} = \emptyset\)); this is the standard computation from the homology of spheres, by Mayer–Vietoris or by the exact sequence of the pair.
  • (H5) If \(X\) is the disjoint union of finitely many subsets \(X_j\), each open in \(X\), and \(A_j \subset X_j\), then \(H_*(X, \bigcup A_j) = \bigoplus_j H_*(X_j, A_j)\).

Lemma D. If \(X \supset Y \supset Z\) and \((X,Y)\), \((Y,Z)\) are of finite type, so is \((X,Z)\), and \(\dim H_\lambda(X,Z) \le \dim H_\lambda(X,Y) + \dim H_\lambda(Y,Z)\) for every \(\lambda\).

Proof. In the exact segment \(H_\lambda(Y,Z) \xrightarrow{i} H_\lambda(X,Z) \xrightarrow{j} H_\lambda(X,Y)\) we have \(\ker j = \operatorname{im} i\), so \(\dim H_\lambda(X,Z) = \dim\ker j + \dim\operatorname{im} j \le \dim H_\lambda(Y,Z) + \dim H_\lambda(X,Y)\). \(\square\)

Definition (Milnor). An integer-valued function \(S\) on pairs of finite type is subadditive if \(S(X,Z) \le S(X,Y) + S(Y,Z)\) whenever \(X \supset Y \supset Z\) with \((X,Y)\) and \((Y,Z)\) of finite type, and additive if equality always holds. Write \(S(X) := S(X, \emptyset)\).

Examples. The \(\lambda\)-th Betti number \(R_\lambda(X,Y) = \dim_F H_\lambda(X,Y;F)\) is subadditive by Lemma D (Milnor: “as is easily seen” from a segment of the exact sequence). The Euler characteristic \(\chi(X,Y) = \sum_\lambda (-1)^\lambda R_\lambda(X,Y)\) is additive: the sequence of the triple is a finite exact sequence \(0 \to V_m \to \dots \to V_0 \to 0\) of finite-dimensional spaces, for which rank–nullity and exactness give \(\dim V_i = \operatorname{rank} d_i + \operatorname{rank} d_{i+1}\) (\(d_i : V_i \to V_{i-1}\)), so \(\sum (-1)^i \dim V_i = 0\); grouping by degree, \(\chi(Y,Z) - \chi(X,Z) + \chi(X,Y) = 0\).

Lemma 5.1. (checked by machine: V3.8, with its hypotheses made explicit) Let \(S\) be subadditive and \(X_0 \subset X_1 \subset \dots \subset X_n\) with every \((X_i, X_{i-1})\) of finite type. Then \((X_n, X_0)\) is of finite type and \(S(X_n, X_0) \le \sum_{i=1}^n S(X_i, X_{i-1})\), with equality if \(S\) is additive. In particular, for \(X_0 = \emptyset\), \[S(X_n) \le \sum_{i=1}^n S(X_i, X_{i-1}). \qquad (1)\]

Proof. Induction on \(n\); for \(n = 1\) there is nothing to prove, and \(n = 2\) is the definition. If the claim holds for \(n - 1\), then \((X_{n-1}, X_0)\) is of finite type, hence so is \((X_n, X_0)\) by Lemma D applied to \(X_n \supset X_{n-1} \supset X_0\), and \[S(X_n, X_0) \le S(X_n, X_{n-1}) + S(X_{n-1}, X_0) \le \sum_{i=1}^n S(X_i, X_{i-1}).\] For additive \(S\) every inequality is an equality. \(\square\)

5. The homology of a slab (Milnor p. 29)

Milnor’s computation on p. 29 is the single line \[H_*(M^{a_i}, M^{a_{i-1}}) = H_*(M^{a_{i-1}} \cup e^{\lambda_i}, M^{a_{i-1}}) = H_*(e^{\lambda_i}, \dot e^{\lambda_i}) \ \text{(by excision)} = \begin{cases} F & \text{in dimension } \lambda_i, \\ 0 & \text{otherwise.} \end{cases}\] The first equality replaces a pair by a homotopy equivalent pair. The second is not literally an excision: one would excise \(A \setminus \dot e\) from \((A \cup e, A)\), but its closure \(A\) is not inside the interior of \(A\) (points of \(\dot e\) are limits of points of the open cell). The repair is to thicken \(A\) first. We also allow several critical points on one level (see §6).

What we use from Chapter 2 (Theorem 3.2 and Remark 3.3, in the form proved there). Let \(c\) be a critical value with \(f^{-1}[c - \varepsilon_0, c + \varepsilon_0]\) compact, whose only critical points \(p_1, \dots, p_r\) lie on the level \(c\) and are nondegenerate, of indices \(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_r\). Then for all sufficiently small \(\varepsilon > 0\) there are pairwise disjoint sets \(e_1, \dots, e_r \subset M^{c+\varepsilon}\) and homeomorphisms \(\sigma_j : D^{\lambda_j} \to e_j\) with \(e_j \cap M^{c-\varepsilon} = \sigma_j(S^{\lambda_j - 1})\), such that \(M^{c-\varepsilon} \cup e_1 \cup \dots \cup e_r\) is a deformation retract of \(M^{c+\varepsilon}\). In Morse coordinates \(u\) around \(p_j\) the cell is \(e_j = \{u_1^2 + \dots + u_{\lambda_j}^2 \le \varepsilon,\ u_{\lambda_j + 1} = \dots = u_n = 0\}\). Milnor proves \(r = 1\); for \(r > 1\) the same construction is made in disjoint coordinate neighbourhoods.

Lemma E (excision for attached cells). Let \(X\) be a Hausdorff space, \(A \subset X\) closed, and \(e_1, \dots, e_r \subset X\) pairwise disjoint, with homeomorphisms \(\sigma_j : D^{\lambda_j} \to e_j\), such that \(X = A \cup e_1 \cup \dots \cup e_r\) and \(A \cap e_j = \sigma_j(S^{\lambda_j - 1})\). Then for any coefficients, \(H_*(X, A) \cong \bigoplus_j H_*(D^{\lambda_j}, S^{\lambda_j - 1})\); over \(F\), \(\dim H_\mu(X, A) = \#\{j : \lambda_j = \mu\}\).

Proof. Each \(e_j\) is compact, hence closed in \(X\), and so is \(\sigma_j(S^{\lambda_j - 1})\). The complement of \(e_j \setminus \sigma_j(S^{\lambda_j-1})\) is \(A \cup \bigcup_{i \ne j} e_i \cup \sigma_j(S^{\lambda_j - 1})\), a closed set, so the open cell \(e_j \setminus \sigma_j(S^{\lambda_j-1})\) is open in \(X\), and with it \(O_j := \sigma_j(\{|x| < \tfrac12\})\). Let \(K_j = \{x \in D^{\lambda_j} : \tfrac12 \le |x| \le 1\}\) (empty if \(\lambda_j = 0\)) and \[A' := X \setminus \textstyle\bigcup_j O_j = A \cup \bigcup_j \sigma_j(K_j).\]

Thickening. \(A\) is a deformation retract of \(A'\): let \(\rho_s\) be the identity on \(A\) and \(\rho_s(\sigma_j(x)) = \sigma_j\big((1-s)x + s\,x/|x|\big)\) on \(\sigma_j(K_j)\), \(0 \le s \le 1\). The pieces are finitely many closed sets agreeing on their overlaps \(\sigma_j(S^{\lambda_j-1})\), where both formulas give the identity, so \(\rho\) is continuous on \(A' \times [0,1]\). By (H2), \(H_*(A', A) = 0\), and the sequence of the triple \((X, A', A)\) shows that \(H_*(X, A) \to H_*(X, A')\) is an isomorphism.

Excision. Let \(Z = X \setminus \bigcup_j e_j\). Its closure lies in the closed set \(A\). The set \(X \setminus \bigcup_j \sigma_j(\{|x| \le \tfrac12\})\) is open, contained in \(A'\), and contains \(A\) (because \(A \cap e_j = \sigma_j(S^{\lambda_j - 1})\)). So \(\bar Z \subset \operatorname{int} A'\), and (H3) gives \(H_*(X \setminus Z, A' \setminus Z) \cong H_*(X, A')\). Here \(X \setminus Z = \bigcup_j e_j\) and \(A' \setminus Z = \bigcup_j \sigma_j(K_j)\).

Counting. The \(e_j\) are disjoint closed sets, hence each is open in their union, so by (H5) \(H_*(\bigcup e_j, \bigcup \sigma_j(K_j)) \cong \bigoplus_j H_*(D^{\lambda_j}, K_j)\). Finally \(S^{\lambda_j - 1} \subset K_j\) is a homotopy equivalence (radial retraction), so the five lemma on the sequences of the pairs gives \(H_*(D^{\lambda_j}, K_j) \cong H_*(D^{\lambda_j}, S^{\lambda_j - 1})\), which is (H4). \(\square\)

Proposition F (one critical level). Let \(a < b\), let \(f^{-1}[a,b]\) be compact, and suppose its only critical points lie on one level \(c \in (a,b)\), are nondegenerate, and have indices \(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_r\). Then for any coefficients \(H_*(M^b, M^a) \cong \bigoplus_j H_*(D^{\lambda_j}, S^{\lambda_j-1})\). With coefficients in \(F\): \((M^b, M^a)\) is of finite type, \(R_\mu(M^b, M^a) = \#\{j : \lambda_j = \mu\}\), and \(\chi(M^b, M^a) = \sum_j (-1)^{\lambda_j}\).

Proof. Choose \(\varepsilon\) as in the statement quoted above, with \(a < c - \varepsilon < c + \varepsilon < b\), and let \(Y = M^{c-\varepsilon} \cup e_1 \cup \dots \cup e_r\). By Theorem 3.1, \(M^a\) is a deformation retract of \(M^{c-\varepsilon}\), and \(M^{c+\varepsilon}\) is one of \(M^b\); so the inclusions \(M^a \subset M^{c-\varepsilon}\) and \(Y \subset M^{c+\varepsilon} \subset M^b\) are homotopy equivalences. By (H2), \(H_*(M^{c-\varepsilon}, M^a) = 0\), and the sequence of the triple \((M^b, M^{c-\varepsilon}, M^a)\) gives \(H_*(M^b, M^a) \cong H_*(M^b, M^{c-\varepsilon})\). By (H2) again, \(H_*(Y, M^{c-\varepsilon}) \cong H_*(M^b, M^{c-\varepsilon})\). Lemma E applies to \(X = Y\) and \(A = M^{c-\varepsilon}\), which is closed in the Hausdorff space \(M\). \(\square\)

6. The Morse inequalities (Milnor pp. 29–31)

Let \(M\) be a compact manifold, \(f\) a Morse function on \(M\), and \(C_\lambda\) the (finite) number of critical points of index \(\lambda\). Let \(c_1 < \dots < c_m\) be the critical values and choose \[a_0 < c_1 < a_1 < c_2 < a_2 < \dots < a_{m-1} < c_m < a_m, \qquad a_0 < \min f, \quad a_m \ge \max f .\] Then \(\emptyset = M^{a_0} \subset M^{a_1} \subset \dots \subset M^{a_m} = M\), each \(f^{-1}[a_{i-1}, a_i]\) is compact and contains exactly one critical value, and Proposition F, summed over \(i\), gives \[\sum_{i=1}^m R_\mu(M^{a_i}, M^{a_{i-1}}) = C_\mu, \qquad \sum_{i=1}^m \chi(M^{a_i}, M^{a_{i-1}}) = \sum_\mu (-1)^\mu C_\mu . \qquad (5)\]

A hidden hypothesis. Milnor chooses \(a_1 < \dots < a_k\) “such that \(M^{a_i}\) contains exactly \(i\) critical points”. Such numbers exist only if distinct critical points have distinct critical values, which is not assumed and fails in natural examples: for the two-rotor potential of §7 with \(\kappa = 0\), all nine minima lie on the level \(0\). Placing one critical value in each slab and using Remark 3.3 removes the issue.

Theorem 5.2 (weak Morse inequalities). (checked by machine: V3.11, V3.35, in a narrower form; V3.39, with its hypotheses made explicit) For every field \(F\), \[R_\lambda(M) \le C_\lambda \ \text{ for every } \lambda, \qquad (2)\] \[\sum_\lambda (-1)^\lambda R_\lambda(M) = \sum_\lambda (-1)^\lambda C_\lambda . \qquad (3)\] In particular \(H_*(M; F)\) is finite dimensional, and the Euler characteristic \(\chi(M)\) does not depend on \(F\).

Proof. Lemma 5.1 applied to the chain \(M^{a_0} \subset \dots \subset M^{a_m}\) shows that \((M, \emptyset)\) is of finite type; inequality (1) with \(S = R_\lambda\) and the equality case with \(S = \chi\), together with (5), give (2) and (3). The right side of (3) involves no \(F\). \(\square\)

The same argument up to a regular value \(a\) gives \(\chi(M^a) = \sum_\lambda (-1)^\lambda C_\lambda(a)\), with \(C_\lambda(a)\) counting critical points of index \(\lambda\) in \(M^a\).

Lemma 5.3. (checked by machine: V3.12, restated) For each \(\lambda \ge 0\) the function \[S_\lambda(X,Y) = R_\lambda(X,Y) - R_{\lambda-1}(X,Y) + R_{\lambda-2}(X,Y) - \dots \pm R_0(X,Y) = \sum_{\mu=0}^\lambda (-1)^{\lambda-\mu} R_\mu(X,Y)\] is subadditive.

Proof. First an algebraic fact. Let \(A' \xrightarrow{h} A_m \xrightarrow{d_m} A_{m-1} \to \cdots \xrightarrow{d_1} A_0 \to 0\) be exact, with the \(A_i\) finite dimensional. Exactness at \(A_i\) says \(\operatorname{im} d_{i+1} = \ker d_i\), so \(\operatorname{rank} d_{i+1} = \dim A_i - \operatorname{rank} d_i\) (with \(d_{m+1} = h\) and \(d_0 = 0\)). Unwinding from \(i = m\) down to \(i = 0\), \[\operatorname{rank} h = \dim A_m - \dim A_{m-1} + \dim A_{m-2} - \dots \pm \dim A_0 \ \ge\ 0 .\] Apply this to the end of the exact sequence of a triple \(X \supset Y \supset Z\) of pairs of finite type, starting with \(h = \partial : H_{\lambda+1}(X,Y) \to H_\lambda(Y,Z)\): \[H_\lambda(Y,Z) \to H_\lambda(X,Z) \to H_\lambda(X,Y) \to H_{\lambda-1}(Y,Z) \to \cdots \to H_0(X,Z) \to H_0(X,Y) \to 0 .\] The terms \(H_\mu(Y,Z)\), \(H_\mu(X,Z)\), \(H_\mu(X,Y)\) carry the signs \((-1)^{\lambda-\mu}\), \(-(-1)^{\lambda-\mu}\), \((-1)^{\lambda-\mu}\), so \[0 \le \operatorname{rank}\partial = R_\lambda(Y,Z) - R_\lambda(X,Z) + R_\lambda(X,Y) - R_{\lambda-1}(Y,Z) + \dots = S_\lambda(Y,Z) - S_\lambda(X,Z) + S_\lambda(X,Y),\] which is the subadditivity \(S_\lambda(X,Z) \le S_\lambda(X,Y) + S_\lambda(Y,Z)\). \(\square\)

The Morse inequalities. Inequality (1) for \(S = S_\lambda\) and the chain \(\emptyset = M^{a_0} \subset \dots \subset M^{a_m} = M\), together with (5), give for every \(\lambda \ge 0\) \[R_\lambda(M) - R_{\lambda-1}(M) + \dots \pm R_0(M) \ \le\ C_\lambda - C_{\lambda-1} + \dots \pm C_0 . \qquad (4_\lambda)\]

They are sharper than Theorem 5.2. Put \(R_\mu = C_\mu = 0\) for \(\mu < 0\).

  1. Adding \((4_\lambda)\) and \((4_{\lambda-1})\) gives \((2)\), since \(S_\lambda + S_{\lambda-1} = R_\lambda\) and likewise on the right.

  2. For \(\lambda > n = \dim M\) we have \(C_\lambda = 0\) (indices are at most \(n\)), hence \(R_\lambda(M) = 0\) by (2). Then \((4_{n+1})\) reads \(-S_n(M) \le -\sum_{\mu \le n} (-1)^{n-\mu} C_\mu\); together with \((4_n)\) this is the equality \(S_n(M) = \sum_{\mu \le n}(-1)^{n-\mu}C_\mu\), which is (3) multiplied by \((-1)^n\). (Milnor compares “\((4_\lambda)\) with \((4_{\lambda-1})\) for \(\lambda > n\)”; \(\lambda = n + 1\) suffices.)

  3. If \(C_{\lambda+1} = 0\), then \(R_{\lambda+1}(M) = 0\) by (2), and \((4_{\lambda+1})\) becomes \(S_\lambda(M) \ge \sum_{\mu \le \lambda}(-1)^{\lambda-\mu} C_\mu\). With \((4_\lambda)\): \[R_\lambda - R_{\lambda-1} + \dots \pm R_0 = C_\lambda - C_{\lambda-1} + \dots \pm C_0 .\]

  4. If moreover \(C_{\lambda-1} = 0\), then \(R_{\lambda-1} = 0\), and (c) with \(\lambda - 2\) in place of \(\lambda\) gives \(R_{\lambda-2} - R_{\lambda-3} + \dots = C_{\lambda-2} - C_{\lambda-3} + \dots\). Subtracting this from the equality in (c) leaves \(R_\lambda = C_\lambda\):

Corollary 5.4. (checked by machine: V3.15, in a stronger form; V3.37, in a narrower form) If \(C_{\lambda+1} = C_{\lambda-1} = 0\), then \(R_\lambda(M) = C_\lambda\) and \(R_{\lambda+1}(M) = R_{\lambda-1}(M) = 0\).

(As Milnor remarks, this also follows from Theorem 3.5.) For \(\mathbb{C}P^n\), Proposition B gives \(C_\lambda = 1\) for even \(\lambda \le 2n\) and \(0\) otherwise. For even \(\lambda\) both neighbours vanish, so \(R_\lambda = C_\lambda\); for odd \(\lambda\), \(R_\lambda \le C_\lambda = 0\). Hence \(\dim H_\lambda(\mathbb{C}P^n; F) = 1\) for \(\lambda = 0, 2, \dots, 2n\) and \(0\) otherwise, for every field \(F\).

Milnor’s text skips the passage to integers. He notes that the corollary yields the homology groups of complex projective space without the help of Theorem 3.5. Corollary 5.4 gives Betti numbers over every field, not the integral groups of Corollary C. Universal coefficients would finish once \(H_*(\mathbb{C}P^n;\mathbb{Z})\) is known to be finitely generated; here is a direct argument.

Proposition G (lacunary principle). Let \(f\) be a Morse function on a compact manifold \(M\) such that \(C_{\lambda-1} = C_{\lambda+1} = 0\) whenever \(C_\lambda \ne 0\). Then \(H_\lambda(M; \mathbb{Z})\) is free abelian of rank \(C_\lambda\) for every \(\lambda\). In particular Corollary C holds without Theorem 3.5.

Proof. Proposition F with integer coefficients gives \(H_\mu(M^{a_i}, M^{a_{i-1}}; \mathbb{Z}) \cong \mathbb{Z}^{c_\mu^{(i)}}\), where \(c_\mu^{(i)}\) is the number of critical points of index \(\mu\) on the level \(c_i\). We show by induction on \(i\) that \(H_\mu(M^{a_i}; \mathbb{Z})\) is free of rank \(\sum_{i' \le i} c_\mu^{(i')}\); for \(i = 0\), \(M^{a_0} = \emptyset\). In the exact sequence of the pair \((M^{a_i}, M^{a_{i-1}})\), \[H_{\mu+1}(M^{a_i}, M^{a_{i-1}}) \to H_\mu(M^{a_{i-1}}) \to H_\mu(M^{a_i}) \to H_\mu(M^{a_i}, M^{a_{i-1}}) \to H_{\mu-1}(M^{a_{i-1}}),\] if \(C_\mu = 0\) the second and fourth groups vanish (by induction, and by Proposition F), so \(H_\mu(M^{a_i}) = 0\). If \(C_\mu \ne 0\), then \(C_{\mu \pm 1} = 0\), so the first and last groups vanish, and \(0 \to H_\mu(M^{a_{i-1}}) \to H_\mu(M^{a_i}) \to \mathbb{Z}^{c_\mu^{(i)}} \to 0\) is exact; it splits because the right-hand group is free. \(\square\)

An interactive look at the Morse inequalities on a torus

The square is the torus, with opposite edges glued: \(\varphi\) runs horizontally and \(\psi\) vertically, each over one full turn (markers on an edge appear on both glued sides). The shading is the potential \[V(\varphi, \psi) = \tfrac12(1 - \cos k\varphi) + \tfrac12 B\,(1 - \cos k\psi) - \kappa \cos(\varphi - \psi - \delta),\] fading into the page background where \(V\) is lowest (white in the still image). The program finds the critical points numerically (Newton’s method started from a grid of points) and classifies them by the signs of the eigenvalues of the Hessian: minima are filled discs, saddles are crosses, maxima are triangles. Below the picture it reports \(C_0, C_1, C_2\) and checks the three Morse inequalities of the torus, \(C_0 \ge 1\), \(C_1 - C_0 \ge 1\) and \(C_0 - C_1 + C_2 = 0\).

The preset “double pendulum” (\(k = 1\), \(B = \tfrac12\), \(\kappa = 0\)) shows one disc, two crosses and one triangle; “two rotors” (\(k = 3\), \(B = 1\)) shows \(9 + 18 + 9\). (The still image shows the first preset, and the second with \(\kappa = 1.75\), where the counts are \(3 + 12 + 9\).) Drag the coupling \(\kappa\): minima collide with saddles and vanish in pairs, and so do saddles with maxima, but \(C_0 - C_1 + C_2\) stays \(0\) (at a collision the function is degenerate, and the readout says so). The level slider shades the sublevel set \(M^a = \{V \le a\}\); as \(a\) crosses a critical value, \(M^a\) gains a cell of dimension equal to the index, and the readout gives \(\chi(M^a)\), the number of minima minus saddles plus maxima below \(a\).

7. Application: equilibria of a double pendulum and conformers of a two-rotor molecule

The double pendulum. Two rigid rods of lengths \(l_1, l_2\), carrying point masses \(m_1, m_2\) at their far ends, hang in a vertical plane: the first from a fixed pivot, the second from the end of the first. Both may turn through full circles (in the planar model the rods pass each other). The configuration is given by the angles \(\theta_1, \theta_2\) of the rods from the downward vertical, so the configuration space is the torus \(T^2 = S^1 \times S^1\). The heights of the masses are \(-l_1 \cos\theta_1\) and \(-l_1\cos\theta_1 - l_2\cos\theta_2\), so the potential energy is \[V = -(m_1 + m_2)\, g\, l_1 \cos\theta_1 - m_2\, g\, l_2 \cos\theta_2 .\] The equilibria are its critical points: \(\sin\theta_1 = \sin\theta_2 = 0\), the four configurations in which each rod points straight down (\(0\)) or straight up (\(\pi\)). The Hessian is diagonal with entries \((m_1 + m_2) g l_1 \cos\theta_1\) and \(m_2 g l_2 \cos\theta_2\), so all four are nondegenerate:

\((\theta_1, \theta_2)\) configuration index
\((0, 0)\) both rods down \(0\) (stable)
\((\pi, 0)\) first rod up, second hanging down from its top \(1\)
\((0, \pi)\) first rod down, second balanced upright on it \(1\)
\((\pi, \pi)\) both rods up \(2\)

So \((C_0, C_1, C_2) = (1, 2, 1)\).

The Betti numbers of the torus, from the pendulum. Theorem 5.2 gives \(R_0 \le 1\), \(R_1 \le 2\), \(R_2 \le 1\) and \(R_0 - R_1 + R_2 = 0\). The torus is path connected, so \(R_0 = 1\). For a lower bound on \(R_1\), let \(i_1(\theta) = (\theta, 0)\), \(i_2(\theta) = (0, \theta)\) and let \(p_1, p_2\) be the projections. Then \(p_a \circ i_b\) is the identity of \(S^1\) if \(a = b\) and constant if \(a \ne b\), and constant maps induce zero on \(H_1\); so the composite \[H_1(S^1) \oplus H_1(S^1) \xrightarrow{\ i_{1*} + i_{2*}\ } H_1(T^2) \xrightarrow{\ (p_{1*},\, p_{2*})\ } H_1(S^1) \oplus H_1(S^1)\] is the identity, the first map is injective, and \(R_1 \ge 2\dim H_1(S^1;F) = 2\). Hence \((R_0, R_1, R_2) = (1, 2, 1)\) for every field \(F\), and the pendulum’s potential is a perfect Morse function, \(C_\lambda = R_\lambda\).

Every potential on the torus. Now let \(V\) be any Morse function on \(T^2\): the double pendulum with springs or magnets added, a two-joint robot arm under any load, the torsional energy of a molecule with two rotatable bonds. The inequalities \((4_0)\), \((4_1)\), \((4_2)\) with \(R = (1, 2, 1)\) read \[C_0 \ge 1, \qquad C_1 - C_0 \ge 1, \qquad C_2 - C_1 + C_0 \ge 0,\] and (3) makes the last an equality. Therefore \[C_1 = C_0 + C_2, \qquad C_1 \ge C_0 + 1 \ge 2, \qquad C_0 + C_1 + C_2 = 2C_1 \ge 4 .\] There is always at least one more saddle than stable equilibria, and the number of equilibria is even.

For one rotatable bond the configuration space is a circle, \(R = (1, 1)\), and the same reasoning gives \(C_0 = C_1\); butane has three staggered minima (anti and two gauche) and three eclipsed maxima.

Two rotors. A simple model of two coupled threefold rotors is \[V(\varphi, \psi) = \tfrac{V_3}{2}(1 - \cos 3\varphi) + \tfrac{V_3}{2}(1 - \cos 3\psi) - \kappa \cos(\varphi - \psi - \delta),\] a threefold torsional term for each rotor plus a coupling of strength \(\kappa\) (a model, not data for a particular molecule). For \(\kappa = 0\) the critical points are products of those of the two one-variable potentials, each with three minima and three maxima: \(9\) minima, \(9 + 9 = 18\) saddles and \(9\) maxima, and \(18 = 9 + 9\). As the coupling grows, critical points of adjacent index collide and disappear in pairs. With \(V_3 = 1\) and \(\delta = 0\), the numerical search of the figure (confirmed by an independent sign-change search) finds \((C_0, C_1, C_2) = (9, 18, 9)\) at \(\kappa = 0.5\), \(1\) and \(1.5\), then \((3, 12, 9)\) at \(\kappa = 1.75\) and \((3, 9, 6)\) at \(\kappa = 2.5\); with \(\delta = 0.8\) and \(\kappa = 2\) it finds \((6, 12, 6)\). Every case satisfies \(C_1 = C_0 + C_2\). Used in reverse, the relation is a consistency check on a computed list of stationary points: if a search on a two-dihedral energy surface reports \(C_0 - C_1 + C_2 \ne 0\), some stationary point has been missed or one of them is degenerate.

8. Summary of what was silently assumed, now made explicit

Where Milnor says What is actually needed

Checked by machine. Theorem 4.1 (Reeb) has been verified in the Lean proof assistant for compact submanifolds of Euclidean space and, through the Whitney embedding, for compact manifolds. §5 is checked in singular homology over every field. Relative homology, excision, the exact sequences of pairs and triples and the homology of attached cells (Lemma E), absent from Mathlib, were built for this. On every compact submanifold of Euclidean space, and through the Whitney embedding on every compact manifold, each slab between regular values has the homology of its critical points (Proposition F over a field, with several critical points per level), and Lemmas 5.1, D and 5.3, Theorem 5.2, the inequalities \((4_\lambda)\), Corollary 5.4 and the lacunary principle hold for the Betti numbers. Their alternating sum, the same over every field, equals \(\sum_\lambda (-1)^\lambda C_\lambda\) for every Morse function and the index sum of the Poincaré–Hopf theorem, and is \(1 + (-1)^n\) on \(S^n\). The example of \(\mathbb CP^n\) is checked as well, for the compact submanifold of rank-one Hermitian projections: Milnor’s coordinates are coordinates on it, Proposition B holds, and Corollary C holds in the form of one cell in each dimension \(0, 2, \dots, 2n\), with the Betti numbers over every field given by the lacunary principle. Not checked: Remarks 1 and 2, Proposition A, Proposition G (the integral form of the lacunary principle), integral homology, non-compact manifolds and the application. See the verified edition.

Chapter 4Milnor §6pp. 32–38Contents ↑

Chapter 4. Focal points: every manifold has a Morse function

Milnor, “Morse Theory”, §6, rewritten for a first-year graduate student who wants to know what the theorem is for. Every proof is complete; Sard’s theorem, the normal bundle, the index of a nondegenerate zero and the Poincaré–Hopf theorem are quoted from the companion volume (“Topology from the Differentiable Viewpoint”, rewritten), and the Whitney embedding theorem from the literature.

0. Echoes in an oval room

Stand in a room whose wall, seen from above, is an ellipse, and clap once. Some of the sound strikes the wall head-on and comes straight back to you. How many such echoes do you hear, and when?

A sound ray from your position \(p\) returns to \(p\) after one reflection at a point \(q\) of the wall exactly when it meets the wall at right angles: the reflected ray is the mirror image of the incoming one in the normal line, and it points back along the incoming ray only if that ray is the normal. So the echoes correspond to the normals to the wall through \(p\), and these are the critical points of the squared distance \[L_p(q) = |p - q|^2, \qquad q \text{ on the wall},\] because the derivative of \(L_p\) along the wall vanishes exactly when \(p - q\) is perpendicular to the wall. The delay of an echo is \(2|p - q|\) divided by the speed of sound.

The answer depends on where you stand, through a curve you cannot see: the locus of the centres of curvature of the wall, its evolute. Inside the evolute you hear four echoes, outside it two. As you walk across it, two of the echoes slide together in time, merge and vanish; on the evolute itself \(L_p\) has a degenerate critical point.

This chapter proves the general statement behind this, for any submanifold \(M\) of a Euclidean space. \(L_p\) has a degenerate critical point exactly when \(p\) is a focal point of \(M\), a point where infinitely near normals of \(M\) meet (Lemma 6.5). Along each normal line the focal points sit at the principal radii of curvature (Lemma 6.3), and by Sard’s theorem they form a set of measure zero. Hence \(L_p\) is a Morse function for almost every \(p\) (Theorem 6.6). Since every manifold embeds in some \(\mathbb{R}^n\) as a closed subset, every manifold carries a Morse function with compact sublevel sets (Corollary 6.7), and the theory of Chapters 2 and 3 applies to every manifold. Finally, the index of \(L_p\) at \(q\) is the number of focal points between \(q\) and \(p\) (Lemma 6.9): the echoes that come back from beyond a centre of curvature are those of index \(1\). Section 9 does the numbers for an oval room 20 m long and 12 m wide.

1. Normals and focal points (Milnor p. 32)

So far we have studied functions with only nondegenerate critical points, without knowing that any exist. Milnor constructs them on every manifold embedded in Euclidean space.

Setting. Throughout, \(M \subset \mathbb{R}^n\) is a smooth submanifold of dimension \(k < n\) (Milnor: “differentiably embedded”; \(M\) need not be compact or closed). Every point of \(M\) has a neighbourhood \(x(U)\) in \(M\), where \(U \subset \mathbb{R}^k\) is open and \(x : U \to \mathbb{R}^n\) is a parametrization: smooth, with injective derivative, and a homeomorphism onto \(x(U)\). Its inverse gives coordinates \(u = (u^1, \dots, u^k)\), and \(TM_q\) is the image of \(dx\) at \(q\). We cite the companion volume by chapter and number.

Definition (Milnor). The normal bundle is \(N = \{(q, v) \in M \times \mathbb{R}^n : v \perp TM_q\}\), and the endpoint map is \(E : N \to \mathbb{R}^n\), \(E(q, v) = q + v\).

Fact A (the normal bundle). \(N\) is a smooth \(n\)-dimensional submanifold of \(\mathbb{R}^{2n}\). Concretely, let \(x : U \to M\) be a parametrization and \(w_1, \dots, w_{n-k} : U \to \mathbb{R}^n\) smooth maps such that \(w_1(u), \dots, w_{n-k}(u)\) is an orthonormal basis of \((TM_{x(u)})^\perp\) for each \(u\). Then \[\Psi(u, t) = \Big(x(u),\ \sum_{\alpha=1}^{n-k} t^\alpha w_\alpha(u)\Big), \qquad (u,t) \in U \times \mathbb{R}^{n-k},\] is a parametrization of \(N\) onto the open subset \(N \cap (x(U) \times \mathbb{R}^n)\). Such frames exist near every point of \(M\): apply Gram–Schmidt to \(\partial_1 x, \dots, \partial_k x\) followed by \(n - k\) standard basis vectors completing them to a basis at one point (they then do so nearby). This is proved in Chapter 6 of the companion volume (Topology from the Differentiable Viewpoint, rewritten), in the proof of Proposition 4.1; see also its Chapter 8, Problem 11. That proof assumes \(M\) compact but is local. (In brief: \(\Psi\) is smooth and injective; its derivative sends \(\partial/\partial u^i\) and \(\partial/\partial t^\beta\) to \((\partial_i x, \ast)\) and \((0, w_\beta)\), which are independent; and its inverse \((q, v) \mapsto (x^{-1}(q), (v \cdot w_\alpha(x^{-1}(q)))_\alpha)\) is continuous.)

\(E\) is smooth, as the restriction of the linear map \((q, v) \mapsto q + v\) of \(\mathbb{R}^{2n}\).

Definition (Milnor). A point \(e \in \mathbb{R}^n\) is a focal point of \((M, q)\) with multiplicity \(\mu\) if \(e = q + v\) with \((q, v) \in N\) and the derivative \(dE_{(q,v)} : TN_{(q,v)} \to \mathbb{R}^n\) has a kernel of dimension \(\mu > 0\). It is a focal point of \(M\) if it is a focal point of \((M, q)\) for some \(q \in M\).

Both spaces have dimension \(n\), so \((q, v)\) is then a critical point of \(E\). Intuitively a focal point is where nearby normals meet: if \(dE\) kills a tangent vector to \(N\) at \((q, v)\), then the normal lines through nearby points of \(M\), followed for the right length, arrive at \(e\) to first order (Milnor’s figure on p. 32).

Example. For the sphere \(M = S^{n-1}(r)\) of radius \(r\) about \(0\), the normal space at \(q\) is spanned by \(q\), and in the parametrization \(\Psi(u, s) = (x(u), s\,x(u)/r)\) we get \(E(\Psi(u,s)) = (1 + s/r)\, x(u)\), with partial derivatives \((1 + s/r)\,\partial_i x\) and \(x/r\). These are dependent exactly when \(s = -r\), and then the kernel has dimension \(n - 1\). So the centre is a focal point of \((M, q)\) for every \(q\), of multiplicity \(n - 1\), and there are no others: all normals of a sphere meet at its centre.

2. Sard’s theorem and the measure of the focal set (Milnor p. 33)

A set \(Z \subset \mathbb{R}^n\) has measure zero if for each \(\eta > 0\) it can be covered by countably many cubes of total volume less than \(\eta\). A countable union of such sets has measure zero, and a set of measure zero contains no ball, so its complement is dense. A critical point of a \(C^1\) map between manifolds of the same dimension is a point where its derivative is singular.

Theorem 6.1 (Sard). (checked by machine: V4.3, in a narrower form)1 If \(M_1\) and \(M_2\) are manifolds with countable bases, of the same dimension, and \(f : M_1 \to M_2\) is of class \(C^1\), then the image of the set of critical points has measure zero in \(M_2\) (its trace in each chart is carried to a set of measure zero).

Milnor does not prove it and cites de Rham, Variétés différentiables, p. 10. We apply it only to smooth maps into \(\mathbb{R}^n\), and that case is proved in Chapter 3 of the companion volume: Theorem 1.1 there is Sard’s theorem for smooth maps between open subsets of vector spaces, and the proof of its Theorem 2.1 passes to a manifold domain by covering it with countably many charts \(\varphi_i\), the critical values of \(f\) being the union of those of the maps \(f \circ \varphi_i^{-1}\).

How much smoothness. “Of class \(C^1\)” suffices because the dimensions are equal. From higher-dimensional manifolds Sard’s theorem needs more derivatives, and Whitney’s \(C^1\) example shows that they are necessary (companion volume, Chapter 3). Every map below is smooth.

Corollary 6.2. (checked by machine: V4.4, with its hypotheses made explicit) For almost all \(x \in \mathbb{R}^n\) (all but a set of measure zero), \(x\) is not a focal point of \(M\).

Proof. \(N\) is an \(n\)-manifold (Fact A), with a countable basis since it is a subset of \(\mathbb{R}^{2n}\), and \(E : N \to \mathbb{R}^n\) is smooth. By definition, \(x\) is a focal point of \(M\) if and only if \(x = E(q, v)\) for a point \((q, v) \in N\) at which \(dE\) is singular, that is, if and only if \(x\) is a critical value of \(E\). By Theorem 6.1 these form a set of measure zero. \(\square\)

3. The second fundamental form (Milnor pp. 33–34)

Fix a parametrization \(x(u) = (x_1(u), \dots, x_n(u))\) of a neighbourhood of \(q\) in \(M\), write \(\partial_i = \partial/\partial u^i\), and let \(u_q\) be the coordinates of \(q\). (Milnor writes vectors with arrows; we drop them.)

Definition (Milnor). The first fundamental form is the symmetric matrix of functions \(g_{ij} = \partial_i x \cdot \partial_j x\); it is positive definite because the \(\partial_i x\) are independent. The vector \(\partial_i\partial_j x\) at a point of \(M\) is the sum of a vector tangent to \(M\) and a vector normal to \(M\); the normal part is denoted \(\ell_{ij}\), and the matrix \((\ell_{ij})\) of vector-valued functions, symmetric in \(i, j\), is the second fundamental form. For a unit normal vector \(v\) at \(q\), the symmetric matrix \[\big(v \cdot \partial_i\partial_j x\big) = \big(v \cdot \ell_{ij}\big)\] is the second fundamental form of \(M\) at \(q\) in the direction \(v\). The two expressions agree because \(v\) is orthogonal to the tangent part.

It simplifies matters to have \(g_{ij}(u_q) = \delta_{ij}\). A linear change of coordinates achieves this: if \(P\) is invertible with \(P^{\mathsf T} g(u_q) P = I\) (for instance \(P = g(u_q)^{-1/2}\)), then \(\tilde x(\tilde u) = x(u_q + P\tilde u)\) has \(\tilde g(0) = I\).

Definition (Milnor). With \(g_{ij}(u_q) = \delta_{ij}\), the eigenvalues \(K_1, \dots, K_k\) of the symmetric \(k \times k\) matrix \((v \cdot \ell_{ij})\) at \(q\) are the principal curvatures of \(M\) at \(q\) in the normal direction \(v\), and the reciprocals \(K_i^{-1}\) of the nonzero ones are the principal radii of curvature. (Milnor writes \(K_1, \dots, K_n\); there are \(k\) of them.) If the matrix is singular some \(K_i\) vanish, and the corresponding radii are not defined.

Claim B. The principal curvatures, with multiplicities, do not depend on the coordinates with \(g_{ij}(u_q) = \delta_{ij}\). In arbitrary coordinates they are the eigenvalues of \(g^{-1}(v \cdot \ell)\) at \(q\).

Proof. Let \(\tilde u\) be other coordinates near \(q\) and \(J = (\partial u^i/\partial \tilde u^a)\) at \(q\). By the chain rule \(\partial x/\partial\tilde u^a = \sum_i J_{ia}\,\partial_i x\), so \(\tilde g = J^{\mathsf T} g J\), and \[\frac{\partial^2 x}{\partial \tilde u^a \partial \tilde u^b} = \sum_{i,j} J_{ia} J_{jb}\, \partial_i\partial_j x + \sum_i \frac{\partial^2 u^i}{\partial\tilde u^a \partial\tilde u^b}\, \partial_i x .\] The last sum is tangent, so \(v \cdot \tilde\ell = J^{\mathsf T}(v \cdot \ell) J\). If \(g = \tilde g = I\) at \(q\) then \(J^{\mathsf T} J = I\), and \(v \cdot \tilde\ell = J^{-1}(v \cdot \ell) J\) has the same eigenvalues. In general \(\tilde g^{-1}(v \cdot \tilde\ell) = J^{-1} g^{-1}(v \cdot \ell) J\), which for \(g = I\) is the matrix of the definition. \(\square\)

Example. For the sphere of radius \(r\) and the inward normal \(v = -q/r\): differentiating \(x \cdot x = r^2\) twice gives \(\partial_i\partial_j x \cdot x = -g_{ij}\), so \(v \cdot \ell_{ij} = g_{ij}/r\). All principal curvatures equal \(1/r\) and all radii equal \(r\), in agreement with §1.

4. Focal points along a normal line (Milnor pp. 34–35)

Let \(v\) be a unit normal vector at \(q\) and \(\ell = \{q + tv : t \in \mathbb{R}\}\) the normal line.

Lemma 6.3. (checked by machine: V4.7, in a stronger form) The focal points of \((M, q)\) on \(\ell\) are exactly the points \(q + K_i^{-1} v\) with \(K_i \ne 0\), where \(K_1, \dots, K_k\) are the principal curvatures in the direction \(v\); the multiplicity of \(q + K^{-1}v\) is the multiplicity of \(K\) as an eigenvalue. Hence there are at most \(k\) focal points of \((M, q)\) on \(\ell\), counted with multiplicity.

Proof. Choose \(x\) and a normal frame \(w_1, \dots, w_{n-k}\) near \(q\) (Fact A) and use the coordinates \((u, t)\) on \(N\) given by \(\Psi\). Then \(e(u, t) := E(\Psi(u,t)) = x(u) + \sum_\alpha t^\alpha w_\alpha(u)\), with \[\frac{\partial e}{\partial u^i} = \partial_i x + \sum_\alpha t^\alpha\, \partial_i w_\alpha, \qquad \frac{\partial e}{\partial t^\beta} = w_\beta .\] Since \(d\Psi\) is an isomorphism onto the tangent space of \(N\), the kernel of \(dE\) at \(\Psi(u,t)\) has the dimension of the kernel of the \(n \times n\) Jacobian matrix of \(e\). Take the inner products of these \(n\) vectors with the basis \(\partial_1 x, \dots, \partial_k x, w_1, \dots, w_{n-k}\) of \(\mathbb{R}^n\). This multiplies the Jacobian by an invertible matrix and so does not change the dimension of the kernel. Since \(w_\alpha \cdot \partial_j x = 0\) and \(w_\alpha \cdot w_\beta = \delta_{\alpha\beta}\), with rows indexed by \(u^i\) then \(t^\beta\), and columns by \(\partial_j x\) then \(w_\beta\), the result is \[\begin{pmatrix} \partial_i x\cdot\partial_j x + \sum_\alpha t^\alpha\,\partial_i w_\alpha \cdot \partial_j x & \sum_\alpha t^\alpha\,\partial_i w_\alpha \cdot w_\beta \\ 0 & I \end{pmatrix}.\] Differentiating \(w_\alpha \cdot \partial_j x = 0\) gives \(\partial_i w_\alpha \cdot \partial_j x = -w_\alpha \cdot \partial_i\partial_j x = -w_\alpha \cdot \ell_{ij}\), so the upper left block is \(\big(g_{ij} - \sum_\alpha t^\alpha\, w_\alpha \cdot \ell_{ij}\big)\). Subtracting multiples of the identity rows clears the upper right block, so the kernel of the whole matrix has the dimension of the kernel of the upper left block. At the point \((q, tv)\) of \(N\) we have \(\sum_\alpha t^\alpha w_\alpha = tv\), hence \(\sum_\alpha t^\alpha w_\alpha \cdot \ell_{ij} = t\,v \cdot \ell_{ij}\). We have proved:

Assertion 6.4. (checked by machine: V4.9, in a stronger form) \(q + tv\) is a focal point of \((M, q)\) with multiplicity \(\mu\) if and only if the matrix \[\big(g_{ij} - t\, v \cdot \ell_{ij}\big) \qquad (\ast)\] at \(q\) is singular, with nullity \(\mu\).

Now take coordinates with \(g_{ij}(u_q) = \delta_{ij}\) and let \(L = (v \cdot \ell_{ij}(u_q))\). For \(t = 0\) the matrix \((\ast)\) is \(I\), so \(q\) itself is never a focal point of \((M, q)\). For \(t \ne 0\), \(I - tL = -t(L - t^{-1} I)\) is singular if and only if \(1/t\) is an eigenvalue of \(L\), and its nullity is the dimension of the \(1/t\)-eigenspace, which for the symmetric matrix \(L\) is the multiplicity of \(1/t\) as an eigenvalue. So the focal points on \(\ell\) are the points \(q + tv\) with \(1/t = K_i\), with the stated multiplicities, which add up to at most \(k\). \(\square\)

Milnor’s text skips three small points. (1) The fields \(w_\alpha\), which he writes as functions of \(u\), need Gram–Schmidt to exist near each point (Fact A), and in general they exist only locally, not along all of \(M\): a Möbius band in \(\mathbb{R}^3\) has no nowhere-zero normal field. (2) “Thus the rank is equal to the rank of the upper left hand block”: the rank of the \(n \times n\) matrix is that rank plus \(n - k\); it is the nullities that agree, which is what the argument uses. (3) The case \(t = 0\) must be set aside before dividing by \(t\), and “multiplicity as eigenvalue” equals the nullity because \((v \cdot \ell_{ij})\) is symmetric.

5. The squared distance function (Milnor pp. 35–36)

For \(p \in \mathbb{R}^n\) let \(L_p : M \to \mathbb{R}\), \(L_p(q) = |q - p|^2\). In coordinates, \(f(u) := L_p(x(u)) = x \cdot x - 2\,x \cdot p + p \cdot p\), so \[\partial_i f = 2\,\partial_i x \cdot (x - p), \qquad \partial_i\partial_j f = 2\big(\partial_i x \cdot \partial_j x + \partial_i\partial_j x \cdot (x - p)\big).\] The first formula shows that \(q\) is a critical point of \(L_p\) if and only if \(q - p\) is normal to \(M\) at \(q\), that is, \((q, p - q) \in N\). So the critical points of \(L_p\) are the first components of the points of \(E^{-1}(p)\).

At a critical point \(q \ne p\) write \(p = q + tv\), where \(t > 0\) is the distance from \(q\) to \(p\) and \(v = (p - q)/t\) is a unit normal. Then \(\partial_i\partial_j x \cdot (x - p) = -t\,v \cdot \partial_i\partial_j x = -t\, v \cdot \ell_{ij}\), so the Hessian is \[\partial_i\partial_j f(u_q) = 2\big(g_{ij} - t\, v \cdot \ell_{ij}\big). \qquad (\ast\ast)\] If \(p = q\), the Hessian is \(2g_{ij}\), nondegenerate of index \(0\) (\(q\) is the minimum). Recall from Chapter 1 that at a critical point the Hessian is a well-defined symmetric bilinear form on \(TM_q\), so its nullity and index do not depend on the coordinates.

Lemma 6.5. (checked by machine: V4.11, with its hypotheses made explicit) The point \(q \in M\) is a degenerate critical point of \(L_p\) if and only if \(p\) is a focal point of \((M, q)\). The nullity of \(q\) as a critical point equals the multiplicity of \(p\) as a focal point.

Proof. If \(q\) is not critical, then \(p - q\) is not normal at \(q\) and \(p\) is not a focal point of \((M, q)\). If \(q\) is critical and \(q = p\), the Hessian \(2g\) is nondegenerate and \(p = q\) is not a focal point of \((M,q)\) (Lemma 6.3, \(t = 0\)). If \(q\) is critical and \(q \ne p\), the Hessian \((\ast\ast)\) is twice the matrix \((\ast)\) of Assertion 6.4, so the nullities agree. \(\square\)

Theorem 6.6. (checked by machine: V4.12, in a stronger form) For almost all \(p \in \mathbb{R}^n\), the function \(L_p : M \to \mathbb{R}\) has no degenerate critical points.

Proof. By Lemma 6.5, \(L_p\) has a degenerate critical point if and only if \(p\) is a focal point of \((M, q)\) for some \(q\), that is, a focal point of \(M\). By Corollary 6.2 these \(p\) form a set of measure zero. \(\square\)

6. Every manifold carries a Morse function (Milnor pp. 36–37)

Here \(M\) is an abstract manifold (smooth, Hausdorff, with a countable basis), of dimension \(m\). To use Theorem 6.6 we need it inside a Euclidean space.

Whitney embedding theorem (quoted). Every smooth \(m\)-manifold that is Hausdorff and has a countable basis admits a smooth embedding into \(\mathbb{R}^{2m+1}\) whose image is a closed subset. (Milnor cites Whitney, Geometric Integration Theory, p. 113; a modern proof is in J. Lee, Introduction to Smooth Manifolds, 2nd ed., Chapter 6.)

For compact \(M\) an easy version suffices. Cover \(M\) by charts \(\varphi_i : U_i \to \mathbb{R}^m\), \(i = 1, \dots, r\), and choose smooth \(\rho_i : M \to [0,1]\) supported in \(U_i\) such that the interiors of the sets \(\{\rho_i = 1\}\) cover \(M\). Then \(F = (\rho_1\varphi_1, \dots, \rho_r\varphi_r, \rho_1, \dots, \rho_r)\) is injective (if \(F(a) = F(b)\) and \(\rho_i(a) = 1\), then \(\rho_i(b) = 1\), both points lie in \(U_i\), and \(\varphi_i(a) = \varphi_i(b)\)) and an immersion (near a point with \(\rho_i = 1\) the component \(\rho_i\varphi_i = \varphi_i\) is a chart), hence an embedding, \(M\) being compact.

Corollary 6.7. (checked by machine: V4.13, V4.17, in a narrower form) On any manifold \(M\) there is a smooth function with no degenerate critical points for which each \(M^a\) is compact.

Proof. Embed \(M\) as a closed subset of \(\mathbb{R}^{2m+1}\) and identify it with its image. By Theorem 6.6 choose \(p\) such that \(L_p\) has no degenerate critical points. Then \(M^a = L_p^{-1}(-\infty, a] = M \cap \bar B(p, \sqrt a)\) (empty for \(a < 0\)) is closed and bounded in \(\mathbb{R}^{2m+1}\), hence compact. \(\square\)

A hidden hypothesis. “Any manifold” must be Hausdorff with a countable basis, as Whitney’s theorem requires, and the corollary fails without it: on the long line every continuous real function is eventually constant, so some sublevel set contains a closed unbounded piece of the line and is not compact. The closedness of the embedding is what makes \(M^a\) compact; an embedding onto a non-closed set would not do.

Application 1 (Milnor). Every manifold has the homotopy type of a CW complex, with one cell of dimension \(\lambda\) for each critical point of index \(\lambda\) of the function of Corollary 6.7. Proof. Theorem 3.5 (Chapter 2) applies to that function. \(\square\)

Application 2 (Milnor). Let \(M\) be compact and \(f\) a Morse function on \(M\) (one exists by Theorem 6.6). Then: (i) \(\chi(M) = \sum_\lambda (-1)^\lambda C_\lambda\); (ii) for any Riemannian metric, the zeros of \(\operatorname{grad} f\) are the critical points of \(f\), and the index of \(\operatorname{grad} f\) at a critical point of index \(\lambda\) is \((-1)^\lambda\); hence (iii) the vector field \(\operatorname{grad} f\) has index sum \(\chi(M)\), and so does every vector field on \(M\) with isolated zeros.

Proof. (i) is Theorem 5.2, equation (3), of Chapter 3. (ii) In coordinates \(\operatorname{grad} f\) has components \(X^i = \sum_j g^{ij}\partial_j f\), which vanish exactly where \(df = 0\). At a critical point the terms containing \(\partial_j f\) drop out of \(\partial_k X^i\), so the Jacobian matrix of \(X\) there is \(G^{-1}H\), with \(G = (g_{ij})\) and \(H\) the Hessian. Its determinant \(\det H/\det G\) is nonzero, with the sign of \(\det H\), which is \((-1)^\lambda\) since \(H\) has \(\lambda\) negative and \(m - \lambda\) positive eigenvalues. A nondegenerate zero has index equal to the sign of this determinant (companion volume, Chapter 6, Lemmas 3.1 and 3.2). (iii) Embed \(M\) in some \(\mathbb{R}^N\). The index sum of a tangent vector field with isolated zeros does not depend on the field: companion volume, Chapter 6, Theorem 4.2 for nondegenerate zeros and the remark on degenerate zeros that follows it (Milnor cites Steenrod, The Topology of Fibre Bundles, 39.7). \(\square\)

Milnor’s text skips the hypothesis in (i): “for any differentiable function \(f\) on \(M\)” must read “for any function without degenerate critical points”. This application is also the identification that the companion volume (Chapter 6) quotes from this book: the Euler number defined there by vector fields equals the homological Euler characteristic.

7. Approximation by Morse functions (Milnor p. 37)

Corollary 6.8. (checked by machine: V4.21, in a stronger form; V4.22, in a narrower form) Let \(M\) be a manifold of dimension \(m\), \(f : M \to \mathbb{R}\) a bounded smooth function, \(K \subset M\) compact and \(k \ge 0\) an integer. Fix finitely many charts \(\varphi_j : U_j \to \mathbb{R}^m\) and compact sets \(K_j \subset U_j\) with \(K = \bigcup_j K_j\). Then for every \(\eta > 0\) there is a smooth \(g : M \to \mathbb{R}\) without degenerate critical points such that \(|g - f| < \eta\) on \(M\), and every partial derivative of order between \(1\) and \(k\) of \((g - f) \circ \varphi_j^{-1}\) has absolute value less than \(\eta\) on \(\varphi_j(K_j)\), for every \(j\).

Milnor asks that on the compact set \(K\) the derivatives of \(g\) of order \(i \le k\) uniformly approximate those of \(f\). Derivatives on a manifold make sense only in charts, so the charts must be fixed in advance; finitely many suffice because \(K\) is compact. (Milnor compares M. Morse, Trans. Amer. Math. Soc. 33 (1931), 71–91.)

Proof. Step 1: a bounded embedding whose first coordinate is \(f\). Let \(h' : M \to \mathbb{R}^{n-1}\) be an embedding (Whitney), \(\beta(y) = y/\sqrt{1 + |y|^2}\), a diffeomorphism of \(\mathbb{R}^{n-1}\) onto the open unit ball, and \(h = (f, \beta \circ h') : M \to \mathbb{R}^n\). Then \(h\) is smooth, injective and an immersion (because its second component is), and a homeomorphism onto its image (its inverse is \((\beta\circ h')^{-1}\) composed with the projection forgetting the first coordinate). So \(h\) is an embedding with \(h_1 = f\), and \(|h| \le B := (\sup f^2 + 1)^{1/2}\).

Step 2: Milnor’s “short computation”. For \(c > 0\) and \(\varepsilon = (\varepsilon_1, \dots, \varepsilon_n)\) put \(p = (-c + \varepsilon_1, \varepsilon_2, \dots, \varepsilon_n)\) and \(g = (L_p \circ h - c^2)/(2c)\). Expanding \(|h - p|^2 = (h_1 + c - \varepsilon_1)^2 + \sum_{i \ge 2} (h_i - \varepsilon_i)^2\), \[g = f + \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{h_i^2}{2c} - \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{\varepsilon_i h_i}{c} + \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{\varepsilon_i^2}{2c} - \varepsilon_1 .\]

Step 3: estimates. The formula says \(g - f = |h - \varepsilon|^2/(2c) - \varepsilon_1\), so \(|g - f| \le (B + |\varepsilon|)^2/(2c) + |\varepsilon|\). In the derivatives of order \(\ge 1\) the constants drop out; the functions \(h_i \circ \varphi_j^{-1}\) and their squares are smooth on \(\varphi_j(U_j)\), so their partial derivatives of orders \(1\) to \(k\) are bounded on the compact sets \(\varphi_j(K_j)\) by one constant \(D\). Hence each such derivative of \((g - f)\circ\varphi_j^{-1}\) is at most \(nD/(2c) + n|\varepsilon| D/c\). Choose \(c > \max\{(B+1)^2/\eta,\ 3nD/(2\eta),\ 1\}\); then every \(\varepsilon\) with \(|\varepsilon| < \min\{1, \eta/2\}\) gives both estimates with bound \(\eta\).

Step 4: nondegeneracy. By Theorem 6.6 for the submanifold \(h(M) \subset \mathbb{R}^n\), the points \(p\) for which \(L_p\) has a degenerate critical point on \(h(M)\) form a set of measure zero, which contains no ball. So some \(\varepsilon\) in the allowed range makes \(L_p \circ h\) a Morse function, and then so is \(g\), which has the same critical points and Hessians multiplied by \(1/(2c) > 0\). \(\square\)

Why “bounded”. Boundedness of \(f\) is what makes \(h\) bounded, and hence the error terms \(\sum h_i^2/2c\) uniformly small. Without it the statement is still true but needs another argument (density of Morse functions in the strong topology; M. Hirsch, Differential Topology, Chapter 6, §1).

8. The index of \(L_p\) (Milnor pp. 37–38)

Lemma 6.9 (index theorem for \(L_p\)). (checked by machine: V4.23, restated) The index of \(L_p\) at a nondegenerate critical point \(q \in M\) equals the number of focal points of \((M, q)\) on the segment from \(q\) to \(p\), each counted with its multiplicity.

Proof. If \(p = q\), the index is \(0\) and the segment \(\{q\}\) contains no focal point of \((M, q)\) (Lemma 6.3, \(t = 0\)). Otherwise write \(p = q + tv\) with \(t > 0\) as in §5 and take coordinates with \(g_{ij}(u_q) = \delta_{ij}\). The index of the Hessian \((\ast\ast)\) is the number of negative eigenvalues of \(I - tL\), \(L = (v \cdot \ell_{ij})\): by the spectral theorem a symmetric matrix is negative definite on the span of its eigenvectors with negative eigenvalues and nonnegative on a complement. The eigenvalues of \(I - tL\) are \(1 - tK_i\), and \(1 - tK_i < 0\) if and only if \(K_i > 1/t\), that is, \(K_i > 0\) and \(K_i^{-1} < t\). By Lemma 6.3 the focal points of \((M, q)\) on the line are the points \(q + K_i^{-1} v\); such a point lies on the segment from \(q\) to \(p = q + tv\) if and only if \(0 < K_i^{-1} \le t\), and \(K_i^{-1} = t\) is excluded because \(p\) is not a focal point of \((M, q)\) (\(q\) is nondegenerate; Lemma 6.5). Counting multiplicities on both sides gives the claim. \(\square\)

Milnor writes “eigenvalues … which are \(\ge 1/t\)”; by the last remark \(\ge\) and \(>\) agree here. An analogous statement in Part III, the Morse index theorem, will be of fundamental importance: there the straight segment becomes a geodesic, focal points become conjugate points, and \(L_p\) becomes the energy of paths.

An interactive look at focal points

The figure shows an oval room: the wall \(M\) is an ellipse with semi-axes \(a = 10\) m and \(b\) (a slider), and the dashed closed curve with four cusps is the evolute, the set of focal points of \(M\). Drag the point \(p\), or use its sliders. The program solves \(dL_p/d\theta = 0\) along the wall and draws every normal from \(p\) to the wall: solid for minima of \(L_p\) (index \(0\)), dashed for maxima (index \(1\)). On each normal a small circle marks the focal point of \((M, q)\), the centre of curvature at its foot \(q\); a normal has index \(1\) exactly when that circle lies between \(q\) and \(p\), as Lemma 6.9 says. Below, the graph of the distance from \(p\) along the wall shows the same critical points, and the readout lists the echo delays \(2|p - q|/(343\ \text{m/s})\). Drag \(p\) across the evolute: a minimum and a maximum approach each other, merge into a degenerate critical point on the evolute, and disappear. The wavefront slider draws the curve at distance \(s\) from the wall along the inward normals, where a sound front emitted by the whole wall at once would be after travelling a distance \(s\); its cusps run along the evolute. (The still image shows the listeners at \((3, 2)\), inside the evolute, and \((8, 1)\), outside it, with their distance graphs side by side.)

9. Application: echoes in an oval room

The wall and its focal points. Let the wall be the ellipse \(M = \{X^2/a^2 + Y^2/b^2 = 1\}\), \(a > b > 0\), parametrized by \(x(\theta) = (a\cos\theta, b\sin\theta)\); here \(k = 1\) and \(n = 2\). Put \(s(\theta) = |x'(\theta)| = (a^2\sin^2\theta + b^2\cos^2\theta)^{1/2}\) and let \(\nu = -(b\cos\theta, a\sin\theta)/s\) be the inward unit normal. Since \(x'' = -x\), the second fundamental form in the direction \(\nu\) is \(\nu \cdot x'' = ab/s\), and \(g_{11} = s^2\). By Claim B the principal curvature is \(K = ab/s^3 > 0\), the curvature of the ellipse, and by Lemma 6.3 the only focal point of \((M, x(\theta))\) is the centre of curvature \(x + K^{-1}\nu\). (In the direction \(-\nu\) the curvature is \(-K\) and the focal point is the same.) Using \(a^2 - s^2 = (a^2 - b^2)\cos^2\theta\) and \(b^2 - s^2 = -(a^2 - b^2)\sin^2\theta\), \[x + K^{-1}\nu = \Big(\frac{a^2 - b^2}{a}\cos^3\theta,\ -\frac{a^2 - b^2}{b}\sin^3\theta\Big).\] So the focal set of \(M\) is the evolute \((a|X|)^{2/3} + (b|Y|)^{2/3} = (a^2 - b^2)^{2/3}\), a closed curve with cusps at \((\pm(a^2-b^2)/a, 0)\) and \((0, \pm(a^2-b^2)/b)\).

The count. The normals from \(p = (p_1, p_2)\) are the critical points of \(L_p(\theta) = |x(\theta) - p|^2\), and \[\tfrac12 L_p'(\theta) = (b^2 - a^2)\sin\theta\cos\theta + a p_1 \sin\theta - b p_2 \cos\theta .\]

  • By Lemma 6.5 and the computation above, \(L_p\) is a Morse function if and only if \(p\) is off the evolute.
  • By Theorem 5.2 of Chapter 3 for the circle (\(R_0 = R_1 = 1\)), \(C_0 = C_1 \ge 1\): off the evolute the number of echoes is even and at least \(2\).
  • By Lemma 6.9, a foot \(q\) has index \(1\) (a local maximum of the distance along the wall) if and only if the centre of curvature at \(q\) lies between \(q\) and \(p\).
  • The number of normals is constant on each component of the complement of the evolute. It is \(\#E^{-1}(p)\) (§5), and \(E\) is proper: on \(N = \{(x(\theta), \tau\nu(\theta))\}\) we have \(|E| \ge |\tau| - a\), so preimages of bounded sets are bounded and closed. For a proper smooth map between manifolds of the same dimension, \(\#E^{-1}(p)\) is finite and locally constant on the regular values: see Theorems 5.1 and 5.2 of Chapter 1 of the companion volume, whose proofs use the compactness of the domain only to know that \(E^{-1}(p)\) is compact and that \(E\) maps closed sets to closed sets; proper maps into \(\mathbb{R}^2\) have both properties. The regular values of \(E\) are the points off the evolute.
  • The complement of the evolute has two components, \(\{F < F_0\}\) and \(\{F > F_0\}\) with \(F = (a|X|)^{2/3} + (b|Y|)^{2/3}\) and \(F_0 = (a^2 - b^2)^{2/3}\). Both are connected because \(F(\lambda X, \lambda Y) = \lambda^{2/3} F(X, Y)\): the first is star-shaped about \(0\), and every point of the second can be pushed radially out to a large circle lying in it.
  • At \(p = 0\), \(L_p' = 0\) if and only if \(\sin\theta\cos\theta = 0\): four normals. At \(p = (R, 0)\) with \(R > (a^2 - b^2)/a\), \(\tfrac12 L_p' = \sin\theta\,(aR - (a^2 - b^2)\cos\theta)\) vanishes only where \(\sin\theta = 0\): two normals.

So a listener inside the evolute hears four echoes and one outside it two, as promised in §0. (Apollonius studied the normals from a point to a conic in Book V of the Conics; the boundary between two and four normals is implicit there.)

Numbers. Take a room 20 m by 12 m: \(a = 10\) m, \(b = 6\) m, \(a^2 - b^2 = 64\) m\(^2\). The evolute has cusps at \((\pm 6.4, 0)\) and \((0, \pm 10.7)\), so it pokes out through the long walls; the foci are \((\pm 8, 0)\). With the speed of sound \(343\) m/s (air at \(20\,^\circ\)C), an echo from a foot at distance \(d\) arrives after \(2d/343\) s. Solving \(L_p' = 0\) numerically:

listener at feet of the normals: distance (index) echo delays
\((0, 0)\), centre \((0, \pm 6)\): 6 m \((0)\); \((\pm 10, 0)\): 10 m \((1)\) 35.0 ms (two), 58.3 ms (two)
\((5, 0)\) \((7.81, \pm 3.75)\): 4.68 m \((0)\); \((10, 0)\): 5 m \((1)\); \((-10, 0)\): 15 m \((1)\) 27.3 ms (two), 29.2 ms, 87.5 ms
\((8, 0)\), a focus \((10, 0)\): 2 m \((0)\); \((-10, 0)\): 18 m \((1)\) 11.7 ms, 105.0 ms
\((3, 2)\) 3.64 m \((0)\), 7.43 m \((0)\), 7.57 m \((1)\), 13.21 m \((1)\) 21.2, 43.3, 44.2, 77.0 ms

Check one index with Lemma 6.9. For the listener at \((5, 0)\) the radius of curvature of the wall at \((10, 0)\) is \(b^2/a = 3.6\) m, so the centre of curvature \((6.4, 0)\) lies between \((10, 0)\) and the listener: index \(1\). Indeed the 5 m foot is a local maximum of the distance along the wall, flanked by the two feet at 4.68 m, where the radius of curvature, 7.93 m, exceeds the distance: index \(0\). Walk from \((5, 0)\) toward the end wall and the three near feet slide together; at the cusp \((6.4, 0)\) they merge into one degenerate critical point, and beyond it only \((10, 0)\) is left, now a minimum. The pair of echoes at 27.3 ms and the echo at 29.2 ms fuse into one. The model is idealized: specular reflection, a point listener, and only single reflections.

Where Milnor says What is actually needed

Checked by machine. Milnor’s §6 has been verified in the Lean proof assistant for submanifolds of Euclidean space, closed or not: Theorem 6.1 for smooth maps into a vector space, Corollary 6.2, focal points and their multiplicities, Lemma 6.3 (with principal curvatures as eigenvalues of the shape operator), Assertion 6.4, Lemmas 6.5 and 6.9, Theorem 6.6, and Corollary 6.7 for closed submanifolds. Corollary 6.8 is proved differently, by adding to \(f\) a small linear function of a bounded embedding instead of using \(L_p\), and \(f\) need not be bounded. Through Mathlib’s Whitney embedding, which exists only for compact manifolds, it is checked that every compact manifold carries a Morse function, that Corollary 6.8 holds on it, and that \(\chi(M)\) is well defined: \(\sum_\lambda (-1)^\lambda C_\lambda\) is the same for every Morse function and equals the index sum of every vector field on any embedded copy, as in Application 2, and the homological Euler characteristic (Chapter 3). Not checked: Corollary 6.7 for non-compact manifolds, Application 1, and the oval room of §9. See the verified edition.
