Chapter 5Milnor §7pp. 39–42Contents ↑

Chapter 5. Hyperplane sections: complex manifolds have no high cells

Milnor, “Morse Theory”, §7, rewritten for a first-year graduate student who wants to know what the theorem is for. Every proof is complete, except that the triangulability of algebraic varieties, the Lefschetz duality theorem and two standard lemmas of homotopy theory are quoted, with references.

0. Why a soap film never bulges away from you

Bend a wire into a closed loop, dip it in soapy water and pull it out: a film spans the wire. Now fix a point \(p\) in the room, your eye for instance. Is there a point of the film, away from the wire, that is farther from \(p\) than all nearby points of the film? Look at any soap film and you will not find one. The film may sag towards you or away from you, but it never forms a dome with a farthest point. The farthest point of the film from \(p\) is always on the wire, and consequently the film lies inside every ball that contains the wire, hence inside the convex hull of the wire.

The reason is curvature. The air pressure is the same on both sides of a soap film, so by the Young–Laplace law its mean curvature is zero: at every point it bends one way in one principal direction exactly as much as it bends the other way in the perpendicular direction. Its principal curvatures are \(\kappa\) and \(-\kappa\). In Chapter 4 (Milnor §6) we computed the Hessian of the squared distance \(L_p(x) = \|x - p\|^2\) on a surface at a critical point \(q\), where \(p = q + t\nu\) for a unit normal \(\nu\): in principal directions it is diagonal with entries \(2(1 - t\kappa_1)\) and \(2(1 - t\kappa_2)\). For the film these are \(2(1 - t\kappa)\) and \(2(1 + t\kappa)\), which add up to \(4\). At least one of them is positive, so \(q\) is never a local maximum. It can be a minimum (index \(0\)) or a saddle (index \(1\)), never index \(2\).

This chapter is about the same mechanism in complex geometry. The set of complex solutions of a polynomial equation such as \(z^3 + w^3 = 1\) is a real surface in \(\mathbb{C}^2 = \mathbb{R}^4\), and Andreotti and Frankel observed that it too curves equally in opposite directions, in every normal direction at once: multiplication by \(i\) turns its second fundamental form into its negative. So the squared distance from a point, restricted to a complex curve, has critical points of index \(0\) and \(1\) only, and on a complex manifold of complex dimension \(k\), of index at most \(k\): half the real dimension. Morse theory (Theorem 3.5 of Chapter 2) converts this into topology. A closed complex submanifold of \(\mathbb{C}^n\) of complex dimension \(k\) is built, up to homotopy, from cells of dimension at most \(k\) (Theorem 7.2). Applied to the complement of a hyperplane section of a projective variety, this gives the Lefschetz hyperplane theorem (Corollary 7.3 and Theorem 7.4): a projective variety and its hyperplane section have the same homology and homotopy groups below the middle dimension.

At the end (§6) we prove the statement about soap films, and we compute: the complex curve \(z^3 + w^3 = 1\) has the homotopy type of a wedge of four circles, and a numerical search finds exactly one minimum and four saddle points of a distance function on it, and no maximum.

1. The theorems, and what they rest on (Milnor p. 39)

We identify \(\mathbb{C}^n\) with \(\mathbb{R}^{2n}\). Besides the Hermitian product \(\langle a, b\rangle = \sum_\alpha a_\alpha \bar b_\alpha\) there is the real inner product \(a \cdot b = \operatorname{Re}\langle a, b\rangle\), which is the Euclidean inner product of \(\mathbb{R}^{2n}\). Multiplication by \(i\) preserves both; in particular it is an orthogonal map of \(\mathbb{R}^{2n}\).

A complex submanifold of \(\mathbb{C}^n\) of complex dimension \(k\) is a subset \(M\) such that each \(q \in M\) has a neighbourhood \(W\) in \(\mathbb{C}^n\) and a holomorphic map \(w : B \to \mathbb{C}^n\), \(B \subset \mathbb{C}^k\) open, which is a homeomorphism onto \(M \cap W\) and whose complex derivative has rank \(k\) at every point; \(z = w^{-1}\) is a holomorphic chart. Milnor’s complex analytic manifold of dimension \(k\), “bianalytically embedded as a closed subset” of \(\mathbb{C}^n\), means exactly: a complex submanifold of \(\mathbb{C}^n\) of complex dimension \(k\) which is a closed subset. Such an \(M\) is a smooth submanifold of \(\mathbb{R}^{2n}\) of dimension \(2k\), and each tangent space \(TM_q\), the image of the complex-linear map \(dw\), is a complex subspace of \(\mathbb{C}^n\). A non-singular affine algebraic variety is a common zero set of finitely many polynomials which is a complex submanifold (checked in practice by the Jacobian criterion and the holomorphic implicit function theorem). A zero set of continuous functions is closed.

Theorem 7.1. (checked by machine: V5.16, in a narrower form)1 If \(M \subset \mathbb{C}^n\) is a non-singular affine algebraic variety of real dimension \(2k\), then \(H_i(M;\mathbb{Z}) = 0\) for \(i > k\).

Theorem 7.2. (checked by machine: V5.15, restated) A complex submanifold \(M\) of \(\mathbb{C}^n\) of complex dimension \(k\) which is a closed subset of \(\mathbb{C}^n\) has the homotopy type of a CW-complex of dimension at most \(k\).

Milnor’s statement says “a \(k\)-dimensional CW-complex” (his proof ends, p. 41, with “dimension \(\le k\)”). The proof produces one cell of dimension \(\lambda\) for each critical point of index \(\lambda\) of a function, with every \(\lambda \le k\), so “of dimension at most \(k\)” is what is proved, and it is what is true: \(\mathbb{C}\) is contractible.

Proof of Theorem 7.1 from Theorem 7.2. \(M\) is closed and a complex submanifold of dimension \(k\), so \(M\) is homotopy equivalent to a CW-complex \(X\) of dimension at most \(k\). Singular homology is a homotopy invariant, and \(H_i(X;\mathbb{Z}) = 0\) for \(i > \dim X\) for every CW-complex, finite or not (Hatcher, Algebraic Topology, Lemma 2.34). \(\square\)

If the components of \(M\) have different dimensions, \(k\) is the largest of them; the proof of 7.2 bounds the index at a point by the complex dimension of the component through it, so the conclusion is unchanged.

What is used from earlier chapters. From Chapter 4 (Milnor §6), for a smooth submanifold \(M \subset \mathbb{R}^N\) of dimension \(m\) and a point \(p \in \mathbb{R}^N\):

  1. \(q \in M\) is a critical point of \(L_p|_M\) if and only if \(p - q\) is normal to \(M\) at \(q\) (Milnor p. 35).

  2. In local coordinates \(u = (u^1, \dots, u^m)\) on \(M\), with \(x = x(u)\) the inclusion, let \(g_{ij} = \frac{\partial x}{\partial u^i}\cdot\frac{\partial x}{\partial u^j}\) (the first fundamental form) and, for a unit normal \(v\) at \(q\), let \((v \cdot \ell_{ij}) = (v\cdot \partial^2 x/\partial u^i\partial u^j)\) (the second fundamental form in the direction \(v\); only the normal component \(\ell_{ij}\) of the second derivative contributes). At a critical point \(q\) with \(p = q + tv\), \[\frac{\partial^2 L_p}{\partial u^i \partial u^j}(q) = 2\big(g_{ij} - t\, v\cdot\ell_{ij}\big).\] We refer to this as formula (1.1) (Milnor pp. 36, 38).

  3. Assertion 6.4: \(q + tv\) is a focal point of \((M, q)\) of multiplicity \(\mu\) if and only if the matrix \((g_{ij} - t\,v\cdot\ell_{ij})\) is singular with nullity \(\mu\). Lemma 6.3: the focal points on the normal line \(\{q + tv\}\) are the points \(q + K_i^{-1} v\), where the \(K_i \neq 0\) are the nonzero eigenvalues of \((v\cdot\ell_{ij})\) relative to \((g_{ij})\), the principal curvatures; so there are at most \(m\) of them, counted with multiplicity.

  4. Lemma 6.5: \(q\) is a degenerate critical point of \(L_p\) if and only if \(p\) is a focal point of \((M,q)\). Theorem 6.6: for almost every \(p\), \(L_p|_M\) has no degenerate critical points. Lemma 6.9 (index theorem for \(L_p\)): the index of \(L_p\) at a nondegenerate critical point \(q\) equals the number of focal points of \((M, q)\) on the segment from \(q\) to \(p\), counted with multiplicity.

From Chapter 2 (Milnor §3) we use Theorem 3.5: if \(f\) is a smooth function on a manifold \(M\) with no degenerate critical points, and each \(M^a = f^{-1}(-\infty, a]\) is compact, then \(M\) has the homotopy type of a CW-complex with one cell of dimension \(\lambda\) for each critical point of index \(\lambda\). (When there are infinitely many critical points, its proof uses the Appendix.) In §5 we shall also need the ingredients of that proof, Theorems 3.1 and 3.2 and Remark 3.3, in a slightly more general setting.

2. A quadratic form that is its own negative (Milnor p. 39)

Let \(Q(z^1, \dots, z^k) = \sum_{h,j} b_{hj}\, z^h z^j\), with complex coefficients \(b_{hj} = b_{jh}\), be a quadratic form in \(k\) complex variables. Substituting \(z^h = x^h + i y^h\) and taking the real part gives a real quadratic form in \(2k\) real variables, \[Q'(x^1,\dots,x^k,y^1,\dots,y^k) = \operatorname{Re} \sum_{h,j} b_{hj}\,(x^h + iy^h)(x^j + iy^j).\] Write \(Q'(u) = u^{\mathsf T} A u\) with \(A\) a real symmetric \(2k \times 2k\) matrix; the eigenvalues of \(Q'\) are those of \(A\). Let \(J\) be the real linear map \(J(x, y) = (-y, x)\), which is multiplication by \(i\) in the variable \(z = x + iy\). It is orthogonal and \(J^2 = -1\).

Assertion 1. (checked by machine: V5.3, restated) If \(e\) is an eigenvalue of \(Q'\) with multiplicity \(\mu\), then \(-e\) is also an eigenvalue, with the same multiplicity \(\mu\).

Proof. \(Q\) is homogeneous of degree \(2\), so \(Q(iz^1, \dots, iz^k) = i^2 Q(z) = -Q(z)\). Taking real parts, \(Q'(Ju) = -Q'(u)\) for all \(u\), that is \(J^{\mathsf T} A J = -A\). Since \(J^{\mathsf T} = J^{-1}\) this says \(AJ = -JA\). If \(Au = eu\) then \(A(Ju) = -J(Au) = -e\,(Ju)\), so \(J\) maps the \(e\)-eigenspace of \(A\) injectively into the \((-e)\)-eigenspace. By the same argument it maps the \((-e)\)-eigenspace injectively into the \(e\)-eigenspace. The two eigenspaces have the same dimension. \(\square\)

For \(k = 1\) and \(Q = b z^2\), the matrix of \(Q' = \operatorname{Re}\big(b(x + iy)^2\big)\) has trace \(0\) and determinant \(-|b|^2\): its eigenvalues are \(\pm|b|\).

What the next section actually needs is the same statement relative to a \(J\)-invariant inner product, because focal points are eigenvalues relative to the first fundamental form:

Assertion 1a. Let \(G\) and \(B\) be real symmetric \(2k \times 2k\) matrices with \(J^{\mathsf T} G J = G\) and \(J^{\mathsf T} B J = -B\). Then for every real \(t\) the matrices \(G - tB\) and \(G + tB\) have the same nullity.

Proof. \(J^{\mathsf T}(G - tB)J = G + tB\), and \(J\) is invertible. \(\square\)

3. Focal points of a complex submanifold come in symmetric pairs (Milnor p. 40)

Let \(M \subset \mathbb{C}^n\) be a complex submanifold of complex dimension \(k\) and \(q \in M\).

Lemma 3.1. Let \(T \subset \mathbb{C}^n\) be a complex linear subspace and \(v \in \mathbb{C}^n\) with \(a \cdot v = 0\) for all \(a \in T\). Then \(\langle a, v\rangle = 0\) for all \(a \in T\).

Proof. \(\operatorname{Re}\langle a, v\rangle = a\cdot v = 0\), and \(\operatorname{Im}\langle a, v\rangle = -\operatorname{Re}\big(i\langle a, v\rangle\big) = -\operatorname{Re}\langle ia, v\rangle = -(ia)\cdot v = 0\), because \(ia \in T\). \(\square\)

Assertion 2. (checked by machine: V5.7, restated) The focal points of \((M, q)\) along any normal line occur in pairs situated symmetrically about \(q\): if \(v\) is a unit normal vector at \(q\), \(t \neq 0\), and \(q + tv\) is a focal point of multiplicity \(\mu\), then \(q - tv\) is a focal point of multiplicity \(\mu\).

Proof. Choose holomorphic coordinates \(z^1, \dots, z^k\) for \(M\) near \(q\) with \(z(q) = 0\). The inclusion \(M \to \mathbb{C}^n\) is given by \(n\) holomorphic functions \(w_\alpha(z^1, \dots, z^k)\). Writing \(z^h = x^h + iy^h\), the \(2k\) functions \(u = (x, y)\) are real coordinates for \(M\), and we compute the quantities of (b) and (c) in these coordinates.

Step 1: the first fundamental form is \(J\)-invariant. By the Cauchy–Riemann equations, \(\partial w/\partial y^h = i\,\partial w/\partial x^h\). Let \(J\) act on coordinate vectors by \(\partial_{x^h} \mapsto \partial_{y^h}\), \(\partial_{y^h} \mapsto -\partial_{x^h}\); this is the matrix \(J\) of §2. Then \(dw(J\xi) = i\,dw(\xi)\) for every \(\xi \in \mathbb{R}^{2k}\). Since multiplication by \(i\) is orthogonal, the matrix \(G = (g_{ij})\) satisfies \(G(J\xi, J\eta) = (i\,dw\,\xi)\cdot(i\,dw\,\eta) = (dw\,\xi)\cdot(dw\,\eta) = G(\xi, \eta)\), that is \(J^{\mathsf T} G J = G\), at every point.

Step 2: the second fundamental form is \(J\)-anti-invariant. Let \(v\) be a unit vector orthogonal to \(M\) at \(q\), in the real sense. The Hermitian product \(h(z) = \langle w(z), v\rangle = \sum_\alpha w_\alpha(z)\,\bar v_\alpha\) is a holomorphic function of \(z\) near \(0\), with a convergent power series \[h(z) = h(0) + \sum_h c_h z^h + Q(z) + (\text{terms of order} \ge 3),\] \(Q\) a homogeneous quadratic polynomial. The linear coefficients are \(c_h = \langle \partial w/\partial z^h(0), v\rangle\), and they vanish by Lemma 3.1 applied to the complex subspace \(T = TM_q\). (Milnor: “the linear terms vanish since \(v\) is orthogonal to \(M\)”; the lemma is needed because orthogonality is meant in the real sense.) Taking real parts, the real function \(\varphi(u) := w(u)\cdot v = \operatorname{Re} h\) has the Taylor expansion \[\varphi(u) = q\cdot v + Q'(x, y) + O(|u|^3).\] On the other hand \(\partial^2 \varphi/\partial u^i\partial u^j(0) = v\cdot \partial^2 w/\partial u^i\partial u^j(0) = v\cdot\ell_{ij}\), because \(v\) is constant and normal at \(q\). Comparing with Taylor’s formula, \((v\cdot\ell_{ij}) = 2A\), where \(A\) is the matrix of \(Q'\). This is the precise content of Milnor’s remark that \(Q'\) determines the second fundamental form in the direction \(v\). By §2, \(J^{\mathsf T}(v\cdot\ell_{ij})J = -(v\cdot\ell_{ij})\).

Step 3. By Assertion 6.4 the multiplicity of \(q + tv\) as a focal point is the nullity of \(G - t(v\cdot\ell_{ij})\), and that of \(q - tv\) is the nullity of \(G + t(v\cdot\ell_{ij})\). By Steps 1 and 2 and Assertion 1a these are equal. \(\square\)

Milnor’s text skips a normalization. Milnor concludes from Assertion 1 that the eigenvalues of \(Q'\) come in opposite pairs, and “hence” that the focal points do. But Assertion 1 is about eigenvalues with respect to the standard inner product of the coordinate space \(\mathbb{R}^{2k}\), while focal points are governed by the eigenvalues of \((v\cdot\ell_{ij})\) relative to \((g_{ij})\); Lemma 6.3 even assumes coordinates with \(g_{ij}(q) = \delta_{ij}\). The two notions agree when the real coordinates are orthonormal at \(q\), not in general. One can arrange this by a complex-linear change of the coordinates \(z\) that makes the vectors \(\partial w/\partial z^h(0)\) Hermitian-orthonormal (then the real vectors \(\partial w/\partial x^h(0)\), \(\partial w/\partial y^h(0)\) are orthonormal), or bypass it, as above, by the \(J\)-invariance of \((g_{ij})\).

Corollary 3.2. In every unit normal direction \(v\) at \(q\), the principal curvatures of \(M\) are \(K_1, \dots, K_k, -K_1, \dots, -K_k\) for suitable \(K_1, \dots, K_k \ge 0\). In particular the mean curvature of a complex submanifold is zero in every normal direction, and in any normal direction at most \(k\) principal curvatures are positive.

Proof. The principal curvatures are the eigenvalues of \(S = G^{-1}L\), where \(L = (v\cdot\ell_{ij})\); \(S\) is self-adjoint for the inner product \(G\), hence diagonalizable with real eigenvalues. From \(J^{\mathsf T} G J = G\) we get \(G^{-1}(J^{\mathsf T})^{-1} = JG^{-1}\), and with \(J^{\mathsf T}LJ = -L\) this gives \(SJ = G^{-1}(J^{\mathsf T})^{-1}(J^{\mathsf T}LJ) = -JG^{-1}L = -JS\). As in Assertion 1, \(J\) maps the \(e\)-eigenspace of \(S\) isomorphically onto the \((-e)\)-eigenspace. The positive eigenvalues are therefore matched with the negative ones, at most \(k\) of each among \(2k\); and the trace of \(S\) (the mean curvature, up to normalization) is zero. \(\square\)

4. Proof of Theorem 7.2 (Milnor pp. 40–41)

Proof of Theorem 7.2. Regard \(M\) as a \(2k\)-dimensional submanifold of \(\mathbb{R}^{2n}\). By Theorem 6.6 choose \(p \in \mathbb{C}^n\) such that \(L_p : M \to \mathbb{R}\) has no degenerate critical points. Each set \(M^a = L_p^{-1}[0, a]\) is the intersection of the closed set \(M\) with the closed ball of radius \(\sqrt a\) about \(p\), hence compact.

Let \(q\) be a critical point, of index \(\lambda\). If \(q = p\) then \(q\) is the absolute minimum and \(\lambda = 0\). Otherwise, by (a), \(p = q + tv\) with \(v\) a unit normal at \(q\) and \(t = \|p - q\| > 0\). By Lemma 6.9, \(\lambda\) is the number of focal points \(q + sv\) with \(0 < s < t\), counted with multiplicity. (Neither end of the segment is focal: \(s = 0\) would make \(G\) singular, and \(p\) is not focal by Lemma 6.5, because \(q\) is nondegenerate.) By Lemma 6.3 these are the points \(q + K_i^{-1}v\) with \(K_i > 1/t\), so \(\lambda \le \#\{i : K_i > 0\} \le k\) by Corollary 3.2. Milnor’s version: at most \(2k\) focal points on the whole normal line, symmetric about \(q\) (Assertion 2), hence at most \(k\) between \(q\) and \(p\).

By Theorem 3.5, \(M\) has the homotopy type of a CW-complex with one cell of dimension \(\lambda\) for each critical point of index \(\lambda\), and every \(\lambda\) is at most \(k\). \(\square\)

(If \(k = n\), then \(M\) is open and closed in \(\mathbb{C}^n\), so it is empty or all of \(\mathbb{C}^n\), and the statement is trivial; Chapter 4 assumes \(\dim M < N\) but nothing above uses it.)

A shorter route to the index bound. Steps 1 and 2 give the bound directly, without focal points. Let \(q\) be a critical point and \(\nu = p - q\). By formula (1.1) the Hessian of \(L_p\) at \(q\) is \(H(X, X) = 2\big(G(X,X) - \mathrm{II}_\nu(X, X)\big)\) with \(\mathrm{II}_\nu(X,X) = \sum_{i,j} X^iX^j\, \nu\cdot\partial^2 w/\partial u^i\partial u^j\). Steps 1 and 2 (with \(v = \nu/\|\nu\|\); if \(\nu = 0\), \(\mathrm{II}_\nu = 0\)) say \(G(JX,JX) = G(X,X)\) and \(\mathrm{II}_\nu(JX,JX) = -\mathrm{II}_\nu(X,X)\). Hence \[H(JX, JX) = 4\,G(X, X) - H(X, X).\] If \(H\) is negative definite on a subspace \(W\), it is positive definite on \(JW\); so \(W \cap JW = 0\) and \(2\dim W \le 2k\). This bounds the index by \(k\) at every critical point, degenerate or not, and uses neither Lemma 6.3 nor Lemma 6.9; it is the Andreotti–Frankel mechanism without focal points. It also shows that \(H\) is not negative semidefinite on any nonzero \(J\)-invariant subspace, in particular on \(TM_q\): if \(X \ne 0\) and \(H(X,X) \le 0\) then \(H(JX, JX) \ge 4G(X,X) > 0\). So \(L_p\) has no local maximum on a complex submanifold of positive dimension. For a formalization this is the route to take.

An interactive look at the index bound

The simplest curved complex curve is \(M = \{(z, w) \in \mathbb{C}^2 : w = z^2/2\}\), parametrized by \(z = x + iy\). At \(q = 0\) its tangent plane is the \(z\)-axis, and its normal plane is the \(w\)-axis, a copy of \(\mathbb{C}\). For an observer at \(p = (0, P)\) in the normal plane, \[L_p(z) = |z|^2 + \big|z^2/2 - P\big|^2 = |P|^2 + |z|^2 - \operatorname{Re}(\bar P z^2) + \tfrac14|z|^4 .\] The Hessian at \(q\) has eigenvalues \(2(1 - |P|)\) and \(2(1 + |P|)\): the term \(|z|^2\) is \(g_{ij} = \delta_{ij}\), and the term \(-\operatorname{Re}(\bar P z^2)\) is \(-t\,v\cdot\ell_{ij}\), whose eigenvalues \(\pm|P|\) are the pair of Assertion 1. The focal points of \((M, q)\) form the circle \(|P| = 1\) in the normal plane, one symmetric pair on each normal line. Inside the circle \(q\) is the minimum of \(L_p\); outside it \(q\) is a saddle, and two minima appear at \(z = \pm\sqrt{2(|P| - 1)}\, e^{i\arg(P)/2}\) (solve \(\partial L_p/\partial\bar z = z + \bar z\,(z^2/2 - P) = 0\)).

The figure shows the normal plane on the left, with the focal circle; drag the observer \(p\). On the right is a contour map of \(L_p\) over the \(z\)-plane, with the critical points marked and their indices listed. The button switches to the real paraboloid \(h = (x^2 + y^2)/2\) in \(\mathbb{R}^3\), whose normal line at \(0\) has a single double focal point at height \(1\). For an observer at height \(P\), \(L_p = P^2 + (1 - P)r^2 + r^4/4\); both Hessian eigenvalues are \(2(1 - P)\), and for \(P > 1\) the origin is a local maximum (index \(2\)), surrounded by a ring of minima. The complex curve never does this: however far you drag \(p\), the index at \(q\) stays at most \(1\).

5. Hyperplane sections: Corollary 7.3 and Theorem 7.4 (Milnor pp. 41–42)

A projective algebraic variety \(V \subset \mathbb{C}P_n\) is the common zero set of finitely many homogeneous polynomials; it is closed in \(\mathbb{C}P_n\), hence compact. A point of \(V\) is non-singular if \(V\) is a complex submanifold of \(\mathbb{C}P_n\) near it, and the singular points are the others. Let \(P\) be a hyperplane. After a linear change of homogeneous coordinates \(P = \{Z_0 = 0\}\), and \([Z_0 : \dots : Z_n] \mapsto (Z_1/Z_0, \dots, Z_n/Z_0)\) is a biholomorphism of \(\mathbb{C}P_n - P\) onto \(\mathbb{C}^n\), Milnor’s “affine space \(\mathbb{C}P_n - P\)”. It carries \(V - P\) onto the zero set of the dehomogenized polynomials, a closed subset of \(\mathbb{C}^n\), which is a complex submanifold when all singular points of \(V\) lie in \(P\). Write \(A = V \cap P\).

A hidden hypothesis. “An algebraic variety of complex dimension \(k\)” must be read as of pure dimension \(k\): every irreducible component has dimension \(k\). Otherwise \(V - P\) may have components of smaller dimension, which are invisible to the dimension count, and both results fail. Example: in \(\mathbb{C}P_4\) let \(V = \Pi \cup L\), where \(\Pi\) is a hyperplane (\(\cong\mathbb{C}P_3\)) and \(L\) a line meeting \(\Pi\) in one point \(s\); \(\dim V = 3\) and the only singular point is \(s\). For a hyperplane \(P \ne \Pi\) through \(s\) not containing \(L\), \(V \cap P = \Pi \cap P \cong \mathbb{C}P_2\), and \(H_2(V\cap P) = \mathbb{Z} \to H_2(V) = \mathbb{Z}^2\) is not onto, contrary to Corollary 7.3 with \(k = 3\). Under pure dimensionality, \(V - P\) is a closed complex submanifold of \(\mathbb{C}^n\) of pure complex dimension \(k\), in particular an oriented \(2k\)-manifold.

Corollary 7.3 (Lefschetz). (checked by machine: V5.18, in a narrower form) Let \(V \subset \mathbb{C}P_n\) be an algebraic variety of pure complex dimension \(k\), and \(P\) a hyperplane containing the singular points of \(V\). Then the inclusion \(V \cap P \to V\) induces isomorphisms \(H_r(V\cap P;\mathbb{Z}) \to H_r(V;\mathbb{Z})\) for \(r < k - 1\), and a surjection for \(r = k - 1\).

Proof (Milnor’s). In the exact sequence of the pair, \[H_{r+1}(V, A) \to H_r(A) \to H_r(V) \to H_r(V, A),\] if \(H_s(V, A) = 0\) for all \(s \le k - 1\) then \(H_r(A) \to H_r(V)\) is injective for \(r + 1 \le k - 1\) and surjective for \(r \le k - 1\). So it suffices to show \(H_r(V, A;\mathbb{Z}) = 0\) for \(r \le k - 1\). By Lefschetz duality (stated below), \[H_r(V, A;\mathbb{Z}) \cong H^{2k - r}(V - A;\mathbb{Z}).\] Now \(V - A\) is a closed complex submanifold of \(\mathbb{C}P_n - P \cong \mathbb{C}^n\) of complex dimension \(k\), so by Theorem 7.2 it has the homotopy type of a CW-complex of dimension at most \(k\), and its cohomology vanishes in degrees above \(k\). Since \(2k - r > k\) exactly when \(r < k\), the group vanishes for \(r \le k - 1\). \(\square\)

The duality theorem, stated. Milnor does not say which form of Lefschetz duality he uses. The form that applies is: if \(X\) is compact, \(A \subset X\) is closed, \(X - A\) is an oriented \(m\)-manifold, and the pair \((X, A)\) is triangulable, then \(H_r(X, A;\mathbb{Z}) \cong H^{m-r}(X - A;\mathbb{Z})\) for all \(r\) (see Spanier, Algebraic Topology, Ch. 6; for compact manifolds with boundary, Hatcher, Algebraic Topology, Theorem 3.43). Some niceness of \(A\) is needed; for \((V, V\cap P)\) it comes from the triangulation theorem quoted below, the same input as for Theorem 7.4. The proof of Corollary 7.3 given after Theorem 7.4 avoids duality altogether.

Theorem 7.4 (Lefschetz). (checked by machine: V5.19, restated) Under the hypotheses of Corollary 7.3, the relative homotopy group \(\pi_r(V, V\cap P)\) is zero for \(r < k\), for every base point in \(V \cap P\). (For \(r = 0\) this means that every point of \(V\) can be joined to \(V\cap P\) by a path.)

Milnor bases the proof on the following hypothesis, which he says can be proved using “the theorem that algebraic varieties can be triangulated”.

Hypothesis (N). There are a neighbourhood \(U\) of \(A\) in \(V\) and a homotopy \(H : U \times [0,1] \to V\) with \(H_0\) the inclusion, \(H_1(U) \subset A\), and \(H_t(a) = a\) for all \(a \in A\) and all \(t\).

It holds: there is a triangulation of \(V\) in which \(V\cap P\) is a subcomplex (Łojasiewicz, Triangulation of semi-analytic sets, 1964), and a subcomplex of a CW-complex is a deformation retract, keeping it pointwise fixed, of some open neighbourhood (Hatcher, Proposition A.5). We quote both facts.

A hidden hypothesis. Milnor asks only that \(U\) “can be deformed into \(V\cap P\) within \(V\)”. The deformation must keep \(V \cap P\) fixed: it is composed with maps of pairs \((I^r, \partial I^r) \to (U, V\cap P)\), which must remain maps of pairs with a fixed base point.

Step 1: the function. By Theorem 6.6 choose \(p \in \mathbb{C}^n = \mathbb{C}P_n - P\) such that \(L_p\) has no degenerate critical points on \(V - P\). Define \(f : V \to [0, 1]\) by \[f(x) = 0 \ \ (x \in A), \qquad f(x) = \frac{1}{1 + L_p(x)} \ \ (x \in V - P).\] (Milnor uses \(1/L_p\), which is infinite at \(p\) if \(p \in V\); the extra \(1\) changes nothing else.) Then:

  1. \(f\) is continuous, and \(f^{-1}(0) = A\). On \(V - P\) it is smooth. At points of \(A\): the function \(\rho([Z]) = |Z_0|^2/\sum_\alpha |Z_\alpha|^2\) is well defined and continuous on \(\mathbb{C}P_n\), vanishes exactly on \(P\), and the affine coordinates of a point of \(\mathbb{C}P_n - P\) satisfy \(\|x\|^2 = (1 - \rho)/\rho\). So as \(x \to A\) within \(V - P\), \(\|x\| \to \infty\), hence \(L_p(x) \ge (\|x\| - \|p\|)^2 \to \infty\) and \(f(x) \to 0\).

  2. For \(0 < \varepsilon \le 1\), the set \(f^{-1}[\varepsilon, 1] = \{x \in V - P : L_p(x) \le 1/\varepsilon - 1\}\) is a closed bounded subset of \(\mathbb{C}^n\), hence compact. Nondegenerate critical points are isolated, so \(f\) has only finitely many critical points in \(f^{-1}[\varepsilon, 1]\), and its critical values in \((0, 1]\) can accumulate only at \(0\).

  3. The critical points of \(f\) are those of \(L_p\) on \(V - P\), since \(df = -dL_p/(1 + L_p)^2\). At such a point the Hessian is \(-\operatorname{Hess}L_p/(1 + L_p)^2\), so a critical point where \(L_p\) has index \(\lambda\) is a nondegenerate critical point of \(f\) of index \(2k - \lambda\). Here pure dimensionality enters: the real dimension of \(V - P\) at the point is \(2k\). By Theorem 7.2’s index bound, \(\lambda \le k\), so every critical point of \(f\) has index \(\ge 2k - k = k\).

Step 2: Morse theory away from \(A\). For \(a > 0\) put \(V^a = f^{-1}[0, a]\); these contain \(A\), and \(V^a = V\) for \(a \ge 1\).

Lemma 5.1. (i) If \(0 < a < b\) and \([a, b]\) contains no critical value of \(f\), then \(V^a\) is a deformation retract of \(V^b\) by a deformation that keeps \(V^a\) pointwise fixed. (ii) If \(c > 0\) is a critical value and \(q_1, \dots, q_j\) are the critical points on the level \(c\), of indices \(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_j\), then for all small \(\delta > 0\) there are cells \(e^{\lambda_1}, \dots, e^{\lambda_j} \subset V\), attached to \(V^{c-\delta}\) along their boundary spheres, such that \(V^{c-\delta} \cup e^{\lambda_1} \cup \dots \cup e^{\lambda_j}\) is a deformation retract of \(V^{c+\delta}\) keeping it pointwise fixed.

Proof. \(V\) is not a manifold, but Milnor’s proofs of Theorem 3.1, Theorem 3.2 (its Assertions 3 and 4) and Remark 3.3 never leave the compact set \(f^{-1}[a, b]\), respectively \(f^{-1}[c - \delta, c + \delta]\), and small neighbourhoods of it, all inside the manifold \(V - A\). They use a Riemannian metric on \(V - A\), the vector field \(\rho\cdot\operatorname{grad} f\) with \(\rho\) supported in a compact neighbourhood \(K\) of that set inside \(V - A\), Morse charts at the \(q_i\), and a modification \(F\) of \(f\) near the \(q_i\). The flow of a compactly supported field is complete and is the identity outside \(K\); extended by the identity on \(V - K\), an open neighbourhood of \(A\), it is continuous on \(V\). The deformation retractions Milnor builds from it fix the smaller set pointwise. \(\square\)

Step 3: pushing maps off high cells.

Lemma 5.2. Let \(Y = X \cup e^{\lambda_1} \cup \dots \cup e^{\lambda_j}\) be a space obtained by attaching cells, and \(g : I^r \to Y\) continuous with \(r < \min_i \lambda_i\). Then \(g\) is homotopic, relative to \(g^{-1}(X)\), to a map into \(X\).

This is the lemma behind the cellular approximation theorem. By Hatcher’s Lemma 4.10, applied with \(W = X \cup e^{\lambda_2} \cup \dots \cup e^{\lambda_j}\), \(g\) is homotopic relative to \(g^{-1}(W)\) to a map that is piecewise linear over a small simplex in the open cell \(e^{\lambda_1}\); since there is no linear surjection \(\mathbb{R}^r \to \mathbb{R}^{\lambda_1}\) for \(r < \lambda_1\), the new map misses a point \(y_1\) of that cell. The radial deformation retraction of \(Y - \{y_1\}\) onto \(W\), which fixes \(W\) pointwise, then pushes the map into \(W\). Repeat for the other cells. In our situation the cells of Lemma 5.1 are subsets of the compact Hausdorff space \(V\), and \(V^{c-\delta} \cup e^{\lambda_1} \cup \dots\) carries the topology of the abstract attaching space (a continuous bijection from a compact space onto a Hausdorff space is a homeomorphism), so the lemma applies.

Step 4: proof of Theorem 7.4. Let \(r < k\), \(x_0 \in A\), and \(g : (I^r, \partial I^r, J^{r-1}) \to (V, A, x_0)\) represent an element of \(\pi_r(V, A, x_0)\). By (ii) of Step 1 and Hypothesis (N) choose a regular value \(\varepsilon > 0\) of \(f\) with \(V^\varepsilon \subset U\): the sets \(V^\varepsilon - U\) are compact, decrease as \(\varepsilon \downarrow 0\), and have empty intersection (because \(\bigcap_\varepsilon V^\varepsilon = A \subset U\)), so one of them is empty. List the finitely many critical values of \(f\) in \([\varepsilon, 1]\) as \(c_1 < \dots < c_m\) (the value \(1\) is critical if \(p \in V\)) and choose regular values \(\varepsilon = a_0 < c_1 < a_1 < \dots < c_m < a_m = 2\), so that \(V^{a_m} = V\).

Suppose \(g\) maps into \(V^{a_i}\) (true for \(i = m\)). By Lemma 5.1(i) on \([c_i + \delta, a_i]\), deform \(g\) into \(V^{c_i + \delta}\); by Lemma 5.1(ii), into \(V^{c_i - \delta} \cup e^{\lambda_1} \cup \dots\) with all \(\lambda\)’s \(\ge k > r\) (Step 1(iii)); by Lemma 5.2, into \(V^{c_i - \delta}\); by Lemma 5.1(i) on \([a_{i-1}, c_i - \delta]\), into \(V^{a_{i-1}}\). Each deformation fixes \(A \supset g(\partial I^r)\) pointwise, so all homotopies are relative to \(\partial I^r\). After \(m\) rounds, \(g\) is homotopic relative to \(\partial I^r\) to a map \(g'\) into \(V^\varepsilon \subset U\). Then \(H_t \circ g'\) is a homotopy relative to \(\partial I^r\) (since \(H\) fixes \(A\)) from \(g'\) to a map into \(A\). By the compression criterion (Hatcher, §4.1: a map of triples \((I^r, \partial I^r, J^{r-1}) \to (V, A, x_0)\) represents \(0\) if it is homotopic relative to \(\partial I^r\) to a map into \(A\)), \([g] = 0\). For \(r = 0\) the same deformations join any point of \(V\) to \(A\) by a path. \(\square\)

A proof of Corollary 7.3 without duality. The same ingredients give the homology statement directly. (1) The map \(H_r(V^\varepsilon, A) \to H_r(V, A)\) induced by inclusion is zero: the inclusion of pairs \((V^\varepsilon, A) \to (V, A)\) is homotopic through maps of pairs (by \(H_t|_{V^\varepsilon}\), which maps \(A\) into \(A\)) to \(H_1|_{V^\varepsilon}\), which factors through the pair \((A, A)\), and \(H_r(A, A) = 0\). (2) \(H_r(V, V^\varepsilon) = 0\) for \(r < k\): by Lemma 5.1 and the five lemma, \(H_r(V^{a_i}, V^{a_{i-1}}) \cong H_r(V^{c_i-\delta} \cup e^{\lambda_1} \cup \dots, V^{c_i - \delta}) \cong \bigoplus_l \tilde H_r(S^{\lambda_l})\) (Hatcher, Proposition 2.22, for the good pair of a space with cells attached), which vanishes for \(r < k\); the exact sequences of the triples \((V^{a_i}, V^{a_{i-1}}, V^\varepsilon)\) and induction on \(i\) give the claim. (3) In the exact sequence of the triple \((V, V^\varepsilon, A)\), \[H_r(V^\varepsilon, A) \xrightarrow{\;0\;} H_r(V, A) \to H_r(V, V^\varepsilon) = 0 \qquad (r < k),\] so \(H_r(V, A) = 0\) for \(r \le k - 1\), and the exact sequence of the pair finishes the proof as before. \(\square\)

Example 5.3 (hypersurfaces are simply connected). Let \(X = \{F = 0\} \subset \mathbb{C}P_n\), \(n \ge 2\), be a hypersurface, \(F\) homogeneous of degree \(d \ge 1\), singular or not. Then \(\pi_r(X) \to \pi_r(\mathbb{C}P_n)\) is an isomorphism for \(r < n - 1\) and onto for \(r = n - 1\); in particular a hypersurface in \(\mathbb{C}P_n\), \(n \ge 3\), is simply connected (for instance every smooth surface in \(\mathbb{C}P_3\)). Proof. The Veronese map \(\nu_d : \mathbb{C}P_n \to \mathbb{C}P_N\), \([Z] \mapsto [Z^m]_{|m| = d}\), \(N = \binom{n+d}{d} - 1\), is a holomorphic embedding whose image \(W\) is a non-singular projective variety of dimension \(n\) (cut out by the quadrics \(Y_mY_{m'} = Y_{m''}Y_{m'''}\) for \(m + m' = m'' + m'''\)). Writing \(F = \sum c_m Z^m\), the hyperplane \(P_F = \{\sum c_m Y_m = 0\}\) satisfies \(W \cap P_F = \nu_d(X)\), and it contains all singular points of \(W\) (there are none). Theorem 7.4 with \(k = n\) gives \(\pi_r(W, W\cap P_F) = 0\) for \(r < n\), and the exact homotopy sequence of the pair gives the claim. \(\square\)

6. Application: soap films, and the four loops of a complex cubic

Soap films lie in the convex hull of their wire. Let \(\Sigma \subset \mathbb{R}^3\) be a compact smooth surface with boundary curve \(\Gamma\), with mean curvature zero at its interior points, as a soap film has. Fix \(p \in \mathbb{R}^3\) and let \(q\) be a point of \(\Sigma\) where \(L_p\) is largest. If \(q\) were an interior point, \(L_p\) would have a local maximum there, so its Hessian would be negative semidefinite. But \(q \neq p\) (otherwise \(\max L_p = 0\) and \(\Sigma\) is a point), so \(p = q + t\nu\) with \(\nu\) a unit normal, and in principal directions the Hessian (1.1) is \(\operatorname{diag}\big(2(1 - t\kappa), 2(1 + t\kappa)\big)\), of trace \(4 > 0\): a contradiction. So \(\max_\Sigma L_p = \max_\Gamma L_p\), and \(\Sigma\) lies in every closed ball containing \(\Gamma\). The intersection of all closed balls containing the compact set \(\Gamma\) is its closed convex hull: if \(x\) lies outside the hull, a plane separates \(x\) from \(\Gamma\), and a ball of very large radius whose boundary sphere nearly coincides with that plane contains \(\Gamma\) but not \(x\). So \(\Sigma\) lies in the convex hull of \(\Gamma\).

A concrete case: the film spanning two coaxial rings of radius \(1\) at heights \(\pm 0.5\) is the catenoid \(r = a\cosh(h/a)\) with \(a = 0.848\), the stable root of \(a\cosh(0.5/a) = 1\). At the waist its principal curvatures are \(\pm 1/a = \pm 1.18\), and the focal points on the normal line through a waist point sit at distance \(a\) on either side: one is the centre of the waist circle. Seen from that centre the film is nearest along the whole waist circle (distance \(0.848\), a degenerate minimum, as Lemma 6.5 predicts for a focal point) and farthest on the rings (\(\sqrt{1.25} = 1.118\)).

Complex manifolds are soap films. By Corollary 3.2 a complex submanifold of \(\mathbb{C}^n\) has zero mean curvature, and by the remark in §4 the Hessian of \(L_p\) is never negative semidefinite on it. The argument above therefore shows that a compact complex submanifold with boundary lies in the convex hull of its boundary, and that a compact complex submanifold of \(\mathbb{C}^n\) without boundary has dimension \(0\), so it is a finite set: on a component of positive dimension \(L_p\) would attain a maximum.

The complex cubic \(C = \{(z, w) \in \mathbb{C}^2 : z^3 + w^3 = 1\}\). It is closed, and it is a complex submanifold because the gradient \((3z^2, 3w^2)\) vanishes only at \(z = w = 0\), which is not on \(C\). By Theorem 7.2 it has the homotopy type of a graph, and by Theorem 7.1 \(H_2(C) = 0\): although \(C\) is a surface, it carries no \(2\)-cycle. To see the graph, we located all critical points of \(L_p\) on \(C\) for \(p = (0.3 + 0.2i,\ -0.1 + 0.4i)\), solving numerically the four real equations \[z^3 + w^3 = 1, \qquad (z - 0.3 - 0.2i)\,\bar w^2 = (w + 0.1 - 0.4i)\,\bar z^2\] (the second says that \(p - (z, w)\) is Hermitian-orthogonal to the tangent vector \((w^2, -z^2)\), which by (a) and Lemma 3.1 is the critical point condition), with a Newton-type solver started from 20,000 random points of \(C\) with \(|z| \le 6\). Exactly five solutions appear. Writing \(C\) near a solution as a graph \(w = w(z)\), the quadratic part of \(L_p\) is \(\alpha|\zeta|^2 + \operatorname{Re}(\beta\zeta^2)\), with \(\alpha = 1 + |w'|^2\) and \(\beta = \overline{(w - b)}\,w''\) (\(b\) the second coordinate of \(p\)), whose eigenvalues are \(\alpha \pm |\beta|\): the Lefschetz mechanism in one line, since \(\alpha > 0\). The results, confirmed by finite-difference Hessians:

critical point \((z, w)\) \(L_p\) index
\((0.386 + 0.142i,\ -0.477 + 0.867i)\) \(0.370\) \(0\)
\((-0.250 + 0.711i,\ 0.872 + 0.100i)\) \(1.598\) \(1\)
\((-0.303 + 0.613i,\ -0.419 - 0.778i)\) \(2.023\) \(1\)
\((-0.456 - 0.713i,\ 0.740 + 0.050i)\) \(2.233\) \(1\)
\((-0.349 - 0.722i,\ -0.449 - 0.660i)\) \(2.517\) \(1\)

By Theorem 3.5, \(C\) has the homotopy type of one \(0\)-cell with four \(1\)-cells attached: a wedge of four circles. So \(C\) is connected, \(H_1(C;\mathbb{Z}) = \mathbb{Z}^4\), and \(H_i(C) = 0\) for \(i \ge 2\). A cross-check from outside this book: the closure of \(C\) in \(\mathbb{C}P_2\) is a smooth cubic, which is a torus (genus formula for plane curves), with Euler number \(0\) (proved in Chapter 6 of the companion volume, Topology from the Differentiable Viewpoint, rewritten); it meets the line at infinity in the three points \(Z^3 + W^3 = 0\), and removing them gives \(\chi(C) = -3 = 1 - 4\). The same search for \(z^2 + w^2 = 1\) gives one minimum and one saddle (\(C \simeq S^1\), indeed \(C \cong \mathbb{C}^*\) via \(z + iw\)), and for \(z^4 + w^4 = 1\) six minima and fourteen saddles: a graph with Euler characteristic \(-8\), which, being connected (the curve is irreducible), is a wedge of nine circles. In general \(z^d + w^d = 1\) is a wedge of \((d - 1)^2\) circles, by the same Euler characteristic count. In every case the search found no critical point of index \(2\), as Theorem 7.2 demands.

7. Summary of what was silently assumed, now made explicit

Where Milnor says What is actually needed
p. 39 “has the homotopy type of a \(k\)-dimensional CW-complex” of dimension at most \(k\) (Theorem 7.2)
p. 39 7.1 is “a consequence of” 7.2 “non-singular” means a closed complex submanifold; homotopy invariance of homology and \(H_i = 0\) above the dimension of a CW-complex
p. 39 Assertion 1 “clearly follows” \(J^{\mathsf T}AJ = -A\), so \(J\) maps the \(e\)-eigenspace onto the \((-e)\)-eigenspace (§2)
p. 40 “The linear terms vanish since \(v\) is orthogonal to \(M\)” real orthogonality to a complex subspace implies Hermitian orthogonality (Lemma 3.1)
p. 40 “Clearly the quadratic terms \(Q'\) determine the second fundamental form” the Hessian of \(w\cdot v\) at \(q\) is \((v\cdot\ell_{ij}) = 2A\) (Step 2)
p. 40 eigenvalues of \(Q'\) in opposite pairs, “hence” focal points in symmetric pairs focal points are eigenvalues relative to \((g_{ij})\); need orthonormal coordinates at \(q\) or the \(J\)-invariance of \((g_{ij})\) (Steps 1, 3, Assertion 1a)
p. 41 “at most \(2k\) focal points”, so “at most \(k\) of them can lie between \(p\) and \(q\)” Lemma 6.3 with \(\dim_{\mathbb{R}} M = 2k\); \(p\) not focal (Lemma 6.5); the case \(p = q\)
p. 41 Corollary 7.3, Theorem 7.4 for “an algebraic variety of complex dimension \(k\)” \(V\) of pure dimension \(k\); counterexample \(\Pi \cup L\) otherwise (§5)
p. 41 “the Lefschetz duality theorem asserts” a form for compact pairs with \(X - A\) an oriented manifold and \((X, A)\) triangulable; or avoid it (proof after Theorem 7.4)
p. 42 “\(U\) can be deformed into \(V\cap P\) within \(V\)” the deformation must fix \(V \cap P\) (Hypothesis (N)); triangulation of the pair and regular neighbourhoods
p. 42 \(f = 1/L_p\) infinite at \(p\) if \(p \in V\), use \(1/(1 + L_p)\); continuity at \(V \cap P\); Hessian \(= -\operatorname{Hess}L_p/(1+L_p)^2\) at critical points (Step 1)
p. 42 “\(V\) has the homotopy type of \(V^\varepsilon\) with finitely many cells … attached” Theorems 3.1, 3.2, Remark 3.3 on \(V - P\), where \(f\) is smooth; compactness of \(f^{-1}[\varepsilon, 1]\); \(\varepsilon\) a regular value (Lemma 5.1)
p. 42 “Choose \(\varepsilon\) small enough so that \(V^\varepsilon \subset U\)” decreasing compact sets with intersection \(V \cap P\) (Step 4)
p. 42 “since \(r < k\), … can be deformed into …” cellular approximation: push maps of \(r\)-cubes off cells of dimension \(> r\), relative to \(\partial I^r\) (Lemma 5.2); compression criterion

Checked by machine. Milnor’s §7 has been verified in the Lean proof assistant, for submanifolds of \(\mathbb C^n = \mathbb R^{2n}\) whose tangent spaces are complex subspaces. The algebra: Assertions 1 and 1a, Lemma 3.1, and the content of Assertion 2 in holomorphic coordinates, that the Hessians of \(L_{q+tv}\) and \(L_{q-tv}\) at \(q\) have the same nullity. The index bound, by the shorter route at the end of §4 and not through focal points: at every critical point of \(L_p\) on such a submanifold of complex dimension \(k\), degenerate or not, the index is at most \(k\). Theorem 7.2, for such a submanifold closed in \(\mathbb C^n\), as a countable cell complex all of whose cells have dimension at most \(k\); and Theorem 7.1 over every field. Under the hypothesis that a neighbourhood of \(V \cap P\) can be deformed into \(V \cap P\) keeping it fixed: Corollary 7.3 over every field, by the route of §5 without Lefschetz duality, and Theorem 7.4, for a closed \(V \subseteq \mathbb CP_n\) whose affine part is a complex submanifold of complex dimension \(k\), and for the hyperplane \(z_0 = 0\). Not checked: integral coefficients; that algebraic varieties satisfy these hypotheses, and the deformation hypothesis itself; Corollary 3.2 and Milnor’s route through Lemmas 6.3 and 6.9; Lemmas 5.1 and 5.2 as stated (the pushing lemma of Chapter 13 plays their role); Example 5.3; and the application. See the verified edition.

Chapter 6. Covariant derivatives and curvature: why Foucault’s pendulum turns

Milnor, “Morse Theory”, §8–§9, rewritten for a first-year graduate student who wants to know what the theorem is for. Every proof is complete, except that the smooth dependence of solutions of linear differential equations on parameters is quoted.

0. Why does Foucault’s pendulum turn?

In 1851 Léon Foucault hung a 28 kg bob on a 67 m wire from the dome of the Panthéon in Paris and set it swinging. The plane of the swing did not stay put relative to the building: seen from above, it turned clockwise by about \(11^\circ\) every hour. Foucault’s sine law says that at latitude \(\varphi\) the plane turns by \(360^\circ \sin\varphi\) per sidereal day (23.93 hours): once a day at the North Pole, not at all at the equator, and in Paris (\(\sin 48.85^\circ = 0.753\)) by \(271^\circ\) a day, \(11.3^\circ\) an hour, one full turn in \(31.8\) hours. Why the sine?

Here is the geometric answer, which this chapter makes precise. During one sidereal day the suspension point is carried once around its circle of latitude. Nothing pushes the swing sideways, so the pendulum carries its direction of swing along that circle without turning it. On a flat table, a direction carried around a closed loop without turning comes back to itself. On a sphere it does not: it comes back turned, and the angle is the curvature of the sphere integrated over the enclosed cap. For the cap above latitude \(\varphi\) on the unit sphere the area is \(2\pi(1 - \sin\varphi)\), and a turn by that angle is the same as a turn by \(-2\pi\sin\varphi\).

To make “carry a vector along a curve without turning it” mean something on a curved manifold, Milnor introduces affine connections, covariant derivatives along curves and parallel transport (§§1–2 below). On a Riemannian manifold there is exactly one connection that is compatible with the metric and symmetric, the Levi-Civita connection (§§3–4). The curvature tensor measures the failure of covariant derivatives to commute, equivalently the failure of parallel transport to be independent of the path (§§5–6), and it has four symmetries (§7). These tools are used in every later chapter: the second variation of energy, Jacobi fields and conjugate points are all written in terms of \(D/dt\) and \(R\). In §8 we solve the parallel-transport equation on the sphere explicitly and obtain Foucault’s sine law.

Throughout, \(M\) is a smooth manifold of dimension \(n\), \(C^\infty(M)\) its smooth functions and \(\mathfrak X(M)\) its smooth vector fields. A tangent vector \(X_p\) acts on functions by the directional derivative \(X_p f\), and \([X, Y]f = X(Yf) - Y(Xf)\). We keep Milnor’s notation \(X \vdash Y\) for what is now written \(\nabla_X Y\). We use bump functions: for every open \(U \ni p\) there is \(\psi \in C^\infty(M)\) with values in \([0,1]\), support a compact subset of \(U\), and \(\psi = 1\) on a neighbourhood of \(p\). (In a chart it is \(\theta(\|u - u(p)\|^2)\) for a smooth \(\theta\) built from \(\lambda(\tau) = e^{-1/\tau}\), as in Chapter 4, §1 and §3 of the companion volume, Topology from the Differentiable Viewpoint, rewritten.) With them, every tangent vector extends to a vector field, and every function or vector field defined near \(p\) agrees near \(p\) with a globally defined one.

1. Affine connections (Milnor pp. 43–45)

Definition. An affine connection at \(p\) assigns to each \(X_p \in TM_p\) and each vector field \(Y\) a vector \(X_p \vdash Y \in TM_p\), the covariant derivative of \(Y\) in the direction \(X_p\), which is bilinear in \((X_p, Y)\) and satisfies \[X_p \vdash (fY) = (X_p f)\,Y_p + f(p)\,X_p \vdash Y \qquad (f \in C^\infty(M)).\]

Definition. A global affine connection, or connection, assigns to each \(p\) an affine connection \(\vdash_p\) at \(p\) such that (1) for smooth \(X, Y\) the vector field \(X \vdash Y\), defined by \((X\vdash Y)_p = X_p \vdash_p Y\), is smooth. It then satisfies (2) \(X \vdash Y\) is bilinear in \(X\) and \(Y\); (3) \((fX)\vdash Y = f\,(X\vdash Y)\); (4) \(X \vdash (fY) = (Xf)\,Y + f\,(X\vdash Y)\).

Lemma 1.1 (locality). If \(Y = Y'\) on a neighbourhood of \(p\), then \(X_p\vdash Y = X_p\vdash Y'\).

Proof. \(Z = Y - Y'\) vanishes on a neighbourhood \(W\) of \(p\). Take \(\psi \in C^\infty(M)\) with \(\psi = 0\) near \(p\) and \(\psi = 1\) outside \(W\) (\(1\) minus a bump function supported in \(W\)). Then \(\psi Z = Z\), so \(X_p\vdash Z = (X_p\psi)Z_p + \psi(p)\,X_p\vdash Z = 0\), as \(Z_p = 0\) and \(\psi(p) = 0\). \(\square\)

So \(X_p \vdash Y\) makes sense for a field \(Y\) defined only near \(p\) (extend it by a bump function; the result does not depend on the extension), and a connection restricts to a connection on every open subset. Milnor uses this silently when he writes \(\partial_i \vdash \partial_j\) for coordinate fields, which exist only on a chart.

Lemma 1.2 (tensoriality). Let \(A\) be a map from \(\mathfrak X(M)^r\) to \(\mathfrak X(M)\) or to \(C^\infty(M)\) that is \(\mathbb{R}\)-multilinear and \(C^\infty(M)\)-linear in each variable. Then the value of \(A(X_1, \dots, X_r)\) at \(p\) depends only on \(X_1(p), \dots, X_r(p)\), so \(A\) is a multilinear map \(TM_p^r \to TM_p\) (or \(\to\mathbb{R}\)) at each point.

Proof. By multilinearity it suffices to show \(A(X_1, \dots)_p = 0\) when \(X_1(p) = 0\). Take a chart \((U; u^1, \dots, u^n)\) at \(p\), write \(X_1 = \sum_i x^i\partial_i\) on \(U\), and let \(\psi\) be a bump function supported in \(U\), equal to \(1\) near \(p\). Then \(\psi x^i\) and \(\psi\partial_i\), extended by zero, are global, and \(X_1 = \sum_i (\psi x^i)(\psi\partial_i) + (1 - \psi^2)X_1\). Hence \(A(X_1,\dots)_p = \sum_i x^i(p)\,A(\psi\partial_i, \dots)_p + (1 - \psi(p)^2)\,A(X_1, \dots)_p = 0\). \(\square\)

Proposition 1.3 (Milnor: conditions (1)–(4) “can be taken as the definition”). Every map \(\vdash : \mathfrak X(M)\times\mathfrak X(M)\to\mathfrak X(M)\) satisfying (2), (3), (4) comes from exactly one global affine connection.

Proof. By (2) and (3), \(X \mapsto X\vdash Y\) is \(C^\infty(M)\)-linear, so by the argument of Lemma 1.2 \((X\vdash Y)_p\) depends only on \(X_p\). Define \(X_p\vdash_p Y = (X\vdash Y)_p\) for any field \(X\) through \(X_p\). Bilinearity and the Leibniz rule at \(p\) follow from (2) and (4), and (1) holds by construction. Uniqueness is clear. \(\square\)

Christoffel symbols. On a chart \((U; u^1,\dots,u^n)\) with \(\partial_k = \partial/\partial u^k\), the restricted connection gives smooth functions \(\Gamma^k_{ij}\) on \(U\) (\(n^3\) of them) by \[\partial_i \vdash \partial_j = \sum_k \Gamma^k_{ij}\,\partial_k. \tag{5}\] For \(X = \sum_i x^i\partial_i\) and \(Y = \sum_j y^j\partial_j\), rules (2), (3), (4) give \(X\vdash Y = \sum_i x^i \sum_j \big((\partial_i y^j)\partial_j + y^j\,\partial_i\vdash\partial_j\big)\), that is \[X\vdash Y = \sum_k\Big(\sum_i x^i\,y^k_{\,,i}\Big)\partial_k, \qquad y^k_{\,,i} = \partial_i y^k + \sum_j \Gamma^k_{ij}\,y^j. \tag{6}\] Conversely, any smooth functions \(\Gamma^k_{ij}\) on \(U\) define by (6) a connection on \(U\) satisfying (1)–(5). Conditions (1), (2), (3) are evident; (5) is (6) with \(X = \partial_i\), \(Y = \partial_j\); and for (4), replacing \(y^k\) by \(fy^k\) turns \(y^k_{\,,i}\) into \((\partial_i f)y^k + f\,y^k_{\,,i}\), which gives \(X\vdash(fY) = (Xf)Y + f\,X\vdash Y\). Evaluated at \(p\), (6) shows that \(X_p\vdash Y\) depends only on \(X_p\), on \(Y_p\), and on the derivatives \(X_p y^k\) of the components of \(Y\) in the direction \(X_p\).

(Milnor does not claim that every manifold has a connection; that needs a partition of unity. For a Riemannian manifold, Lemma 8.6 provides one.)

2. Covariant derivatives along curves, and parallel transport (Milnor pp. 45–47)

Definitions. A parametrized curve is a smooth map \(c : I \to M\) from an open interval (Milnor takes \(I = \mathbb{R}\); everything below is local in \(t\), and curves on closed intervals are restrictions of curves on open ones). A vector field along \(c\) assigns to each \(t\) a vector \(V_t \in TM_{c(t)}\) such that \(t\mapsto V_t f\) is smooth for every \(f\in C^\infty(M)\). The velocity is \(dc/dt = c_*(d/dt)\), i.e. \((dc/dt)f = d(f\circ c)/dt\).

Lemma 2.1. In a chart, write \(u^i(t) = u^i(c(t))\) and \(V_t = \sum_j v^j(t)\,\partial_j\) for \(t \in c^{-1}(U)\). Then \(V\) is smooth if and only if every \(v^j\) is smooth, and \(dc/dt = \sum_i (du^i/dt)\,\partial_i\).

Proof. \(V_t f = \sum_j v^j(t)\,(\partial_j f)(c(t))\), which is smooth if the \(v^j\) are. Conversely, near \(t_0\) take \(f = \psi u^j\) with \(\psi\) a bump function equal to \(1\) near \(c(t_0)\); then \(V_t f = v^j(t)\) for \(t\) near \(t_0\). The formula for \(dc/dt\) is the chain rule. \(\square\)

Now let \(M\) carry a connection. Milnor characterizes the covariant derivative \(V\mapsto DV/dt\) of fields along \(c\) by three axioms:

  1. \(D(V + W)/dt = DV/dt + DW/dt\);

  2. \(D(fV)/dt = (df/dt)\,V + f\,DV/dt\) for every smooth \(f : I \to\mathbb{R}\);

  3. if \(V\) is induced by a vector field \(Y\) on \(M\), \(V_t = Y_{c(t)}\), then \(DV/dt = (dc/dt)\vdash Y\).

Lemma 8.1. (checked by machine: V6.6, in a narrower form)1 There is one and only one operation \(V\mapsto DV/dt\) satisfying a), b), c). In a chart it is \[\frac{DV}{dt} = \sum_k\Big(\frac{dv^k}{dt} + \sum_{i,j}\frac{du^i}{dt}\,\Gamma^k_{ij}(c(t))\, v^j\Big)\partial_k. \tag{2.1}\]

Proof. Uniqueness. Let \(D\) satisfy a), b), c). (i) Locality: if \(V = 0\) on an open interval \(J \ni t_0\), take \(f\) smooth on \(I\) with \(f = 0\) near \(t_0\) and \(f = 1\) outside \(J\). Then \(fV = V\), so by b) \(DV/dt(t_0) = f'(t_0)V_{t_0} + f(t_0)\,DV/dt(t_0) = 0\). (ii) The formula: given \(t_0\), choose a chart \(U\ni c(t_0)\), a bump function \(\psi\) supported in \(U\) with \(\psi = 1\) on a neighbourhood \(W\) of \(c(t_0)\), and an interval \(J\ni t_0\) with \(c(J)\subset W\). The fields \(E_j = \psi\partial_j\) are global and equal \(\partial_j\) on \(W\). Let \(\chi\) be smooth on \(I\), supported in \(J\), equal to \(1\) near \(t_0\). The field \(\tilde V = \sum_j(\chi v^j)\,E_j\circ c\) is smooth along all of \(c\) and equals \(V\) near \(t_0\). By (i), a), b), c) and Lemma 1.1, \[\frac{DV}{dt}(t_0) = \frac{D\tilde V}{dt}(t_0) = \sum_j\Big(\frac{dv^j}{dt}\,\partial_j + v^j\,\frac{dc}{dt}\vdash E_j\Big)(t_0) = \sum_j\Big(\frac{dv^j}{dt}\,\partial_j + v^j\sum_i\frac{du^i}{dt}\,\partial_i\vdash\partial_j\Big)(t_0),\] which is (2.1). So \(D\) is determined.

Existence. Define \(DV/dt\) by (2.1) on \(c^{-1}(U)\). It is smooth by Lemma 2.1, a) is clear, b) follows from \(d(fv^k)/dt = f'v^k + f\,dv^k/dt\), and c) holds because for \(v^j = y^j\circ c\) we have \(dv^k/dt = \sum_i (du^i/dt)(\partial_i y^k)(c(t))\), so (2.1) becomes (6) with \(x^i = du^i/dt\). Two charts give the same result on the overlap: on a subinterval mapped into both charts, the formula of each chart satisfies a), b), c), and the uniqueness argument, run in the other chart, shows that it equals the other formula. \(\square\)

A vector field \(V\) along \(c\) is parallel if \(DV/dt \equiv 0\). In a chart this is the linear system \(dv^k/dt = -\sum_{i,j}(du^i/dt)\,\Gamma^k_{ij}(c(t))\,v^j\). Milnor cites Graves for the following fact; here is the short proof.

Fact 2.2 (linear ODE). Let \(A : J\to\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) be continuous on an open interval \(J\), \(t_0\in J\), \(v_0\in\mathbb{R}^n\). There is exactly one \(C^1\) map \(v : J\to\mathbb{R}^n\) with \(v' = A(t)v\) and \(v(t_0) = v_0\), defined on all of \(J\). It depends linearly on \(v_0\), and it is smooth if \(A\) is.

Proof. On a compact interval \(K\ni t_0\) in \(J\) let \(C = \max_K\|A\|\). The Picard iterates \(v_0(t) = v_0\), \(v_{m+1}(t) = v_0 + \int_{t_0}^t A(s)v_m(s)\,ds\) satisfy \(|v_{m+1}(t) - v_m(t)|\le |v_0|\,(C|t - t_0|)^{m+1}/(m+1)!\), so they converge uniformly on \(K\) to a solution of the integral equation, i.e. of the ODE. If \(w\) is a solution with \(w(t_0) = 0\), then \(|w(t)| \le C\,|\int_{t_0}^t|w(s)|\,ds|\), and iterating, \(|w(t)|\le\max_K|w|\,(C|t - t_0|)^m/m!\to 0\); so solutions are unique, and the solutions on increasing compact intervals fit together on \(J\). Linearity follows from uniqueness, and \(v' = Av\) shows inductively that \(v\) is \(C^{m+1}\) when it is \(C^m\) and \(A\) is smooth. \(\square\)

Lemma 8.2. (checked by machine: V6.8, in a narrower form) Given a curve \(c : I\to M\), \(t_0\in I\) and \(V_0\in TM_{c(t_0)}\), there is one and only one parallel vector field \(V\) along \(c\) with \(V_{t_0} = V_0\).

Proof. Uniqueness. If \(V, W\) are parallel with \(V_{t_0} = W_{t_0}\), the set \(\{t : V_t = W_t\}\) is closed, and it is open, because near any of its points both are solutions of the same linear system in a chart with the same value there (Fact 2.2). As \(I\) is connected, \(V = W\). Existence. Fix a compact interval \([\alpha,\beta]\subset I\) containing \(t_0\). By the Lebesgue number lemma there are \(\alpha = s_0 < s_1 < \dots < s_m = \beta\) such that each \(c([s_{l-1}, s_l])\) lies in a chart \(U_l\), and then an open interval \(J_l\supset[s_{l-1},s_l]\) with \(c(J_l) \subset U_l\). Solve the linear system on the \(J_l\) successively, starting from the one containing \(t_0\) and passing the value at each \(s_l\) on to the neighbouring interval (Fact 2.2). On the overlaps the solutions agree by uniqueness, so they define a parallel field on a neighbourhood of \([\alpha,\beta]\); exhausting \(I\) by such intervals and using uniqueness again gives \(V\) on all of \(I\). \(\square\)

\(V_t\) is obtained from \(V_0\) by parallel translation along \(c\). The map \(P_t : TM_{c(t_0)}\to TM_{c(t)}\), \(V_0\mapsto V_t\), is linear (sums and constant multiples of parallel fields are parallel, by a) and b)) and injective (a parallel field vanishing at one time vanishes everywhere, by uniqueness), hence a linear isomorphism.

3. Connections compatible with a metric (Milnor pp. 47–48)

Now let \(M\) be a Riemannian manifold, with inner product \(\langle X_p, Y_p\rangle\) on each tangent space, smooth in the sense that \(g_{ij} = \langle\partial_i,\partial_j\rangle\) is smooth in every chart.

Definition. A connection is compatible with the metric if parallel translation preserves inner products: for every curve \(c\) and all parallel fields \(P, P'\) along \(c\), \(\langle P, P'\rangle\) is constant.

Milnor proves that compatibility implies a product rule along curves (Lemma 8.3) and for vector fields (Corollary 8.4). For the existence half of Lemma 8.6 we need the converse as well, so we prove all equivalences at once.

Lemma 3.1. For a connection on a Riemannian manifold the following are equivalent.

  1. The connection is compatible with the metric.

  2. (Lemma 8.3) For every curve \(c\) and all fields \(V, W\) along \(c\), \[\frac{d}{dt}\langle V, W\rangle = \Big\langle\frac{DV}{dt}, W\Big\rangle + \Big\langle V, \frac{DW}{dt}\Big\rangle.\]

  3. (Corollary 8.4) For all vector fields \(Y, Y'\) and all \(X_p\): \(X_p\langle Y, Y'\rangle = \langle X_p\vdash Y, Y'_p\rangle + \langle Y_p, X_p\vdash Y'\rangle\).

  4. In every chart, \(\partial_i g_{jk} = \Gamma_{ij,k} + \Gamma_{ik,j}\), where \(\Gamma_{ij,k} := \langle\partial_i\vdash\partial_j, \partial_k\rangle = \sum_l \Gamma^l_{ij}\, g_{lk}\).

Proof. (i) \(\Rightarrow\) (ii), Milnor’s proof of 8.3. By Lemma 8.2 choose parallel fields \(P_1, \dots, P_n\) along \(c\) that are orthonormal at one time; by (i) they are orthonormal at every time, hence a basis of each \(TM_{c(t)}\). Then \(V = \sum_i v^iP_i\) and \(W = \sum_j w^jP_j\) with \(v^i = \langle V, P_i\rangle\) and \(w^j = \langle W, P_j\rangle\) smooth (in a chart they are sums of products of smooth functions). By a) and b), \(DV/dt = \sum_i (dv^i/dt)P_i\) and \(DW/dt = \sum_j (dw^j/dt)P_j\), so \[\Big\langle\frac{DV}{dt}, W\Big\rangle + \Big\langle V,\frac{DW}{dt}\Big\rangle = \sum_i\Big(\frac{dv^i}{dt}w^i + v^i\frac{dw^i}{dt}\Big) = \frac{d}{dt}\sum_i v^iw^i = \frac{d}{dt}\langle V, W\rangle.\]

  1. \(\Rightarrow\) (iii), Milnor’s proof of 8.4. Take a curve with \(c(0) = p\) and \(\dot c(0) = X_p\), for instance \(c(t) = u^{-1}(u(p) + ta)\) for small \(|t|\) in a chart, where \(a\) is the coordinate vector of \(X_p\). Apply (ii) to \(V = Y\circ c\), \(W = Y'\circ c\) at \(t = 0\): the left side is \(X_p\langle Y, Y'\rangle\), and by c) \(DV/dt(0) = X_p\vdash Y\), \(DW/dt(0) = X_p\vdash Y'\).

  2. \(\Rightarrow\) (iv). Apply (iii) on the chart (Lemma 1.1) to \(X = \partial_i\), \(Y = \partial_j\), \(Y' = \partial_k\).

  3. \(\Rightarrow\) (ii). On a subinterval where \(c\) stays in a chart, write \(V = \sum v^j\partial_j\), \(W = \sum w^k\partial_k\). By (2.1), \[\Big\langle\frac{DV}{dt}, W\Big\rangle + \Big\langle V, \frac{DW}{dt}\Big\rangle = \sum_{j,k}g_{jk}\Big(\frac{dv^j}{dt}w^k + v^j\frac{dw^k}{dt}\Big) + \sum_{i,j,k} \frac{du^i}{dt}\big(\Gamma_{ij,k} + \Gamma_{ik,j}\big)v^jw^k,\] and by (iv) the last sum is \(\sum_{i,j,k}(du^i/dt)(\partial_i g_{jk})v^jw^k\). The total is \(\frac{d}{dt}\sum_{j,k}g_{jk}(u(t))v^jw^k = \frac{d}{dt}\langle V, W\rangle\).

  4. \(\Rightarrow\) (i). For parallel \(P, P'\), (ii) gives \(\frac{d}{dt}\langle P, P'\rangle = 0\), so \(\langle P, P'\rangle\) is constant on the interval \(I\). \(\square\)

4. Symmetric connections and the fundamental lemma (Milnor pp. 48–49)

Definition 8.5. (checked by machine: V6.13, with its hypotheses made explicit) A connection is symmetric if \(X\vdash Y - Y\vdash X = [X, Y]\) for all vector fields \(X, Y\).

The torsion \(T(X, Y) = X\vdash Y - Y\vdash X - [X, Y]\) is \(C^\infty(M)\)-bilinear: using \([fX, Y] = f[X, Y] - (Yf)X\), one finds \(T(fX, Y) = f\,X\vdash Y - (Yf)X - f\,Y\vdash X - f[X,Y] + (Yf)X = fT(X,Y)\), and \(T(Y, X) = -T(X,Y)\). By Lemma 1.2, \(T\) is a tensor, and since \([\partial_i, \partial_j] = 0\), \(T(\partial_i,\partial_j) = \sum_k(\Gamma^k_{ij} - \Gamma^k_{ji})\partial_k\). Therefore: a connection is symmetric if and only if \(\Gamma^k_{ij} = \Gamma^k_{ji}\) in every chart. (This is Milnor’s “using formula (6) it is not difficult to verify”.)

Milnor’s footnote: symmetry as symmetry of second derivatives. Define the covariant second derivative of \(f\in C^\infty(M)\) by \(\nabla^2 f(X_p, Y_p) = X_p(Yf) - (X_p\vdash Y)f\), where \(Y\) extends \(Y_p\). The expression \(X(Yf) - (X\vdash Y)f\) is \(C^\infty(M)\)-linear in \(X\), and also in \(Y\): replacing \(Y\) by \(gY\) gives \((Xg)(Yf) + g\,X(Yf) - (Xg)(Yf) - g\,(X\vdash Y)f\). By Lemma 1.2 it depends only on \(X_p\) and \(Y_p\), so \(\nabla^2 f\) is well defined. Moreover \(\nabla^2f(X, Y) - \nabla^2f(Y, X) = [X, Y]f - (X\vdash Y - Y\vdash X)f = -T(X,Y)f\). Since a tangent vector that annihilates every function is zero, \(\nabla^2 f\) is symmetric for all \(f\) if and only if the connection is symmetric. At a critical point of \(f\), \(\nabla^2 f\) is the Hessian \(f_{**}\) of Milnor §2, because \((X_p\vdash Y)f = df_p(X_p\vdash Y) = 0\) there.

Lemma 8.6 (fundamental lemma of Riemannian geometry). (checked by machine: V6.14, in a narrower form) A Riemannian manifold possesses one and only one symmetric connection which is compatible with its metric.

Proof of uniqueness. Let \(\vdash\) be symmetric and compatible. In a chart, Lemma 3.1(iv) and the symmetry \(\Gamma_{ij,k} = \Gamma_{ji,k}\) give \[\partial_i g_{jk} = \Gamma_{ij,k} + \Gamma_{ik,j},\qquad \partial_j g_{ik} = \Gamma_{ij,k} + \Gamma_{jk,i},\qquad \partial_k g_{ij} = \Gamma_{ik,j} + \Gamma_{jk,i}.\] Adding the first two and subtracting the third gives the first Christoffel identity \[\langle\partial_i\vdash\partial_j,\partial_k\rangle = \Gamma_{ij,k} = \tfrac12\big(\partial_i g_{jk} + \partial_j g_{ik} - \partial_k g_{ij}\big).\] Its left side is \(\sum_l\Gamma^l_{ij}g_{lk}\); multiplying by the inverse matrix \((g^{kl})\) of \((g_{lk})\) gives the second Christoffel identity \[\Gamma^l_{ij} = \sum_k\tfrac12\big(\partial_i g_{jk} + \partial_j g_{ik} - \partial_k g_{ij}\big)g^{kl}.\] So the \(\Gamma^l_{ij}\), and with (6) the connection, are determined by the metric on every chart.

Proof of existence. On each chart, define \(\Gamma^l_{ij}\) by the second Christoffel identity and a connection on the chart by (6) (§1). It is symmetric, since the formula is symmetric in \(i, j\). It is compatible: \(\Gamma_{ij,k} = \sum_l\Gamma^l_{ij}g_{lk}\) equals \(\frac12(\partial_i g_{jk} + \partial_j g_{ik} - \partial_k g_{ij})\), so \(\Gamma_{ij,k} + \Gamma_{ik,j} = \partial_i g_{jk}\), which is condition (iv) of Lemma 3.1. On the overlap of two charts both connections are symmetric and compatible (Lemma 3.1 is local), so they coincide by uniqueness. Hence they define one connection on \(M\), smooth because it is given locally by (6). \(\square\)

A possible misprint in Milnor’s proof. Milnor writes that permuting \(i, j, k\) gives three linear equations in “the three quantities \(\langle\partial_i\vdash\partial_j,\partial_k\rangle\), \(\langle\partial_j\vdash\partial_i,\partial_k\rangle\), and \(\langle\partial_k\vdash\partial_j, \partial_i\rangle\)”. By symmetry the first two are equal. The three unknowns are \(\Gamma_{ij,k}\), \(\Gamma_{ik,j}\) and \(\Gamma_{jk,i}\), as above. Also, “Conversely … one can verify that the resulting connection is … compatible with the metric” needs the implication (iv) \(\Rightarrow\) (i) of Lemma 3.1, which Milnor does not state, and the patching of the local connections, which uses uniqueness.

From now on, a Riemannian manifold carries this connection, the Levi-Civita connection.

5. Parametrized surfaces (Milnor pp. 49–50)

A parametrized surface is a smooth map \(s : \mathbb{R}^2\to M\) (an open subset of \(\mathbb{R}^2\) works equally well). A vector field along \(s\) assigns to each \((x, y)\) a vector \(V_{(x,y)}\in TM_{s(x,y)}\), smooth in the sense of §2. Examples are the velocity fields \(\partial s/\partial x = s_*(\partial/\partial x)\) and \(\partial s/\partial y\). For each fixed \(y_0\), \(V\) restricts to a field along the curve \(x\mapsto s(x, y_0)\); its covariant derivative is \(DV/\partial x\) at \((x, y_0)\). Likewise \(DV/\partial y\). In a chart, with \(s^i = u^i\circ s\) and \(V = \sum v^k\partial_k\), (2.1) gives \[\frac{DV}{\partial x} = \sum_k\Big(\frac{\partial v^k}{\partial x} + \sum_{i,j}\frac{\partial s^i}{\partial x}\,\Gamma^k_{ij}(s)\,v^j\Big)\partial_k,\] which shows that \(DV/\partial x\) is smooth in \((x, y)\) jointly, a point Milnor does not mention. \(\frac{D}{\partial x}\frac{\partial s}{\partial x}\) is the acceleration of the curves \(x\mapsto s(x, y_0)\), but the mixed derivatives have no such description.

Lemma 8.7. (checked by machine: V6.15, in a narrower form) If the connection is symmetric, then \(\dfrac{D}{\partial x}\dfrac{\partial s}{\partial y} = \dfrac{D}{\partial y}\dfrac{\partial s}{\partial x}\).

Proof. With \(v^k = \partial s^k/\partial y\) in the formula above, \[\frac{D}{\partial x}\frac{\partial s}{\partial y} = \sum_k\Big(\frac{\partial^2s^k}{\partial x\,\partial y} + \sum_{i,j}\Gamma^k_{ij}(s)\,\frac{\partial s^i}{\partial x}\frac{\partial s^j}{\partial y}\Big)\partial_k.\] Exchanging \(x\) and \(y\) gives the same expression, by equality of mixed partial derivatives and \(\Gamma^k_{ij} = \Gamma^k_{ji}\). \(\square\)

The converse holds too, which makes this the “alternative characterization of symmetry” Milnor announces: for \(s(x,y) = u^{-1}(u(p) + xe_i + ye_j)\) near \(0\), the two sides at \((0,0)\) are \(\sum_k \Gamma^k_{ij}\partial_k\) and \(\sum_k\Gamma^k_{ji}\partial_k\).

6. The curvature tensor (Milnor pp. 51–53)

The curvature tensor measures how far the second covariant derivative \(\partial_i\vdash (\partial_j\vdash Z)\) is from being symmetric in \(i\) and \(j\). For vector fields \(X, Y, Z\) Milnor defines \[R(X, Y)Z = -X\vdash(Y\vdash Z) + Y\vdash(X\vdash Z) + [X, Y]\vdash Z.\]

Watch the sign. This is the negative of the convention of Nomizu and of most modern texts, \(R^{\mathrm{std}}(X,Y)Z = \nabla_X\nabla_YZ - \nabla_Y\nabla_XZ - \nabla_{[X,Y]}Z\): \(R = -R^{\mathrm{std}}\). Milnor’s footnote gives the reason: with his sign, \(\langle R(\partial_h,\partial_i)\partial_j, \partial_k\rangle\) is the classical symbol \(R_{hijk}\). The sectional curvature of an orthonormal pair is \(\langle R(X, Y)X, Y\rangle\) in Milnor’s convention (p. 100; §7 below) and \(\langle R^{\mathrm{std}}(X, Y)Y, X\rangle\) in the other, the same number. A formalization against a library using the other convention must insert this sign.

Lemma 9.1. (checked by machine: V6.17, in a narrower form) The value of \(R(X, Y)Z\) at \(p\) depends only on \(X_p, Y_p, Z_p\), and \((X_p, Y_p, Z_p)\mapsto R(X_p, Y_p)Z_p\) is trilinear. Briefly, \(R\) is a tensor.

Proof. \(R\) is \(\mathbb{R}\)-trilinear. Replacing \(X\) by \(fX\), the three terms become \(-f\,X\vdash(Y\vdash Z)\), then \((Yf)(X\vdash Z) + f\,Y\vdash(X\vdash Z)\), then \(-(Yf)(X\vdash Z) + f\,[X,Y]\vdash Z\) (as \([fX, Y] = f[X, Y] - (Yf)X\)). Adding, \(R(fX, Y)Z = fR(X,Y)Z\). Since \([Y,X] = -[X,Y]\), the definition gives \(R(Y, X)Z = -R(X, Y)Z\), so \(R\) is also \(C^\infty\)-linear in \(Y\). For \(Z\): by (4), \(X\vdash(Y\vdash fZ) = X(Yf)\,Z + (Yf)\,X\vdash Z + (Xf)\,Y\vdash Z + f\,X\vdash(Y\vdash Z)\), and symmetrically in \(X, Y\); also \([X,Y]\vdash fZ = ([X,Y]f)Z + f\,[X,Y]\vdash Z\). In \(R(X,Y)(fZ)\) the terms with one derivative of \(f\) cancel in pairs, and those with two derivatives give \(\big(-X(Yf) + Y(Xf) + [X,Y]f\big)Z = 0\). So \(R(X, Y)(fZ) = fR(X,Y)Z\), and Lemma 1.2 finishes the proof. \(\square\)

Milnor finishes with coordinates instead: \(R(X, Y)Z = \sum_{i,j,k}x^iy^jz^k\,R(\partial_i, \partial_j)\partial_k\), which presupposes that \(R\) can be computed on a chart; it can, because \(\vdash\) and \([\ ,\ ]\) are local. From (5), \(R(\partial_i,\partial_j)\partial_k = \sum_l R^l_{ijk}\partial_l\) with \[R^l_{ijk} = \partial_j\Gamma^l_{ik} - \partial_i\Gamma^l_{jk} + \sum_m\big(\Gamma^m_{ik} \Gamma^l_{jm} - \Gamma^m_{jk}\Gamma^l_{im}\big).\]

Lemma 9.2. (checked by machine: V6.19, in a narrower form) For a parametrized surface \(s\) and a vector field \(V\) along \(s\), \[\frac{D}{\partial y}\frac{D}{\partial x}V - \frac{D}{\partial x}\frac{D}{\partial y}V = R\Big(\frac{\partial s}{\partial x},\frac{\partial s}{\partial y}\Big)V.\]

Proof. In a chart let \(E_k = \partial_k\circ s\), so \(V = \sum_k v^kE_k\), and by c) applied to the coordinate curves, \(DE_k/\partial x = \sum_i(\partial_x s^i)(\partial_i\vdash\partial_k)\circ s\). Then \[\frac{D}{\partial y}\frac{D}{\partial x}V = \sum_k\Big(\partial_y\partial_x v^k\,E_k + \partial_x v^k\,\frac{DE_k}{\partial y} + \partial_y v^k\,\frac{DE_k}{\partial x} + v^k\,\frac{D}{\partial y}\frac{DE_k}{\partial x}\Big),\] and the first three terms are symmetric in \(x, y\). Next, by b) and c), \[\frac{D}{\partial y}\frac{DE_k}{\partial x} = \sum_i\partial_y\partial_xs^i\,(\partial_i \vdash\partial_k) + \sum_{i,j}\partial_xs^i\,\partial_ys^j\,\partial_j\vdash(\partial_i\vdash \partial_k).\] Subtracting the same expression with \(x\) and \(y\) exchanged, the second derivatives of \(s^i\) cancel, and what is left is \(\sum_{i,j}\partial_xs^i\,\partial_ys^j\,\big[\partial_j\vdash (\partial_i\vdash\partial_k) - \partial_i\vdash(\partial_j\vdash\partial_k)\big] = \sum_{i,j} \partial_xs^i\,\partial_ys^j\,R(\partial_i,\partial_j)\partial_k\), because \([\partial_i, \partial_j] = 0\). Multiplying by \(v^k\), summing, and using Lemma 9.1 gives \(R(\partial s/\partial x,\partial s/\partial y)V\). \(\square\)

Note that Lemma 9.2 holds for every affine connection; symmetry is not used.

Proposition 6.1 (Milnor’s remark on pp. 52–53). Suppose \(R = 0\). Then for every parametrized surface \(s\), defined on \(\mathbb{R}^2\) or on an open square centred at \(0\), and every \(P_0\in TM_{s(0,0)}\), there is exactly one vector field \(P\) along \(s\) with \(DP/\partial x = DP/\partial y = 0\) and \(P_{(0,0)} = P_0\). Conversely, if such fields exist for all such \(s\) and \(P_0\), then \(R = 0\).

Proof. Let \(P_{(x,0)}\) be the parallel field along the \(x\)-axis with value \(P_0\) at \(0\), and for each \(x_0\) let \(y\mapsto P_{(x_0,y)}\) be the parallel field along \(y\mapsto s(x_0, y)\) with the value \(P_{(x_0,0)}\) at \(y = 0\) (Lemma 8.2). This defines \(P\) on the domain of \(s\). It is smooth in \((x, y)\) jointly: on a small rectangle in a chart, \(P\) solves the linear system \(\partial P^k/\partial y = -\sum_{i,j}\Gamma^k_{ij}(s)\,(\partial s^i/\partial y)\,P^j\), whose coefficients depend smoothly on the parameter \(x\), with initial values smooth in \(x\); solutions of such systems depend smoothly on parameters and initial values (see Hartman, Ordinary Differential Equations, Chapter V), and covering a compact rectangle by finitely many chart rectangles as in Lemma 8.2 gives smoothness everywhere. By construction \(DP/\partial y = 0\) everywhere and \(DP/\partial x = 0\) on the \(x\)-axis. By Lemma 9.2 with \(R = 0\), \[\frac{D}{\partial y}\Big(\frac{DP}{\partial x}\Big) = \frac{D}{\partial x}\frac{D}{\partial y}P + R\Big(\frac{\partial s}{\partial x},\frac{\partial s}{\partial y}\Big)P = 0,\] so for each \(x_0\) the field \(DP/\partial x\) is parallel along \(y\mapsto s(x_0, y)\) and vanishes at \(y = 0\); by uniqueness in Lemma 8.2 it vanishes identically. Uniqueness of \(P\) follows from uniqueness of parallel transport along the \(x\)-axis and then along each curve \(y\mapsto s(x_0, y)\). For the converse, given \(p\) and \(X_p, Y_p, Z_p\), take \(s(x, y) = u^{-1}(u(p) + xa + yb)\) near \(0\) in a chart, \(a, b\) the coordinate vectors of \(X_p, Y_p\), and \(P\) with \(P_0 = Z_p\): Lemma 9.2 gives \(R(X_p, Y_p)Z_p = 0\). \(\square\)

So in a flat manifold, parallel transport along the boundary of any small parametrized square returns every vector to itself, while curvature is exactly the obstruction to this. The figure below shows the obstruction on the sphere.

An interactive look at parallel transport

The figure shows a sphere and a circle of latitude \(\varphi\). A tangent vector starts at the marked point pointing due north and is carried eastward along the circle by parallel transport, that is, by solving the equations of Lemma 8.2 for the Levi-Civita connection of the sphere. (The solution is derived in §8: relative to the local north and east directions, the vector turns clockwise at the constant rate \(\sin\varphi\) per radian of longitude.) Drag the longitude travelled slider, or press play, and watch the vector come back after a full circuit turned by \(360^\circ\sin\varphi\). Move the latitude slider: near the pole the vector hardly moves in space while the local frame spins under it; at the equator, a great circle, nothing turns at all. The panel also shows the area of the cap above the circle, in degrees of angle: it always adds up with the turning angle to \(360^\circ\), which is the curvature at work. Two more sliders tilt and turn the view, and the check box lets the camera ride along with the pendulum, the way Foucault’s audience saw it.

7. The symmetries of the curvature tensor (Milnor pp. 53–54)

From now on \(M\) is a Riemannian manifold with its Levi-Civita connection.

Lemma 9.3. (checked by machine: V6.20, in a narrower form; V6.21, in a stronger form) The curvature tensor satisfies

  1. \(R(X, Y)Z + R(Y, X)Z = 0\);

  2. \(R(X, Y)Z + R(Y, Z)X + R(Z, X)Y = 0\);

  3. \(\langle R(X, Y)Z, W\rangle + \langle R(X, Y)W, Z\rangle = 0\);

  4. \(\langle R(X, Y)Z, W\rangle = \langle R(Z, W)X, Y\rangle\).

Proof. (1) was noted in the proof of Lemma 9.1; it holds for every connection.

A preliminary remark used for (2) and (3): all expressions involved are tensors (Lemma 9.1), so it suffices to prove them at a point \(p\) for arbitrary vectors \(X_p, Y_p, Z_p, W_p\), and we may choose the extensions. Extend each to a field whose components are constant in a chart near \(p\) (cut off by a bump function away from \(p\)). Brackets of such fields vanish near \(p\), and by locality their covariant derivatives at \(p\) vanish too.

  1. uses only symmetry. With all brackets zero near \(p\), the left side of (2) is \[\begin{aligned}&-X\vdash(Y\vdash Z) + Y\vdash(X\vdash Z) - Y\vdash(Z\vdash X) + Z\vdash(Y\vdash X) \\ &\quad - Z\vdash(X\vdash Y) + X\vdash(Z\vdash Y) = X\vdash[Z, Y] + Y\vdash[X, Z] + Z\vdash[Y, X] = 0\end{aligned}\] at \(p\), since \(Y\vdash Z - Z\vdash Y = [Y, Z]\) and so on: the terms cancel in pairs.

  2. uses only compatibility. The bilinear form \(B(Z, W) = \langle R(X,Y)Z, W\rangle\) is skew-symmetric if and only if \(B(Z, Z) = 0\) for all \(Z\), because \(B(Z+W, Z+W) - B(Z,Z) - B(W,W) = B(Z, W) + B(W, Z)\). With \([X, Y] = 0\) near \(p\), \(\langle R(X,Y)Z, Z\rangle = \langle -X\vdash (Y\vdash Z) + Y\vdash(X\vdash Z), Z\rangle\), so we must show that \(\langle Y\vdash(X\vdash Z), Z\rangle\) is symmetric in \(X\) and \(Y\). By Corollary 8.4 (Lemma 3.1(iii)) applied twice, \[YX\langle Z, Z\rangle = Y\big(2\langle X\vdash Z, Z\rangle\big) = 2\langle Y\vdash(X\vdash Z), Z\rangle + 2\langle X\vdash Z, Y\vdash Z\rangle.\] The left side is symmetric in \(X, Y\) because \(XY\langle Z,Z\rangle - YX\langle Z,Z\rangle = [X, Y]\langle Z, Z\rangle = 0\), and the last term is visibly symmetric. Hence so is \(\langle Y\vdash (X\vdash Z), Z\rangle\).

  3. is pure algebra from (1), (2), (3). Write \([XYZW] = \langle R(X,Y)Z, W\rangle\); by (1) and (3) it changes sign when the first two or the last two entries are exchanged. Milnor places the six quantities \[T = [XYZW],\quad B = [ZWXY],\quad L = [XWYZ],\quad K = [YWZX],\quad Q = [YZXW],\quad F = [ZXYW]\] at the vertices of an octahedron (top, bottom, and four around the middle) and shades four faces, each labelled by a letter. Face \(W\): identity (2) for \(X, Y, Z\), paired with \(W\), reads \(T + Q + F = 0\). Face \(Z\): identity (2) for \(X, Y, W\), paired with \(Z\), reads \([XYWZ] + [YWXZ] + [WXYZ] = 0\), which by (1), (3) is \(-(T + K + L) = 0\). Face \(X\): (2) for \(Y, Z, W\) paired with \(X\) gives \([YZWX] + [ZWYX] + [WYZX] = -(Q + B + K) = 0\). Face \(Y\): (2) for \(Z, W, X\) paired with \(Y\) gives \([ZWXY] + [WXZY] + [XZWY] = B + L + F = 0\). Adding the top two faces and subtracting the bottom two, \[(T + Q + F) + (T + K + L) - (Q + B + K) - (B + L + F) = 2T - 2B = 0,\] which is (4). \(\square\)

Sectional curvature (Milnor p. 100). Milnor defines it in §19, but it belongs here. If \(A, B\in TM_p\) are orthonormal, \(K(A, B) = \langle R(A, B)A, B\rangle\) is the sectional curvature determined by \(A\) and \(B\). More generally, for linearly independent \(X, Y\) put \[K(X, Y) = \frac{\langle R(X, Y)X, Y\rangle}{|X|^2|Y|^2 - \langle X, Y\rangle^2}.\]

Lemma 7.1. \(K(X, Y)\) depends only on the plane \(\sigma\) spanned by \(X\) and \(Y\).

Proof. Let \(X' = aX + bY\), \(Y' = cX + dY\) be another basis of \(\sigma\). By (1), \(R(X', Y') = (ad - bc)R(X, Y)\), and by (3), the bilinear form \((Z, W)\mapsto\langle R(X, Y)Z, W\rangle\) is skew, so \(\langle R(X,Y)X', Y'\rangle = (ad - bc)\langle R(X,Y)X, Y\rangle\). Thus the numerator gets multiplied by \((ad - bc)^2\), and so does the Gram determinant in the denominator. \(\square\)

Lemma 7.2. The sectional curvatures determine \(R\): if \(R\) and \(R'\) satisfy (1)–(4) and \(\langle R(X,Y)X, Y\rangle = \langle R'(X,Y)X, Y\rangle\) for all \(X, Y\), then \(R = R'\).

Proof. \(D = R - R'\) satisfies (1)–(4), and \([XYXY] = 0\) for all \(X, Y\), where now \([XYZW] = \langle D(X,Y)Z, W\rangle\). Replacing \(X\) by \(X + Z\) and using (4): \([XYZY] + [ZYXY] = 2[XYZY] = 0\). Replacing \(Y\) by \(Y + W\) in \([XYZY] = 0\): \([XYZW] = -[XWZY] = [XWYZ]\), using (3). So \([XYZW]\) is unchanged by cyclically permuting its last three entries. Now by (2), \(0 = [XYZW] + [YZXW] + [ZXYW]\); here \([YZXW] = [XWYZ] = [XYZW]\) by (4) and the cyclic rule, and \([ZXYW] = -[XZYW] = -[XYWZ] = [XYZW]\) by (1), the cyclic rule and (3). So \(3[XYZW] = 0\). \(\square\)

Corollary 7.3. If all sectional curvatures at \(p\) equal \(\kappa\), then \(R(X, Y)Z = \kappa\big(\langle X, Z\rangle Y - \langle Y, Z\rangle X\big)\) at \(p\).

Proof. \(R_0(X,Y)Z = \langle X, Z\rangle Y - \langle Y, Z\rangle X\) satisfies (1)–(4) (direct check; for (2), the six terms cancel in pairs) and \(\langle R_0(X, Y)X, Y\rangle = |X|^2|Y|^2 - \langle X, Y\rangle^2\). Apply Lemma 7.2 to \(R\) and \(\kappa R_0\). \(\square\)

On a surface there is one plane at each point, \(K\) is a function (the Gaussian curvature), and \(R(X, Y)Z = K(\langle X, Z\rangle Y - \langle Y, Z\rangle X)\).

8. Application: Foucault’s pendulum, and the curvature of the sphere

The sphere’s connection.
