Let \(S\) be the sphere of radius \(\rho\) in \(\mathbb{R}^3\) with the induced metric, and use latitude \(\varphi\in(-\pi/2,\pi/2)\) and longitude \(\lambda\) as coordinates: \(x(\varphi, \lambda) = \rho(\cos\varphi\cos\lambda, \cos\varphi\sin\lambda, \sin\varphi)\). From \(\partial_\varphi x = \rho(-\sin\varphi\cos\lambda, -\sin\varphi\sin\lambda, \cos\varphi)\) and \(\partial_\lambda x = \rho(-\cos\varphi\sin\lambda, \cos\varphi\cos\lambda, 0)\), \[g_{\varphi\varphi} = \rho^2,\qquad g_{\lambda\lambda} = \rho^2\cos^2\varphi,\qquad g_{\varphi\lambda} = 0.\] The only nonzero derivative of the metric is \(\partial_\varphi g_{\lambda\lambda} = -2\rho^2\cos\varphi\sin\varphi\), and the second Christoffel identity gives \[\Gamma^\varphi_{\lambda\lambda} = -\tfrac12\,\partial_\varphi g_{\lambda\lambda}/g_{\varphi\varphi} = \sin\varphi\cos\varphi,\qquad \Gamma^\lambda_{\varphi\lambda} = \Gamma^\lambda_{\lambda\varphi} = \tfrac12\,\partial_\varphi g_{\lambda\lambda}/g_{\lambda\lambda} = -\tan\varphi,\] all others zero. (They do not depend on \(\rho\).)

Transport around a circle of latitude. Let \(c(t) = (\varphi_0, \lambda_0 + t)\), the circle of latitude \(\varphi_0\) traversed eastward. Here \(du^\varphi/dt = 0\) and \(du^\lambda/dt = 1\), so the parallel transport equations of Lemma 8.2 are \[\frac{dv^\varphi}{dt} = -\sin\varphi_0\cos\varphi_0\,v^\lambda,\qquad \frac{dv^\lambda}{dt} = \tan\varphi_0\,v^\varphi.\] In terms of the components \(a = \rho v^\varphi\) and \(b = \rho\cos\varphi_0\,v^\lambda\) along the unit vectors pointing north and east, they read \(a' = -\sin\varphi_0\,b\), \(b' = \sin\varphi_0\,a\), with solution \[\begin{pmatrix}a(t)\\ b(t)\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}\cos(t\sin\varphi_0) & -\sin(t\sin\varphi_0)\\ \sin(t\sin\varphi_0) & \cos(t\sin\varphi_0)\end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix}a(0)\\ b(0)\end{pmatrix}.\] The transported vector keeps its length (compatibility at work) and turns from north towards east, which seen from outside the sphere is clockwise, at the rate \(\sin\varphi_0\) per radian of longitude. After a full circuit, \(t = 2\pi\), the north–east frame is back where it started and the vector has turned clockwise by \[2\pi\sin\varphi_0.\]

The numbers. In Foucault’s model the suspension point makes one circuit per sidereal day, \(23.934\) hours, and the swing direction is transported in this way. At the Panthéon (\(\varphi_0 = 48.85^\circ\), \(\sin\varphi_0 = 0.7530\)) the swing plane turns \(360^\circ\times 0.7530 = 271.1^\circ\) per sidereal day, that is \(11.33^\circ\) per hour, and a full turn takes \(23.934/0.7530 = 31.8\) hours, as observed. At \(45^\circ\) the rate is \(10.6^\circ\) per hour; at the North Pole it is \(15.04^\circ\) per hour (the Earth simply turns under the pendulum); at the equator, a great circle, it is \(0\); in the southern hemisphere \(\sin\varphi_0 < 0\) and the turning is counterclockwise. (That the swing direction is parallel transported is the standard geometric reading of Foucault’s sine law, valid for a long pendulum with small swings, and the sine law itself is confirmed by Foucault pendulums in museums around the world. We take this piece of physics as given.)

The curvature. From the coordinate formula of §6, \(R^\lambda_{\varphi\lambda\varphi} = -\partial_\varphi\Gamma^\lambda_{\lambda\varphi} - \Gamma^\lambda_{\lambda\varphi}\Gamma^\lambda_{\varphi\lambda} = \sec^2\varphi - \tan^2\varphi = 1\), so \(R(\partial_\varphi,\partial_\lambda)\partial_\varphi = \partial_\lambda\) and \[K = \frac{\langle R(\partial_\varphi,\partial_\lambda)\partial_\varphi, \partial_\lambda\rangle} {g_{\varphi\varphi}g_{\lambda\lambda} - g_{\varphi\lambda}^2} = \frac{\rho^2\cos^2\varphi} {\rho^4\cos^2\varphi} = \frac{1}{\rho^2}.\] The round sphere has positive curvature (in either sign convention, each with its own formula for \(K\)), and by Corollary 7.3, \(R(X, Y)Z = \rho^{-2}(\langle X, Z\rangle Y - \langle Y, Z\rangle X)\) in Milnor’s.

Turning angle equals enclosed curvature. The cap \(\{\varphi > \varphi_0\}\) has area \(2\pi\rho^2(1 - \sin\varphi_0)\), so curvature times area is \(2\pi(1 - \sin\varphi_0)\). A counterclockwise turn by this angle (the circle goes counterclockwise around the cap, seen from above the North Pole) is the same as a clockwise turn by \(2\pi\sin\varphi_0\), which is what we computed. For Paris, the cap above the circle accounts for \(88.9^\circ\), and \(88.9^\circ + 271.1^\circ = 360^\circ\). This is the Gauss–Bonnet theorem for a disc, which is not proved in this book, but Lemma 9.2 explains its infinitesimal version. Transport \(V\) around the image of the square with corners \((0,0), (\varepsilon,0), (\varepsilon,\varepsilon), (0,\varepsilon)\), in that order. With \(P\) built as in the proof of Proposition 6.1 (along the \(x\)-axis, then up each vertical line), Lemma 9.2 gives \(\frac{D}{\partial y}\frac{DP}{\partial x} = R(\partial_x s,\partial_y s)P\), so on the top edge \(DP/\partial x \approx \varepsilon R(\partial_x s,\partial_y s)V\), and the vector comes back as \(V + \varepsilon^2R(\partial_x s, \partial_y s)V\) up to higher order. On the sphere, with \(\partial_x s, \partial_y s\) a positively oriented orthonormal pair \(e_1, e_2\) and \(V = e_1\), Corollary 7.3 turns this into \(e_1 + \varepsilon^2K e_2\): a counterclockwise turn by curvature times area, which is the sign found above. The convention affects the formula, not the geometry: with \(R^{\mathrm{std}} = -R\) the returning vector is written \(V - \varepsilon^2R^{\mathrm{std}}(\partial_x s, \partial_y s)V\), the same vector.

9. Summary of what was silently assumed, now made explicit

Where Milnor says What is actually needed
p. 43 \(X_p\vdash Y\) for a vector field \(Y\) it depends only on \(Y\) near \(p\) (Lemma 1.1, bump functions); needed to use coordinate fields \(\partial_j\), defined only on a chart
p. 44 “Conditions (1), (2), (3), (4) can be taken as the definition” \(C^\infty\)-linearity in \(X\) implies dependence on \(X_p\) only (Lemma 1.2, Proposition 1.3)
p. 45 “The result clearly satisfies the conditions (1), …, (5)” the Leibniz rule (4) for formula (6), checked in §1
p. 45 smoothness of a vector field along a curve equivalent to smoothness of its components (Lemma 2.1)
p. 46 Lemma 8.1: formula (2.1) “follows from (a), (b), and (c)” locality in \(t\), and extension of the coordinate fields by bump functions; existence needs independence of the chart
p. 47 the equations are linear, so the solutions “can be defined for all relevant values of \(t\)” global existence for linear ODEs (Fact 2.2) and patching across charts by compactness (Lemma 8.2)
p. 47 Lemma 8.3 the parallel orthonormal frame exists by Lemma 8.2 and stays orthonormal by compatibility
p. 48 Corollary 8.4: choose a curve with velocity \(X_p\) at \(t = 0\) a coordinate line on a small interval; Milnor’s curves on all of \(\mathbb{R}\) are unnecessary
p. 48 symmetry iff \(\Gamma^k_{ij} = \Gamma^k_{ji}\), “not difficult to verify” the torsion is a tensor (§4)
p. 48 (footnote) the covariant second derivative “does not depend on the choice of \(Y\)” \(C^\infty\)-linearity in \(Y\) and Lemma 1.2 (§4)
p. 49 “three quantities … \(\langle\partial_j\vdash\partial_i,\partial_k\rangle\) …” possible misprint: the unknowns are \(\Gamma_{ij,k}, \Gamma_{ik,j}, \Gamma_{jk,i}\)
p. 49 “one can verify that the resulting connection is symmetric and compatible” compatibility from \(\partial_ig_{jk} = \Gamma_{ij,k} + \Gamma_{ik,j}\) (Lemma 3.1(iv) \(\Rightarrow\) (i)); patching charts by uniqueness
p. 49 \(DV/\partial x\) “along the entire parametrized surface” joint smoothness in \((x,y)\), from the coordinate formula (§5)
p. 50 Lemma 8.7: “express both sides … and compute” the computation in §5; the converse also holds
p. 51 Lemma 9.1: “corresponding identities for \(Y\) and \(Z\) are easily obtained” \(Y\) by skew-symmetry, \(Z\) by the computation in §6; pointwise dependence by Lemma 1.2 or locality
p. 51 sign of \(R\) opposite to the modern convention; sectional curvature is \(\langle R(X,Y)X,Y\rangle\)
p. 52 Lemma 9.2: “express both sides … and compute” the computation in §6; valid for every affine connection
pp. 52–53 flat surfaces carry parallel fields joint smoothness of \(P\) (smooth dependence of ODE solutions on parameters); converse via Lemma 9.2 (Proposition 6.1)
p. 53 “it is sufficient to prove (2)” when the brackets of \(X, Y, Z\) are zero extend vectors to fields with constant coordinate components near \(p\); tensoriality
p. 53 skew-symmetry in \(Z, W\) is “clearly equivalent” to \(\langle R(X,Y)Z,Z\rangle = 0\) polarization of a bilinear form
p. 54 the octahedron the four Bianchi identities with signs, made explicit (§7)
p. 100 sectional curvature for orthonormal \(A, B\) independent of the basis of the plane (Lemma 7.1); determines \(R\) (Lemma 7.2)

Checked by machine. Milnor’s §§8–9 have been verified in the Lean proof assistant for submanifolds of Euclidean space with the induced metric, where the connection is \(X \vdash Y = P(dY(X))\), with \(P\) the orthogonal projection onto the tangent space: rules (1)–(4), Lemmas 8.1–8.3, parallel translation as a linear isometry, Corollary 8.4, symmetry, Lemma 8.6 (existence and uniqueness), Lemmas 8.7, 9.1, 9.2 and 9.3, and sectional curvature \(1\) for the unit sphere. The curvature is computed from the second fundamental form by the Gauss equation, with Milnor’s sign, and parallel fields come from one linear equation with skew-adjoint coefficients instead of chart-by-chart solutions. Lemmas 7.1 and 7.2 and Corollary 7.3 are checked as linear algebra, with (4) of Lemma 9.3 derived from (1)–(3) by the octahedron. On an abstract Riemannian manifold only the uniqueness half of Lemma 8.6 is checked: Mathlib has no curvature, parallel transport or Levi-Civita connection. Not checked: Lemmas 1.1, 1.2 and 2.1, the equivalences of Lemma 3.1, Proposition 1.3 and the Christoffel symbols on an abstract manifold, Proposition 6.1, and Foucault’s pendulum. See the verified edition.

  1. Checked by machine: the result has been verified in the Lean proof assistant. The numbers are those of the verified edition and of the comparison, which give the checked statement in full. As stated: the same statement. Restated: an equivalent statement in other terms. With its hypotheses made explicit: a hypothesis the book uses silently is stated. In a stronger form: the checked statement says more than the book’s. In a narrower form: it covers less, a special setting or a weaker conclusion. With a sign corrected: the book’s statement has a slip. Not checked: no part of the result has been verified. The section “Checked by machine” at the end of the chapter says which forms were checked, and covers the results that carry no such note.↩︎

Chapter 7Milnor §10pp. 55–66Contents ↑

Chapter 7. The shortest way round: geodesics and completeness

Milnor, “Morse Theory”, §10, rewritten for a first-year graduate student who wants to know what the theorem is for. Every proof is complete.

0. Why does the flight to New York go north?

A flight from London Heathrow to New York JFK sets off towards the west-north-west, although New York lies eleven degrees of latitude further south. On a sphere of radius 6,371 km the shortest track climbs to \(53.7^\circ\)N, over the Atlantic west of Ireland, before turning south towards Newfoundland. A route of constant compass heading, the one that looks straight on a Mercator chart, is about 4% longer. Behind the pilot’s choice are three questions that make sense on any curved space.

  • Is there a shortest route? Not always. In the plane with the origin removed, \((-1,0)\) and \((1,0)\) are joined by paths of length as close to \(2\) as we like, but by none of length exactly \(2\): the only candidate, the segment, runs through the missing point.
  • How is a shortest route recognized locally? A particle confined to a frictionless surface, with no force but the constraint, has acceleration normal to the surface: it goes “straight ahead”. Such curves are the geodesics. Short pieces of them are shortest routes, and shortest routes are made of them.
  • How many geodesics join two points? The great circle through London and New York gives infinitely many (go round once more), exactly one of them shortest. For London and its antipode, infinitely many are shortest.

This chapter answers these questions on any Riemannian manifold. Geodesics solve a second-order differential equation (§1) and are packaged into the exponential map (§2). Short geodesics are shortest paths and shortest paths are geodesics (§3), which makes the manifold a metric space (§4). The Hopf–Rinow theorem (§5): if every geodesic can be continued indefinitely, any two points are joined by a shortest geodesic. This is exactly what fails in the punctured plane. The application (§7) does the London–New York computation and counts geodesics on a sphere, a cylinder and a torus. The rest of the book rests on this chapter: the critical points of the energy on the path space are the geodesics, and completeness is the hypothesis of the fundamental theorem of Morse theory (§17).

1. Geodesics as solutions of a differential equation (Milnor pp. 55–57)

Conventions. Manifolds are smooth, Hausdorff and second countable. \(M\) is a connected Riemannian manifold with its Levi-Civita connection (Lemma 8.6, in Chapter 6 of this book, on Milnor §8–§9); \(\frac{D}{dt}\) is covariant differentiation along curves (Lemma 8.1). A piecewise smooth path \(\omega:[a,b]\to M\) is continuous with every \(\omega|[t_{i-1},t_i]\) smooth for some subdivision \(a=t_0<\dots<t_k=b\) (Milnor p. 67). Its length \(L(\omega)=\int_a^b\|\frac{d\omega}{dt}\|\,dt\) is integrated piece by piece; it is additive under concatenation and unchanged by reversal or affine reparametrization.

Definition. A smooth curve \(\gamma:I\to M\) on an interval \(I\) is a geodesic if \(\frac{D}{dt}\frac{d\gamma}{dt}\equiv0\): its velocity field is parallel along \(\gamma\).

By Lemma 8.3, \(\frac{d}{dt}\langle\frac{d\gamma}{dt},\frac{d\gamma}{dt}\rangle=2\langle\frac{D}{dt} \frac{d\gamma}{dt},\frac{d\gamma}{dt}\rangle=0\), so a geodesic has constant speed \(c\) and arc length \(s(t)=ct+\text{const}\): the parameter is a linear function of arc length, equal to it iff \(c=1\).

In a chart with coordinates \(u^1,\dots,u^n\), the coordinate formula for \(\frac{D}{dt}\) (Lemma 8.1, with \(V=\sum_j\frac{du^j}{dt}\partial_j\)) turns the geodesic condition into \[\frac{d^2u^k}{dt^2}+\sum_{i,j}\Gamma^k_{ij}(u^1,\dots,u^n)\frac{du^i}{dt}\frac{du^j}{dt}=0, \qquad k=1,\dots,n.\qquad(1)\]

If \(u(t)\) solves (1), so does \(u(ct)\) for a constant \(c\): both terms acquire the factor \(c^2\). So if \(t\mapsto\gamma(t)\) is a geodesic, so is \(t\mapsto\gamma(ct)\) (Milnor’s “homogeneity”, p. 57).

Theorem 10.1 (existence and uniqueness). (checked by machine: V7.4, in a stronger form)1 Let \(\vec F\) be an \(n\)-tuple of \(C^\infty\) functions on an open set \(U\subseteq\mathbb R^{2n}\), and \((\vec u_1,\vec v_1)\in U\). There are a neighbourhood \(W\) of \((\vec u_1,\vec v_1)\) and \(\varepsilon>0\) such that for each \((\vec u_0,\vec v_0)\in W\) the equation \(\frac{d^2\vec u}{dt^2}=\vec F(\vec u,\frac{d\vec u}{dt})\) has a unique solution \(t\mapsto\vec u(t)\), \(|t|<\varepsilon\), with \((\vec u(t),\vec u\,'(t))\in U\), \(\vec u(0)=\vec u_0\), \(\vec u\,'(0)=\vec v_0\); and \((\vec u_0,\vec v_0,t)\mapsto\vec u(t)\) is \(C^\infty\) on \(W\times(-\varepsilon,\varepsilon)\).

Proof. With \(\vec v=\frac{d\vec u}{dt}\) the equation becomes the first-order system \(\frac{d\vec u}{dt}=\vec v\), \(\frac{d\vec v}{dt}=\vec F(\vec u,\vec v)\), i.e. \(x'=G(x)\) with \(G(\vec u,\vec v)=(\vec v,\vec F(\vec u,\vec v))\) smooth on \(U\). We quote the standard theorem for such systems (Picard–Lindelöf with smooth dependence on initial conditions): for \(G\) smooth on an open \(U\subseteq\mathbb R^m\) and \(x_1\in U\) there are a neighbourhood \(W\) of \(x_1\) and \(\varepsilon>0\) such that for \(x_0\in W\) a solution \(x:(-\varepsilon,\varepsilon)\to U\) with \(x(0)=x_0\) exists, \((x_0,t)\mapsto x(t)\) is \(C^\infty\), and two solutions with the same value at \(0\) agree on their common interval of definition. (Milnor cites Graves, The Theory of Functions of Real Variables, p. 166; see also Hartman, Ordinary Differential Equations, Ch. V, or Lee, Introduction to Smooth Manifolds, 2nd ed., Appendix D. The same facts are quoted, in global Lipschitz form, in Chapter 4 of the companion volume, Topology from the Differentiable Viewpoint, rewritten.) \(\square\)

Theorem 10.1 asserts uniqueness only inside one chart. Milnor’s repeated “the unique geodesic” needs uniqueness in the large.

Lemma A (uniqueness in the large). Let \(\gamma_1,\gamma_2:I\to M\) be geodesics on the same interval with \(\gamma_1(t_0)=\gamma_2(t_0)\) and \(\gamma_1'(t_0)=\gamma_2'(t_0)\) for some \(t_0\in I\). Then \(\gamma_1=\gamma_2\).

Proof. \(J=\{t:\gamma_1(t)=\gamma_2(t),\ \gamma_1'(t)=\gamma_2'(t)\}\ni t_0\) is closed in \(I\), as the set where two continuous maps into the Hausdorff space \(TM\) agree. It is open: near \(t_1\in J\) both curves lie in one chart and solve (1) with the same data at \(t_1\), so they agree near \(t_1\) by the uniqueness clause of Theorem 10.1. As \(I\) is connected, \(J=I\). \(\square\)

A hidden hypothesis. Hausdorff is essential. On the line with two origins (two copies of \(\mathbb R\) glued along \(\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}\)), with the flat metric, the curves \(t\mapsto t\) through the two origins are geodesics that agree for \(t<0\) and differ at \(t=0\).

Lemma 10.2. (checked by machine: V7.6, in a stronger form) For every \(p_0\in M\) there are a neighbourhood \(U\) of \(p_0\) and \(\varepsilon>0\) such that for each \(p\in U\) and each \(v\in TM_p\) with \(\|v\|<\varepsilon\) there is a unique geodesic \(\gamma_v:(-2,2)\to M\) with \(\gamma_v(0)=p\), \(\frac{d\gamma_v}{dt}(0)=v\). Moreover \((p,v,t)\mapsto\gamma_v(t)\) is smooth.

Proof. Take a chart \(u:U_0\to\mathbb R^n\) around \(p_0\) and apply Theorem 10.1 to \(\vec F(\vec u,\vec v)=-\big(\sum_{i,j}\Gamma^k_{ij}(\vec u)v^iv^j\big)_{k}\) on \(u(U_0)\times\mathbb R^n\) at \((u(p_0),0)\); call the resulting time \(2\varepsilon_2\). Choose \(a,b>0\) with \(\bar B(u(p_0),a)\subseteq u(U_0)\) and \(B(u(p_0),a)\times B(0,b)\subseteq W\). The smallest eigenvalue of the positive definite matrix \((g_{ij}(\vec u))\) is continuous, so it has a positive minimum \(\lambda\) on the compact ball \(\bar B(u(p_0),a)\), where therefore \(\|v\|^2=\sum g_{ij}v^iv^j\ge\lambda|\vec v|^2\). Put \(U=u^{-1}B(u(p_0),a)\) and \(\varepsilon_1=b\sqrt\lambda\). For \(p\in U\) and \(\|v\|<\varepsilon_1\) the coordinates of \((p,v)\) lie in \(W\), so Theorem 10.1 gives a geodesic with initial velocity \(v\) on \((-2\varepsilon_2,2\varepsilon_2)\), staying in the chart, smooth in \((p,v,t)\), and unique by Lemma A. Now fix \(0<\varepsilon<\varepsilon_1\varepsilon_2\). If \(\|v\|<\varepsilon\) and \(|t|<2\), then \(\|v/\varepsilon_2\|<\varepsilon_1\) and \(|\varepsilon_2t|<2\varepsilon_2\), so \[\gamma_v(t):=\gamma_{v/\varepsilon_2}(\varepsilon_2t)\] is defined. It is a geodesic by homogeneity, with initial velocity \(\varepsilon_2\cdot v/\varepsilon_2=v\), smooth in \((p,v,t)\), and unique by Lemma A. \(\square\)

Milnor’s text skips… the comparison \(\|v\|^2\ge\lambda|\vec v|^2\) on a compact coordinate ball, needed to turn the neighbourhood \(W\) of Theorem 10.1 into “\(p\in U\), \(\|v\|<\varepsilon_1\)”.

Definition (the exponential). Let \(v\in TM_q\). If there is a geodesic \(\gamma:[0,1]\to M\) with \(\gamma(0)=q\), \(\frac{d\gamma}{dt}(0)=v\), then \(\exp_q(v):=\gamma(1)\), the exponential of \(v\). By Lemma A there is at most one such \(\gamma\), so \(\exp_q(v)\), if defined at all, is uniquely defined. For \(0\le t\le1\) the curve \(s\mapsto\gamma(ts)\) is a geodesic on \([0,1]\) with initial velocity \(tv\), so \[\gamma(t)=\exp_q(tv),\qquad0\le t\le1.\] By Lemma 10.2, \(\exp_q(v)\) is defined when \(\|v\|\) is small, uniformly for \(q\) near a given point; in general not for large \(v\). Milnor’s footnote explains the name: on the unitary group, \(\exp_I\) is the matrix exponential. That depends on the metric; see §6.

2. The exponential map and uniformly normal neighbourhoods (Milnor pp. 58–59)

Definition. \(M\) is geodesically complete if \(\exp_q(v)\) is defined for all \(q\in M\) and \(v\in TM_q\).

To compare this with Milnor’s reformulation, and to know that \(\exp\) is smooth wherever it is defined (needed in Corollary 10.10), we use the global ODE theorem.

Fact (flows). Let \(G\) be a smooth vector field on a manifold \(N\). There are an open set \(\mathcal D\subseteq\mathbb R\times N\) containing \(\{0\}\times N\) and a smooth map \(\theta:\mathcal D\to N\) such that for each \(x\in N\), \(\{t:(t,x)\in\mathcal D\}\) is an open interval and \(t\mapsto\theta(t,x)\) is an integral curve of \(G\) starting at \(x\) that extends every other one. (Lee, Introduction to Smooth Manifolds, 2nd ed., Theorem 9.12.)

Lemma B (the geodesic flow). (i) Every geodesic extends to a unique maximal geodesic, defined on an open interval. (ii) The set \(\mathcal E\subseteq TM\) of \((q,v)\) for which \(\exp_q(v)\) is defined is open and contains all zero vectors, and \(\exp:\mathcal E\to M\) is smooth.

Proof. Over a chart domain \(U\), with coordinates \((u,v)\) on \(TU\) (described below), let \[G_U=\sum_kv^k\frac{\partial}{\partial u^k}-\sum_k\Big(\sum_{i,j}\Gamma^k_{ij}(u)v^iv^j\Big) \frac{\partial}{\partial v^k}.\] Its integral curves are the \((u(t),v(t))\) with \(v=\frac{du}{dt}\) and \(u\) solving (1): the lifts \((\gamma,\gamma')\) of geodesics in \(U\). Through a point of \(TU\cap TU'\) the integral curves of \(G_U\) and \(G_{U'}\) are lifts of geodesics with the same initial data, equal for small \(t\) by Lemma A, so \(G_U=G_{U'}\) there. Thus the \(G_U\) form one smooth vector field \(G\) on \(TM\), the geodesic spray, whose integral curves are the lifts of geodesics. Apply the Fact. (i) A geodesic lifts into a maximal integral curve, whose projection is the maximal geodesic; uniqueness by Lemma A. (ii) \((q,v)\in\mathcal E\) iff \((1,(q,v))\in\mathcal D\), an open condition, and \(\exp=\pi\circ\theta(1, \cdot)\) with \(\pi:TM\to M\) the projection. \(\square\)

Milnor’s reformulation: \(M\) is geodesically complete iff every geodesic segment \(\gamma_0:[a,b]\to M\) extends to a geodesic \(\gamma:\mathbb R\to M\). Suppose \(\exp\) is defined everywhere and let \(\gamma:(\alpha,\beta)\to M\) be the maximal geodesic extending \(\gamma_0\). If \(\beta<\infty\), choose \(T>\beta-a\); with \(q=\gamma_0(a)\), \(v=\gamma_0'(a)\) there is a geodesic \(\sigma:[0,1]\to M\) with initial velocity \(Tv\), and \(t\mapsto\sigma((t-a)/T)\) is a geodesic on \([a,a+T]\) with the data of \(\gamma\) at \(a\). By Lemma A and maximality, \([a,a+T]\subseteq(\alpha, \beta)\), contradicting \(a+T>\beta\). Likewise \(\alpha=-\infty\). Conversely, a geodesic with initial velocity \(v\) exists on a short interval (rescale Lemma 10.2); extended to \(\mathbb R\) and restricted to \([0,1]\), it shows \(\exp_q(v)\) is defined.

The tangent manifold. A chart \(u^1,\dots,u^n\) on \(U\subseteq M\) gives coordinates \((u^1,\dots,u^n,t^1,\dots,t^n)\) on \(TU\), where \(v=\sum t^i\partial_i\). A change of chart \(\tilde u=\varphi(u)\) gives \((u,t)\mapsto(\varphi(u),D\varphi(u)t)\), smooth; so \(TM\) is a smooth \(2n\)-manifold, Hausdorff and second countable.

By Lemma 10.2, for each \(p\in M\), \((q,v)\mapsto\exp_q(v)=\gamma_v(1)\) is defined and smooth on the neighbourhood \(V=\{(q,v):q\in U,\ \|v\|<\varepsilon\}\) of \((p,0)\). Consider \[F:V\to M\times M,\qquad F(q,v)=(q,\exp_q(v)).\] In coordinates \((u,t)\) on \(TU\) and \((u_1,u_2)\) on \(U\times U\), \(F(u,t)=(u,E(u,t))\). As \(\exp_q(0)=q\), \(E(u,0)=u\) and \(\partial E/\partial u=I\) at \(t=0\); as \(t\mapsto\exp_q(tv)\) has velocity \(v\) at \(t=0\), \(d(\exp_q)_0\) is the identity and \(\partial E/\partial t=I\) at \(t=0\). So \[F_*\Big(\frac{\partial}{\partial u^i}\Big)=\frac{\partial}{\partial u_1^i}+\frac{\partial}{\partial u_2^i},\qquad F_*\Big(\frac{\partial}{\partial t^j}\Big)=\frac{\partial}{\partial u_2^j},\] and the Jacobian \(\begin{pmatrix}I&0\\I&I\end{pmatrix}\) (Milnor prints its transpose) is nonsingular. By the inverse function theorem on manifolds (Milnor says “implicit”; it is proved from the Euclidean one in Chapter 1, Theorem 4.1, of the companion volume, and the proof works verbatim in charts), \(F\) maps a neighbourhood \(V''\) of \((p,0)\) diffeomorphically onto a neighbourhood of \((p,p)\). The sets \(V(U',\varepsilon')=\{(q,v):q\in U',\ \|v\|<\varepsilon'\}\), \(U'\) an open neighbourhood of \(p\), are open and form a neighbourhood base of \((p,0)\) in \(TM\): by \(\|v\|^2\ge\lambda|t|^2\), the coordinate box \(\{u\in B(u(p),a'),|t|<b'\}\) contains \(V(u^{-1}B(u(p),a'),b'\sqrt\lambda)\). So choose \(V'=V(U',\varepsilon)\subseteq V''\) (a new \(\varepsilon\)) and a neighbourhood \(W\subseteq U'\) of \(p\) with \(W\times W\subseteq F(V')\).

Lemma 10.3. (checked by machine: V7.9, V7.10, restated) For each \(p\in M\) there are a neighbourhood \(W\) of \(p\) and \(\varepsilon>0\) such that:

  1. any two points \(q_1,q_2\) of \(W\) are joined by a unique geodesic \(\gamma:[0,1]\to M\) of length \(<\varepsilon\);
  2. this geodesic depends smoothly on the two points: \(\gamma(t)=\exp_{q_1}(tv)\), and \((q_1,q_2)\mapsto(q_1,v)\in TM\) is smooth on \(W\times W\);
  3. for each \(q\in W\), \(\exp_q\) maps the open \(\varepsilon\)-ball \(B_\varepsilon(q)=\{v\in TM_q: \|v\|<\varepsilon\}\) diffeomorphically onto an open set \(U_q\supseteq W\).

Proof. Take \(W,\varepsilon,V'\) as above. (1) As \(F\) keeps the first coordinate, \((q_1,q_2)\in F(V')\) gives \((q_1,q_2)=F(q_1,v)\) with \(\|v\|<\varepsilon\), and \(t\mapsto \exp_{q_1}(tv)\) is a geodesic from \(q_1\) to \(q_2\) of length \(\|v\|\). If \(\sigma:[0,1]\to M\) is a geodesic from \(q_1\) to \(q_2\) with \(L(\sigma)<\varepsilon\) and \(w=\sigma'(0)\), then \(\|w\|=L(\sigma)<\varepsilon\), so \((q_1,w)\in V'\) and \(F(q_1,w)=F(q_1,v)\); injectivity gives \(w=v\), and \(\sigma=\gamma\) by Lemma A. (2) \((q_1,v)=(F|_{V'})^{-1}(q_1,q_2)\). (3) For \(q\in W\), \(\exp_q|B_\varepsilon(q)\) is \(v\mapsto\mathrm{pr}_2F(q,v)\), injective; its image \(U_q=\{q':(q,q')\in F(V')\}\) is open and contains \(W\); its inverse \(q'\mapsto\mathrm{pr}_2(F|_{V'})^{-1}(q,q')\) is smooth. \(\square\)

Call \(\varepsilon>0\) a normal radius at \(q\) if \(\exp_q\) is defined on \(B_\varepsilon(q)\) and maps it diffeomorphically onto an open set \(U_q\); by item 3 (at \(p=q\)) every point has one. For \(0<s<\varepsilon\) write \[\mathcal B_s(q)=\exp_qB_s(q),\qquad\bar{\mathcal B}_s(q)=\exp_q\bar B_s(q),\qquad S_s(q)=\exp_q\{v:\|v\|=s\},\] the normal ball, its closed version and the spherical shell of radius \(s\). \(\mathcal B_s(q)\) is open; \(\bar{\mathcal B}_s(q)\) is compact, hence closed in the Hausdorff space \(M\), so it contains the closure of \(\mathcal B_s(q)\); and \(\bar{\mathcal B}_s(q)\setminus\mathcal B_s(q)=S_s(q)\).

Remark (Milnor). With more care \(W\) can be chosen so that the geodesic of length \(<\varepsilon\) joining any two of its points lies in \(W\) (J. H. C. Whitehead, Convex regions in the geometry of paths, Quart. J. Math. Oxford 3 (1932), 33–42). The book does not use this; it is proved in §4.

3. Short geodesics are shortest: the Gauss lemma (Milnor pp. 59–61)

Theorem 10.4. (checked by machine: V7.15, V7.16, in a stronger form) Let \(W\) and \(\varepsilon\) be as in Lemma 10.3, let \(\gamma:[0,1]\to M\) be the geodesic of length \(<\varepsilon\) joining two points of \(W\), and let \(\omega:[0,1]\to M\) be any piecewise smooth path joining the same two points. Then \[\int_0^1\Big\|\frac{d\gamma}{dt}\Big\|\,dt\le\int_0^1\Big\|\frac{d\omega}{dt}\Big\|\,dt,\] and if equality holds, \(\omega=\gamma\circ\rho\) for a continuous nondecreasing surjection \(\rho:[0,1]\to[0,1]\); in particular \(\omega([0,1])=\gamma([0,1])\). Thus \(\gamma\) is the shortest path joining its endpoints.

Milnor’s equality clause says only that the point sets coincide; Corollary 10.7 needs the sharper form. In the two lemmas below, \(\varepsilon\) is a normal radius at \(q\) (for \(q\in W\), the \(\varepsilon\) of 10.3 is one).

Lemma 10.5 (Gauss). (checked by machine: V7.12, in a stronger form) In \(U_q\), the geodesics through \(q\) are the orthogonal trajectories of the hypersurfaces \(S_r(q)=\{\exp_q(v):\|v\|=r\}\), \(0<r<\varepsilon\).

These are hypersurfaces since \(\exp_q\) is a diffeomorphism on \(B_\varepsilon(q)\), and each tangent vector of \(S_{r_0}(q)\) at \(\exp_q(r_0v_0)\) is \(\frac{d}{dt}\exp_q(r_0v(t))|_{t=0}\) for a smooth curve \(v(t)\) on the unit sphere of \(TM_q\) with \(v(0)=v_0\). So the claim is that for every such curve the curves \(t\mapsto\exp_q(r_0v(t))\) are orthogonal to the radial geodesics \(r\mapsto\exp_q(rv(t_0))\).

Proof. Let \(f(r,t)=\exp_q(rv(t))\), \(|r|<\varepsilon\), a smooth parametrized surface. By Lemma 8.3, \[\frac{\partial}{\partial r}\Big\langle\frac{\partial f}{\partial r},\frac{\partial f}{\partial t} \Big\rangle=\Big\langle\frac{D}{\partial r}\frac{\partial f}{\partial r},\frac{\partial f}{\partial t}\Big\rangle+\Big\langle\frac{\partial f}{\partial r},\frac{D}{\partial r}\frac{\partial f} {\partial t}\Big\rangle.\] The first term vanishes because \(r\mapsto f(r,t)\) is a geodesic. By the symmetry Lemma 8.7, \(\frac{D}{\partial r}\frac{\partial f}{\partial t}=\frac{D}{\partial t}\frac{\partial f}{\partial r}\), so the second term is \[\Big\langle\frac{\partial f}{\partial r},\frac{D}{\partial t}\frac{\partial f}{\partial r}\Big \rangle=\frac12\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\Big\langle\frac{\partial f}{\partial r},\frac{\partial f} {\partial r}\Big\rangle=0,\] since \(\|\frac{\partial f}{\partial r}\|\) is the constant speed \(\|v(t)\|=1\) of the geodesic \(r\mapsto\exp_q(rv(t))\). Hence \(\langle\frac{\partial f}{\partial r},\frac{\partial f}{\partial t} \rangle\) does not depend on \(r\). At \(r=0\), \(f(0,t)=q\) for all \(t\), so \(\frac{\partial f}{\partial t} (0,t)=0\). Therefore \(\langle\frac{\partial f}{\partial r},\frac{\partial f}{\partial t}\rangle\equiv0\). \(\square\)

Polar coordinates. For piecewise smooth \(\omega:[a,b]\to U_q\setminus\{q\}\), the functions \(w(t)=\exp_q^{-1}\omega(t)\ne0\), \(r(t)=\|w(t)\|\in(0,\varepsilon)\) and \(v(t)=w(t)/r(t)\) are piecewise smooth (the norm is smooth away from \(0\)), and \(\omega(t)=\exp_q(r(t)v(t))\) uniquely.

Lemma 10.6. (checked by machine: V7.13, in a narrower form) \(\int_a^b\|\frac{d\omega}{dt}\|\,dt\ge|r(b)-r(a)|\), with equality only if \(r(t)\) is monotone and \(v(t)\) is constant. Thus the shortest path joining two concentric spherical shells around \(q\) is a radial geodesic.

Proof. On each smooth piece, with \(f(r,t)=\exp_q(rv(t))\), \(\omega(t)=f(r(t),t)\) and \[\frac{d\omega}{dt}=\frac{\partial f}{\partial r}\,r'(t)+\frac{\partial f}{\partial t}.\] The terms are orthogonal (Lemma 10.5) and \(\|\frac{\partial f}{\partial r}\|=1\), so \[\Big\|\frac{d\omega}{dt}\Big\|^2=|r'(t)|^2+\Big\|\frac{\partial f}{\partial t}\Big\|^2\ge |r'(t)|^2,\] with equality only where \(\frac{\partial f}{\partial t}=d(\exp_q)_{rv}(r\,v'(t))=0\), i.e. (as \(d(\exp_q)_{rv}\) is injective and \(r>0\)) where \(v'(t)=0\). Hence \[\int_a^b\Big\|\frac{d\omega}{dt}\Big\|\,dt\ge\int_a^b|r'(t)|\,dt\ge\Big|\int_a^br'(t)\,dt\Big|= |r(b)-r(a)|.\] If equality holds throughout, then on each piece the continuous functions \(\|\omega'\|-|r'|\ge0\) and \(|r'|\mp r'\ge0\) (sign of \(r(b)-r(a)\)) have integral \(0\), so vanish: \(v'=0\) on every piece, so the continuous \(v\) is constant, and \(r'\) has one sign, so \(r\) is monotone. \(\square\)

Milnor’s proof of 10.4 then asserts that the path contains a segment running from the shell of radius \(\delta\) to the shell of radius \(r\) and lying between the two. But a competing path may leave \(U_q\) and come back; the assertion holds because closed normal balls are closed in \(M\).

Lemma C (crossing the shells). Let \(0<\delta<r<\varepsilon\) and let \(\omega:[a,b]\to M\) be piecewise smooth with \(\omega(a)\in\bar{\mathcal B}_\delta(q)\) and \(\omega(b)\notin\mathcal B_r(q)\). Then there are \(a\le t_1<t_2\le b\) with \(\omega(t_1)\in S_\delta(q)\), \(\omega(t_2)\in S_r(q)\) and \(\omega([t_1,t_2])\subseteq\bar{\mathcal B}_r(q)\setminus\mathcal B_\delta(q)\). Consequently \(L(\omega)\ge r-\delta\), and every path from \(q\) to a point outside \(\mathcal B_r(q)\) has length \(\ge r\).

Proof. Let \(t_1\) be the largest \(t\) with \(\omega(t)\in\bar{\mathcal B}_\delta(q)\) (a closed set); \(t_1<b\). If \(\omega(t_1)\) lay in the open set \(\mathcal B_\delta(q)\), so would \(\omega(t)\) for \(t\) slightly larger; so \(\omega(t_1)\in S_\delta(q)\). Let \(t_2\) be the least \(t\ge t_1\) with \(\omega(t)\notin\mathcal B_r(q)\) (a closed set containing \(b\)); \(t_2>t_1\). As \(\omega(t)\in \mathcal B_r(q)\) for \(t_1\le t<t_2\), \(\omega(t_2)\) lies in the closure of \(\mathcal B_r(q)\), inside \(\bar{\mathcal B}_r(q)\), hence in \(S_r(q)\). On \([t_1,t_2]\) the path stays in \(\bar{\mathcal B}_r(q) \setminus\mathcal B_\delta(q)\subseteq U_q\setminus\{q\}\), with \(r(t_1)=\delta\), \(r(t_2)=r\), so Lemma 10.6 gives \(L(\omega)\ge r-\delta\). For paths from \(q\), let \(\delta\to0\). \(\square\)

Proof of Theorem 10.4. Let \(q=\gamma(0)\), \(\gamma(t)=\exp_q(tw)\) with \(\|w\|=L(\gamma)< \varepsilon\), and \(q'=\gamma(1)\). If \(w=0\) all is trivial (equality forces \(\omega\) constant). Otherwise \(r=\|w\|\) and \(q'=\exp_q(rv)\) with \(v=w/r\), so \(q'\in S_r(q)\), \(q'\notin\mathcal B_r(q)\), and Lemma C gives \(L(\omega)\ge r=L(\gamma)\).

Suppose \(L(\omega)=r\). Let \(T_0\) be the last time with \(\omega(T_0)=q\) and \(T_1\) the first time after \(T_0\) with \(\omega(T_1)\notin\mathcal B_r(q)\); as in Lemma C, \(\omega(T_1)\in S_r(q)\) and \(\omega(t)\in\mathcal B_r(q)\setminus\{q\}\) for \(T_0<t<T_1\). In polar coordinates on \((T_0,T_1]\), \(r(t)\to0\) as \(t\downarrow T_0\) and \(r(T_1)=r\). For \(T_0<s'<s<T_1\) Lemma 10.6 gives \(L(\omega|[s',s])\ge r(s)-r(s')\) and \(L(\omega|[s,T_1])\ge r-r(s)\); letting \(s'\downarrow T_0\), \(L(\omega|[T_0,s])\ge r(s)\). Adding, \[r=L(\omega)\ge L(\omega|[0,T_0])+r(s)+\big(r-r(s)\big)+L(\omega|[T_1,1]).\] So \(\omega\) has length \(0\), hence is constant, on \([0,T_0]\) and \([T_1,1]\), and \(L(\omega|[s,T_1])=r-r(s)\) for all \(s\in(T_0,T_1)\). By the equality case of Lemma 10.6, \(v\) is constant on \((T_0,T_1]\) and \(r\) is nondecreasing there. Then \(\exp_q(rv(T_1))=\omega(T_1)=q'= \exp_q(rv)\) gives \(v(T_1)=v\). Thus \(\omega(t)=\gamma(r(t)/r)\) on \((T_0,T_1]\), \(\omega=\gamma(0)\) on \([0,T_0]\), \(\omega=\gamma(1)\) on \([T_1,1]\): \(\omega=\gamma\circ\rho\). \(\square\)

Milnor’s text skips… that a competing path may leave \(U_q\), so the shell-crossing step needs Lemma C; and “we easily obtain a strict inequality” is the equality analysis above (last visit to \(q\), first arrival at \(S_r(q)\)).

Corollary 10.7. (checked by machine: V7.17, in a stronger form) Suppose a path \(\omega:[0,\ell]\to M\), parametrized by arc length (piecewise smooth, \(\|\omega'\|=1\) on each piece), has length less than or equal to that of any other path from \(\omega(0)\) to \(\omega(\ell)\). Then \(\omega\) is a geodesic; in particular it is smooth.

Proof. Every segment \(\omega|[\alpha,\beta]\) is shortest between its endpoints, since a shorter path between them, inserted in place of the segment, would shorten \(\omega\). Fix \(t_*\in[0,\ell]\), take \(W,\varepsilon\) from Lemma 10.3 for \(\omega(t_*)\), and a neighbourhood \([\alpha,\beta]\) of \(t_*\) in \([0,\ell]\) with \(\omega([\alpha,\beta])\subseteq W\), \(\beta-\alpha<\varepsilon\). Let \(\gamma\) be the geodesic of length \(<\varepsilon\) from \(\omega(\alpha)\) to \(\omega(\beta)\). By 10.4, \(L(\gamma)\le\beta-\alpha\); by minimality of the segment, \(\beta-\alpha\le L(\gamma)\). So equality holds, and the proof of 10.4 gives, with \(q=\omega(\alpha)\): \(\omega\) is constant on \([\alpha,T_0]\) and \([T_1,\beta]\), so \(T_0=\alpha\), \(T_1=\beta\) by unit speed; and on \((\alpha,\beta]\), \(\omega(t)=\exp_q(r(t)v)\) with \(v\) fixed, \(r\) nondecreasing and \(\|\omega'\|=|r'|=1\), so \(r'=1\) on each piece and \(r(t)=t-\alpha\). Thus \(\omega(t)=\exp_q((t-\alpha)v)\) on \([\alpha,\beta]\), a geodesic, smooth even at a break point \(t_*\). Every \(t_*\) has such a neighbourhood. \(\square\)

Milnor’s text skips… that equal point sets do not make \(\omega\) a geodesic (a path running along \(\gamma\) at varying speed has the same image). One needs the monotone reparametrization, the unit speed, minimality of sub-paths, and segments containing the break points in their interiors.

Definition. A geodesic \(\gamma:[a,b]\to M\) is minimal if its length is at most that of any other piecewise smooth path joining its endpoints.

By Theorem 10.4 every sufficiently small segment of a geodesic is minimal: a short segment around \(\gamma(t_*)\) lies in the \(W\) of Lemma 10.3 for \(\gamma(t_*)\) and has length \(<\varepsilon\), so it is the geodesic of 10.3(1). A long geodesic need not be minimal: a great-circle arc on the unit sphere is a geodesic (§6), and if its length \(\ell\) exceeds \(\pi\) the complementary arc joins the same endpoints with length \(2\pi-\ell<\ell\). Minimal geodesics need not be unique: antipodal points of the sphere are joined by infinitely many (§6).

4. The Riemannian distance (Milnor p. 62)

Definition. The distance \(\rho(p,q)\) is the greatest lower bound of the lengths of piecewise smooth paths from \(p\) to \(q\).

Milnor calls the metric property clear, and says that compatibility with the topology of \(M\) “follows easily from 10.4”. The first claim needs Lemma C.

Proposition D. (i) \(\rho\) is a metric. (ii) If \(\varepsilon\) is a normal radius at \(p\) and \(0<r\le\varepsilon\), the metric ball \(\{q:\rho(p,q)<r\}\) equals \(\mathcal B_r(p)\), and points of \(S_s(p)\), \(0<s<\varepsilon\), are at distance exactly \(s\) from \(p\). (iii) The metric topology is the manifold topology, and \(\rho\) is continuous on \(M\times M\).

Proof. (i) Finiteness: the points joined to \(p\) by a piecewise smooth path form an open set (straight segments in a coordinate ball are smooth paths) with open complement, so all of the connected \(M\). Symmetry, triangle inequality, \(\rho(p,p)=0\): reverse and concatenate paths; use the constant path. Positivity: for \(p\ne q\) and a normal radius \(\varepsilon\) at \(p\), take \(r\in(0,\varepsilon)\) arbitrary if \(q\notin U_p\), and \(r=\|w\|\) if \(q=\exp_p(w)\), \(0<\|w\|< \varepsilon\). Then \(q\notin\mathcal B_r(p)\), and Lemma C gives \(\rho(p,q)\ge r>0\).

  1. For \(q=\exp_p(w)\), \(\|w\|<r\), the radial geodesic has length \(<r\). For \(r<\varepsilon\) and \(q\notin\mathcal B_r(p)\), Lemma C gives \(\rho(p,q)\ge r\). For \(r=\varepsilon\) take the union. A point of \(S_s(p)\) is at distance \(\le s\) (radial geodesic) and \(\ge s\) (Lemma C).

  2. A \(\rho\)-open set contains around each point \(p\) some \(\mathcal B_r(p)\), open in \(M\). If \(N\ni p\) is open in \(M\), then \(\exp_p^{-1}(N\cap U_p)\) contains some \(B_r(p)\), so \(N\) contains the metric ball \(\mathcal B_r(p)\). Finally \(|\rho(x,y)-\rho(x',y')|\le\rho(x,x')+\rho(y,y')\). \(\square\)

Corollary 10.8. (checked by machine: V7.20, restated) Given a compact set \(K\subseteq M\) there is \(\delta>0\) such that any two points of \(K\) with distance less than \(\delta\) are joined by a unique geodesic of length less than \(\delta\). This geodesic is minimal, and depends differentiably on its endpoints.

Proof. Take \((W_p,\varepsilon_p)\) from Lemma 10.3 for each \(p\in K\), and \(W_{p_1},\dots,W_{p_m}\) covering \(K\). By Proposition D, \(K\) is a compact metric space, so the cover has a Lebesgue number \(\lambda>0\). Let \(\delta=\min(\lambda,\varepsilon_{p_1},\dots,\varepsilon_{p_m})\). If \(x,y\in K\), \(\rho(x,y)<\delta\), they lie in some \(W_{p_j}\), and 10.3 gives a geodesic \(\gamma\) from \(x\) to \(y\) of length \(<\varepsilon_{p_j}\), minimal by 10.4, so \(L(\gamma)=\rho(x,y)<\delta\). A geodesic from \(x\) to \(y\) of length \(<\delta\le\varepsilon_{p_j}\) equals \(\gamma\) by 10.3(1). The initial vector of \(\gamma\) is the smooth map of 10.3(2) on each \(W_{p_j}\times W_{p_j}\); these agree on overlaps by uniqueness, so \((x,y)\mapsto\gamma'(0)\) is smooth on the open set \(\bigcup_j\{(x,y)\in W_{p_j}\times W_{p_j}:\rho(x,y)<\delta\}\), which contains all pairs in \(K\) at distance \(<\delta\). \(\square\)

Milnor’s text skips… the finite subcover and \(\delta\le\min_j\varepsilon_{p_j}\), without which uniqueness does not follow from 10.3; “differentiably” means smoothness on an open set of pairs.

Proof of the Remark after Lemma 10.3 (convex neighbourhoods). Fix \(p\), its \(W,\varepsilon\), and normal coordinates \(x\) on \(U_p\), \(x(\exp_p\sum_ix^ie_i)=(x^1,\dots,x^n)\) for an orthonormal basis \((e_i)\) of \(TM_p\). Then \(\mathcal B_s(p)=\{|x|<s\}\) and \(|x(y)|=\rho(p,y)\) (Proposition D). Let \(\Gamma(x)\) be the bilinear map \((a,b)\mapsto(\sum_{i,j}\Gamma^k_{ij}(x)a^ib^j)_k\), \(C\) the maximum of its norm over \(|x|\le\varepsilon/2\), and \(r_0=\min(\varepsilon/2,1/(2C))\) (\(\varepsilon/2\) if \(C=0\)). For a nonconstant geodesic with coordinates \(x(t)\), \(|x(t)|<r_0\), we have \(x'\ne0\) and by (1) \[\frac{d^2}{dt^2}|x|^2=2|x'|^2+2\langle x,x''\rangle=2|x'|^2-2\langle x,\Gamma(x)(x',x')\rangle\ge 2|x'|^2(1-C|x|)\ge|x'|^2>0,\] so \(\rho(p,\cdot)^2\) is strictly convex along it. Choose \(s>0\) with \(3s\le r_0\) and \(\mathcal B_s(p) \subseteq W\), and let \(W'=\mathcal B_s(p)\). For \(q_1,q_2\in W'\) the geodesic \(\gamma\) of length \(<\varepsilon\) joining them is minimal, so \(L(\gamma)=\rho(q_1,q_2)<2s\) and \(\gamma\) stays within distance \(<3s\le r_0\) of \(p\). Along \(\gamma\), \(\rho(p,\cdot)^2\) is convex and \(<s^2\) at both ends, hence \(<s^2\) throughout: \(\gamma\subseteq W'\). Items 1–3 of 10.3 still hold for \(W'\subseteq W\). \(\square\)

5. Completeness: the Hopf–Rinow theorem (Milnor pp. 62–64)

Theorem 10.9 (Hopf and Rinow). (checked by machine: V7.26, in a stronger form) If \(M\) is geodesically complete, then any two points can be joined by a minimal geodesic.

(Milnor cites G. de Rham, Sur la réductibilité d’un espace de Riemann, Comment. Math. Helv. 26 (1952), p. 341, and H. Hopf and W. Rinow, Über den Begriff der vollständigen differentialgeometrischen Fläche, Comment. Math. Helv. 3 (1931), 209–225.)

Proof. Let \(p,q\in M\) with \(r=\rho(p,q)>0\) (if \(p=q\) use a constant geodesic). Let \(\varepsilon\) be a normal radius at \(p\), fix \(0<\delta<\min(\varepsilon,r)\), and let \(S=S_\delta(p)\).

Step 1: \(\rho(p,q)=\delta+\min_{s\in S}\rho(s,q)\). As \(\rho(p,q)>\delta\), \(q\notin\mathcal B_\delta(p)\) (Proposition D). For a path \(\omega\) from \(p\) to \(q\), the first \(t\) with \(\omega(t) \notin\mathcal B_\delta(p)\) has \(\omega(t)\) in the closure of \(\mathcal B_\delta(p)\), hence in \(S\): every path from \(p\) to \(q\) passes through \(S\). Splitting there, and using \(\rho(p,s)=\delta\) on \(S\), \(L(\omega)\ge\delta+\rho(\omega(t),q)\ge\delta+\inf_S\rho(\cdot,q)\); the reverse inequality is the triangle inequality. \(S\) is compact and \(\rho(\cdot,q)\) continuous, so the infimum is attained at some \(p_0=\exp_p(\delta v)\), \(\|v\|=1\), and \(\rho(p_0,q)=r-\delta\).

Step 2: the moving point gets closer. By completeness \(\gamma(t)=\exp_p(tv)\) is defined for all \(t\ge0\), a unit-speed geodesic with \(\gamma(\delta)=p_0\). We show that for every \(t\in[\delta,r]\) \[\rho(\gamma(t),q)=r-t.\qquad(1_t)\] Step 1 is \((1_\delta)\). The set of \(t\in[\delta,r]\) with \((1_t)\) is closed, as \(t\mapsto\rho(\gamma(t) ,q)\) is continuous; let \(t_0\) be its largest element and suppose \(t_0<r\). Take a normal radius \(\varepsilon'\) at \(\gamma(t_0)\), \(0<\delta'<\min(\varepsilon',r-t_0)\), \(S'=S_{\delta'}(\gamma(t_0))\), and \(p_0'\in S'\) nearest to \(q\) (Milnor’s Diagram 10). As \(\rho(\gamma(t_0),q)=r-t_0>\delta'\), Step 1 at \(\gamma(t_0)\) gives \(\rho(\gamma(t_0),q)=\delta'+\rho(p_0',q)\), so \[\rho(p_0',q)=(r-t_0)-\delta'.\qquad(2)\] Then \(\rho(p,p_0')\ge\rho(p,q)-\rho(p_0',q)=t_0+\delta'\). But following \(\gamma\) from \(p\) to \(\gamma(t_0)\) and then the radial geodesic to \(p_0'\), both at unit speed, is a broken geodesic of length exactly \(t_0+\delta'\): a shortest path parametrized by arc length, hence by Corollary 10.7 an unbroken geodesic \(\sigma\). As \(\sigma=\gamma\) on \([0,t_0]\) with \(t_0>0\), they share the velocity at \(t_0\), and Lemma A gives \(\sigma=\gamma\) on \([0,t_0+\delta']\). So \(p_0'=\gamma(t_0+\delta')\), and (2) is \((1_{t_0+\delta'})\) with \(t_0<t_0+\delta'\le r\), a contradiction. Hence \(t_0=r\).

Conclusion. \((1_r)\) gives \(\gamma(r)=q\), and \(\gamma|[0,r]\) has length \(r=\rho(p,q)\): a minimal geodesic. \(\square\)

Milnor’s text skips… that \(\delta\) must also be smaller than \(\rho(p,q)\) (else “every path from \(p\) to \(q\) must pass through \(S\)” can fail), and likewise \(\delta'<r-t_0\); that \(\rho(p,s)=\delta\) on \(S\) and the continuity of \(\rho\) come from Proposition D; and that “hence coincides with \(\gamma\)” is Lemma A. Completeness is used only for \(\exp_p(tv)\), \(t\le r\): if \(\exp_p\) is defined on all of \(TM_p\) for one \(p\), every point is joined to \(p\) by a minimal geodesic.

Corollary 10.10. (checked by machine: V7.27, in a stronger form) If \(M\) is geodesically complete, every bounded subset of \(M\) has compact closure. Consequently \(M\) is complete as a metric space (every Cauchy sequence converges).

Proof. Let \(X\) be nonempty of diameter \(d\), and \(p\in X\). For \(x\in X\), Theorem 10.9 gives a minimal geodesic \(t\mapsto\exp_p(tw)\) from \(p\) to \(x\) with \(\|w\|=\rho(p,x)\le d\), so \(X\subseteq\exp_p(\bar B_d(p))\). This set is compact because \(\exp_p\) is continuous on all of \(TM_p\), by Lemma B and completeness; so it is closed and contains the closure of \(X\), which is therefore compact. A Cauchy sequence is bounded, so it has a convergent subsequence, hence converges. \(\square\)

A hidden hypothesis. Continuity of \(\exp_p\) on the whole disk of radius \(d\) is not given by Lemma 10.2, which concerns small vectors; it is the global smooth dependence of Lemma B.

Milnor states the converse, that metric completeness implies geodesic completeness, calls it “not difficult, using Lemma 10.3”, and refers to Hopf and Rinow for details. Here they are.

Proposition (converse of 10.10). If \((M,\rho)\) is a complete metric space, then \(M\) is geodesically complete.

Proof. Let \(\gamma:(\alpha,\beta)\to M\) be a nonconstant maximal geodesic (Lemma B), of unit speed after a linear change of parameter, and suppose \(\beta<\infty\). As \(\rho(\gamma(t),\gamma(t'))\le |t-t'|\), \(\gamma(t_n)\) is Cauchy for \(t_n\uparrow\beta\), converges to some \(x\), and \(\gamma(t)\to x\) as \(t\uparrow\beta\). Take \(U,\varepsilon\) for \(p_0=x\) from Lemma 10.2: for \(y\in U\) and a unit \(u\in TM_y\), \(t\mapsto\gamma_{\varepsilon u/2}(2t/\varepsilon)\) is a geodesic with initial velocity \(u\) on \(|t|<\varepsilon\). Choose \(t_*\in(\beta-\varepsilon/2,\beta)\) with \(\gamma(t_*)\in U\), and let \(\sigma\) be this geodesic for \(u=\gamma'(t_*)\). By Lemma A, \(\gamma\) and \(s\mapsto\sigma(s-t_*)\) agree where both are defined, and together form a geodesic on \((\alpha,t_*+\varepsilon)\), with \(t_*+\varepsilon>\beta\): this contradicts maximality. Likewise \(\alpha=-\infty\). \(\square\)

Henceforth, as Milnor says, the two notions are not distinguished: \(M\) is a complete Riemannian manifold. Compact Riemannian manifolds are complete. The punctured plane of §0 is not: the geodesic \(t\mapsto(t,0)\) starting at \(t=-1\) cannot be continued past \(t=0\), and \((\pm1,0)\) have no minimal geodesic between them.

6. Familiar examples of geodesics (Milnor pp. 65–66)

Euclidean space. In \(\mathbb R^n\) with metric \(dx_1\otimes dx_1+\dots+dx_n\otimes dx_n\), \(g_{ij}=\delta_{ij}\), so \(\Gamma^k_{ij}=0\) (second Christoffel identity, Lemma 8.6), and (1) is \(\frac{d^2x_i}{dt^2}=0\): the geodesics are the lines \(x(t)=a+tb\). Milnor adds that the integral \(\int(\sum_i(\frac{dx_i}{dt})^2)^{1/2}dt\) “coincides with” the supremum of the lengths of inscribed polygons, so straight lines are minimal, hence geodesics by Corollary 10.7. Proof: polygons are no longer, as \(|\omega(t_i)-\omega(t_{i-1})|=|\int_{t_{i-1}}^{t_i}\omega'|\le\int_{t_{i-1}}^{t_i} |\omega'|\); and for a partition containing the break points, so fine that \(|\omega'(s)-\omega'(t_i)|<\eta\) on each \([t_{i-1},t_i]\) (uniform continuity), \(|\omega(t_i)- \omega(t_{i-1})|\ge\int_{t_{i-1}}^{t_i}|\omega'|-2\eta(t_i-t_{i-1})\), so the polygon is longer than \(L(\omega)-2\eta(b-a)\). Minimality of segments is quicker still: \(\int|\omega'|\ge|\int\omega'|\).

Lemma E (isometries). Let \(I:M\to M\) be an isometry (a diffeomorphism whose derivative preserves inner products). Then \(I\) preserves lengths and distances, and carries geodesics to geodesics. If \(x,y\) are fixed by \(I\) and joined by a unique minimal geodesic \(\gamma:[0,1]\to M\), then \(\gamma\) lies in the fixed point set of \(I\).

Proof. \(\|(I\circ\omega)'\|=\|dI(\omega')\|=\|\omega'\|\), and \(I^{-1}\) is an isometry too. A short segment of a nonconstant geodesic is minimal (end of §3); its image, parametrized by arc length, is again shortest, so a geodesic by Corollary 10.7; being a geodesic is local. If \(x,y\) are fixed, \(I\circ\gamma\) is a minimal geodesic from \(x\) to \(y\) on \([0,1]\), so \(I\circ\gamma=\gamma\). \(\square\)

Spheres. The geodesics of the unit sphere \(S^n\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+1}\) (induced metric) are the great circles, \(S^n\cap(\text{plane through }0)\), at constant speed: \(t\mapsto(\cos ct)\,x+(\sin ct)\,u\) with \(x\in S^n\), \(u\perp x\) a unit vector, \(c\ge0\).

Proof (Milnor’s, completed). Let \(E^2\) be a plane through \(0\), and \(I\) the reflection fixing \(E^2\) and reversing \((E^2)^\perp\): an orthogonal map, so an isometry of \(S^n\) with fixed set the great circle \(C=S^n\cap E^2\). Apply Corollary 10.8 to \(K=S^n\), with \(\delta\le\pi\): points at distance \(<\delta\) have a unique geodesic of length \(<\delta\), which is minimal, and every minimal geodesic between them has length \(<\delta\), so they have a unique minimal geodesic. Let \(x\in C\), \(u\in E^2\) a unit vector orthogonal to \(x\), \(y=(\cos s)x+(\sin s)u\), \(0<s<\delta\); then \(\rho(x,y)\le s\) (an arc of \(C\)). By Lemma E the minimal geodesic \(C'\) from \(x\) to \(y\) lies in \(C\): \(C'(t)=(\cos\theta(t))x+(\sin\theta(t))u\), \(\theta\) smooth, \(\theta(0)=0\). Its speed \(|\theta'|\) is a constant \(\ell=L(C')\in(0,\pi)\), so \(\theta=\pm\ell t\), and \(C'(1)=y\) gives \(\cos\ell=\cos s\), \(\pm\sin\ell=\sin s>0\): \(\theta(t)=st\). By homogeneity the geodesic with initial velocity \(u\) is \(\sigma(t)=(\cos t)x+(\sin t)u\) for \(t\in[0,s]\). Since \(\sigma(t_0+t)=(\cos t)\sigma(t_0)+(\sin t)\sigma'(t_0)\) with \(\sigma'(t_0)\perp\sigma(t_0)\) a unit vector of \(E^2\), the same applies at every \(\sigma(t_0)\), so \(\sigma\) is a geodesic on \(\mathbb R\). A great circle passes through any point in any direction, so by Lemma A the \(\sigma(ct)\) are all the geodesics. \(\square\)

(Lemma F below gives a one-line check: \(\sigma''=-\sigma\) is normal to \(S^n\).) All geodesics of \(S^n\) are defined on \(\mathbb R\): \(S^n\) is complete.

Pairs of points. Milnor states that antipodal points are joined by a continuum of minimal geodesics, and every other pair by a unique minimal geodesic and infinitely many non-minimal ones. Let \(x\ne y\), \(\theta=\arccos\langle x,y\rangle\in(0,\pi]\). A geodesic \(\sigma:[0,1]\to S^n\) from \(x\) to \(y\) is \(\sigma(t)=(\cos\ell t)x+(\sin\ell t)u\) with \(\ell=L(\sigma)>0\), \(u\perp x\) a unit vector, \(y=(\cos\ell)x+(\sin\ell)u\).

  • If \(y=-x\): every unit \(u\perp x\), with \(\ell\in\{\pi,3\pi,\dots\}\), works. A minimal geodesic exists (Theorem 10.9) and is among these, so \(\rho(x,-x)=\pi\) and all the half great circles \(t\mapsto(\cos\pi t)x+(\sin\pi t)u\) are minimal.
  • If \(y\ne\pm x\): write \(y=(\cos\theta)x+(\sin\theta)u_0\), \(u_0\perp x\) a unit vector. Then \(u\perp x\) forces \(\cos\ell=\cos\theta\), \(u=(\sin\theta/\sin\ell)u_0\): either \(u=u_0\) and \(\ell\in\{\theta,\theta+2\pi,\dots\}\), or \(u=-u_0\) and \(\ell\in\{2\pi-\theta,4\pi-\theta,\dots\}\), all along one great circle. The minimal geodesic (Theorem 10.9) is the shortest, \(\ell=\theta\), unique as \(\theta<\pi<2\pi-\theta\). So \(\rho(x,y)=\theta\).

In particular a unit-speed geodesic from \(x\) is minimal on \([0,t]\) exactly for \(t\le\pi\).

Surfaces of revolution. Milnor adds that, by the same reasoning, the meridians of a surface of revolution are geodesics. Rotate an embedded smooth curve in \(\{(x,0,z):x>0\}\) about the \(z\)-axis. Reflection in the plane through the axis and a meridian is an isometry of the surface whose fixed set is that meridian and the opposite one, two disjoint curves. By Corollary 10.8 (on a compact neighbourhood) and Lemma E, two nearby points \(x,y\) of the meridian have a unique minimal geodesic \(\gamma\), lying in the meridian by connectedness. With \(s\) the arc length along the meridian, \(\|\gamma'\|=|(s\circ\gamma)'|\), so \(L(\gamma)\ge|s(y)-s(x)|\ge\rho(x,y)=L(\gamma)\), which forces \(s\circ\gamma\) to be affine: the meridian, parametrized by arc length, is locally, hence globally, a geodesic.

Cylinders. On \(Z=\{x^2+y^2=1\}\subseteq\mathbb R^3\), Milnor says, the geodesics are the generating lines, the circles cut by planes perpendicular to them, and the helices. The map \(P(\theta,z)=(\cos\theta,\sin\theta,z)\) carries the orthonormal pair \(\partial_\theta,\partial_z\) to an orthonormal pair. For a generating line \(L=\{\theta=\theta_0\}\), \(P\) maps the strip \((\theta_0,\theta_0+2\pi)\times\mathbb R\) bijectively onto \(Z\setminus L\) with injective derivative: an isometry, whose inverse is Milnor’s \(I\), “rolling \(Z\) onto \(\mathbb R^2\)”. In the coordinates \((\theta,z)\) the metric is \(d\theta^2+dz^2\), so \(\Gamma^k_{ij}=0\) and geodesics are \(\theta=\theta_1+at\), \(z=z_1+ct\). Every point lies off some generating line, so by Lemma A every geodesic is \(t\mapsto(\cos(\theta_1+at),\sin(\theta_1+at),z_1+ct)\): a generating line (\(a=0\)), a circle (\(c=0\)), a helix (\(ac\ne0\)) or a point. The points \(P(\theta_1,z_1)\), \(P(\theta_2,z_2)\) are joined by the geodesics \(t\mapsto P(\theta_1+t(\theta_2+2\pi k-\theta_1),z_1+t(z_2-z_1))\), \(k\in\mathbb Z\), of lengths \(\sqrt{(\theta_2-\theta_1+2\pi k)^2+(z_2-z_1)^2}\): infinitely many.

The unitary group (Milnor’s footnote, p. 57). The claim \(\exp_I(A)=I+A+\frac1{2!}A^2+\cdots\) for skew-Hermitian \(A\) holds for the metric \(\langle A,B\rangle=\operatorname{Re}\operatorname{tr}(AB^*)\) induced from \(\mathbb C^{n\times n}=\mathbb R^{2n^2}\), by the following lemma.

Lemma F (submanifolds). If \(M\subseteq\mathbb R^k\) has the induced metric, then \(\frac{DV}{dt}=\pi(\frac{dV}{dt})\), the orthogonal projection to \(TM_{c(t)}\) of the ordinary derivative. So a curve in \(M\) is a geodesic iff its acceleration in \(\mathbb R^k\) is normal to \(M\).

Proof. \(X\vdash Y:=\pi(dY(X))\) is a connection, symmetric because \(dY(X)-dX(Y)=[X,Y]\) is tangent, and compatible because \(X\langle Y,Z\rangle=\langle dY(X),Z\rangle+\langle Y,dZ(X)\rangle\) with \(Y,Z\) tangent. By Lemma 8.6 it is the Levi-Civita connection, and by the uniqueness in Lemma 8.1 its covariant derivative along curves is \(\pi(\frac{dV}{dt})\). \(\square\)

For \(U(n)\), differentiating \(gg^*=I\) gives \(TM_g=\{gY:Y^*=-Y\}\). The space \(\{gH:H^*=H\}\) is orthogonal to it, since \(\operatorname{Re}\operatorname{tr}(gY(gH)^*)=\operatorname{Re}\operatorname {tr}(YH)\) and \(\overline{\operatorname{tr}(YH)}=\operatorname{tr}(H^*Y^*)=-\operatorname{tr}(YH)\); by dimension (\(n^2+n^2\)) it is the normal space. For skew-Hermitian \(A\), \(\gamma(t)=e^{tA}\) has \(\gamma''=e^{tA}A^2\) with \(A^2\) Hermitian: a geodesic with \(\gamma'(0)=A\), so \(\exp_I(A)=e^A\).

An interactive look at the exponential map of the sphere

The figure shows the unit sphere with a base point \(p\). Thin curves are radial geodesics \(t\mapsto\exp_p(tv)\); the dashed circle is the shell \(S_t(p)\), which by the Gauss lemma meets each of them at a right angle. The thick curve is one geodesic \(\gamma(t)=\exp_p(tv)\) of length \(t\). Drag the length slider: up to \(t=\pi\), \(\gamma\) is minimal and \(\rho(p,\gamma(t))=t\). At \(t=\pi\) all geodesics from \(p\) meet at the antipode and the shell collapses to a point; beyond it \(\gamma\) (now drawn in a second colour) is not minimal, and the inset graph of \(\rho(p,\gamma(t))\) turns down along \(2\pi-t\). The direction slider changes \(v\), the tilt slider turns the sphere. The meeting point is the first conjugate point of \(p\) (Chapter 9), the source of the cells of dimension \(n-1,2(n-1),\dots\) in the path space of \(S^n\) (Chapter 10).

7. Application: London to New York, and counting geodesics

The shortest route. Take the Earth to be a sphere of radius \(R=6371\) km, its mean radius (the Earth is flattened by about one part in 300, which changes the figures below by a fraction of a percent). London Heathrow is at \(\varphi_1=51.47^\circ\)N, \(\lambda_1=0.45^\circ\)W; New York JFK at \(\varphi_2=40.64^\circ\)N, \(\lambda_2=73.78^\circ\)W. With unit vectors \((\cos\varphi\cos\lambda,\cos\varphi\sin\lambda,\sin\varphi)\), \[\cos\theta=\sin\varphi_1\sin\varphi_2+\cos\varphi_1\cos\varphi_2\cos(\lambda_2-\lambda_1)=0.6451, \qquad\theta=49.83^\circ=0.8696\text{ rad}.\] By §6 the minimal geodesic is the shorter arc of the great circle through the two cities, unique, of length \(R\theta\approx5540\) km. That great circle reaches its highest latitude, \(53.66^\circ\)N, at \(22.9^\circ\)W, between the cities: the northward bulge of the track. A rhumb line (constant heading) has length \(R\sqrt{\Delta\varphi^2+(\Delta\varphi/\Delta\psi)^2\Delta\lambda^2}\approx5759\) km, where \(\psi=\ln\tan(\frac\pi4+\frac\varphi2)\) is the Mercator coordinate: 219 km, or 4%, longer.

The other geodesics. By §6 every geodesic from London to New York runs along the same great circle, with length \(R(\theta+2\pi k)\) or \(R(2\pi(k+1)-\theta)\), \(k\ge0\): \[5540,\ 34490,\ 45570,\ 74520,\ 85600,\ 114550,\ \dots\ \text{km},\] five of them under 100,000 km and about \(L/(\pi R)\) under \(L\). Only the first is minimal. A geodesic leaving London stops being minimal after \(\pi R\approx20{,}015\) km, at London’s antipode (\(51.47^\circ\)S, \(179.55^\circ\)E), in the Pacific south-east of New Zealand near the Antipodes Islands, named for lying close to the point antipodal to Greenwich. The second geodesic leaves London heading east-south-east and passes the antipodes of New York and of London before arriving.

Cylinders and tori. On the cylinder the geodesics between two points are indexed by \(k\in\mathbb Z\), and the number of length \(\le L\) grows linearly in \(L\), as on the sphere. On the flat torus \(T=\mathbb R^2/\mathbb Z^2\) the argument for the cylinder (the projection \(\mathbb R^2\to T\) is a local isometry) shows that the geodesics from \(p\) to \(q\) correspond to the vectors \(w\in(q-p)+\mathbb Z^2\), of length \(|w|\). Those of length \(\le L\) are the points of a translated lattice in a disk of radius \(L\), about \(\pi L^2\) of them: for \(q=p\) and \(L=10\) there are 317 lattice points, so 316 nonconstant geodesic loops at \(p\) of length at most 10, against \(\pi L^2\approx314\). The minimal geodesic is the shortest \(w\); it need not be unique: for \(q-p=(\frac12,0)\), \(w=(\pm\frac12,0)\) give two.

On every compact manifold Hopf–Rinow gives at least one geodesic between two points. That two non-conjugate points are joined by infinitely many when the manifold is not contractible is a theorem of Morse theory (Chapter 10, after Milnor §17).

Milnor’s §10 has been verified in the Lean proof assistant for submanifolds of Euclidean space with the induced metric, where geodesics are the curves with normal acceleration (Lemma F); every Riemannian manifold is such a submanifold by Nash’s embedding theorem (quoted, not proved).
