Chapter 12Milnor §§20–21pp. 109–117Contents ↑

Chapter 12. Every full turn counts twice: symmetric spaces and Lie groups

Milnor, “Morse Theory”, §20–§21, rewritten for a first-year graduate student who wants to know what the theorem is for. Every proof is complete. The standard facts of Lie theory that Milnor quotes are listed in §3, with references, and are used exactly as stated there.

0. A ball spinning in space

A perfectly balanced ball floats in space, far from any torque: a rigid body whose three principal moments of inertia are equal, a spherical top. Its configuration is an orientation \(R \in SO(3)\). In how many ways can the ball, moving freely, turn from a prescribed orientation \(A\) to a prescribed orientation \(B\) in one second? And how stable is each of these motions?

A spherical top moves freely by turning at constant angular speed about a fixed axis. If \(BA^{-1}\) is the rotation through \(\varphi_0\) about the axis \(n\), \(0 < \varphi_0 < \pi\), the ball can turn through \(\varphi_0\) about \(n\), through \(2\pi - \varphi_0\) the other way, through \(2\pi + \varphi_0\), through \(4\pi - \varphi_0\) the other way, and so on. Each motion is a critical point of the action \(\int_0^1 T\,dt\), \(T\) the kinetic energy, and its stability is measured by its Morse index: the largest number of independent perturbations, with fixed ends and fixed travel time, that lower the action to second order. We will prove (§6) that the motion turning through the total angle \(\varphi\) has index \[\lambda = 2\left\lfloor \frac{\varphi}{2\pi}\right\rfloor .\] Each full turn adds \(2\) to the index. It never adds \(1\).

The pairing is not peculiar to balls. The kinetic energy of a spherical top is a Riemannian metric on the rotation group unchanged by rotating the body and by rotating the laboratory, a bi-invariant metric, and the free motions are its geodesics. On every Lie group with a bi-invariant metric the curvature is given by brackets, \(R(X,Y)Z = \frac14[[X,Y],Z]\), and the Jacobi equation along a geodesic has constant coefficients, with coefficient matrix \(-\frac14(\operatorname{ad}V)^2\) and \(\operatorname{ad}V\) skew-symmetric. The nonzero eigenvalues of such a matrix come in equal pairs, so conjugate points have even multiplicity and geodesics have even index. The fundamental theorem of Chapter 10 (Milnor’s 17.3) turns this into Bott’s theorem: the loop space of a compact, simply connected Lie group has the homotopy type of a CW complex with only even-dimensional cells, finitely many in each dimension.

The natural setting is that of symmetric spaces, Riemannian manifolds with a reflection through every point, where Jacobi fields can be written down explicitly (§1–§2); Lie groups are the main example (§3–§5). In §6 we count the free motions of the ball and their indices, and then do the same for \(SU(3)\), where the indices give the homology of the loop space, free of ranks \(1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 4, 4\) in degrees \(0, 2, \dots, 14\), and as a by-product \(\pi_2(SU(3)) = 0\) and \(\pi_3(SU(3)) \cong \mathbb Z\).

1. Symmetric spaces (Milnor pp. 109–110)

\(M\) is a Riemannian manifold with its Levi-Civita connection; Milnor writes \(X \vdash Y\) for \(\nabla_XY\). We keep his sign for the curvature (Chapter 6, §9), \[R(X,Y)Z = -\nabla_X\nabla_YZ + \nabla_Y\nabla_XZ + \nabla_{[X,Y]}Z ,\] so that the Jacobi equation along a geodesic with velocity \(V\) is \(\frac{D^2J}{dt^2} + R(V,J)V = 0\) (Chapter 9, §14) and \(\langle R(X,Y)X,Y\rangle\) is the sectional curvature of an orthonormal pair. “Complete” means that every geodesic extends to \(\mathbb R\); by Hopf–Rinow (Chapter 7, Milnor’s 10.9 and 10.10) this is metric completeness, and any two points of a connected complete manifold are joined by a minimal geodesic.

Lemma A (isometries). Let \(\varphi : M \to M\) be an isometry. Then \(\varphi_*(\nabla_XY) = \nabla_{\varphi_*X}\varphi_*Y\). Hence \(\varphi\) carries geodesics to geodesics, parallel fields along \(c\) to parallel fields along \(\varphi\circ c\), Jacobi fields to Jacobi fields (so conjugate points to conjugate points, with multiplicity), and \(R(\varphi_*X,\varphi_*Y)\varphi_*Z = \varphi_*R(X,Y)Z\).

Proof. \(\nabla'_XY := \varphi_*^{-1}(\nabla_{\varphi_*X}\varphi_*Y)\) is a connection, symmetric because \(\varphi_*[X,Y] = [\varphi_*X,\varphi_*Y]\) and compatible with the metric because \(\varphi\) preserves inner products. By uniqueness (Milnor’s 8.6) \(\nabla' = \nabla\); everything else is defined from \(\nabla\). \(\square\)

Definition (Milnor). A symmetric space is a connected Riemannian manifold \(M\) such that for each \(p \in M\) there is an isometry \(I_p : M \to M\) which leaves \(p\) fixed and reverses geodesics through \(p\): if \(\gamma\) is a geodesic with \(\gamma(0) = p\) then \(I_p(\gamma(t)) = \gamma(-t)\).

The domain of \(\gamma\) is not specified; we read the condition as “whenever both sides are defined”. This costs nothing:

Lemma B (reflections extend geodesics). Let \(M\) be a symmetric space and \(p \in M\). (a) \((dI_p)_p = -\mathrm{id}\). Conversely, an isometry \(I\) with \(I(p) = p\) and \(dI_p = -\mathrm{id}\) reverses all geodesics through \(p\). (b) A geodesic \(\gamma : J \to M\) with \(0 \in J\), \(\gamma(0) = p\), extends to a geodesic on \(J\cup(-J)\), on which \(I_p(\gamma(t)) = \gamma(-t)\). (c) Every geodesic is defined on all of \(\mathbb R\).

Proof. (a) Differentiate \(I_p(\gamma_v(t)) = \gamma_v(-t)\) at \(t = 0\), \(\gamma_v\) the geodesic with initial velocity \(v\) (Milnor’s 10.1). Conversely, \(I\circ\gamma\) (on \(J\)) and \(t \mapsto \gamma(-t)\) (on \(-J\)) are geodesics with the same initial point and velocity \(-\gamma'(0)\), so they agree on \(J\cap(-J)\). (b) Put \(\hat\gamma = \gamma\) on \(J\) and \(\hat\gamma(t) = I_p(\gamma(-t))\) on \(-J\). By (a) the two agree on \(J\cap(-J)\), so \(\hat\gamma\) is a geodesic on \(J\cup(-J)\); then \(I_p\circ\hat\gamma\) and \(t\mapsto\hat\gamma(-t)\) are geodesics on this symmetric interval with the same initial data, hence equal. (c) Let \(\gamma : (\alpha,\beta) \to M\) admit no extension and let \(s \in (\alpha,\beta)\). Applying (b) at \(\gamma(s)\) to \(t \mapsto \gamma(s+t)\), defined on \(J = (\alpha-s,\beta-s)\) and admitting no extension, gives \(-J \subseteq J\). With \(\alpha, \beta\) finite this forces \(s = (\alpha+\beta)/2\) for every \(s\); with one of them finite it is false. So \((\alpha,\beta) = \mathbb R\). \(\square\)

Examples. \(\mathbb R^n\) with \(I_p(x) = 2p - x\). The unit sphere \(S^n\) with \(I_p(x) = 2\langle x,p\rangle p - x\), the reflection in the line \(\mathbb Rp\), which is \(-\mathrm{id}\) on \(TS^n_p = p^\perp\) (Lemma B(a)). Flat tori. Lie groups with bi-invariant metrics (§3).

Lemma 20.1. Let \(\gamma\) be a geodesic in a symmetric space, \(p = \gamma(0)\), \(q = \gamma(c)\). Then \(I_qI_p(\gamma(t)) = \gamma(t+2c)\). Moreover, if \(V\) is a parallel field along \(\gamma\) then \((I_qI_p)_*V(t) = V(t+2c)\).

(Milnor assumes “\(\gamma(t)\) and \(\gamma(t+2c)\) are defined”; his proof also uses \(\gamma(-t)\). By Lemma B(c) everything is defined.)

Proof. With \(\beta(s) = \gamma(s+c)\) and Lemma B(b) at \(p\) and at \(q\): \(I_qI_p(\gamma(t)) = I_q(\beta(-t-c)) = \beta(t+c) = \gamma(t+2c)\). For parallel \(V\), the fields \(t \mapsto I_{p*}V(t)\) and \(t \mapsto -V(-t)\) are both parallel along \(t \mapsto \gamma(-t)\) (Lemma A, and \(\frac{D}{dt}[V(-t)] = -\frac{DV}{dt}(-t)\)), and both equal \(-V(0)\) at \(t = 0\); so \(I_{p*}V(t) = -V(-t)\) (Milnor’s 8.2). Likewise \(I_{q*}V(c+s) = -V(c-s)\), and \(I_{q*}I_{p*}V(t) = -I_{q*}V(c+(-t-c)) = V(t+2c)\). \(\square\)

Corollary 20.2. A symmetric space is complete. (This is Lemma B(c). Milnor’s “20.1 shows that geodesics can be indefinitely extended” is the same idea: \(I_qI_p\) slides \(\gamma\) along itself.)

Corollary 20.3. \(I_p\) is unique.

Proof. If \(I, I'\) both qualify and \(x \in M\), join \(p\) to \(x\) by a geodesic \(\gamma\), \(\gamma(1) = x\) (Hopf–Rinow; \(M\) is connected and complete). Then \(I(x) = \gamma(-1) = I'(x)\). \(\square\)

Corollary 20.4. If \(U, V, W\) are parallel along a geodesic \(\gamma\), so is \(R(U,V)W\).

Proof. Let \(X\) be parallel, \(p = \gamma(0)\), \(c \in \mathbb R\), and \(T = I_{\gamma(c/2)}I_p\). By 20.1, \(T(\gamma(t)) = \gamma(t+c)\) and \(T_*Y(t) = Y(t+c)\) for parallel \(Y\); by Lemma A, \[\langle R(U,V)W,X\rangle(c) = \langle R(T_*U(0),T_*V(0))T_*W(0),T_*X(0)\rangle = \langle R(U,V)W,X\rangle(0).\] Taking for \(X\) a parallel frame \(E_1,\dots,E_n\), orthonormal everywhere (Milnor’s 8.3), the coefficients of \(R(U,V)W = \sum_i\langle R(U,V)W,E_i\rangle E_i\) are constant, which is the step Milnor calls clear. \(\square\)

Definition. A Riemannian manifold, not necessarily complete, is locally symmetric if the conclusion of 20.4 holds along every geodesic. Since \(\frac{D}{dt}(R(U,V)W) = (\nabla_{\gamma'}R) (U,V)W\) for parallel \(U,V,W\), and any vectors at a point extend to parallel fields along a geodesic with any given velocity, this is the usual condition \(\nabla R = 0\).

Milnor quotes, and we never use: (É. Cartan) a complete, simply connected, locally symmetric manifold is symmetric (Helgason, Differential Geometry, Lie Groups, and Symmetric Spaces, 1978, Ch. IV; Cheeger–Ebin, Comparison Theorems in Riemannian Geometry, 1975, Ch. 1).

2. Jacobi fields in a locally symmetric manifold (Milnor pp. 110–111)

Let \(\gamma\) be a geodesic in a locally symmetric \(n\)-manifold, defined on an open interval \(J \ni 0\), with \(p = \gamma(0)\), \(V = \gamma'(0)\). Define \[K_V : TM_p \to TM_p, \qquad K_V(W) = R(V,W)V ,\] (not to be confused with the Ricci tensor \(K\) of Chapter 11; \(K(V,V) = \operatorname{trace}K_V\)), and let \(e_1,\dots,e_n\) be its eigenvalues, with multiplicity.

Theorem 20.5. (checked by machine: V12.18, V14.18, in a narrower form; V14.7, restated)1 For \(t_0 \in J\setminus\{0\}\), the parameters \(0\) and \(t_0\) are conjugate along \(\gamma\) iff \(t_0 = \pi k/\sqrt{e_i}\) for some \(e_i > 0\) and some integer \(k \neq 0\). The multiplicity of \(\gamma(t_0)\) as a conjugate point is the number of \(i\) with \(e_i > 0\) and \(t_0\) an integer multiple of \(\pi/\sqrt{e_i}\).

Proof. By Milnor’s Lemma 9.3(4), \(\langle R(X,Y)Z,T\rangle = \langle R(Z,T)X,Y\rangle\), so \(\langle K_VW,W'\rangle = \langle R(V,W')V,W\rangle = \langle W,K_VW'\rangle\): \(K_V\) is self-adjoint, and \(TM_p\) has an orthonormal basis \(U_1,\dots,U_n\) with \(K_VU_i = e_iU_i\). Extend the \(U_i\) to parallel fields along \(\gamma\). By local symmetry \(R(\gamma',U_i)\gamma'\) is parallel, as is \(e_iU_i\), and they agree at \(t = 0\); so \(R(\gamma',U_i)\gamma' = e_iU_i\) along \(\gamma\). Any field along \(\gamma\) is uniquely \(W = \sum_iw_iU_i\) with \(w_i = \langle W,U_i\rangle\) smooth; then \(\frac{D^2W}{dt^2} = \sum_iw_i''U_i\) and \(R(\gamma',W)\gamma' = \sum_ie_iw_iU_i\), so the Jacobi equation is equivalent to \[w_i'' + e_iw_i = 0, \qquad i = 1,\dots,n .\] The solution with \(w_i(0) = 0\), \(w_i'(0) = c_i\) is \(c_is_i\), where \(s_i(t) = \sin(\sqrt{e_i}\,t)/\sqrt{e_i}\) if \(e_i > 0\), \(s_i(t) = t\) if \(e_i = 0\), \(s_i(t) = \sinh(\sqrt{|e_i|}\,t)/\sqrt{|e_i|}\) if \(e_i < 0\). So the Jacobi fields vanishing at \(0\) are the \(\sum_ic_is_iU_i\), \(c \in \mathbb R^n\). Such a field vanishes at \(t_0 \neq 0\) iff \(c_is_i(t_0) = 0\) for all \(i\); \(s_i(t_0) \neq 0\) when \(e_i \le 0\), and when \(e_i > 0\), \(s_i(t_0) = 0\) iff \(\sqrt{e_i}\,t_0 \in \pi\mathbb Z\). Hence the Jacobi fields vanishing at \(0\) and \(t_0\) form a space whose dimension is the number in the statement; by definition (Chapter 9, §14) this is the multiplicity. \(\square\)

Remarks. \(K_VV = 0\), with Jacobi field \(t\gamma'(t)\) (Milnor’s 14.2). \(K_{aV} = a^2K_V\), as reparametrization requires. The statement concerns parameter values, not points (Milnor’s footnote on p. 77), and holds on any interval \(J\), which matters when \(M\) is not complete; Milnor writes \(\gamma : \mathbb R \to M\).

3. Lie groups with a bi-invariant metric (Milnor pp. 112–113)

\(G\) is a Lie group with identity \(e\), \(L_\tau(\sigma) = \tau\sigma\), \(R_\tau(\sigma) = \sigma\tau\) (the subscript distinguishes \(R_\tau\) from the curvature). We quote these standard facts (Chevalley, Theory of Lie Groups, 1946; Warner, Foundations of Differentiable Manifolds and Lie Groups, 1983, Ch. 3; Bröcker–tom Dieck, Representations of Compact Lie Groups, 1985, Ch. I).

(L1) A vector field \(X\) is left invariant if \((L_a)_*X_b = X_{ab}\) for all \(a, b\). Left-invariant fields are smooth, \(X \mapsto X_e\) identifies the space \(\mathfrak g\) of them with \(TG_e\), and the bracket of left-invariant fields is left invariant. With the Jacobi identity \([[X,Y],Z] + [[Y,Z],X] + [[Z,X],Y] = 0\), valid for all vector fields, \(\mathfrak g\) is a Lie algebra, the Lie algebra of \(G\). We write \(\operatorname{ad}X(Y) = [X,Y]\).

(L2) A one-parameter subgroup is a smooth homomorphism \(\theta : \mathbb R \to G\). If \(\theta'(0) = X_e\), then \(t \mapsto \sigma\theta(t)\) is the integral curve of \(X\) through \(\sigma\), since \(\frac{d}{dt}\sigma\theta(t) = \frac{d}{ds}|_{s=0}\,\sigma\theta(t)\theta(s) = (L_{\sigma\theta(t)})_*X_e\). By uniqueness of integral curves, two one-parameter subgroups with the same tangent vector at \(0\) coincide. Each \(X\) has one, written \(t \mapsto \exp(tX)\); for a group of matrices it is \(e^{tX}\). If \([X,Y] = 0\) then \(\exp X\) and \(\exp Y\) commute and \(\exp(X+Y) = \exp X\exp Y\).

(L3) A compact Lie group has a Borel probability measure \(\mu\) (Haar measure) invariant under all \(L_\tau\) and \(R_\tau\). (A left-invariant volume form \(\omega\) satisfies \(R_a^*\omega = \Delta(a)\omega\) with \(\Delta : G \to \mathbb R^\times\) a continuous homomorphism; its compact image lies in \(\{\pm1\}\); normalize \(|\omega|\).)

(L4) (i) If \(G\) is simply connected and \(\mathfrak g = \mathfrak g_1\oplus\mathfrak g_2\) with \(\mathfrak g_i\) ideals, there are simply connected Lie groups \(G_i\) with Lie algebras \(\mathfrak g_i\) and an isomorphism \(G_1\times G_2 \to G\) whose differential at \(e\) is the sum of the inclusions (simply connected groups with isomorphic Lie algebras are isomorphic). (ii) A connected, simply connected, abelian \(k\)-dimensional Lie group is isomorphic to \((\mathbb R^k,+)\).

(L5) (É. Cartan) A closed subgroup of a Lie group is an embedded Lie subgroup. A compact connected abelian Lie group \(A\) of dimension \(m\) is a torus: \(\exp : \mathfrak a \to A\) is a surjective homomorphism whose kernel is a lattice of rank \(m\).

A metric on \(G\) is bi-invariant if all \(L_\tau\) and \(R_\tau\) are isometries. Any inner product on \(TG_e\) gives a left-invariant metric \(\langle u,v\rangle_\sigma = \langle(L_{\sigma^{-1}})_*u, (L_{\sigma^{-1}})_*v\rangle_e\); if \(G\) is commutative, \(L_\tau = R_\tau\) and it is bi-invariant. If \(G\) is compact, Milnor averages:

Lemma C. Let \(G\) be compact, \(\langle\,,\rangle\) any Riemannian metric, \(\mu\) the Haar measure. Then \(\langle\!\langle V,W\rangle\!\rangle = \int_{G\times G}\langle(L_\sigma)_*(R_\tau)_*V, (L_\sigma)_*(R_\tau)_*W\rangle\,d\mu(\sigma)\,d\mu(\tau)\) is a bi-invariant Riemannian metric.

Proof. For \(V, W \in TG_x\) the integrand \(F_{V,W}(\sigma,\tau)\) is continuous on the compact \(G\times G\); in a chart it depends smoothly on \(x\) and on \(V, W\), so differentiation under the integral sign gives smoothness. For \(V \neq 0\), \(F_{V,V}\) has a positive minimum, so the integral is positive. Since \(L_\sigma R_\tau L_a = L_{\sigma a}R_\tau\) and \(L_\sigma R_\tau R_a = L_\sigma R_{a\tau}\), we have \(F_{(L_a)_*V,(L_a)_*W}(\sigma,\tau) = F_{V,W}(\sigma a,\tau)\) and \(F_{(R_a)_*V,(R_a)_*W}(\sigma,\tau) = F_{V,W}(\sigma,a\tau)\), and the invariance of \(\mu\) gives the invariance of the integral. \(\square\)

A practical test. Let \(\operatorname{Ad}(\tau) = d(c_\tau)_e\), \(c_\tau(\sigma) = \tau\sigma \tau^{-1}\). Since \(R_\tau L_\sigma = L_{\sigma\tau}c_{\tau^{-1}}\), a left-invariant metric is bi-invariant iff \(\langle\,,\rangle_e\) is \(\operatorname{Ad}\)-invariant. For matrix groups \(\operatorname{Ad}(\tau)X = \tau X\tau^{-1}\), so \(\langle X,Y\rangle = -\operatorname{trace}(XY)\) is a bi-invariant metric on \(SU(n)\).

Lemma 21.1. (checked by machine: V12.16, in a narrower form) If \(G\) has a bi-invariant metric, then for every \(\tau\) the map \(I_\tau(\sigma) = \tau\sigma^{-1}\tau\) is an isometry fixing \(\tau\) and reversing geodesics through \(\tau\). If \(G\) is connected, it is a symmetric space.

Proof. \(I_e(\sigma) = \sigma^{-1}\) is a diffeomorphism. Differentiating \(\sigma I_e(\sigma) = e\) at \(e\), where multiplication has differential \((u,w) \mapsto u + w\), gives \((dI_e)_e = -\mathrm{id}\). The identity \(I_e = R_{\sigma^{-1}}I_eL_{\sigma^{-1}}\) (indeed \((\sigma^{-1}x)^{-1}\sigma^{-1} = x^{-1}\)), differentiated at \(\sigma\), writes \((dI_e)_\sigma\) as the composite of \((L_{\sigma^{-1}})_*\), \((dI_e)_e\) and \((R_{\sigma^{-1}})_*\), each preserving inner products. So \(I_e\) is an isometry with \((dI_e)_e = -\mathrm{id}\), and it reverses geodesics through \(e\) by the converse in Lemma B(a), which uses only that \(I_e\) is an isometry. Finally \(I_\tau = R_\tau I_eR_\tau^{-1}\), since \((\sigma\tau^{-1})^{-1}\tau = \tau\sigma^{-1}\tau\), an isometry fixing \(\tau\) with \((dI_\tau)_\tau = -\mathrm{id}\). \(\square\)

A hidden hypothesis. “Symmetric space” includes connectedness, so 21.1 needs \(G\) connected. For disconnected \(G\), each component is a translate of the identity component \(G_0\), which is symmetric, hence complete (20.2); so geodesics of \(G\) are defined on \(\mathbb R\), and 21.2 and 21.3 below hold verbatim. Connectedness becomes essential in 21.5.

Lemma 21.2. (checked by machine: V12.15, in a narrower form) The geodesics \(\gamma : \mathbb R \to G\) with \(\gamma(0) = e\) are precisely the one-parameter subgroups of \(G\).

Proof. Let \(\gamma\) be such a geodesic; it lies in the symmetric space \(G_0\). By 20.1 with \(p = e\), \(q = \gamma(t)\), the map \(I_{\gamma(t)}I_e : \sigma \mapsto \gamma(t)\sigma\gamma(t)\) takes \(\gamma(u)\) to \(\gamma(u+2t)\): \[\gamma(t)\gamma(u)\gamma(t) = \gamma(u+2t)\qquad\text{for all } t, u. \tag{*}\] With \(u = -t\): \(\gamma(-t) = \gamma(t)^{-1}\). With \(u = (n-1)t\): \(\gamma((n+1)t) = \gamma(t)\gamma((n-1)t)\gamma(t)\), so by induction \(\gamma(nt) = \gamma(t)^n\) for \(n \ge 0\), hence for all \(n \in \mathbb Z\). If \(t'' \neq 0\) and \(t'/t'' = a/b\) (\(a, b \in \mathbb Z\), \(b > 0\)), put \(t = t''/b\): then \(\gamma(t'+t'') = \gamma(t)^{a+b} = \gamma(t')\gamma(t'')\). For fixed \(t''\) such \(t'\) are dense and both sides are continuous in \(t'\), so \(\gamma\) is a homomorphism. Conversely, if \(\theta\) is a one-parameter subgroup and \(\gamma\) the geodesic with \(\gamma'(0) = \theta'(0)\), then \(\gamma\) is a one-parameter subgroup, so \(\gamma = \theta\) by (L2). \(\square\)

Consequences. (i) The Lie-theoretic \(\exp\) is the Riemannian \(\exp_e\) (Milnor’s footnote on p. 57). (ii) The geodesics through \(\sigma\) are \(t \mapsto \sigma\exp(tX) = \exp(tY)\sigma\), \(Y = \operatorname{Ad}(\sigma)X\), since \(L_\sigma\) and \(R_\sigma\) are isometries. (iii) If \(G\) is connected, every element is \(\exp X\) for some \(X\) (Hopf–Rinow).

Milnor then defines left-invariant fields and the Lie algebra \(\mathfrak g\), as in (L1).

4. The curvature of a bi-invariant metric (Milnor pp. 113–115)

Theorem 21.3. (checked by machine: V12.3, V12.5, V12.6, restated; V12.17, in a narrower form) Let \(G\) have a bi-invariant metric and let \(X, Y, Z, W \in \mathfrak g\). Then (a) \(\langle[X,Y],Z\rangle = \langle X,[Y,Z]\rangle\); (b) \(R(X,Y)Z = \frac14[[X,Y],Z]\); (c) \(\langle R(X,Y)Z,W\rangle = \frac14\langle[X,Y],[Z,W]\rangle\); and (d) \(\nabla_XY = \frac12[X,Y]\).

(Milnor states (a)–(c); (d) is proved, with that label, inside his proof.)

Proof. \(\nabla_XX = 0\). For \(\sigma \in G\), \(c(t) = \sigma\exp(tX)\) is the integral curve of \(X\) through \(\sigma\) (L2) and a geodesic (21.2 and the isometry \(L_\sigma\)). So \(0 = \frac{D}{dt}c' = \frac{D}{dt}(X\circ c) = (\nabla_XX)(c(t))\) by Milnor’s 8.1(c); take \(t = 0\).

(d). By the above applied to \(X\), \(Y\), \(X+Y\): \(\nabla_XY + \nabla_YX = 0\). Symmetry of the connection (Milnor’s 8.5): \(\nabla_XY - \nabla_YX = [X,Y]\). Add.

(a). \(\langle X,Z\rangle_\sigma = \langle X_e,Z_e\rangle\) is constant, so by Milnor’s 8.4 and (d), \(0 = Y\langle X,Z\rangle = \frac12\langle[Y,X],Z\rangle + \frac12\langle X,[Y,Z]\rangle\).

(b). Brackets of left-invariant fields are left invariant, so by (d) \[R(X,Y)Z = -\nabla_X\nabla_YZ + \nabla_Y\nabla_XZ + \nabla_{[X,Y]}Z = -\tfrac14[X,[Y,Z]] + \tfrac14[Y,[X,Z]] + \tfrac12[[X,Y],Z] ,\] and by the Jacobi identity \([X,[Y,Z]] - [Y,[X,Z]] = -[Z,[X,Y]] = [[X,Y],Z]\), so \(R(X,Y)Z = \frac14[[X,Y],Z]\).

(c). By (b), then (a) for the triple \([X,Y], Z, W\). \(\square\)

Since \(R\) is a tensor (Milnor’s 9.1) and every vector is the value of a left-invariant field, this determines \(R\) everywhere. Milnor’s footnote: by (a), \(\omega(X,Y,Z) = \langle[X,Y],Z\rangle\) changes sign under \(X\leftrightarrow Y\) and under \(Y \leftrightarrow Z\) (\(\langle X,[Y,Z]\rangle = -\langle[X,Z],Y\rangle\)), so it is alternating, a left-invariant \(3\)-form; Cartan used it to show \(H^3(G;\mathbb R) \neq 0\) for compact connected non-abelian \(G\) (La topologie des espaces représentatifs des groupes de Lie, 1936). Quoted, not used.

Corollary 21.4. (checked by machine: V12.8, in a stronger form) The sectional curvature \(\langle R(X,Y)X,Y\rangle = \frac14\langle[X,Y],[X,Y] \rangle\) is always \(\ge 0\), with equality iff \([X,Y] = 0\). (Take \(Z = X\), \(W = Y\) in (c).)

For a unit \(X\) and an orthonormal basis \(X_1,\dots,X_n\) of \(\mathfrak g\), the Ricci curvature is therefore \[K(X,X) = \sum_i\langle R(X,X_i)X,X_i\rangle = \tfrac14\sum_i|[X,X_i]|^2 = -\tfrac14\operatorname{trace}(\operatorname{ad}X)^2 ,\] using that \(\operatorname{ad}X\) is skew-symmetric by (a): \(-\frac14\) times the Killing form. The centre \(\mathfrak c\) of \(\mathfrak g\) is the set of \(X\) with \([X,Y] = 0\) for all \(Y\).

Corollary 21.5. (checked by machine: V12.9, in a narrower form) If \(G\) is connected, has a bi-invariant metric, and \(\mathfrak g\) has trivial centre, then \(G\) is compact with finite fundamental group.

A hidden hypothesis. Milnor omits “connected”, which cannot be dropped: \(SO(3)\times\mathbb Z\) (\(\mathbb Z\) discrete) has Lie algebra \(\mathfrak{so}(3)\), with trivial centre, and a bi-invariant metric, but is not compact.

Proof. If \(\dim G = 0\), \(G = \{e\}\). A one-dimensional Lie algebra is its own centre, so \(n = \dim G \ge 2\). For a unit \(X\) some \([X,X_i] \neq 0\), since otherwise \(X\) would be central; so \(K(X,X) > 0\), and by compactness of the unit sphere \(K(X,X) \ge \kappa = (n-1)/r^2 > 0\), at every point by left invariance. \(G\) is symmetric (21.1), hence complete (20.2), so Myers’ theorem (Milnor’s 19.5, Chapter 11) makes \(G\) compact, of diameter \(\le \pi r\). The universal covering \(\tilde G\), with the pulled-back metric, has the same Ricci bound and is complete (geodesics project, extend, and lift back), so it is compact too; the fibre over \(e\) is closed and discrete in \(\tilde G\), hence finite, and its cardinality is \(|\pi_1(G)|\). \(\square\)

Corollary 21.6. (checked by machine: V12.10, in a narrower form) A simply connected Lie group \(G\) with a bi-invariant metric splits as a product \(G'\times\mathbb R^k\), where \(G'\) is compact with Lie algebra of trivial centre and \(\mathbb R^k\) is a vector group. Conversely, any such product has a bi-invariant metric.

Proof. Let \(\mathfrak g'\) be the orthogonal complement of the centre \(\mathfrak c\). For \(X \in \mathfrak g'\), \(Y \in \mathfrak g\), \(C \in \mathfrak c\), by 21.3(a) \(\langle[X,Y],C\rangle = \langle X,[Y,C]\rangle = 0\), so \([X,Y] \in \mathfrak g'\). (Milnor takes \(Y \in \mathfrak g'\), showing \(\mathfrak g'\) is a subalgebra; the same line shows it is an ideal.) As \([\mathfrak g',\mathfrak c] = 0\), \(\mathfrak g = \mathfrak g'\oplus\mathfrak c\) is a direct sum of ideals, and (L4)(i) gives \(G \cong G'\times G''\) with \(G', G''\) simply connected with Lie algebras \(\mathfrak g'\), \(\mathfrak c\). \(G''\) is abelian (a connected group is generated by exponentials, which commute here), so \(G'' \cong \mathbb R^k\) by (L4)(ii). The metric of \(G\) restricts to a bi-invariant metric on the closed subgroup \(G' = G'\times\{e\}\). The centre of \(\mathfrak g'\) is trivial: an element commuting with \(\mathfrak g'\) also commutes with \(\mathfrak c\), so lies in \(\mathfrak c\cap\mathfrak g' = 0\). By 21.5, \(G'\) is compact. Conversely, Lemma C on \(G'\), any inner product on \(\mathbb R^k\), and the product metric. \(\square\)

Milnor’s text skips the Lie theory behind “Hence \(G\) splits as a Cartesian product”: an ideal decomposition of \(\mathfrak g\) integrates to a product decomposition of a simply connected group, and simply connected abelian groups are vector groups. These are (L4); he refers to Chevalley.

5. Bott’s theorem: only even cells (Milnor pp. 116–117)

\(\Omega(M;p,q)\) is Milnor’s space of piecewise smooth paths, \(\Omega^*(M;p,q)\) the space of continuous paths (compact-open topology), and \(\Omega \to \Omega^*\) is a homotopy equivalence (Theorem 17.1, Chapter 10). The loop space \(\Omega(G)\) is \(\Omega(G;e,e)\). Milnor works with other endpoints, so:

Lemma D (endpoints do not matter). If \(X\) is path connected, \(\Omega^*(X;p,q) \simeq \Omega^*(X;p',q')\).

Proof. Move one endpoint at a time. For a path \(\beta\) from \(q\) to \(q'\) put \(\Phi(\omega) = \omega\cdot\beta\) and \(\Psi(\omega') = \omega'\cdot\bar\beta\). The standard homotopies proving that \(\pi_1\) is a group (Hatcher, Algebraic Topology, §1.1) give \(\Psi\Phi(\omega) \simeq \omega\) and \(\Phi\Psi(\omega') \simeq \omega'\) by formulas continuous in \(\omega\), \(\omega'\). Starting points are moved by precomposing with a path. \(\square\)

Theorem 21.7 (Bott). (not checked by machine) Let \(G\) be a compact, simply connected Lie group. Then \(\Omega(G)\) has the homotopy type of a CW complex with no odd-dimensional cells and only finitely many \(\lambda\)-cells for each even \(\lambda\). Thus \(H_\lambda(\Omega(G);\mathbb Z)\) is zero for \(\lambda\) odd and free abelian of finite rank for \(\lambda\) even.

Proof. Give \(G\) a bi-invariant metric (Lemma C). If \(\dim G = 0\), \(\Omega(G)\) is a point; let \(n = \dim G \ge 1\).

Step 1: trivial centre. By 21.6, \(G \cong G'\times\mathbb R^k\); \(G\) is compact, so \(k = 0\) and \(\mathfrak g\) has trivial centre. As in 21.5 there is \(\kappa > 0\) with \[\|\operatorname{ad}X\|^2 := \sum_i|[X,X_i]|^2 \ge 4\kappa|X|^2 \qquad (X \in \mathfrak g). \tag{1}\]

Step 2: the Morse complex. Choose \(p, q\) not conjugate along any geodesic (Milnor’s 18.2, Chapter 11, which rests on Sard’s theorem, proved in Chapter 3 of the companion volume, Topology from the Differentiable Viewpoint, rewritten). By 17.3, \(\Omega(G;p,q)\) has the homotopy type of a CW complex with one \(\lambda\)-cell for each geodesic from \(p\) to \(q\) of index \(\lambda\).

Step 3: every index is even. Let \(\gamma\) be a geodesic from \(p\) with velocity \(V\). The isometry \(L_{p^{-1}}\) takes it to \(\gamma_0(t) = \exp(tV_0)\), \(V_0 = (L_{p^{-1}})_*V \in \mathfrak g\), with the same conjugate points (Lemma A). \(G\) is locally symmetric (21.1, 20.4), and by 21.3(b) \[K_{V_0}(W) = \tfrac14[[V_0,W],V_0] = -\tfrac14(\operatorname{ad}V_0)^2W .\] \(A = \operatorname{ad}V_0\) is skew-symmetric by 21.3(a). Milnor uses its normal form without proof:

There is an orthonormal basis in which \(A\) is block diagonal, with blocks \(\begin{pmatrix}0 & a_j\\-a_j & 0\end{pmatrix}\), \(a_j > 0\) (\(j = 1,\dots,s\)), and zeros. Indeed \(A^2\) is symmetric with \(\langle A^2w,w\rangle = -|Aw|^2\), so \(\mathfrak g\) is the orthogonal sum of its eigenspaces, each \(A\)-invariant, with eigenvalues \(-a^2 \le 0\). On the eigenvalue \(0\), \(A = 0\). On \(-a^2 < 0\), a unit \(w\) gives the orthonormal pair \((w,-Aw/a)\) spanning an \(A\)-invariant plane with the displayed matrix; its orthogonal complement in the eigenspace is \(A\)-invariant (\(A\) is skew); induct.

So \(K_{V_0}\) has eigenvalues \(a_1^2/4, a_1^2/4, \dots, a_s^2/4, a_s^2/4\) and \(0\): the nonzero eigenvalues are positive and occur in pairs. By 20.5 the conjugate points are at \(t = 2\pi m/a_j\), \(m \ge 1\), with multiplicity \(2\,\#\{j : ta_j \in 2\pi\mathbb Z\}\), and the index theorem (Milnor’s 15.1, Chapter 9) gives Bott’s formula \[\lambda(\gamma) = 2\sum_{j=1}^s\#\{m \ge 1 : 2\pi m < a_j\} , \tag{2}\] an even number.

Step 4: finitely many cells in each dimension. \(\|\operatorname{ad}V_0\|^2 = \operatorname{trace}(A^{\mathsf T}A) = 2\sum_ja_j^2\), so by (1), with \(L = |V|\) the length of \(\gamma\), \(2\sum_ja_j^2 \ge 4\kappa L^2\). If \(L > 0\) then \(s \ge 1\), and as \(s \le n/2\), \(a_{\max}^2 \ge 2\kappa L^2/s \ge 4\kappa L^2/n\); by (2) \[\lambda(\gamma) \ge 2\Big(\frac{a_{\max}}{2\pi} - 1\Big) \ge \frac{2L}{\pi}\sqrt{\frac\kappa n} - 2.\] So a geodesic of index \(\le \lambda\) has length \(\le L_\lambda = \frac\pi2(\lambda+2)\sqrt{n/\kappa}\), and there are only finitely many such geodesics from \(p\) to \(q\) (Theorem 16.3, Chapter 10).

Step 5. So \(\Omega(G;p,q)\), and by 17.1 and Lemma D also \(\Omega(G)\), has the homotopy type of a CW complex with only even cells, finitely many in each dimension. Every cellular boundary map goes between an even and an odd degree, one of which has no cells, so all vanish, and \(H_\lambda\) is free on the \(\lambda\)-cells. \(\square\)

Milnor’s text skips two points. (i) “By §19.4 there are only finitely many \(\lambda\)-cells”: that argument (19.4 and the proof of 19.6, Chapter 11) needs Ricci curvature bounded below by a positive constant, i.e. trivial centre, which holds only because \(G\) is compact and simply connected (21.6). For the compact group \(SO(2)\) the centre is everything and the Ricci curvature vanishes. Step 4 is the same estimate written with (2). (ii) Theorem 17.3 concerns \(\Omega(G;p,q)\); the passage to the loop space is Lemma D with 17.1.

Remark 1 (Milnor). The complex is always infinite dimensional, unless \(G = \{e\}\) (an exception missing in the text). For \(G = S^3\), \(H_i\Omega(S^3) \cong \mathbb Z\) for all even \(i\) (Corollary 17.4). In general, if \(\dim G \ge 1\), take \(p = e\) and \(q \neq e\) not conjugate to \(e\) along any geodesic (18.2); then \(q = \exp X\), \(X \neq 0\) (Consequence (iii) of 21.2). The closure \(A\) of \(\{\exp(tX)\}\) is a closed, connected, abelian subgroup of \(G\), of positive dimension, hence by (L5) a torus whose exponential has a kernel containing some \(Y \neq 0\), and \(X\) lies in its Lie algebra. So \(\exp(X+jY) = q\) for all \(j \in \mathbb Z\): infinitely many geodesics from \(e\) to \(q\), with unbounded indices since only finitely many have index \(\le \lambda\) (Step 4). By Step 5, \(H_\lambda(\Omega(G)) \neq 0\) for infinitely many \(\lambda\); so the complex is infinite dimensional whatever \(p\) and \(q\) are chosen in Step 2.

Remark 2 (Milnor). The theorem holds for non-compact \(G\) provided \(G\) is connected and simply connected (implicit in the text). By Iwasawa (On some types of topological groups, Ann. of Math. 50 (1949), Theorem 6), a connected Lie group \(G\) contains a compact subgroup \(K\) as a deformation retract (\(G\) is homeomorphic to \(K\times\mathbb R^m\), with \(K\) corresponding to \(K\times\{0\}\)). Then \(K\) is connected, \(\pi_1(K) = \pi_1(G) = 0\), and \(\Omega(G) \simeq \Omega(K)\), to which 21.7 applies.

An interactive look at the geodesics of SU(3)

The picture is the plane \(\mathfrak t\) of diagonal matrices \(\operatorname{diag}(i\theta_1,i\theta_2, i\theta_3)\), \(\sum\theta_j = 0\), in \(\mathfrak{su}(3)\), drawn isometrically for \(-\operatorname{trace}(XY)\); the black square is \(0\). Each dot is an \(X\) with \(\exp X = q\) for a fixed regular \(q\) in the diagonal torus; by §6.2 these give all the geodesics \(t \mapsto \exp(tX)\) from \(e\) to \(q\). The grey lines are the walls \(\theta_j - \theta_k \in 2\pi\mathbb Z\). By Bott’s formula (2), the segment from \(0\) to \(X\) crosses a wall exactly at a conjugate point of multiplicity \(2\), so the label of each dot, its index, is twice the number of walls crossed (the dashed walls through \(0\) are never crossed). Tap a dot to draw its segment and mark its conjugate points. Drag the picture to move \(q\): the dots and their indices change, but the table of how many geodesics have each index stays \(1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 3, \dots\), with no odd index. If \(q\) is dragged onto a wall, every dot lies on a wall: \(q\) is conjugate to \(e\) and Theorem 17.3 no longer applies. The slider limits the indices shown.

6. Application: the spinning ball, and the loops of SU(3)

6.1 Free motions of a spherical top

For a motion \(R(t) \in SO(3)\) the angular velocities in the space and body frames, \(\Omega_s = \dot RR^{-1}\) and \(\Omega_b = R^{-1}\dot R\), are conjugate, so have equal length, and the kinetic energy of a spherical top with moment of inertia \(I\) is \(T = \frac I4\operatorname{trace} (\Omega_b^{\mathsf T}\Omega_b)\). Rotating the laboratory (\(R \mapsto R_1R\)) fixes \(\Omega_b\) and rotating the body (\(R \mapsto RR_1\)) fixes \(\Omega_s\): \(T\) is a bi-invariant metric. Free motions are the critical points of \(\int_0^1T\,dt\), i.e. geodesics (Milnor’s 12.3, Chapter 8), and by 21.2 and Consequence (ii) they are \(R(t) = \exp(t\Omega)R(0)\), uniform rotation about a fixed axis, as conservation of angular momentum predicts.

To compute indices, use the double covering \(\rho : SU(2) \to SO(3)\). Here \(SU(2)\) is the unit sphere \(S^3\) of the quaternions, with Lie algebra \(\operatorname{Im}\mathbb H = \mathbb R^3\), \(\rho(q)\) is \(x \mapsto qxq^{-1}\) on \(\operatorname{Im}\mathbb H\), and \(\rho(\cos\frac\varphi2 + u\sin\frac\varphi2)\) is the rotation through \(\varphi\) about the unit vector \(u\). The round metric of \(S^3\) is bi-invariant (\(|axb| = |x|\) for unit \(a, b\)), and \(\rho\) is a local isometry for the metric it induces on \(SO(3)\). Bott’s formula involves only the eigenvalues of \(\operatorname{ad}\), so the indices do not depend on which bi-invariant metric is used. For imaginary quaternions \(uv = -u\cdot v + u\times v\), so \([u,v] = 2u\times v\), and for \(V = \theta u\) (\(|u| = 1\)) \(\operatorname{ad}V\) is zero on \(u\) and \(2\theta\) times a quarter-turn on \(u^\perp\): one block, \(a_1 = 2\theta\). The geodesic \(\exp(tV) = \cos t\theta + u\sin t\theta\) projects to the rotation through \(\varphi = 2\theta\) about \(u\) in unit time, and (2) gives \[\lambda = 2\,\#\{m \ge 1 : 2\pi m < \varphi\} = 2\left\lfloor\frac{\varphi}{2\pi}\right\rfloor\qquad (\varphi \notin 2\pi\mathbb Z),\] as announced in §0. The conjugate points come when the ball has completed whole turns, and their multiplicity \(2\) is visible: a rotation through exactly \(2\pi\) about any axis returns the ball to its starting orientation, so tilting the axis in two independent directions gives free motions that leave and return together, whose variation fields are two independent Jacobi fields vanishing at both ends.

Numbers. Let \(A = 1\) and let \(B\) be the rotation through \(90^\circ\) about the vertical axis \(u\). The free motions in one second turn about \(u\) through the angles below (\(-\) means clockwise from above), at constant angular speed. The last row is the endpoint of the lift to \(SU(2)\) starting at \(1\), with \(\tilde q = \cos45^\circ + u\sin45^\circ\):

total angle \(+90^\circ\) \(-270^\circ\) \(+450^\circ\) \(-630^\circ\) \(+810^\circ\) \(-990^\circ\) \(+1170^\circ\)
index \(\lambda\) 0 0 2 2 4 4 6
lift ends at \(\tilde q\) \(-\tilde q\) \(-\tilde q\) \(\tilde q\) \(\tilde q\) \(-\tilde q\) \(-\tilde q\)

The two classes are the two elements of \(\pi_1(SO(3)) = \mathbb Z/2\) (the “belt trick”), and each class has exactly one motion of each even index: the cells of \(\Omega(S^3)\) in dimensions \(0, 2, 4, \dots\), once for each component of \(\Omega(SO(3))\). In the semiclassical (Van Vleck–Gutzwiller) propagator of a quantum rotor each classical path carries the phase factor \(e^{-i\pi\lambda/2}\) (Gutzwiller, Chaos in Classical and Quantum Mechanics, 1990); on a group manifold these are the signs \((-1)^{\lambda/2}\).

6.2 The loops of SU(3)

Give \(SU(3)\) the metric \(-\operatorname{trace}(XY)\) (§3). Its diagonal torus has Lie algebra \(\mathfrak t = \{\operatorname{diag}(i\theta_1,i\theta_2,i\theta_3) : \sum\theta_j = 0\}\). Let \(q = \exp H\), \(H = \operatorname{diag}(i\eta_1,i\eta_2,i\eta_3)\), be regular: the \(\eta_j\) are distinct modulo \(2\pi\).

Lemma F. The geodesics from \(e\) to \(q\) are \(t \mapsto \exp(tX)\) with \(X = \operatorname{diag}(i\theta_j)\), \(\theta_j = \eta_j + 2\pi n_j\), \(n \in \mathbb Z^3\), \(n_1+n_2+n_3 = 0\), distinct \(n\) giving distinct geodesics. None ends at a conjugate point, and the index of the one given by \(n\) is \(\lambda(n) = 2\sum_{j<k}\lfloor|\theta_j - \theta_k|/2\pi\rfloor\).

Proof. By 21.2 the geodesics from \(e\) are \(t \mapsto e^{tX}\), \(X \in \mathfrak{su}(3)\). If \(e^X = q\), \(X\) commutes with \(q = \sum_kX^k/k!\), so \(X_{jk}(q_k - q_j) = 0\) and \(X\) is diagonal; then \(e^X = q\) iff \(\theta_j - \eta_j \in 2\pi\mathbb Z\), and \(\sum\theta_j = \sum\eta_j = 0\) gives \(\sum n_j = 0\). For \(j < k\) let \(P_{jk} = \operatorname{span}(E_{jk}-E_{kj},\, i(E_{jk}+E_{kj}))\), \(E_{jk}\) the matrix units. Then \([X,E_{jk}-E_{kj}] = (\theta_j-\theta_k)\,i(E_{jk}+E_{kj})\) and \([X,i(E_{jk}+E_{kj})] = -(\theta_j-\theta_k)(E_{jk}-E_{kj})\), the two spanning vectors are orthogonal of equal length, \(\mathfrak{su}(3) = \mathfrak t\oplus P_{12}\oplus P_{13}\oplus P_{23}\) orthogonally, and \(\operatorname{ad}X = 0\) on \(\mathfrak t\). So the \(a_j\) of Step 3 are the numbers \(|\theta_j - \theta_k|\), none of which is a multiple of \(2\pi\) (as \(\theta_j - \theta_k \equiv \eta_j - \eta_k \not\equiv 0\)); \(t = 1\) is not conjugate, and (2) is the stated formula. \(\square\)

So Theorem 17.3 applies directly, without Sard’s theorem: \(\Omega SU(3)\) has the homotopy type of a CW complex with one \(\lambda(n)\)-cell for each \(n\). Take \(H\) in the alcove \(\eta_1 > \eta_2 > \eta_3 > \eta_1 - 2\pi\). Then \((\eta_j - \eta_k)/2\pi \in (0,1)\) for \(j < k\), and \(\lfloor|\delta+d|\rfloor = f(d)\) for \(\delta \in (0,1)\), \(d \in \mathbb Z\), where \(f(d) = d\) for \(d \ge 0\) and \(f(d) = -d-1\) for \(d < 0\). Hence \[\lambda(n) = 2\big[f(n_1-n_2) + f(n_2-n_3) + f(n_1-n_3)\big],\] independent of \(H\) in the alcove. With \(\eta/2\pi = (0.40,-0.05,-0.35)\) the geodesics of index at most \(8\) are:

\(\lambda\) \(n\) \(\theta/2\pi\)
0 \((0,0,0)\) \((0.40,-0.05,-0.35)\)
2 \((-1,0,1)\) \((-0.60,-0.05,0.65)\)
4 \((-1,1,0)\); \((0,-1,1)\) \((-0.60,0.95,-0.35)\); \((0.40,-1.05,0.65)\)
6 \((0,1,-1)\); \((1,-1,0)\) \((0.40,0.95,-1.35)\); \((1.40,-1.05,-0.35)\)
8 \((1,0,-1)\); \((-2,1,1)\); \((-1,-1,2)\) \((1.40,-0.05,-1.35)\); \((-1.60,0.95,0.65)\); \((-0.60,-1.05,1.65)\)

For \(n = (1,-1,0)\), the highlighted segment in the figure, the differences \(|\theta_j-\theta_k|/2\pi\) are \(2.45, 1.75, 0.70\): conjugate points at \(t = 1/2.45,\ 2/2.45,\ 1/1.75\), index \(2(2+1+0) = 6\). Since \(f(d) \ge |d|-1\) and \(|a|+|b|+|a+b| \ge 2\max(|a|,|b|)\), index \(\le 14\) forces \(|n_1-n_2|, |n_2-n_3| \le 5\), so a finite search is exhaustive. It gives the numbers \(N_\lambda\) of geodesics of index \(\lambda\):

\(\lambda\) 0 2 4 6 8 10 12 14 odd
\(N_\lambda\) 1 1 2 2 3 3 4 4 0

Hence \(H_\lambda(\Omega SU(3);\mathbb Z) \cong \mathbb Z^{N_\lambda}\) (Step 5), the coefficients of \(1/((1-t^2)(1-t^4))\), in agreement with Bott’s description of this homology as a polynomial algebra on generators of degrees \(2\) and \(4\) (Bott, An application of the Morse theory to the topology of Lie groups, Bull. Soc. Math. France 84 (1956)). Two homotopy groups come for free. The complex has one \(0\)-cell and no \(1\)-cells, so \(\Omega SU(3)\) is connected and simply connected; as \(\pi_i(\Omega G) \cong \pi_{i+1}(G)\) (the path fibration, Chapter 13, §1), \(\pi_1(SU(3)) = \pi_2(SU(3)) = 0\). By Hurewicz, \(\pi_3(SU(3)) \cong \pi_2(\Omega SU(3)) \cong H_2(\Omega SU(3)) \cong \mathbb Z\), coming from the single \(2\)-cell \(n = (-1,0,1)\). The same count for \(SU(2)\) (one block, \(a = |\theta_1-\theta_2|\)) gives one geodesic of each even index, and \(\pi_3(S^3) \cong \mathbb Z\).

Checked by machine. The algebra of §21 has been verified in the Lean proof assistant, for a real Lie algebra with an ad-invariant inner product: Theorem 21.3, with \(X \vdash Y = \tfrac12[X, Y]\) derived from \(X \vdash X = 0\) as in Milnor and also from the Koszul formula; Corollary 21.4; the algebraic steps of Corollaries 21.5 and 21.6, that the Ricci curvature is positive (the Killing form is negative definite) when the centre is trivial, and that the orthogonal complement of the centre is an ideal; and, for the proof of Theorem 21.7, that \(K_V = -\tfrac14(\operatorname{ad}V)^2\) is self-adjoint and positive semidefinite with even-dimensional eigenspaces for its nonzero eigenvalues, which replaces Milnor’s block normal form. For compact groups of matrices, as submanifolds of the space of matrices with the induced bi-invariant metric, the geometry of §21 has been verified as well: the geodesics are the translates of the one-parameter subgroups and the group is complete (Lemma 21.2); the map \(\sigma \mapsto \tau\sigma^{-1}\tau\) of Lemma 21.1 is the restriction of a linear isometry of the space of matrices, carries the group into itself, fixes \(\tau\) and reverses the geodesics through it; Theorem 21.3 and Corollary 21.4 hold for the curvature of the group, by the Gauss equation; and the Jacobi equation of Theorem 20.5 holds along a one-parameter subgroup. Not checked: §20 for general symmetric spaces, Lie groups not given as matrices (left-invariant fields, Lemma C), Myers’ theorem and the splitting of the group in Corollaries 21.5 and 21.6, the topology of Theorem 21.7, and the application. See the verified edition.

Chapter 13Milnor §22pp. 118–123Contents ↑

Chapter 13. All roads to the antipode: whole manifolds of minimal geodesics

Milnor, “Morse Theory”, §22, rewritten for a first-year graduate student who wants to know what the theorem is for. Every proof is complete. The facts quoted from homotopy theory and from Hanner’s theory of neighbourhood retracts are stated precisely in §1 and §3, with references.

0. Waves that meet at the antipode

A large meteorite strikes a planet. Seismic surface waves run out from the impact along great circles, at the same speed in every direction, and all of them reach the antipode at the same instant. On Mercury the terrain opposite the Caloris impact basin is broken into hills and troughs, the “hilly and lineated terrain”, which is commonly attributed to this focusing of seismic energy (Schultz and Gault, The Moon 12 (1975)). For the geometry of the sphere this pair of points is as far from “general position” as possible: the shortest routes from the impact to the antipode are not finitely many but a whole circle of them, one through each point of the equator, and on the sphere \(S^{n+1}\) a whole \(n\)-sphere.

So far Morse theory has avoided such pairs: Theorem 17.3 needs endpoints that are not conjugate along any geodesic. Bott pointed out that special pairs are better. If the minimal geodesics from \(p\) to \(q\) form a manifold \(\Omega^d\), and every other geodesic has index at least \(\lambda_0\), then \(\Omega^d\) already captures the whole path space in dimensions up to \(\lambda_0 - 2\): \[\pi_i(\Omega^d) \cong \pi_{i+1}(M) \qquad (0 \le i \le \lambda_0 - 2).\] For antipodal points of \(S^{n+1}\) this reads \(\pi_i(S^n) \cong \pi_{i+1}(S^{n+1})\) for \(i \le 2n-2\), the Freudenthal suspension theorem. This chapter proves Bott’s theorem, by way of two lemmas of independent interest: a small perturbation of a function cannot lower the index of its critical points (22.4), and a function whose minimum set is a manifold and whose other critical points have high index is “highly connected” to its minimum set (22.5). Chapters 14 and 15 apply the same theorem to the unitary and orthogonal groups to prove the Bott periodicity theorem. In the application (§5) we compare Corollary 22.3 with the known homotopy groups of spheres, and use it to prove, with no further input, that every map \(S^j \to S^N\) with \(j < N\) is null-homotopic.

1. The theorem and its corollaries (Milnor pp. 118–119)

\(M\) is a complete, connected Riemannian manifold, and \(p, q \in M\) are points at distance \(\rho(p,q) = \sqrt d\). \(\Omega = \Omega(M;p,q)\) is Milnor’s space of piecewise smooth paths \(\omega : [0,1] \to M\) from \(p\) to \(q\), with the metric of Chapter 10 (§16), for which the energy \(E(\omega) = \int_0^1|\dot\omega|^2dt\) is continuous; \(\Omega^a = E^{-1}[0,a]\) and \(\operatorname{Int}\Omega^a = E^{-1}[0,a)\). By Milnor’s Lemma 12.1 (Chapter 8), \(E \ge d\) on \(\Omega\), with equality exactly at the minimal geodesics (parametrized proportionally to arc length). So \[\Omega^d = \{\text{minimal geodesics from } p \text{ to } q\},\] which is not empty, by Hopf–Rinow. Milnor’s notation \(\Omega^{\pi^2}\) on p. 118 is this set for antipodal points of the unit sphere, where \(d = \pi^2\).

We use the following facts from homotopy theory (Hatcher, Algebraic Topology, 2002, Ch. 4; Hu, Homotopy Theory, 1959, which Milnor cites).

(H1) Relative homotopy. Let \((X,A)\) be a pair and \(r \ge 0\) (\(I^0\) is a point and \(\partial I^0 = \emptyset\)). We write \(\pi_r(X,A) = 0\) if every map \(h : (I^r,\partial I^r) \to (X,A)\) is homotopic relative to \(\partial I^r\) to a map into \(A\). For \(r \ge 1\) this holds iff the relative homotopy groups (pointed sets for \(r = 1\)) \(\pi_r(X,A,a)\) vanish for every \(a \in A\), by the compression criterion (Hatcher, §4.1); for \(r = 0\) it says that every path component of \(X\) meets \(A\). (Milnor asks for a homotopy through maps of pairs; the version relative to \(\partial I^r\) is stronger, and it is what the proofs below produce.)

(H2) Exact sequence of a pair (Hatcher, Theorem 4.3): for \(a \in A\), \(\cdots \to \pi_{i+1}(X,A) \to \pi_i(A) \to \pi_i(X) \to \pi_i(X,A) \to \cdots \to \pi_0(X)\) is exact (of groups, then of pointed sets at the end).

(H3) Path fibration. For \(M\) path connected, \(\pi_i(\Omega^*(M;p,q)) \cong \pi_{i+1}(M)\) for all \(i \ge 0\) (a bijection of sets for \(i = 0\)), where \(\Omega^*\) is the space of continuous paths with the compact-open topology. (The paths starting at \(p\) form a contractible space \(P\), and \(\omega \mapsto \omega(1)\) is a fibration \(P \to M\) with fibre \(\Omega^*(M;p,q)\); apply its exact sequence, Hatcher, Theorem 4.41.) By Theorem 17.1 (Chapter 10), \(\Omega \to \Omega^*\) is a homotopy equivalence, so \(\pi_i(\Omega) \cong \pi_{i+1}(M)\).

(H4) Hurewicz. If \(\pi_r(X,A) = 0\) for all \(r < \lambda\), then \(H_r(X,A;\mathbb Z) = 0\) for \(r < \lambda\). (Replace \((X,A)\) by a CW model whose relative cells all have dimension \(\ge \lambda\) and use cellular homology; Hatcher, §4.1–4.2, or Whitehead, Combinatorial Homotopy I, Theorem 2, as Milnor cites. No assumption on \(\pi_1(A)\) is needed for this vanishing statement.)

Theorem 22.1. (checked by machine: V13.2, in a narrower form)1 If the space \(\Omega^d\) of minimal geodesics from \(p\) to \(q\) is a topological manifold, and if every non-minimal geodesic from \(p\) to \(q\) has index \(\ge \lambda_0\), then \(\pi_i(\Omega,\Omega^d) = 0\) for \(0 \le i < \lambda_0\).

The proof occupies §2–§4. First the consequences.

The inclusion. The inclusion \(\Omega^d \to \Omega\) induces bijections \(\pi_i(\Omega^d,\gamma) \to \pi_i(\Omega,\gamma)\) for \(0 \le i \le \lambda_0 - 2\) and every \(\gamma \in \Omega^d\), and a surjection for \(i = \lambda_0 - 1\).

Proof. For \(1 \le i \le \lambda_0 - 1\), exactness of \(\pi_i(\Omega^d) \to \pi_i(\Omega) \to \pi_i(\Omega,\Omega^d) = 0\) gives surjectivity. For \(1 \le i \le \lambda_0 - 2\), exactness of \(0 = \pi_{i+1}(\Omega,\Omega^d) \to \pi_i(\Omega^d) \to \pi_i(\Omega)\) at the group \(\pi_i(\Omega^d)\) gives injectivity. For \(i = 0\): \(\pi_0(\Omega,\Omega^d) = 0\) says every path component of \(\Omega\) meets \(\Omega^d\); and if \(\lambda_0 \ge 2\) and \(\gamma_0, \gamma_1 \in \Omega^d\) are joined by a path in \(\Omega\), this path, as a map \((I,\partial I) \to (\Omega,\Omega^d)\), is homotopic relative to its ends to a path in \(\Omega^d\). \(\square\)

With (H3) this gives:

Corollary 22.2. (checked by machine: V13.4, V13.5, in a narrower form) With the same hypotheses, \(\pi_i(\Omega^d)\) is isomorphic to \(\pi_{i+1}(M)\) for \(0 \le i \le \lambda_0 - 2\).

Similarly, by (H4) \(H_i(\Omega,\Omega^d) = 0\) for \(i < \lambda_0\), and the exact homology sequence of the pair shows that \(H_i(\Omega^d) \to H_i(\Omega)\) is an isomorphism for \(i \le \lambda_0 - 2\) (Milnor’s remark, citing the relative Hurewicz theorem).

The sphere. Let \(M = S^{n+1} \subset \mathbb R^{n+2}\), \(n \ge 1\), with the round metric, \(q = -p\), and let \(S^n = \{u \in S^{n+1} : \langle u,p\rangle = 0\}\) be the equator. The geodesics of \(S^{n+1}\) are the great circles traversed at constant speed (Milnor p. 65, Chapter 7), so the geodesics \([0,1] \to S^{n+1}\) starting at \(p\) are \(\gamma(t) = \cos(Lt)\,p + \sin(Lt)\,u\), with \(L \ge 0\) the length and \(u \in S^n\).

Lemma A. The geodesics from \(p\) to \(-p\) are the curves \(\gamma_{u,m}(t) = \cos(Lt)p + \sin(Lt)u\) with \(u \in S^n\), \(L = (2m+1)\pi\), \(m \ge 0\). The minimal ones are those with \(m = 0\), so \(d = \pi^2\), and \(u \mapsto \gamma_{u,0}\) is a homeomorphism of \(S^n\) onto \(\Omega^d\).

Proof. \(\gamma(1) = -p\) iff \(\cos L = -1\), i.e. \(L = (2m+1)\pi\). A minimal geodesic exists and has one of these lengths, so \(\rho(p,-p) = \pi\) and the minimal geodesics are the \(\gamma_{u,0}\). The map \(u \mapsto \gamma_{u,0}\) is a bijection onto \(\Omega^d\), with inverse \(\omega \mapsto \omega(1/2)\). Milnor’s metric is \(d(\omega,\omega') = \max_t\rho(\omega(t),\omega'(t)) + (\int_0^1(\dot s - \dot s')^2dt)^{1/2}\), \(s, s'\) the arc lengths; for \(\gamma_{u,0}, \gamma_{v,0}\) the speeds are both \(\pi\), so only the first term remains. On the unit sphere \(\rho(x,y)\) is the angle between \(x\) and \(y\), which is \(2\arcsin(|x-y|/2)\), so \(|x-y| \le \rho(x,y) \le \frac\pi2|x-y|\). Since \(|\gamma_{u,0}(t) - \gamma_{v,0}(t)| = \sin(\pi t)|u-v|\), we get \(|u - v| \le d(\gamma_{u,0},\gamma_{v,0}) \le \frac\pi2|u-v|\). \(\square\)

Lemma B. \(\gamma_{u,m}\) has index \(2mn\). In particular every non-minimal geodesic from \(p\) to \(-p\) has index \(\ge 2n\).

Proof. Let \(L = (2m+1)\pi\). For a unit vector \(w \perp p, u\), the curves \(\alpha_s(t) = \cos(Lt)p + \sin(Lt)(\cos s\,u + \sin s\,w)\) are geodesics, so the variation field \(J_w(t) = \sin(Lt)\,w\) is a Jacobi field (Milnor’s 14.3, Chapter 9); so is \(J_0(t) = t\gamma'(t)\) (Remark 14.2). For an orthonormal basis \(w_1,\dots,w_n\) of the vectors orthogonal to \(p\) and \(u\), the \(n+1\) fields \(J_{w_1},\dots,J_{w_n},J_0\) vanish at \(0\) and are independent (their covariant derivatives at \(0\) are \(Lw_1,\dots,Lw_n\) and \(Lu\)), so they span the \((n+1)\)-dimensional space of Jacobi fields vanishing at \(0\) (§14). A combination \(c\,t\gamma'(t) + \sin(Lt)\,w\) (\(w \perp p,u\)) vanishes at \(t_0 > 0\) iff both terms do, since \(\gamma'(t_0) \in \operatorname{span}(p,u) \perp w\); that is, iff \(c = 0\) and \(\sin(Lt_0)w = 0\). So \(\gamma(t_0)\) is conjugate to \(p\) iff \(Lt_0 \in \pi\mathbb Z\), with multiplicity \(n\). For \(0 < t_0 < 1\) this happens at \(t_0 = j/(2m+1)\), \(j = 1,\dots,2m\): the passages of the geodesic through \(-p\) and \(p\). By the index theorem (Milnor’s 15.1) the index is \(2mn\). \(\square\)

(Equivalently: \(S^{n+1}\) is a symmetric space, Chapter 12, and Theorem 20.5 applies.) Milnor’s “Evidently the hypotheses are satisfied with \(\lambda_0 = 2n\)” is Lemmas A and B: a non-minimal geodesic winds one and a half times or more around \(S^{n+1}\) and has at least two conjugate points of multiplicity \(n\) in its interior.

Corollary 22.3 (the Freudenthal suspension theorem). (checked by machine: V13.9, in a stronger form) \(\pi_i(S^n) \cong \pi_{i+1}(S^{n+1})\) for \(i \le 2n-2\).

Proof. Corollary 22.2 with \(M = S^{n+1}\), \(\Omega^d \cong S^n\) (Lemma A) and \(\lambda_0 = 2n\) (Lemma B). \(\square\)

The proof also gives the surjectivity of \(\pi_{2n-1}(S^n) \to \pi_{2n}(S^{n+1})\), the second half of Freudenthal’s theorem, and \(H_i(\Omega S^{n+1}) \cong H_i(S^n)\) for \(i \le 2n-2\). (The composite \(\pi_i(S^n) \cong \pi_i(\Omega^d) \to \pi_i(\Omega) \cong \pi_{i+1}(S^{n+1})\) is the suspension homomorphism; we do not need this. Milnor also notes on p. 97 that Corollary 17.4 leads to a proof.)

2. Jiggling a function does not lower the index (Milnor pp. 119–121)

The index of a critical point \(x\) of a smooth \(f : U \to \mathbb R\), \(U \subseteq \mathbb R^n\) open, is the largest dimension of a subspace on which the Hessian \((\partial^2f/\partial x_i\partial x_j)(x)\) is negative definite; by the spectral theorem it is the number of negative eigenvalues. This makes sense for degenerate critical points too, and it does not depend on the coordinates (the Hessian at a critical point transforms as a quadratic form, Chapter 1). For a real symmetric \(n\times n\) matrix \(A\) let \(e^1(A) \le \dots \le e^n(A)\) be its eigenvalues. Then a critical point has index \(\ge \lambda\) iff \(e^\lambda < 0\) (\(1 \le \lambda \le n\)).

Lemma C (eigenvalues move slowly). (i) \(e^\lambda(A) = \min_{\dim V = \lambda}\ \max_{v \in V, |v| = 1}\langle Av,v\rangle\) (Courant–Fischer). (ii) If \(|a_{ij} - b_{ij}| \le \varepsilon\) for all \(i, j\), then \(|e^\lambda(A) - e^\lambda(B)| \le n\varepsilon\) for every \(\lambda\).

Proof. (i) Let \(u_1,\dots,u_n\) be orthonormal eigenvectors, \(Au_i = e^iu_i\). On \(V_0 = \operatorname{span}(u_1,\dots,u_\lambda)\) the maximum is \(e^\lambda\). Any \(V\) of dimension \(\lambda\) meets \(\operatorname{span}(u_\lambda,\dots,u_n)\) nontrivially (the dimensions add up to \(n+1\)), and a unit \(v\) in the intersection has \(\langle Av,v\rangle = \sum_{i\ge\lambda}e^iv_i^2 \ge e^\lambda\). (ii) For a unit vector \(v\), \(|\langle(A-B)v,v\rangle| \le \varepsilon(\sum_i|v_i|)^2 \le n\varepsilon\) by Cauchy–Schwarz. So \(\langle Av,v\rangle \le \langle Bv,v\rangle + n\varepsilon\), and by (i) \(e^\lambda(A) \le e^\lambda(B) + n\varepsilon\); exchange \(A\) and \(B\). \(\square\)

This is Milnor’s footnote on p. 120; his main text derives continuity of \(e^\lambda\) from the continuous dependence of the roots of a polynomial on its coefficients.

Let \(K\) be a compact subset of \(\mathbb R^n\), \(U\) an open neighbourhood of \(K\), and \(f : U \to \mathbb R\) a smooth function all of whose critical points in \(K\) have index \(\ge \lambda_0\).

Lemma 22.4. (checked by machine: V13.10, in a stronger form) There is \(\varepsilon > 0\) such that every smooth \(g : U \to \mathbb R\) with \[\Big|\frac{\partial g}{\partial x_i} - \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_i}\Big| < \varepsilon,\qquad \Big|\frac{\partial^2g}{\partial x_i\partial x_j} - \frac{\partial^2f}{\partial x_i\partial x_j}\Big| < \varepsilon \qquad (i,j = 1,\dots,n)\] uniformly on \(K\) has all its critical points in \(K\) of index \(\ge \lambda_0\). (\(f\) may have degenerate critical points; in the application \(g\) will have none.)

Proof. Put \(k_g(x) = \sum_i|\partial g/\partial x_i(x)|\), a continuous function vanishing exactly at the critical points of \(g\), and similarly \(k_f\). If \(\lambda_0 = 0\) there is nothing to prove. If \(\lambda_0 > n\), \(f\) has no critical point in \(K\); let \(\delta = \min_Kk_f > 0\) and \(\varepsilon = \delta/n\); then \(k_g > k_f - n\varepsilon \ge 0\) on \(K\), and \(g\) has no critical point in \(K\). Let \(1 \le \lambda_0 \le n\), and put \(e_g(x) = e^{\lambda_0}\big((\partial^2g/\partial x_i\partial x_j)(x)\big)\), continuous by Lemma C(ii); similarly \(e_f\). Let \(m_f = \max(k_f, -e_f)\). At a critical point of \(f\) in \(K\), \(k_f = 0\) and the index is \(\ge \lambda_0\), so \(-e_f > 0\); at other points \(k_f > 0\). So \(m_f > 0\) on \(K\), and \(\delta = \min_Km_f > 0\) by compactness. Let \(\varepsilon = \delta/n\). If \(g\) satisfies the inequalities, then on \(K\) \[|k_g - k_f| \le \sum_i\Big|\frac{\partial g}{\partial x_i} - \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_i}\Big| < \delta, \qquad |e_g - e_f| < \delta \tag{*}\] by Lemma C(ii). At \(x \in K\), either \(k_f(x) \ge \delta\), and then \(k_g(x) > 0\); or \(-e_f(x) \ge \delta\), and then \(-e_g(x) > 0\). At a critical point of \(g\) in \(K\) the first is impossible, so \(e_g < 0\) and the index is \(\ge \lambda_0\). \(\square\)

Milnor leaves the passage from the hypothesis to \((*)\) to “a uniform continuity argument”; Lemma C(ii) makes it the explicit choice \(\varepsilon = \delta/n\).

3. A Morse theorem for a manifold of minima (Milnor pp. 121–122)

Let \(M\) be a smooth manifold and \(f : M \to \mathbb R\) a smooth function with minimum \(0\) such that each \(M^c = f^{-1}[0,c]\) is compact. The set \(M^0 = f^{-1}(0)\) of minimum points is then compact and non-empty.

Lemma 22.5. (checked by machine: V13.14, in a narrower form) If \(M^0\) is a (topological) manifold, and if every critical point in \(M - M^0\) has index \(\ge \lambda_0\), then \(\pi_r(M,M^0) = 0\) for \(0 \le r < \lambda_0\).

We use five facts.

(T1) Hanner’s theorem. A topological manifold is an absolute neighbourhood retract for metrizable spaces; so if a topological manifold \(A\) is a closed subset of a metrizable space \(X\), some open neighbourhood of \(A\) in \(X\) retracts onto \(A\) (O. Hanner, Some theorems on absolute neighborhood retracts, Ark. Mat. 1, pp. 389–408, Theorem 3.3, as Milnor cites). If \(A\) is a compact smooth submanifold, the retraction can instead be taken from a tubular neighbourhood, as in the \(\varepsilon\)-neighbourhood theorem proved in Chapter 6 (Proposition 4.1) of the companion volume, Topology from the Differentiable Viewpoint, rewritten (embed \(M\) in a Euclidean space, retract a neighbourhood there onto \(A\), and restrict).

(T2) Uniformly normal neighbourhoods (Milnor’s 10.8, Chapter 7). For a compact \(K\) in a Riemannian manifold there is \(\delta_K > 0\) such that any two points of \(K\) at distance \(< \delta_K\) are joined by a unique geodesic of length \(< \delta_K\); it is minimal and depends smoothly on its endpoints.

(T3) Approximation (Milnor’s 6.8, Chapter 4). A bounded smooth function \(f\) on a manifold \(W\) can be uniformly approximated by a smooth function \(g\) with no degenerate critical points, whose derivatives of order \(\le 2\) also approximate those of \(f\) uniformly on a given compact set (measured in finitely many charts covering it).

(T4) Handles (Milnor’s 3.1, 3.2 and 3.3, Chapter 2), for a smooth \(g : N \to \mathbb R\) and \(N^a = g^{-1}(-\infty,a]\): (i) if \(g^{-1}[a,b]\) is compact and contains no critical points, then \(N^a\) is a deformation retract of \(N^b\), by a deformation fixing \(N^a\) pointwise; (ii) if \(g^{-1}[c-\varepsilon,c+\varepsilon]\) is compact and its only critical points are non-degenerate ones \(x_1,\dots,x_k\) at level \(c\), of indices \(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_k\), then for small \(\varepsilon\) there are disjoint closed cells \(e^{\lambda_i} \subset N\) with \(e^{\lambda_i}\cap N^{c-\varepsilon} = \partial e^{\lambda_i}\) such that \(N^{c-\varepsilon}\cup e^{\lambda_1}\cup\dots\cup e^{\lambda_k}\) is a deformation retract of \(N^{c+\varepsilon}\), again by a deformation fixing it pointwise. (Both properties are visible in Milnor’s formulas for the retractions \(r_t\).)

(T5) Pushing a disc off a cell (Hatcher, Lemma 4.10, the lemma behind cellular approximation). If \(Y\) is obtained from a subspace \(Z\) by attaching a \(k\)-cell and \(r < k\), every map \((D^r,S^{r-1}) \to (Y,Z)\) is homotopic relative to \(S^{r-1}\) to a map into \(Z\). (Hatcher’s lemma deforms the map, relative to the preimage of \(Z\), so that it misses a point of the open cell; radial projection from that point then pushes it into \(Z\).) In (T4)(ii), \(N^{c-\varepsilon}\cup e^{\lambda_i}\) is obtained from \(N^{c-\varepsilon}\) by attaching a cell: the two pieces are closed and meet in \(\partial e^{\lambda_i}\).

Lemma D (passing critical levels of high index). Let \(g : N \to \mathbb R\) be smooth, \(a < b\) regular values, \(g^{-1}[a,b]\) compact, and every critical point in \(g^{-1}[a,b]\) non-degenerate of index \(\ge \lambda_0\). If \(r < \lambda_0\), every map \(h : (D^r,S^{r-1}) \to (N^b,N^a)\) is homotopic relative to \(S^{r-1}\), within \(N^b\), to a map into \(N^a\).

Proof. Non-degenerate critical points are isolated (Milnor’s 2.3, Chapter 1), so there are finitely many in the compact \(g^{-1}[a,b]\), with critical values \(c_1 < \dots < c_m\) in \((a,b)\). Choose regular values \(a = s_0 < c_1 < s_1 < \dots < c_m < s_m = b\); it suffices to push a map from \(N^{s_j}\) into \(N^{s_{j-1}}\), relative to \(S^{r-1}\) (whose image lies in \(N^a\)), and repeat. Let \(c = c_j\) and choose \(\varepsilon\) as in (T4)(ii) with \([c-\varepsilon,c+\varepsilon] \subset (s_{j-1},s_j)\). Compose the map with the deformation of \(N^{s_j}\) onto \(N^{c+\varepsilon}\) (T4(i)), then with that of \(N^{c+\varepsilon}\) onto \(N^{c-\varepsilon}\cup\bigcup e^{\lambda_i}\) (T4(ii)); both fix \(N^{s_{j-1}}\), so these are homotopies relative to \(S^{r-1}\). Push the result off each cell in turn by (T5), as \(r < \lambda_0 \le \lambda_i\), landing in \(N^{c-\varepsilon}\); finally deform \(N^{c-\varepsilon}\) onto \(N^{s_{j-1}}\) (T4(i)). \(\square\)

Proof of Lemma 22.5. We may assume \(\lambda_0 \ge 1\). Let \(0 \le r < \lambda_0\) and \(h : (I^r,\partial I^r) \to (M,M^0)\).

Step 1: a neighbourhood of \(M^0\) deforms into \(M^0\). Give \(M\) a Riemannian metric (partition of unity); it is metrizable. By (T1) there are an open \(U_1 \supseteq M^0\) and a retraction \(\rho : U_1 \to M^0\). Let \(\delta_1\) be the number of (T2) for the compact set \(K = M^1\), and \[U = \{x \in U_1 : f(x) < 1,\ \operatorname{dist}(x,\rho(x)) < \delta_1\},\] an open set containing \(M^0\). For \(x \in U\) the points \(x\) and \(\rho(x)\) lie in \(K\) at distance \(< \delta_1\); let \(\sigma_x : [0,1] \to M\) be the geodesic of (T2) from \(x\) to \(\rho(x)\), and \(D(x,s) = \sigma_x(s)\). Then \(D\) is continuous, \(D(x,0) = x\), \(D(x,1) = \rho(x) \in M^0\), and \(D(a,s) = a\) for \(a \in M^0\). This is Milnor’s “\(U\) can be deformed into \(M^0\) within \(M\)”.

Step 2: a good approximation. Let \(c = \max f\circ h\). If \(U = M\), put \(h' = h\) and go to the last sentence of Step 3. Otherwise \(f\) has a minimum on the closed set \(M - U\) (each \(M^C\cap(M-U)\) is compact), which is positive because \(M^0 \subseteq U\); call it \(4\delta\). On the open set \(W = f^{-1}(-\infty,c+4\delta)\) the function \(f\) is bounded. The compact set \(K_* = f^{-1}[\delta,c+3\delta] \subset W\) lies in \(M - M^0\); cover it by finitely many compact sets \(K_i\), each in a chart domain. By hypothesis the critical points of \(f\) in \(K_i\) have index \(\ge \lambda_0\); let \(\varepsilon_i\) be the number of Lemma 22.4 for \(f\) and \(K_i\) in that chart. By (T3) there is a smooth \(g : W \to \mathbb R\) with no degenerate critical points, \(|g - f| < \delta\) on \(W\), and derivatives of order \(\le 2\) within \(\varepsilon_i\) of those of \(f\) on each \(K_i\). By Lemma 22.4, every critical point of \(g\) in \(K_*\) is non-degenerate of index \(\ge \lambda_0\).

Step 3: pushing \(h\) down. Write \(W^a = \{x \in W : g(x) \le a\}\). Since \(|g - f| < \delta\): \(g^{-1}[2\delta, c+2\delta] \subseteq f^{-1}(\delta,c+3\delta) \subseteq K_*\), so this set is compact and contains finitely many critical points of \(g\), all non-degenerate of index \(\ge \lambda_0\); choose regular values \(a \in (2\delta,3\delta)\) and \(b \in (c+\delta,c+2\delta)\). Then \(h(I^r) \subseteq M^c \subseteq W^b\); \(M^0 \subseteq W^a\) (there \(g < \delta\)); and \(W^a \subseteq U\) (there \(f < a + \delta < 4\delta\)). By Lemma D, \(h\) is homotopic relative to \(\partial I^r\), within \(W^b\), to a map \(h'\) into \(W^a \subseteq U\). Finally \(s \mapsto D(h'(\cdot),s)\) is a homotopy relative to \(\partial I^r\) (it fixes \(h'(\partial I^r) \subseteq M^0\)) from \(h'\) to a map \(h''\) into \(M^0\). \(\square\)

Milnor’s text skips several points in this proof. (i) \(M^0\) is compact, since \(M^0 \subseteq M^c\), and so is its neighbourhood \(M^1\); this is what makes a single \(\delta_1\) work in Step 1. (ii) He takes \(g\) on the compact set \(M^{c+2\delta}\); a smooth function must live on an open set, here \(W\), where \(f\) is bounded so that 6.8 applies. (iii) That \(g^{-1}(-\infty,c+\delta]\) “has the homotopy type of \(g^{-1}(-\infty,2\delta]\) with cells … attached”: an abstract homotopy equivalence would not do; the argument needs deformations fixing the lower level, which §3 of Milnor provides (T4), and the levels should be regular, which requires the extra room built into Step 2. (iv) “Since \(r < \lambda_0\) it follows that \(h\) is homotopic …”: this is (T5).

4. Proof of Theorem 22.1 (Milnor pp. 122–123)

Let \(0 \le i < \lambda_0\) and \(h : (I^i,\partial I^i) \to (\Omega,\Omega^d)\). We show that \(h\) is homotopic relative to \(\partial I^i\) to a map into \(\Omega^d\).

Step 1: a finite energy bound. \(E\) is continuous on \(\Omega\) and \(h(I^i)\) is compact, so \(E\circ h\) is bounded; choose \(c > d\) larger than its maximum. Then \(h\) maps into \(\operatorname{Int}\Omega^c\), an open set containing \(\Omega^d\). This is Milnor’s “it is sufficient to prove that \(\pi_i(\operatorname{Int}\Omega^c,\Omega^d) = 0\) for arbitrarily large values of \(c\)”.

Step 2: the finite-dimensional model. By Lemma 16.1 and Theorem 16.2 (Chapter 10), for a fine subdivision \(0 = t_0 < \dots < t_k = 1\) the set \(B = \operatorname{Int}\Omega^c(t_0,\dots,t_k)\) of broken geodesics of energy \(< c\) is a smooth manifold (an open subset of \(M^{k-1}\), via \(\omega \mapsto (\omega(t_1),\dots,\omega(t_{k-1}))\), a homeomorphism for the topology of \(\Omega\)); \(E' = E|_B\) is smooth; \(B^a = E'^{-1}[0,a]\) is compact for \(a < c\); and the critical points of \(E'\) are the unbroken geodesics from \(p\) to \(q\) of energy \(< c\), the index of \(E'_{**}\) being that of \(E_{**}\). Moreover there is a homotopy \(r_u : \operatorname{Int}\Omega^c \to \operatorname{Int}\Omega^c\), \(0 \le u \le 1\), with \(r_0 = \mathrm{id}\) and \(r_1\) a retraction onto \(B\), and each \(r_u\) fixes \(B\) pointwise (on a broken geodesic, the minimal geodesics used to define \(r_u\) are its own segments). Every minimal geodesic is an unbroken geodesic of energy \(d < c\), so \(\Omega^d \subseteq B\) and \(r_u\) fixes \(\Omega^d\). Hence \(h \simeq r_1\circ h\) relative to \(\partial I^i\), and \(r_1\circ h\) maps \((I^i,\partial I^i)\) into \((B,\Omega^d)\).

Step 3: a function with minimum \(0\). As Milnor notes, the only difficulty is that \(E\) takes its values in \([d,c)\) rather than \([0,\infty)\). Let \(F : [d,c) \to [0,\infty)\) be a diffeomorphism, e.g. \(F(x) = (x-d)/(c-x)\). Any such \(F\) is increasing with \(F(d) = 0\) (a homeomorphism matches the endpoints, the only points whose removal leaves the interval connected) and \(F' > 0\). Let \(f = F\circ E' : B \to [0,\infty)\). We check the hypotheses of Lemma 22.5 for \((B, f)\): - \(f\) is smooth with minimum \(0\), attained exactly on \(\Omega^d\) (Lemma 12.1), which is non-empty; - \(f^{-1}[0,a] = B^{F^{-1}(a)}\) is compact, since \(F^{-1}(a) < c\); - \(f^{-1}(0) = \Omega^d\) is a topological manifold, by hypothesis; - the critical points of \(f\) are those of \(E'\), as \(F' > 0\); those outside \(\Omega^d\) are non-minimal geodesics, and at such a point the Hessian of \(f\) is \(F'(E)\) times that of \(E'\) (the term \(F''(E)\,dE'\otimes dE'\) vanishes there), so its index is the index of \(E_{**}\), which is \(\ge \lambda_0\).

By Lemma 22.5, \(r_1\circ h\) is homotopic relative to \(\partial I^i\), within \(B\), to a map into \(\Omega^d\). With Step 2 this proves the theorem. \(\square\)

An interactive look at the antipodes

The sphere is \(S^2\), the case \(n = 1\) of \(S^{n+1}\), with \(p\) at the top and \(q = -p\) at the bottom; drag it to turn it. The grey meridians are minimal geodesics from \(p\) to \(q\). Each crosses the blue equator once, at its midpoint, and this is the homeomorphism \(\Omega^d \cong S^n\) of Lemma A. The red curve leaves \(p\) in the direction set by the first slider and makes the number of half-turns set by the second; it is drawn slightly lifted off the sphere so that its passes can be told apart. The open circles are its conjugate points, its passages through \(p\) and \(q\) before the end, each of multiplicity \(n\), and the index \(2mn\) of Lemma B is printed below. The third slider sets \(n\): the sphere is then \(S^{n+1}\) (the picture shows a great \(2\)-sphere through \(p\)), and the text gives \(\lambda_0 = 2n\) and the range of Corollary 22.3. The table lists the groups \(\pi_{n+k}(S^n)\) from Toda’s tables; shaded entries are those that Corollary 22.3 forces to equal the entry below them, and the entries governed by the chosen \(n\) are outlined.

5. Application: the stable range of the homotopy groups of spheres

Maps between spheres of different dimensions. For \(0 \le j < N\), \(\pi_j(S^N) = 0\). By induction on \(N\). For \(j = 0\) this says \(S^N\) is connected. For \(1 \le j < N\) (so \(N \ge 2\)), apply Corollary 22.3 with \(n = N-1\) and \(i = j-1\); the condition \(i \le 2n-2\) reads \(j \le 2N-3\), which holds because \(j \le N-1 \le 2N-3\). So \(\pi_j(S^N) \cong \pi_{j-1}(S^{N-1})\), which is \(0\) by induction since \(j - 1 < N - 1\). In words: every map \(S^j \to S^N\) with \(j < N\) is null-homotopic. The usual proof smooths the map and uses Sard’s theorem (Chapter 3 of the companion volume) to find a point it misses; here the same fact comes from counting conjugate points: the long geodesics between antipodes have index at least \(2n\).

The degree. With \(i = n\), Corollary 22.3 gives \(\pi_n(S^n) \cong \pi_{n+1}(S^{n+1})\) for \(n \ge 2\), so \(\pi_n(S^n) \cong \pi_2(S^2)\) for all \(n \ge 2\). Corollary 22.3 does not say what this group is; Corollary 17.4 (Chapter 10) does. For \(n \ge 2\) it gives \(\Omega S^{n+1}\) cells only in dimensions \(0, n, 2n, \dots\), so \(\Omega S^{n+1}\) is \((n-1)\)-connected and, by (H3) and the Hurewicz theorem, \(\pi_{n+1}(S^{n+1}) \cong \pi_n(\Omega S^{n+1}) \cong H_n(\Omega S^{n+1}) \cong \mathbb Z\). The Hopf degree theorem (Chapter 7, Theorem 6.3, of the companion volume, for smooth maps, to which continuous maps and homotopies can be reduced) identifies the isomorphism with the degree.

The stable stems. Put \(i = n + k\). Corollary 22.3 says that \(\pi_{n+k}(S^n)\) does not depend on \(n\) once \(n \ge k+2\); this common value is the stable \(k\)-stem \(\pi_k^s\). Comparing with the classical computations (H. Toda, Composition Methods in Homotopy Groups of Spheres, 1962), for \(k = 0,1,\dots,7\):

\(k\) 0 1 2 3 4 5 6 7
\(\pi_k^s\) \(\mathbb Z\) \(\mathbb Z/2\) \(\mathbb Z/2\) \(\mathbb Z/24\) \(0\) \(0\) \(\mathbb Z/2\) \(\mathbb Z/240\)
stable from \(n =\) 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 9
last unstable value \(\pi_1(S^1) = \mathbb Z\) \(\pi_3(S^2) = \mathbb Z\) \(\pi_5(S^3) = \mathbb Z/2\) \(\pi_7(S^4) = \mathbb Z\oplus\mathbb Z/12\) \(\pi_9(S^5) = \mathbb Z/2\) \(\pi_{11}(S^6) = \mathbb Z\) \(\pi_{13}(S^7) = \mathbb Z/2\) \(\pi_{15}(S^8) = \mathbb Z\oplus\mathbb Z/120\)

The table in the figure shows the whole range \(1 \le n \le 8\). Every entry with \(n \ge k+2\) equals the entry below it, as the corollary requires, and the range is sharp in several places: \(\pi_3(S^2) = \mathbb Z\) but \(\pi_4(S^3) = \mathbb Z/2\), \(\pi_7(S^4) = \mathbb Z\oplus\mathbb Z/12\) but \(\pi_8(S^5) = \mathbb Z/24\), \(\pi_{11}(S^6) = \mathbb Z\) but \(\pi_{12}(S^7) = 0\). In each of these the map is still onto, as the surjectivity half of the theorem predicts. (In other places the groups happen to agree before the stable range, e.g. \(\pi_5(S^3) = \pi_6(S^4) = \mathbb Z/2\).)

Loops on a sphere. \(H_i(\Omega S^{n+1}) \cong H_i(S^n)\) for \(i \le 2n-2\): for \(n \ge 2\), \(\mathbb Z\) in degrees \(0\) and \(n\) and zero otherwise in this range. This agrees with Corollary 17.4 (Chapter 10), which gives \(\Omega S^{n+1}\) one cell in each of the dimensions \(0, n, 2n, \dots\); the first cell not seen by \(\Omega^d\) has dimension \(2n = \lambda_0\).

Back to the seismic waves. On the \(2\)-sphere (\(n = 1\)) the geodesic from \(p\) to \(-p\) with \(2m+1\) half-turns has index \(2m\): one for each passage through the epicentre or its antipode before arrival. Seismologists observe exactly this count. A surface wave picks up a phase shift of \(\pi/2\) at each such passage, the polar phase shift (Brune, Nafe and Alsop, Bull. Seismol. Soc. Amer. 51 (1961)), which is \(\pi/2\) times the Morse index, as in the semiclassical rule recalled in Chapter 12, §6.1.

6. Summary of what was silently assumed, now made explicit

p. 118 \(\Omega^d\) = the space of minimal geodesics Lemma 12.1: \(E \ge d\), with equality exactly on minimal geodesics

p. 118 “the inclusion homomorphism … is an isomorphism for \(i \le \lambda_0-2\)” the exact sequence for \(i \ge 1\); a direct argument for \(i = 0\); onto for \(i = \lambda_0 - 1\)

Checked by machine. Milnor’s §22 has been verified in the Lean proof assistant, for submanifolds of Euclidean space with the induced metric. Checked: Theorem 22.1, in a relative form (every map of a compact space of small dimension into \(\Omega\) is homotopic, relative to the part already in \(\Omega^d\), to a map into \(\Omega^d\)), with the hypothesis that \(\Omega^d\) is a topological manifold replaced by what the proof uses of it, that \(\Omega^d\) is a retract of an open neighbourhood in \(\Omega\); the corollary on the inclusion \(\Omega^d \to \Omega\), including \(\pi_0\); Corollary 22.2, as a bijection and, for \(i \ge 1\), as an isomorphism of groups, with the change of base point it hides; Lemmas A and B for the sphere, an explicit neighbourhood retraction there, and Corollary 22.3 together with its surjective half; Lemma 22.4 (by an argument that does not need Lemma C), Lemma 22.5 and Lemma D; and the variant of Theorem 22.1 for an open and closed set of paths which Chapter 15 uses. Not checked: Hanner’s theorem (for the sphere, for \(SU(2m)\) and for the spaces of Chapter 15 the retraction is constructed, so the results there do not depend on it), the homological form of the corollary, that the isomorphism of Corollary 22.3 is the suspension homomorphism, and the application.
