Chapter 14Milnor §23pp. 124–132Contents ↑

Chapter 14. Bott periodicity for the unitary group: the Grassmannian of shortest paths

Milnor, “Morse Theory”, §23, rewritten for a first-year graduate student who wants to know what the theorem is for. Every proof is complete, except that, as in Milnor, two facts of homotopy theory are quoted: coset spaces of Lie groups are fibre bundles, and fibre bundles have exact homotopy sequences. The homotopy groups of spheres that are needed are taken from the companion volume. All of this is stated precisely in §3.

0. Why is magnetic charge an integer, and what happens in higher dimensions?

In 1931 Dirac showed that if a magnetic monopole of charge \(g\) exists, then every electric charge \(e\) satisfies \(eg = \tfrac12 N\hbar c\) (Gaussian units) for an integer \(N\). In the language of Wu and Yang (1975), the quantum states of a charged particle on a sphere around the monopole are the sections of a complex line bundle over \(S^2\). Over the northern and over the southern hemisphere the bundle is trivial; it is determined by how the two trivializations are glued along the equator, that is, by a map from the equator \(S^1\) to the group \(U(1)\) of phases. The integer \(N\) is the winding number of this map, an element of \(\pi_1 U(1) = \mathbb Z\).

Ask the same question over higher spheres. A bundle of states with \(N\) internal components over \(S^n\) is glued from two trivial pieces by a map \(S^{n-1} \to U(N)\), so such bundles are classified by \(\pi_{n-1}U(N)\). Over \(S^4\) these are the Yang–Mills instantons, labelled by an element of \(\pi_3 SU(2) = \mathbb Z\) (Belavin, Polyakov, Schwarz and Tyupkin, 1975). Over \(S^3\) there is nothing: every bundle is trivial. What happens over \(S^{100}\)?

Bott’s answer: once \(N \geq n/2\), the group \(\pi_{n-1}U(N)\) no longer depends on \(N\), and it is \(\mathbb Z\) for \(n\) even and \(0\) for \(n\) odd. The twisting alternates forever between “an integer’s worth” and “none”. This chapter proves it by Milnor’s route. On the special unitary group \(SU(2m)\) the shortest paths from \(I\) to \(-I\) form the complex Grassmannian \(G_m(\mathbb C^{2m})\), and every other geodesic from \(I\) to \(-I\) has index at least \(2m+2\). By the theorem of Chapter 13 (Milnor’s Theorem 22.1), the Grassmannian then captures the homotopy groups of the path space up to dimension \(2m\), and a little homotopy theory turns this into \(\pi_{i-1}U \cong \pi_{i+1}U\). In §5 we return to monopoles and instantons and list the complex vector bundles over spheres of dimension up to eight.

1. The unitary group, its exponential and its metric (Milnor pp. 124–126)

Let \(M_n(\mathbb C)\) be the space of complex \(n \times n\) matrices, a real vector space of dimension \(2n^2\) with the Euclidean inner product \[\langle X, Y\rangle = \operatorname{Re}\operatorname{tr}(XY^*) = \operatorname{Re}\sum_{i,j}x_{ij}\bar y_{ij}, \qquad |X| = \langle X, X\rangle^{1/2},\] where \(Y^*\) is the conjugate transpose. Three properties are used throughout: \(|XY| \leq |X|\,|Y|\) (Cauchy–Schwarz entry by entry), \(|X^*| = |X|\), and \(|SXT| = |X|\) for \(S, T\) unitary (because \(\operatorname{tr}(SXTT^*X^*S^*) = \operatorname{tr}(XX^*)\)).

Definition. The unitary group is \(U(n) = \{S \in M_n(\mathbb C) : SS^* = I\}\), the group of linear maps of \(\mathbb C^n\) preserving the Hermitian inner product. For \(A \in M_n(\mathbb C)\), \(\exp A = I + A + A^2/2! + A^3/3! + \cdots\). Since \(|A^k| \leq |A|^k\), the series and all its term-wise derivatives converge uniformly on bounded sets, so \(\exp\) is smooth.

Lemma 1.1 (Milnor’s (1)–(4)). (1) \(\exp(A^*) = (\exp A)^*\) and \(\exp(TAT^{-1}) = T(\exp A)T^{-1}\). (2) If \(AB = BA\), then \(\exp(A+B) = (\exp A)(\exp B)\). (3) \((\exp A)(\exp(-A)) = I\). (4) There is \(\varepsilon > 0\) such that \(\exp\) maps the ball \(B_\varepsilon = \{|A| < \varepsilon\}\) diffeomorphically onto an open neighbourhood of \(I\).

Proof. (1) Term by term, since \((A^k)^* = (A^*)^k\), \((TAT^{-1})^k = TA^kT^{-1}\), and both operations are continuous and linear. (2) The Cauchy product of two absolutely convergent series gives \((\exp A)(\exp B) = \sum_k \sum_{i+j=k} A^iB^j/(i!\,j!) = \sum_k (A+B)^k/k!\), the binomial theorem being valid because \(A\) and \(B\) commute. (3) is (2) with \(B = -A\). (4) \(\exp A = I + A + R(A)\) with \(|R(A)| \leq \sum_{k \geq 2}|A|^k/k! \leq |A|^2e^{|A|}\), so the derivative of \(\exp\) at \(0\) is the identity, and the inverse function theorem (as in Chapter 1 of the companion volume, Topology from the Differentiable Viewpoint, rewritten) applies; shrink the neighbourhood to a ball. \(\square\)

We fix such an \(\varepsilon\), taking also \(\varepsilon \leq 2\pi/\sqrt n\). The ball \(B_\varepsilon\) is invariant under \(A \mapsto -A\), \(A \mapsto A^*\) and \(A \mapsto SAS^{-1}\) for \(S\) unitary, since these preserve \(|\cdot|\). Let \(\mathfrak u(n) = \{A : A + A^* = 0\}\) be the skew-Hermitian matrices, a real subspace of dimension \(n^2\) (\(n\) imaginary diagonal entries and \(n(n-1)/2\) complex entries above the diagonal).

Lemma 1.2. If \(A \in \mathfrak u(n)\), then \(\exp A \in U(n)\). If \(A \in B_\varepsilon\) and \(\exp A \in U(n)\), then \(A \in \mathfrak u(n)\).

Proof. \((\exp A)(\exp A)^* = (\exp A)(\exp A^*) = (\exp A)(\exp(-A)) = I\) by (1) and (3). Conversely \(\exp(A^*) = (\exp A)^* = (\exp A)^{-1} = \exp(-A)\), and \(A^*, -A \in B_\varepsilon\), where \(\exp\) is injective. \(\square\)

Lemma 1.3 (Milnor’s (5) and (6)). \(U(n)\) is a compact smooth submanifold of \(M_n(\mathbb C)\) of dimension \(n^2\) and a Lie group, and its tangent space at \(I\) is \(\mathfrak u(n)\).

Proof. By Lemma 1.2, \(U(n) \cap \exp(B_\varepsilon) = \exp(B_\varepsilon \cap \mathfrak u(n))\). In the chart \(\exp^{-1}\) of \(M_n(\mathbb C)\) near \(I\), therefore, \(U(n)\) is an open piece of the linear subspace \(\mathfrak u(n)\): near \(I\) it is a submanifold with tangent space \(\mathfrak u(n)\). For \(S_0 \in U(n)\), left multiplication \(X \mapsto S_0X\) is a linear automorphism of \(M_n(\mathbb C)\) carrying \(U(n)\) onto itself and \(I\) to \(S_0\), so it transports the chart. \(U(n)\) is closed and bounded (\(|S|^2 = n\)), hence compact; multiplication and inversion \(S \mapsto S^*\) are restrictions of polynomial maps. \(\square\)

The Lie algebra. For \(A \in \mathfrak u(n)\) the field \(X_A(S) = SA\) is left invariant (left translation \(L_T\) is the linear map \(X \mapsto TX\), and \(T(SA) = (TS)A\)), with value \(A\) at \(I\), and every left-invariant field is of this form.

Lemma 1.4 (Milnor’s “computation shows”). \([X_A, X_B] = X_{[A,B]}\), where \([A, B] = AB - BA\) and the bracket of vector fields is \([X,Y]f = X(Yf) - Y(Xf)\) (Milnor 8.5).

Proof. On an open subset of a vector space, let \(X, Y\) be given by smooth maps \(F, G\). Then \(Y\!f(p) = Df_p(G(p))\) and \(X(Y\!f)(p) = D^2f_p(F(p), G(p)) + Df_p(DG_p(F(p)))\); subtracting the same expression with \(F, G\) exchanged, the second-derivative terms cancel by symmetry, so \([X,Y]\) is given by \(DG_p(F(p)) - DF_p(G(p))\). For \(F(S) = SA\), \(G(S) = SB\) on the open set \(GL_n(\mathbb C)\) this is \(SAB - SBA\). These fields are tangent to the submanifold \(U(n)\), and the bracket of fields tangent to a submanifold is tangent to it and restricts to the bracket of the restrictions. \(\square\)

So the Lie algebra \(\mathfrak g\) of \(U(n)\) is \(\mathfrak u(n)\) with the commutator.

The metric. On \(\mathfrak g\) put \(\langle A, B\rangle = \operatorname{Re}\operatorname{tr}(AB^*)\), which is positive definite: \(\langle A, A\rangle = \sum|a_{ij}|^2\). Milnor defines the corresponding left-invariant metric and checks that it is right invariant by checking invariance under the adjoint action. Both facts are contained in the following.

Lemma 1.5. Give \(U(n)\) the Riemannian metric induced from the Euclidean space \(M_n(\mathbb C)\). (a) It is the left-invariant metric determined by \(\langle\,,\rangle\) on \(\mathfrak g\): \(\langle SA, SB\rangle = \langle A, B\rangle\) on \(T U(n)_S = S\mathfrak g\). (b) Left and right translations, and the inner automorphisms \(X \mapsto SXS^{-1}\), are isometries. (c) The derivative of \(X \mapsto SXS^{-1}\) at \(I\) is \(\operatorname{Ad}(S)A = SAS^{-1}\), and \(\langle \operatorname{Ad}(S)A, \operatorname{Ad}(S)B\rangle = \langle A, B\rangle\).

Proof. Multiplication on either side by a unitary matrix is a linear isometry of \(M_n(\mathbb C)\) carrying \(U(n)\) onto itself, so it restricts to an isometry of \(U(n)\); this gives (b), and (a) is \(\operatorname{Re}\operatorname{tr}(SAB^*S^*) = \operatorname{Re}\operatorname{tr}(AB^*)\). In (c) the inner automorphism is the restriction of a linear map, which is its own derivative; and \(\operatorname{tr}(SAS^{-1}(SBS^{-1})^*) = \operatorname{tr}(SAB^*S^{-1}) = \operatorname{tr}(AB^*)\), using \((S^{-1})^* = S\), exactly as on Milnor’s p. 126. \(\square\)

For \(A, B \in \mathfrak g\) the trace \(\operatorname{tr}(AB)\) is real, so \(\langle A, B\rangle = -\operatorname{tr}(AB)\).

Geodesics. By Lemma 21.2 (Chapter 12), the geodesics through \(I\) of a Lie group with a bi-invariant metric are its one-parameter subgroups. For \(A \in \mathfrak g\), \(t \mapsto \exp(tA)\) is a one-parameter subgroup (by (2), since \(sA\) and \(tA\) commute) with velocity \(A\) at \(t = 0\). Conversely, if \(\varphi\) is a one-parameter subgroup with \(\varphi'(0) = A\), differentiating \(\varphi(t+s) = \varphi(t)\varphi(s)\) at \(s = 0\) gives \(\varphi'(t) = \varphi(t)A\), the linear differential equation that \(\exp(tA)\) also solves with the same initial value; so \(\varphi(t) = \exp(tA)\). Hence the geodesic through \(I\) with velocity \(A\) is \(t \mapsto \exp(tA)\), and the Riemannian exponential map of §10 at \(I\) is the matrix exponential (Milnor p. 125). By left translation, the geodesic through \(S\) with velocity \(SA\) is \(t \mapsto S\exp(tA)\), of constant speed \(|A|\).

Diagonal form; \(\exp\) is onto. We quote the spectral theorem: a normal matrix is unitarily diagonalizable (e.g. Axler, Linear Algebra Done Right, the complex spectral theorem). A skew-Hermitian matrix has imaginary eigenvalues and a unitary one has eigenvalues of modulus one. So for \(A \in \mathfrak g\) there is \(T \in U(n)\) with \(TAT^{-1} = \operatorname{diag}(ia_1, \dots, ia_n)\), and for \(S \in U(n)\) there is \(T\) with \(TST^{-1} = \operatorname{diag}(e^{ia_1}, \dots, e^{ia_n})\), the \(a_j\) real. In the second case \(S = \exp(T^{-1}\operatorname{diag}(ia_j)T)\) by (1): \(\exp : \mathfrak g \to U(n)\) is onto, and \(U(n)\) is path connected.

The special unitary group. For \(A \in \mathfrak g\), diagonalizing gives \(\det(\exp A) = e^{\operatorname{tr}A}\). Let \(SU(n) = \{S \in U(n) : \det S = 1\}\) and \(\mathfrak{su}(n) = \{A \in \mathfrak g : \operatorname{tr}A = 0\}\), of dimension \(n^2 - 1\).

Lemma 1.6. \(SU(n)\) is a compact connected submanifold and Lie subgroup of \(U(n)\) with tangent space \(\mathfrak{su}(n)\) at \(I\). With the induced metric it is bi-invariant, its geodesics through \(I\) are \(t \mapsto \exp(tA)\), \(A \in \mathfrak{su}(n)\), and \(\exp : \mathfrak{su}(n) \to SU(n)\) is onto.

Proof. For \(A \in B_\varepsilon \cap \mathfrak g\), \(|\operatorname{tr}A| \leq \sqrt n\,|A| < 2\pi\) (Cauchy–Schwarz on the diagonal), so \(\exp A \in SU(n)\) iff \(\operatorname{tr}A \in 2\pi i\mathbb Z\) iff \(\operatorname{tr}A = 0\). Thus \(SU(n) \cap \exp(B_\varepsilon) = \exp(B_\varepsilon \cap \mathfrak{su}(n))\), and left translation by elements of \(SU(n)\) does the rest, as in Lemma 1.3. Translations by elements of \(SU(n)\) are isometries of \(U(n)\) preserving \(SU(n)\), so the induced metric is bi-invariant, and Lemma 21.2 applies to \(SU(n)\). If \(S = \exp(T^{-1}\operatorname{diag}(ia_j)T) \in SU(n)\), then \(\sum a_j \in 2\pi\mathbb Z\); changing \(a_1\) by a multiple of \(2\pi\) (which does not change \(S\)) makes \(\sum a_j = 0\). \(\square\)

The bracket on \(\mathfrak{su}(n)\) is again the commutator. Milnor writes \(\mathfrak g'\) for \(\mathfrak{su}(n)\).

2. Minimal geodesics from \(I\) to \(-I\) (Milnor pp. 126–128)

All geodesics are parametrized by \([0,1]\). By §1, a geodesic from \(I\) to \(-I\) in \(U(n)\) is \(t \mapsto \exp(tA)\) with \(A \in \mathfrak g\) and \(\exp A = -I\).

Lemma 2.1. For \(A \in \mathfrak g\), \(\exp A = -I\) iff the eigenvalues of \(A\) are \(i\pi k_1, \dots, i\pi k_n\) with every \(k_j\) an odd integer. The geodesic \(t \mapsto \exp(tA)\), \(0 \leq t \leq 1\), then has length \(|A| = \pi(k_1^2 + \cdots + k_n^2)^{1/2}\).

Proof. With \(TAT^{-1} = \operatorname{diag}(ia_j)\): \(\exp A = -I\) iff \(\exp(TAT^{-1}) = \operatorname{diag}(e^{ia_j}) = -I\) iff every \(a_j\) is an odd multiple of \(\pi\). The speed is constantly \(|A|\), and \(|A| = |TAT^{-1}|\). \(\square\)

Corollary 2.2. In \(U(n)\) the distance from \(I\) to \(-I\) is \(\pi\sqrt n\), and the minimal geodesics from \(I\) to \(-I\) are the \(t \mapsto \exp(tA)\) with \(A^2 = -\pi^2 I\). For such \(A\), let \(P\) be the orthogonal projection onto \(E = \operatorname{Eigen}(i\pi) = \{v : Av = i\pi v\}\). Then \(A = i\pi(2P - I)\) and \[\exp(tA) = e^{i\pi t}P + e^{-i\pi t}(I - P). \tag{2.1}\] Conversely, for every complex subspace \(E \subseteq \mathbb C^n\), with projection \(P\), the matrix \(A = i\pi(2P - I)\) lies in \(\mathfrak g\) and satisfies \(A^2 = -\pi^2I\).

Proof. \(U(n)\) is compact, hence complete, so by the Hopf–Rinow theorem (Milnor 10.9) some minimal geodesic from \(I\) to \(-I\) exists. By Lemma 2.1 every geodesic from \(I\) to \(-I\) has length \(\pi(\sum k_j^2)^{1/2} \geq \pi\sqrt n\), with equality iff every \(k_j = \pm 1\), and equality occurs (\(A = i\pi I\)). So the distance is \(\pi\sqrt n\), and the minimal geodesics are those with all \(k_j = \pm 1\), i.e. with \(A\) diagonalizable with eigenvalues \(\pm i\pi\), i.e. \(A^2 = -\pi^2I\). Then \(\mathbb C^n = E \oplus E^\perp\) with \(E^\perp = \operatorname{Eigen}(-i\pi)\), which gives \(A = i\pi P - i\pi(I-P)\) and (2.1). Conversely \(iP\) is skew-Hermitian because \(P\) is Hermitian, and \((2P - I)^2 = I\). \(\square\)

So, as a set, the space of minimal geodesics from \(I\) to \(-I\) in \(U(n)\) is the set of all complex subspaces of \(\mathbb C^n\) (Milnor p. 127). Milnor identifies it with that space; the topology needs a word. Let \(\operatorname{Gr}(\mathbb C^n) = \{P \in M_n(\mathbb C) : P = P^* = P^2\}\), a compact set, and \(G_k(\mathbb C^n) = \{P \in \operatorname{Gr}(\mathbb C^n) : \operatorname{tr}P = k\}\) (projections of rank \(k\)). It is standard that \(G_k(\mathbb C^n)\) is a compact connected manifold of real dimension \(2k(n-k)\): near a subspace \(E_0\), the subspaces of dimension \(k\) are the graphs of the linear maps \(E_0 \to E_0^\perp\).

Lemma 2.3 (the topology). Let \(\Omega = \Omega(U(n); I, -I)\) carry Milnor’s metric (§16) \[d(\omega, \omega') = \max_t \rho(\omega(t), \omega'(t)) + \Bigl(\int_0^1\bigl(\tfrac{ds}{dt} - \tfrac{ds'}{dt}\bigr)^2dt\Bigr)^{1/2}.\] Then \(\Phi(P)(t) = e^{i\pi t}P + e^{-i\pi t}(I - P)\) is a homeomorphism of \(\operatorname{Gr}(\mathbb C^n)\) onto the subspace of minimal geodesics.

Proof. \(\Phi\) is a bijection onto the minimal geodesics by Corollary 2.2 (\(P\) is recovered from \(\Phi(P)'(0) = i\pi(2P - I)\)). All the paths \(\Phi(P)\) have the same constant speed \(\pi\sqrt n\), so the integral term of \(d(\Phi(P), \Phi(Q))\) vanishes. The function \((t, P, Q) \mapsto \rho(\Phi(P)(t), \Phi(Q)(t))\) is continuous on the compact set \([0,1] \times \operatorname{Gr} \times \operatorname{Gr}\) (the distance \(\rho\) is continuous, §10) and vanishes for \(P = Q\); by uniform continuity its maximum over \(t\) tends to \(0\) as \(Q \to P\). So \(\Phi\) is continuous, and a continuous bijection from a compact space to a metric space is a homeomorphism. \(\square\)

A hidden hypothesis. Milnor calls the space of all subspaces “rather inconvenient”, because its components \(G_k(\mathbb C^n)\) have different dimensions. The trouble with \(U(n)\) is worse: there the hypothesis of Theorem 22.1 fails. Take \(k = (3, 1, \dots, 1)\). The index formula of Lemma 4.1 below holds verbatim on \(\mathfrak u(n)\) (the extra direction \(iI\) has eigenvalue \(0\)), and gives index \((n-1)(3 - 1 - 2) = 0\) for this non-minimal geodesic, which lies in a component of \(\Omega(U(n); I, -I)\) that contains no minimal geodesic at all. Indeed, for a path \(\omega\) from \(I\) to \(-I\) let \(\theta_\omega\) be the continuous determination of the argument of \(\det\omega(t)\) with \(\theta_\omega(0) = 0\); then \(\theta_\omega(1)/\pi\) is an integer which cannot change along a continuous family of paths. On the geodesic \(\exp(tA)\), where \(\det\exp(tA) = e^{i\pi t\sum k_j}\), it equals \(\sum k_j\): here \(n + 2\), while every minimal geodesic has \(|\sum k_j| \leq n\). So the hypothesis of Theorem 22.1 (every non-minimal geodesic has index \(\geq \lambda_0\)) fails in \(U(n)\) for every \(\lambda_0 \geq 1\), which is why the argument is run in \(SU(2m)\): its geodesics from \(I\) to \(-I\) are exactly those of \(U(2m)\) with \(\sum k_j = 0\).

In \(SU(n)\), \(\operatorname{tr}A = i\pi\sum k_j\) must vanish, and \(-I \in SU(n)\) requires \(n\) even. Take \(n = 2m\).

Lemma 23.1. (checked by machine: V14.16, V14.17, restated)1 The space of minimal geodesics from \(I\) to \(-I\) in \(SU(2m)\) is homeomorphic to the complex Grassmann manifold \(G_m(\mathbb C^{2m})\) of \(m\)-dimensional subspaces of \(\mathbb C^{2m}\).

Proof. By Lemma 1.6 the geodesics from \(I\) to \(-I\) in \(SU(2m)\) are the \(\exp(tA)\) with \(A \in \mathfrak{su}(2m)\), \(\exp A = -I\): by Lemma 2.1, eigenvalues \(i\pi k_j\) with \(k_j\) odd and \(\sum k_j = 0\), length \(\pi(\sum k_j^2)^{1/2} \geq \pi\sqrt{2m}\). A minimal geodesic exists (\(SU(2m)\) is compact), and length \(\pi\sqrt{2m}\) is attained by \(A = \operatorname{diag}(i\pi I_m, -i\pi I_m)\). So the minimal geodesics are those with all \(k_j = \pm 1\) and \(\sum k_j = 0\): \(m\) of each sign, i.e. \(A = i\pi(2P - I)\) with \(\operatorname{tr}P = m\). Conversely every \(P \in G_m(\mathbb C^{2m})\) gives such an \(A\), with \(\operatorname{tr}A = i\pi(2m - 2m) = 0\). The topology is handled by Lemma 2.3, with \(\rho\) the distance of \(SU(2m)\). \(\square\)

Lemma 23.2. (checked by machine: V14.11, restated; V14.20, as stated) Every non-minimal geodesic from \(I\) to \(-I\) in \(SU(2m)\) has index \(\geq 2m + 2\).

This is proved in §4. With Chapter 13 it gives Bott’s theorem.

Theorem 23.3 (Bott). (checked by machine: V14.22, restated) The inclusion \(G_m(\mathbb C^{2m}) \to \Omega(SU(2m); I, -I)\) of Lemma 23.1 induces isomorphisms of homotopy groups in dimensions \(\leq 2m\). Hence \[\pi_i G_m(\mathbb C^{2m}) \cong \pi_{i+1}SU(2m) \qquad (0 \leq i \leq 2m).\]

Proof. \(SU(2m)\) is compact, hence complete. By Lemma 23.1 the space \(\Omega^d\) of minimal geodesics is a manifold, and by Lemma 23.2 every other geodesic has index \(\geq \lambda_0 = 2m+2\). Theorem 22.1 gives \(\pi_i(\Omega, \Omega^d) = 0\) for \(0 \leq i < 2m+2\). In the exact homotopy sequence of the pair, \[\pi_{i+1}(\Omega, \Omega^d) \to \pi_i(\Omega^d) \to \pi_i(\Omega) \to \pi_i(\Omega, \Omega^d),\] both ends vanish for \(i \leq 2m\), so the middle map is an isomorphism (for \(i = 0\) both spaces are connected: \(G_m\) is, and every component of \(\Omega\) meets \(\Omega^d\)). Finally, \(\pi_i\Omega(M; p, q) \cong \pi_{i+1}M\) for \(M\) path connected: by Theorem 17.1, \(\Omega\) is homotopy equivalent to the space of continuous paths from \(p\) to \(q\); composing with a fixed path from \(q\) to \(p\) is a homotopy equivalence with the loop space at \(p\); and \(\pi_i\) of the loop space is \(\pi_{i+1}M\) (Hu, Homotopy Theory, p. 111, as Milnor cites; or the adjunction between suspension and loops, \(\Sigma S^i = S^{i+1}\)). \(\square\)

For \(m = 1\) this is a theorem about the round \(3\)-sphere \(SU(2)\): \(G_1(\mathbb C^2) = \mathbb CP^1 = S^2\), so \(\pi_1 S^2 \cong \pi_2 S^3 = 0\) and \(\pi_2S^2 \cong \pi_3S^3 \cong \mathbb Z\).

3. Stable homotopy of the unitary groups and the periodicity theorem (Milnor pp. 128–130)

Milnor now uses “standard methods of homotopy theory”. These are the facts quoted.

(Q1) Coset bundles. If \(H\) is a closed subgroup of a Lie group \(G\), then \(G/H\) is a manifold and \(G \to G/H\) is a fibre bundle with fibre \(H\); if \(K \subseteq H \subseteq G\) are closed subgroups, then \(G/K \to G/H\) is a fibre bundle with fibre \(H/K\) (Steenrod, The Topology of Fibre Bundles, §7). If \(G\) is compact and acts continuously and transitively on a Hausdorff space \(X\) with stabilizer \(H\) at \(x\), then \(gH \mapsto gx\) is a homeomorphism \(G/H \to X\) (a continuous bijection from a compact space to a Hausdorff one).

(Q2) Exact homotopy sequence. For a fibre bundle \(F \to E \to B\) with \(B\) path connected there is an exact sequence \(\cdots \to \pi_iF \to \pi_iE \to \pi_iB \to \pi_{i-1}F \to \cdots \to \pi_0E \to \pi_0B\) (Steenrod §17; Hatcher, Algebraic Topology, Theorem 4.41 with Proposition 4.48).

(Q3) Spheres. \(\pi_iS^N = 0\) for \(i < N\): every map of an \(i\)-manifold into \(S^N\) with \(i < N\) is homotopic to a constant, proved in Chapter 8 of the companion volume (Topology from the Differentiable Viewpoint, rewritten), Problem 5 (a free null-homotopy suffices, since \(\pi_1\) acts on \(\pi_i\) fixing the zero element). \(\pi_NS^N \cong \mathbb Z\) by the degree: Hopf’s theorem, proved in Chapter 7 of the companion volume, Theorem 6.3, with Problem 4 of its Chapter 8 to pass from smooth to continuous maps; in particular \(\pi_1S^1 \cong \pi_3S^3 \cong \mathbb Z\). Finally \(\pi_iS^1 = 0\) for \(i \geq 2\), because the covering \(\mathbb R \to S^1\) induces isomorphisms on \(\pi_i\), \(i \geq 2\), and \(\mathbb R\) is contractible (Hatcher, Algebraic Topology, Proposition 4.1).

The bundles needed are the following. \(U(m+1)\) acts transitively on the unit sphere \(S^{2m+1} \subseteq \mathbb C^{m+1}\) (every unit vector is the last vector of an orthonormal basis), and the stabilizer of \(e_{m+1}\) is \(U(m)\), embedded as \(S \mapsto \operatorname{diag}(S, 1)\); so \(U(m+1)/U(m) \cong S^{2m+1}\). Embed \(U(m) \subseteq U(2m)\) by \(S \mapsto \operatorname{diag}(S, I_m)\); the composite of the embeddings \(U(m) \subseteq U(m+1) \subseteq \cdots \subseteq U(2m)\) is this embedding. \(U(2m)\) acts transitively on \(m\)-dimensional subspaces of \(\mathbb C^{2m}\) with stabilizer \(U(m) \times U(m)\) at \(\mathbb C^m \oplus 0\); so \(G_m(\mathbb C^{2m}) \cong U(2m)/U(m)\times U(m)\) (compare Steenrod §7). The complex Stiefel manifold is \(V = U(2m)/U(m)\). Finally \(\det : U(m) \to S^1\) is onto with kernel \(SU(m)\).

Lemma 23.4. (checked by machine: V14.25, in a stronger form; V14.26, restated; V14.27, in a narrower form) For \(1 \leq i \leq 2m\), \(\pi_iG_m(\mathbb C^{2m}) \cong \pi_{i-1}U(m)\). Furthermore \(\pi_{i-1}U(m) \cong \pi_{i-1}U(m+1) \cong \pi_{i-1}U(m+2) \cong \cdots\) for \(i \leq 2m\), the isomorphisms being induced by the inclusions; and \(\pi_jU(m) \cong \pi_jSU(m)\) for \(j \neq 1\).

Proof. Stability. The bundle \(U(m) \to U(m+1) \to S^{2m+1}\) gives the exact sequence \[\pi_{j+1}S^{2m+1} \to \pi_jU(m) \to \pi_jU(m+1) \to \pi_jS^{2m+1}.\] For \(j \leq 2m-1\) both ends vanish by (Q3), so the inclusion induces an isomorphism; for \(j = 2m\) the right end vanishes, so it is onto. Since \(j \leq 2m-1\) implies \(j \leq 2m'-1\) for every \(m' \geq m\), all the later inclusions are isomorphisms too. (For \(j = 0\) these are statements about connected spaces.)

The Stiefel manifold. For \(i \leq 2m\), the map \(\pi_iU(m) \to \pi_iU(2m)\) is onto (onto at the first step, isomorphisms afterwards, since \(i \leq 2m'-1\) for \(m' > m\)), and \(\pi_{i-1}U(m) \to \pi_{i-1}U(2m)\) is injective (\(i-1 \leq 2m-1\)). In the exact sequence of \(U(m) \to U(2m) \to V\), \[\pi_iU(m) \to \pi_iU(2m) \to \pi_iV \to \pi_{i-1}U(m) \to \pi_{i-1}U(2m),\] the first map onto makes \(\pi_iU(2m) \to \pi_iV\) zero, and the last map injective makes \(\pi_iV \to \pi_{i-1}U(m)\) zero; by exactness \(\pi_iV = 0\) for \(i \leq 2m\) (and \(V\) is connected).

The Grassmannian. By (Q1) with \(K = U(m) \subseteq H = U(m)\times U(m) \subseteq G = U(2m)\) there is a bundle \(U(m) \to V \to G_m(\mathbb C^{2m})\). Its sequence \(\pi_iV \to \pi_iG_m \to \pi_{i-1}U(m) \to \pi_{i-1}V\) has vanishing ends for \(1 \leq i \leq 2m\).

\(SU\) versus \(U\). The bundle \(SU(m) \to U(m) \to S^1\) gives \(\pi_{j+1}S^1 \to \pi_jSU(m) \to \pi_jU(m) \to \pi_jS^1\), with vanishing ends for \(j \geq 2\); for \(j = 0\) both groups are connected. \(\square\)

Definition. For \(j \geq 0\) the mutually isomorphic groups \(\pi_jU(m)\), \(2m - 1 \geq j\), are the \(j\)-th stable homotopy group of the unitary group, written \(\pi_jU\). The proof also showed (Milnor p. 129) that \(\pi_{2m}U(m) \to \pi_{2m}U(m+1) \cong \pi_{2m}U\) is onto.

Periodicity theorem. \(\pi_{i-1}U \cong \pi_{i+1}U\) for all \(i \geq 1\).

Proof. Given \(i \geq 1\), choose \(m\) with \(2m \geq i\). Then \[\pi_{i-1}U = \pi_{i-1}U(m) \cong \pi_iG_m(\mathbb C^{2m}) \cong \pi_{i+1}SU(2m) \cong \pi_{i+1}U(2m) = \pi_{i+1}U,\] by Lemma 23.4, Theorem 23.3, Lemma 23.4 again (\(i+1 \geq 2\)), and stability (\(i + 1 \leq 2m+1 \leq 2(2m)-1\)). \(\square\)

Theorem 23.5 (Bott). (checked by machine: V14.29, V14.30, restated) The stable homotopy groups \(\pi_iU\) are periodic of period \(2\): \(\pi_0U \cong \pi_2U \cong \pi_4U \cong \cdots\) are zero, and \(\pi_1U \cong \pi_3U \cong \pi_5U \cong \cdots\) are infinite cyclic.

Proof. \(U(1) = S^1\) and \(0, 1 \leq 2\cdot 1 - 1\), so \(\pi_0U = \pi_0S^1 = 0\) and \(\pi_1U = \pi_1S^1 \cong \mathbb Z\); periodicity does the rest. As a check, independent of periodicity: \(SU(2)\) is the \(3\)-sphere of unit quaternions, and \(2, 3 \leq 2\cdot 2 - 1\), so by Lemma 23.4 \(\pi_2U = \pi_2SU(2) = 0\) and \(\pi_3U = \pi_3SU(2) \cong \mathbb Z\). \(\square\)

Milnor’s isomorphisms are abstract: they are composites of isomorphisms chosen for each \(i\) separately. Bott stated his theorem as a homotopy equivalence of spaces. That form also follows from Theorem 23.3, once one passes to the limit \(m \to \infty\) with some care; it is not in Milnor’s text.

Corollary 23.6 (the space form of Bott’s theorem). Let \(BU = \bigcup_m G_m(\mathbb C^{2m})\), along \(E \mapsto E \oplus \mathbb Ce_{2m+1}\), let \(SU = \bigcup_m SU(2m)\) and \(U = \bigcup_m U(2m)\), along \(S \mapsto \operatorname{diag}(S, I_2)\), each with the colimit topology (a set is closed iff it meets every stage in a closed set), and let \(\Omega X\) be the space of continuous loops at the identity with the compact-open topology. Then there is a map \(\beta : BU \to \Omega SU\) inducing isomorphisms of all homotopy groups, and a map \(\mathbb Z \times BU \to \Omega U\) with the same property.

Proof. Let \(\varphi_m(E)(t) = e^{i\pi t}P_E + e^{-i\pi t}(I - P_E)\) be the minimal geodesic (2.1), let \(E_0 = \operatorname{span}(e_1, e_3, \dots, e_{2m-1})\), and put \(\beta_m(E)(t) = \varphi_m(E)(t)\,\varphi_m(E_0)(t)^{-1}\), a loop at \(I\) in \(SU(2m)\). Pointwise multiplication by the fixed path \(\varphi_m(E_0)^{-1}\) is a homeomorphism from the paths from \(I\) to \(-I\) onto the loops at \(I\) (its inverse multiplies by \(\varphi_m(E_0)\)), so by Theorems 23.3 and 17.1, \(\beta_m\) induces isomorphisms on \(\pi_i\) for \(i \leq 2m\). Since \(\varphi_{m+1}(E \oplus \mathbb Ce_{2m+1}) = \operatorname{diag}(\varphi_m(E), e^{i\pi t}, e^{-i\pi t})\) and \(E_0\) was chosen to be stable in the same way, \(\beta_{m+1}(E \oplus \mathbb Ce_{2m+1}) = \operatorname{diag}(\beta_m(E), I_2)\): the \(\beta_m\) fit together to a map \(\beta\).

Compact sets in a colimit. Let \(X_0 \subseteq X_1 \subseteq \cdots\) be \(T_1\) spaces, each a closed subspace of the next, and \(X = \bigcup X_m\) with the colimit topology. Then each \(X_m\) is a closed subspace of \(X\) (a set closed in \(X_m\) meets each \(X_j\) in a closed set), and every compact \(K \subseteq X\) lies in some \(X_m\): otherwise pick \(x_1, x_2, \ldots \in K\) and \(m_1 < m_2 < \cdots\) with \(x_k \in X_{m_k} \setminus X_{m_{k-1}}\); every subset of \(\{x_k\}\) meets each \(X_j\) in a finite, hence closed, set, so \(\{x_k\}\) is an infinite closed discrete subset of the compact \(K\), which is impossible.

Consequently a map \(S^i \to BU\), or a homotopy \(S^i \times [0,1] \to BU\), factors through some stage, and \(\pi_iBU = \operatorname{colim}_m\pi_iG_m(\mathbb C^{2m})\). A map \(S^i \to \Omega SU\) is the same as a map \(S^i \times S^1 \to SU\) (exponential law; \(S^1\) is compact Hausdorff, Hatcher, Appendix, on the compact-open topology), whose compact image lies in some \(SU(2m)\); so likewise \(\pi_i\Omega SU = \operatorname{colim}_m\pi_i\Omega SU(2m)\). In each degree \(i\) the maps \(\beta_{m*}\) are isomorphisms for \(m \geq i/2\), so \(\beta_*\) is an isomorphism.

For \(U\): \(S \mapsto (S\,D(\det S)^{-1}, \det S)\), with \(D(z) = \operatorname{diag}(z, 1, \dots, 1)\), is a homeomorphism \(U(2m) \cong SU(2m) \times S^1\) compatible with the inclusions. Define \(\mathbb Z \times BU \to \Omega U\) by \((N, E) \mapsto D(e^{2\pi iNt})\,\beta(E)(t)\). The winding number of the determinant of this loop is \(N\), so the map is a bijection on components; on the component \(N\) it is \(\beta\) followed by the inclusion \(\Omega SU \to \Omega_0U\) and by the homeomorphism “multiply by \(D(e^{2\pi iNt})\)”. The inclusion \(\Omega SU \to \Omega_0U\) induces isomorphisms on all \(\pi_i\), since \(\pi_i\Omega SU = \pi_{i+1}SU \cong \pi_{i+1}U = \pi_i\Omega_0U\) for \(i \geq 1\) (Lemma 23.4, passed to the colimit), and both spaces are connected (\(\pi_1SU(2m) \cong \pi_0G_m(\mathbb C^{2m}) = 0\) by Theorem 23.3). \(\square\)

Milnor’s text skips the passage to spaces. To upgrade Corollary 23.6 to homotopy equivalences \(\Omega SU \simeq BU\) and \(\Omega U \simeq \mathbb Z \times BU\) one needs that the spaces involved have the homotopy type of CW complexes, and then Whitehead’s theorem (Hatcher, Theorem 4.5). We quote this. The colimits are taken along smooth embeddings of compact manifolds, which are closed cofibrations (tubular neighbourhoods), so each colimit is homotopy equivalent to the mapping telescope of compact manifolds, a space of CW homotopy type; and the loop space of a space of CW homotopy type has CW homotopy type (J. Milnor, On spaces having the homotopy type of a CW-complex, Trans. AMS 90 (1959)). Milnor appeals to the same two facts, without proof, in the proof of Theorem 24.5 (p. 146). For the homotopy groups, which is all that Theorem 23.5 asserts, they are not needed.

4. The index of a non-minimal geodesic (Milnor pp. 130–132)

We now prove Lemma 23.2. The tools are Theorem 20.5 (Chapter 12): if \(M\) is locally symmetric and \(\gamma\) is a geodesic with \(\gamma(0) = p\) and \(\gamma'(0) = V\), let \(K_V(W) = R(V, W)V\) on \(TM_p\); then the parameters \(t \neq 0\) conjugate to \(0\) along \(\gamma\) are the \(t = \pi s/\sqrt e\), \(s\) a non-zero integer and \(e\) a positive eigenvalue of \(K_V\), and the multiplicity of \(t\) is the number of eigenvalues \(e\), counted with multiplicity, such that \(t\) is a multiple of \(\pi/\sqrt e\). The Index Theorem 15.1 (Chapter 9): the index of a geodesic \(\gamma : [0,1] \to M\) is the number of parameters \(t \in (0,1)\) such that \(\gamma(t)\) is conjugate to \(\gamma(0)\) along \(\gamma\), counted with multiplicity. And Theorem 21.3(b): for left-invariant fields on a Lie group with bi-invariant metric, \(R(X,Y)Z = \tfrac14[[X,Y],Z]\).

Lemma 4.1 (the index formula). Let \(n\) be even and \(A \in \mathfrak{su}(n)\) with eigenvalues \(i\pi k_1, \dots, i\pi k_n\), the \(k_j\) odd with \(\sum k_j = 0\). The index of the geodesic \(t \mapsto \exp(tA)\), \(0 \leq t \leq 1\), from \(I\) to \(-I\) in \(SU(n)\) is \[\lambda = \sum_{k_j > k_l}(k_j - k_l - 2),\] the sum over all pairs of indices \(\{j, l\}\) with \(k_j \neq k_l\), written with the larger first.

Proof. Reduction to diagonal form (Milnor’s “we may assume”). For \(T \in U(n)\), conjugation \(S \mapsto TST^{-1}\) is an isometry of \(SU(n)\) (Lemma 1.5) fixing \(I\) and \(-I\) and carrying \(\exp(tA)\) to \(\exp(tTAT^{-1})\). An isometry carries Jacobi fields to Jacobi fields, so it preserves conjugate points and their multiplicities, hence (Theorem 15.1) indices. Choose \(T\), including a permutation, so that \(A = \operatorname{diag}(i\pi k_1, \dots, i\pi k_n)\) with \(k_1 \geq \cdots \geq k_n\).

The operator \(K_A\). \(SU(n)\) with its bi-invariant metric is a symmetric space (Lemma 21.1), so Theorem 20.5 applies with \(p = I\), \(V = A\). By Theorem 21.3(b) and Lemma 1.4, \[K_A(W) = R(A, W)A = \tfrac14[[A, W], A] = -\tfrac14[A, [A, W]], \qquad W \in \mathfrak{su}(n).\] For \(W = (w_{jl})\), \([A, W]_{jl} = i\pi k_jw_{jl} - w_{jl}\,i\pi k_l = i\pi(k_j - k_l)w_{jl}\), hence \([A,[A,W]]_{jl} = -\pi^2(k_j - k_l)^2w_{jl}\) and \[K_A(W) = \Bigl(\tfrac{\pi^2}{4}(k_j - k_l)^2\,w_{jl}\Bigr).\]

An eigenbasis. For \(j < l\) let \(E_{jl}\) have \(+1\) in place \((j,l)\), \(-1\) in place \((l,j)\) and zeros elsewhere, and let \(E'_{jl}\) have \(i\) in both places. Both lie in \(\mathfrak{su}(n)\) and are eigenvectors with eigenvalue \(\tfrac{\pi^2}{4}(k_j - k_l)^2\). Every diagonal matrix in \(\mathfrak{su}(n)\) is an eigenvector with eigenvalue \(0\). These are \(n(n-1) + (n-1) = n^2 - 1 = \dim\mathfrak{su}(n)\) independent vectors, so they form a basis. The positive eigenvalues of \(K_A\) are therefore the numbers \(e_{jl} = \tfrac{\pi^2}{4}(k_j - k_l)^2\) for the pairs with \(k_j > k_l\), each counted twice.

Conjugate points. For \(e = e_{jl}\), \(\pi/\sqrt e = 2/(k_j - k_l)\), so this eigenvalue produces conjugate points at \(t = 2/(k_j - k_l), 4/(k_j - k_l), \ldots\). Since \(k_j - k_l\) is even, the number of these in the open interval \((0,1)\) is \((k_j - k_l)/2 - 1\).

The index. By Theorems 20.5 and 15.1, \(\lambda\) is the sum over the positive eigenvalues \(e\) (with multiplicity) of the number of multiples of \(\pi/\sqrt e\) in \((0,1)\). Each pair \(k_j > k_l\) contributes \(2\bigl((k_j - k_l)/2 - 1\bigr) = k_j - k_l - 2\). \(\square\)

For a minimal geodesic all \(k_j = \pm 1\), every term is \(1 - (-1) - 2 = 0\), and \(\lambda = 0\), as it should be. Every term of the sum is \(\geq 0\), so any set of pairs gives a lower bound.

Proof of Lemma 23.2. Let \(n = 2m\), \(\sum k_j = 0\), not all \(k_j = \pm 1\). Let \(P\) and \(N\) be the numbers of positive and of negative \(k_j\), so \(P + N = 2m\).

Case 1: \(N \geq m+1\) (Milnor’s “at least \(m+1\) of the \(k_i\) are (say) negative”). Then \(P \leq m-1\), while the positive \(k_j\) add up to \(\sum_{k_l<0}|k_l| \geq N \geq m+1 > P\); so some \(k_{j_0} \geq 3\). Pairing \(k_{j_0}\) with each of the \(N\) negative entries, each term is \(\geq 3 + 1 - 2 = 2\), and \(\lambda \geq 2N \geq 2(m+1)\). The case \(P \geq m+1\) is the same with all signs reversed: the formula is unchanged under \(k \mapsto -k\).

Case 2: \(P = N = m\). Some \(|k_j| \geq 3\); say \(k_{j_0} \geq 3\), the other sign being symmetric. The positive entries then add up to at least \((m-1) + 3 = m+2 > m = N\), and they equal \(\sum_{k_l<0}|k_l|\), so some \(k_{l_0} \leq -3\). Take the pairs \((j_0, l)\) for the \(m-1\) negative \(l \neq l_0\), the pairs \((j, l_0)\) for the \(m-1\) positive \(j \neq j_0\), and the pair \((j_0, l_0)\): \[\lambda \geq (m-1)(3 + 1 - 2) + (m-1)(1 + 3 - 2) + (3 + 3 - 2) = 4m \geq 2(m+1).\] In either case \(\lambda \geq 2m+2\). \(\square\)

This completes the proof of Theorem 23.3, and with it of Theorem 23.5. Both bounds are attained: for \(m = 2\), \(k = (3, -1, -1, -1)\) gives \(\lambda = 6 = 2m+2\) and \(k = (3, 1, -1, -3)\) gives \(\lambda = 8 = 4m\).

An interactive look at the eigenvalue braid

Along the geodesic \(t \mapsto \exp(tA)\) the eigenvalues of \(\exp(tA)\) are \(e^{i\pi k_jt}\): they leave \(1\) together at \(t = 0\), run around the unit circle at speeds \(k_j\), and all arrive at \(-1\) at \(t = 1\). Two of them, with \(k_j \neq k_l\), coincide exactly when \(t\) is a multiple of \(2/(k_j - k_l)\), which is where the proof of Lemma 4.1 finds the conjugate points coming from the pair \((j, l)\). So the index is twice the number of collisions strictly between \(t = 0\) and \(t = 1\). The figure draws the eigenvalue at time \(t\) at radius \(1 + t\), so that each eigenvalue traces a spiral from the inner circle to the outer one and each collision is a crossing of two spirals. Drag the time slider to move the eigenvalues along; choose \(m\); load a minimal geodesic (no crossings: half the eigenvalues turn one way, half the other), a random non-minimal one, or “pump” the extreme speeds apart (\(k_1 \mapsto k_1 + 2\), \(k_{2m} \mapsto k_{2m} - 2\)). The panel shows the collisions passed so far, the index from the formula, and Milnor’s bound \(2m+2\).

5. Application: complex vector bundles over spheres

Clutching. A complex vector bundle of rank \(N\) over \(S^n\) is trivial over each closed hemisphere (a contractible space), so it is obtained from two trivial bundles by gluing along the equator \(S^{n-1}\) with a map \(f : S^{n-1} \to GL_N(\mathbb C)\), and isomorphism classes of bundles correspond to homotopy classes of such maps (Steenrod §18; Hatcher, Vector Bundles and K-Theory, Proposition 1.11). Gram–Schmidt deforms \(GL_N(\mathbb C)\) onto \(U(N)\), and since \(U(N)\) is a connected topological group, free homotopy classes of maps \(S^{n-1} \to U(N)\) are the same as elements of \(\pi_{n-1}U(N)\). So \[\{\text{rank } N \text{ complex bundles over } S^n\}/\cong \;\;=\;\; \pi_{n-1}U(N).\] By Lemma 23.4 this is the stable group \(\pi_{n-1}U\) as soon as \(n - 1 \leq 2N - 1\), i.e. \(N \geq n/2\), and by Theorem 23.5:

sphere \(S^1\) \(S^2\) \(S^3\) \(S^4\) \(S^5\) \(S^6\) \(S^7\) \(S^8\)
\(\pi_{n-1}U\) \(0\) \(\mathbb Z\) \(0\) \(\mathbb Z\) \(0\) \(\mathbb Z\) \(0\) \(\mathbb Z\)
stable for \(N \geq 1\) \(N \geq 1\) \(N \geq 2\) \(N \geq 2\) \(N \geq 3\) \(N \geq 3\) \(N \geq 4\) \(N \geq 4\)

\(S^2\): monopoles. \(\pi_1U(1) = \mathbb Z\), and the clutching map of the bundle with integer \(N\) is \(z \mapsto z^N\) on the equator. This is Dirac’s integer. The tautological line bundle of \(\mathbb CP^1 = S^2\) has \(|N| = 1\); the tangent bundle of \(S^2\), a complex line bundle, has clutching map \(z \mapsto z^{\pm 2}\), so \(|N| = 2\), and this \(2\) is the Euler number \(\chi(S^2)\) (Chapter 6 of the companion volume, where the Poincaré–Hopf theorem is proved). By stability, every complex bundle over \(S^2\) of any rank is a line bundle plus a trivial bundle.

\(S^4\): instantons. \(\pi_3U(2) = \pi_3SU(2) = \mathbb Z\), already stable. The clutching map \(S^3 \to SU(2)\) that identifies the unit quaternions with \(SU(2)\) has degree one; the resulting rank-\(2\) bundle is the quaternionic Hopf bundle over \(\mathbb HP^1 = S^4\), and the integer is the instanton number of Yang–Mills theory (the BPST instanton has instanton number \(1\)).

Odd spheres. Since \(\pi_{2k}U = 0\), every complex bundle of rank \(\geq k+1\) over \(S^{2k+1}\) is trivial, and every complex bundle over \(S^1\) or \(S^3\) is trivial.

Below the stable range the answer is irregular, which is why the theorem is about \(U\) and not about a fixed \(U(N)\). Since \(U(2) \cong SU(2) \times S^1\) as spaces and \(SU(2) = S^3\), rank-\(2\) bundles over \(S^{n}\) are classified by \(\pi_{n-1}S^3\) for \(n \geq 3\), and the standard values \(\pi_4S^3 = \mathbb Z/2\), \(\pi_5S^3 = \mathbb Z/2\), \(\pi_6S^3 = \mathbb Z/12\) give: over \(S^5\) there is exactly one non-trivial rank-\(2\) bundle, and it becomes trivial when a trivial line bundle is added (rank \(3\) is stable, and \(\pi_4U = 0\)); over \(S^6\) the rank-\(2\) bundles form \(\mathbb Z/2\) but those of rank \(\geq 3\) form \(\mathbb Z\); over \(S^7\) the rank-\(2\) bundles form \(\mathbb Z/12\), those of rank \(\geq 4\) are all trivial.

In K-theory language. The reduced K-group \(\widetilde K(S^n)\) of stable bundles is \(\pi_{n-1}U\), and Theorem 23.5 reads \(\widetilde K(S^{n+2}) \cong \widetilde K(S^n)\). The integer attached to a stable bundle over \(S^2\) is its first Chern number, and the same integer, for the bundle of occupied electron states over the two-dimensional Brillouin torus, is the quantized Hall conductance in units of \(e^2/h\) (Thouless, Kohmoto, Nightingale and den Nijs, 1982). In Kitaev’s classification of topological insulators (2009), insulators without symmetries in \(d\) dimensions carry an integer invariant of this kind exactly when \(\widetilde K(S^d) = \pi_{d-1}U\) is \(\mathbb Z\), that is, for \(d\) even: the period two of that column of Kitaev’s table is the period two of Theorem 23.5.

Checked by machine. Milnor’s §23 has been verified in the Lean proof assistant. The algebra and counting of §§2 and 4: for \(A = \operatorname{diag}(i\pi k_1, \dots, i\pi k_n)\), \(\exp A = -I\) iff every \(k_j\) is odd; \(|A|^2 = \pi^2 \sum k_j^2 \geq \pi^2 n\), with equality iff all \(k_j = \pm 1\), and then \(m\) of each sign in \(SU(2m)\); Milnor’s formula for \(K_A\), with eigenvectors shown to span; and, from this spectrum, the index formula of Lemma 4.1, Lemma 23.2, and the non-minimal geodesic \(k = (3, 1, \dots, 1)\) of index \(0\) in \(U(n)\). For every skew-Hermitian \(A\), \(A^2 = -\pi^2 I\) iff \(A = i\pi(2P - I)\) with \(P\) a Hermitian projection, the algebraic content of Corollary 2.2 and Lemma 23.1. The geometry and the topology: \(U(n)\) and \(SU(n)\) as compact submanifolds of \(M_n(\mathbb C)\) with the induced bi-invariant metric; that every geodesic from \(I\) to \(-I\) in \(SU(n)\) is \(t \mapsto \exp(tA)\) with \(A\) unitarily conjugate to the diagonal form; the distance from \(I\) to \(-I\) in \(SU(2m)\) and its minimal geodesics; Lemma 23.1, as a homeomorphism for the initial velocities and, in the path space, as a homotopy equivalence (a homeomorphism after identifying paths that agree on \([0, 1]\)); Theorem 20.5 for \(SU(n)\), so that the index formula of Lemma 4.1 and Lemma 23.2 hold for the geodesics themselves, by the Index Theorem; an explicit neighbourhood retraction, which makes Theorem 23.3 independent of Hanner’s theorem; Theorem 23.3; the bundles of Lemma 23.4 on concrete Stiefel manifolds and Grassmannians, with their exact homotopy sequences, and Lemma 23.4; the periodicity theorem, inside one \(U(m)\) for \(1 \le i \le 2m - 2\) and between any two groups in the stable range; and Theorem 23.5. Each isomorphism is a bijection of pointed sets and, in the range of one \(U(m)\) and where both sides are groups, an isomorphism of groups. Not checked: \(U(n)\) beyond what \(SU(2m)\) needs (its minimal geodesics, the connectedness of \(U(n)\) and \(SU(n)\), Lemma 2.3 for \(U(n)\)), the stable groups \(\pi_iU\) as homotopy groups of a limit, Corollary 23.6, and the application. Chapter 15Milnor §24pp. 133–148Contents ↑

Chapter 15. Bott periodicity for the orthogonal group: complex structures and Clifford modules

Milnor, “Morse Theory”, §24, rewritten for a first-year graduate student who wants to know what the theorem is for. Milnor calls his treatment “rather sketchy”; the missing details are supplied, and every proof is complete, except that, as in Chapter 14, coset fibrations, exact homotopy sequences and two facts about CW complexes are quoted.

0. How many independent directions can be combed on a sphere?

On the sphere of directions \(S^2\) no tangent vector field is nowhere zero (the hairy ball theorem, proved in Chapter 5 of the companion volume, Topology from the Differentiable Viewpoint, rewritten, Theorem 5.1). On the unit quaternions \(S^3\) there are three at once, \(x \mapsto ix, jx, kx\), orthonormal and tangent at every point; on \(S^7\) octonion multiplication gives seven. How many pointwise independent tangent fields does \(S^{n-1}\) carry? The answer, due to Radon and Hurwitz (lower bound, 1922–23) and Adams (upper bound, 1962), is \(\rho(n) - 1\), where for \(n = 2^{4a+b}\cdot(\text{odd})\), \(0 \leq b \leq 3\), \[\rho(n) = 8a + 2^b.\] The lower bound comes from linear algebra: if \(J_1, \dots, J_k\) are orthogonal \(n \times n\) matrices with \(J_\alpha^2 = -I\) and \(J_\alpha J_\beta = -J_\beta J_\alpha\), then \(J_1x, \dots, J_kx\) are orthonormal and perpendicular to \(x\). The \(8\) in the formula is Bott’s \(8\), \(\pi_iO \cong \pi_{i+8}O\), and this is no coincidence: Milnor’s proof of the periodicity theorem runs through these families of anti-commuting “complex structures”. The minimal geodesics from \(I\) to \(-I\) in \(O(n)\) are the complex structures \(J_1\); those from \(J_1\) to \(-J_1\) in the space of complex structures are the \(J_2\) anti-commuting with \(J_1\); and so on. After eight steps one is back at an orthogonal group, and Morse theory shifts homotopy groups by one at each step. §7 returns to vector fields and to real vector bundles over spheres.

1. The orthogonal group and its minimal geodesics (Milnor pp. 133–136)

\(O(n) = \{T \in M_n(\mathbb R) : TT^{\mathsf T} = I\}\). Chapter 14, §1, holds verbatim for real matrices: \(O(n)\) is a compact Lie group with Lie algebra \(\mathfrak o(n)\) of skew-symmetric matrices, the metric \(\langle A, B\rangle = \operatorname{tr}(AB^{\mathsf T})\) induced from \(M_n(\mathbb R)\) (the restriction of that of \(U(n)\)) is bi-invariant, conjugations are isometries, and the geodesic through \(S\) with velocity \(SA\) is \(t \mapsto S\exp(tA)\); geodesics from \(I\) stay in \(SO(n)\). We quote the normal form (real spectral theorem, e.g. Axler): for \(A \in \mathfrak o(2m)\) there is \(T \in O(2m)\) with \[TAT^{-1} = \operatorname{diag}(a_1J_0, \dots, a_mJ_0), \qquad J_0 = \begin{pmatrix}0 & 1\\ -1 & 0\end{pmatrix}, \quad a_j \geq 0,\] and \(\exp(\theta J_0) = \cos\theta\, I + \sin\theta\, J_0\) (Milnor p. 134).

Definition. For \(n\) even, a complex structure on \(\mathbb R^n\) is a \(J \in O(n)\) with \(J^2 = -I\). \(\Omega_1(n)\) denotes the set of complex structures.

Lemma 1.1. \(J \in M_n(\mathbb R)\) is a complex structure iff \(J^{\mathsf T} = -J\) and \(J^2 = -I\). For a complex structure, \(\exp(\theta J) = \cos\theta\, I + \sin\theta\, J\), \(|J|^2 = n\), and \(J\) is conjugate in \(O(n)\) to \(\operatorname{diag}(J_0, \dots, J_0)\).

Proof. If \(J\) is orthogonal, \(J^{\mathsf T} = J^{-1} = -J\); if \(J\) is skew, \(JJ^{\mathsf T} = -J^2 = I\). The series for \(\exp\) uses \(J^{2k} = (-1)^kI\), and \(|J|^2 = \operatorname{tr}(JJ^{\mathsf T}) = n\). In the normal form, \(TJ^2T^{-1} = \operatorname{diag}(-a_j^2I_2) = -I\) forces every \(a_j = 1\). \(\square\)

Remark (Milnor p. 133). Fix \(J_1 \in \Omega_1(n)\) and let \(U(n/2) = \{T \in O(n) : TJ_1 = J_1T\}\), the unitary group of \(\mathbb R^n\) made complex by \(i = J_1\). Then \(\Omega_1(n) \cong O(n)/U(n/2)\). Indeed \(O(n)\) acts on \(\Omega_1(n)\) by \(T\cdot J = TJT^{-1}\), transitively by the last part of Lemma 1.1, with stabilizer \(U(n/2)\) at \(J_1\); apply (Q1) of Chapter 14.

Lemma 24.1. (checked by machine: V15.26, restated)1 The space of minimal geodesics from \(I\) to \(-I\) in \(O(n)\) is homeomorphic to \(\Omega_1(n)\), by \(J \mapsto \gamma_J\), \(\gamma_J(t) = \exp(\pi tJ) = \cos(\pi t)\,I + \sin(\pi t)\,J\).

Proof. A geodesic from \(I\) to \(-I\) is \(\gamma(t) = \exp(\pi tA)\), \(A \in \mathfrak o(n)\), \(\exp(\pi A) = -I\); in the normal form this says every \(a_j\) is an odd integer. Its length is \(|\pi A| = \pi(2\sum a_j^2)^{1/2} \geq \pi\sqrt n\), with equality iff every \(a_j = 1\), i.e. \(A^2 = -I\), i.e. \(A \in \Omega_1(n)\). A minimal geodesic exists (\(O(n)\) is compact; Milnor 10.9), so the minimal geodesics are the \(\gamma_J\). The map \(J \mapsto \gamma_J\) is injective (\(J = \gamma_J'(0)/\pi\)), continuous (constant speed, as in Chapter 14, Lemma 2.3), and \(\Omega_1(n)\) is compact. \(\square\)

Lemma 24.2. (checked by machine: V15.3, restated; V15.30, in a narrower form) Every non-minimal geodesic from \(I\) to \(-I\) in \(O(2m)\) has index \(\geq 2m - 2\).

Proof. Conjugating by an orthogonal matrix (an isometry fixing \(\pm I\), so preserving indices, as in Chapter 14, Lemma 4.1), take \(A = \operatorname{diag}(a_1J_0, \dots, a_mJ_0)\), the \(a_j\) odd and positive, \(a_1 \geq \cdots \geq a_m\). The velocity is \(V = \pi A\), and by Theorems 21.3(b) and 20.5 the conjugate points are governed by \(K_V = \pi^2K_A\), \(K_A(W) = -\tfrac14[A, [A, W]]\).

Eigenvalues of \(K_A\) (Milnor’s “computation shows”). Write \(W \in \mathfrak o(2m)\) in \(2 \times 2\) blocks, \(W_{ji} = -W_{ij}^{\mathsf T}\), and split \(M_2(\mathbb R) = C_+ \oplus C_-\), where \(C_+ = \operatorname{span}(I, J_0)\) commutes with \(J_0\) and \(C_- = \operatorname{span}(\operatorname{diag}(1,-1), \bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{smallmatrix}\bigr))\) anti-commutes with it; \(J_0C_\pm = C_\pm\). For \(i < j\) and \(X \in C_\pm\) let \(W^{(ij)}_X\) have block \(X\) at \((i,j)\), \(-X^{\mathsf T}\) at \((j,i)\), zeros elsewhere. The \((i,j)\) block of \([A, W]\) is \(a_iJ_0W_{ij} - a_jW_{ij}J_0\), so \([A, W^{(ij)}_X] = W^{(ij)}_{(a_i \mp a_j)J_0X}\) and \(K_AW^{(ij)}_X = \tfrac14(a_i \mp a_j)^2W^{(ij)}_X\); the diagonal blocks lie in \(\mathbb RJ_0\) and commute with \(A\). Since \(4\cdot m(m-1)/2 + m = \dim\mathfrak o(2m)\), the non-zero eigenvalues of \(K_A\) are \((a_i + a_j)^2/4\) (\(i < j\)) and \((a_i - a_j)^2/4\) (\(a_i > a_j\)), each twice.

Conjugate points. An eigenvalue \(e^2\) of \(K_A\) gives conjugate points at \(t = \pi s/\sqrt{\pi^2e^2} = s/e\) (Theorem 20.5); for \(e = (a_i \pm a_j)/2\), an integer, \(e - 1\) of them lie in \((0,1)\). By the Index Theorem 15.1, \[\lambda = \sum_{i<j}(a_i + a_j - 2) + \sum_{a_i > a_j}(a_i - a_j - 2),\] all terms \(\geq 0\). For a minimal geodesic all \(a_j = 1\) and \(\lambda = 0\); otherwise \(a_1 \geq 3\) and \(\lambda \geq \sum_{j=2}^m(3 + 1 - 2) = 2m - 2\). \(\square\)

Theorem 24.3 (Bott). (checked by machine: V15.32, restated) The inclusion \(\Omega_1(n) \to \Omega(O(n); I, -I)\) of Lemma 24.1 induces isomorphisms of homotopy groups in dimensions \(\leq n - 4\). Hence \(\pi_i\Omega_1(n) \cong \pi_{i+1}O(n)\) for \(i \leq n - 4\).

Proof. As in Chapter 14, Theorem 23.3, in the compact manifold \(SO(n)\): \(\Omega_1(n)\) is a manifold (the Remark, or Lemma 24.4), \(\lambda_0 = n - 2\) (Lemma 24.2), and \(\pi_i\Omega(SO(n); I, -I) \cong \pi_{i+1}SO(n) = \pi_{i+1}O(n)\). \(\square\)

2. Anti-commuting complex structures and the spaces \(\Omega_k(n)\) (Milnor pp. 136–138)

Definition. Fix complex structures \(J_1, \dots, J_{k-1}\) on \(\mathbb R^n\) that anti-commute, \(J_rJ_s + J_sJ_r = 0\) for \(r \neq s\) (they make \(\mathbb R^n\) a module over a Clifford algebra, §5). Let \(\Omega_k(n)\) be the set of complex structures anti-commuting with \(J_1, \dots, J_{k-1}\), and \(\Omega_0(n) = O(n)\): \(\Omega_k(n) \subseteq \cdots \subseteq \Omega_1(n) \subseteq O(n)\), all compact.

Products of anti-commuting complex structures obey simple sign rules. Let \(J_1, \dots, J_k\) anti-commute pairwise, and for \(S = \{s_1 < \cdots < s_p\} \subseteq \{1, \dots, k\}\) put \(J_S = J_{s_1}\cdots J_{s_p}\), \(J_\emptyset = I\).

Lemma 2.1 (sign rules). (a) \(J_S\) is orthogonal and \(J_S^{\mathsf T} = (-1)^{p(p+1)/2}J_S\): for \(p \equiv 0, 3 \pmod 4\) it is symmetric with \(J_S^2 = I\), for \(p \equiv 1, 2 \pmod 4\) it is a complex structure. (b) \(J_SJ_T = (-1)^{pq - |S \cap T|}J_TJ_S\) for \(|T| = q\); in particular \(J_\alpha\) commutes with \(J_S\) iff \(p - [\alpha \in S]\) is even. (c) \(J_SJ_T = \pm J_{S \triangle T}\), the sign depending only on \(S\) and \(T\).

Proof. (a) \(J_S^{\mathsf T} = (-1)^pJ_{s_p}\cdots J_{s_1}\), and reversing \(p\) anti-commuting factors costs \((-1)^{p(p-1)/2}\); with \(J_S^{\mathsf T}J_S = I\) this gives \(J_S^2 = \pm I\) with the same sign. (b) Moving the \(q\) factors of \(J_T\) past the \(p\) factors of \(J_S\) costs a sign for each pair of distinct indices. (c) Bring equal factors together and use \(J_\alpha^2 = -I\). \(\square\)

Milnor calls a submanifold totally geodesic if each of its geodesics (for the induced metric) is a geodesic of the larger manifold.

Lemma 2.2. Let \(N\) be a submanifold of a Riemannian manifold \(M\), with the induced metric. (a) If for every \(v \in TN_x\) the \(M\)-geodesic \(t \mapsto \exp^M_x(tv)\) stays in \(N\) for small \(|t|\), then \(N\) is totally geodesic. (b) If \(N\) is totally geodesic, then \(R^N(X,Y)Z = R^M(X,Y)Z\) for \(X, Y, Z \in TN_x\). (c) An isometry of \(M\) that maps \(N\) onto \(N\) restricts to an isometry of \(N\).

Proof. (a) Let \(c(t) = \exp^M_x(tv)\) lie in \(N\) for \(|t| < \varepsilon\). For small \(\delta\), \(c|[0,\delta]\) is no longer than any path in \(M\) between its endpoints (Theorem 10.4), in particular than any path in \(N\), which has the same length in both. So it is a minimal path of \(N\) parametrized proportionally to arc length, hence a geodesic of \(N\) (Corollary 10.7, applied in \(N\)). By uniqueness, the \(N\)-geodesic with velocity \(v\) coincides with \(c\) near \(t = 0\); as \(x\) and \(v\) are arbitrary, every \(N\)-geodesic is locally, hence globally, an \(M\)-geodesic. (b) For \(X, Y\) tangent to \(N\), the tangential part of \(\nabla^M_XY\) is a symmetric connection compatible with the metric, hence is \(\nabla^N_XY\) (Lemma 8.6). The rest, \(\mathrm{II}(X,Y) = \nabla^M_XY - \nabla^N_XY\), is tensorial and symmetric, and the same splitting holds along curves. Along an \(N\)-geodesic \(c\), an \(M\)-geodesic by hypothesis, \(0 = D^Mc'/dt = \mathrm{II}(c', c')\); so \(\mathrm{II} = 0\) by polarization, \(\nabla^M = \nabla^N\) on fields tangent to \(N\), and \(R(X,Y)Z = -\nabla_X\nabla_YZ + \nabla_Y\nabla_XZ + \nabla_{[X,Y]}Z\) is the same in \(N\) and \(M\). (c) Its inverse also preserves \(N\). \(\square\)

Lemma 24.4. (checked by machine: V15.23, restated) (i) Each \(\Omega_k(n)\) is a smooth, totally geodesic submanifold of \(O(n)\); its tangent space at \(J\) is \(J\mathcal T_J\), where \[\mathcal T_J = \{A \in \mathfrak o(n) : AJ = -JA,\ AJ_\alpha = J_\alpha A \text{ for } \alpha < k\}.\] (ii) Each component of \(\Omega_k(n)\) is a symmetric space. (iii) Let \(J_k \in \Omega_k(n)\) (and \(J_0 = I\)), let \(\Omega_{k+1}(n)\) be the set of \(J' \in \Omega_k(n)\) anti-commuting with \(J_k\), and suppose \(\Omega_{k+1}(n) \neq \emptyset\). Then the minimal geodesics from \(J_k\) to \(-J_k\) in \(\Omega_k(n)\) are exactly the semicircles \[\gamma_{J'}(t) = \cos(\pi t)\,J_k + \sin(\pi t)\,J', \qquad J' \in \Omega_{k+1}(n),\] and \(J' \mapsto \gamma_{J'}\) is a homeomorphism of \(\Omega_{k+1}(n)\) onto the space of minimal geodesics.

For \(k = 0\), (i) is Chapter 14’s chart argument and (iii) is Lemma 24.1; assume \(k \geq 1\). Milnor’s version of (iii), “for \(0 \leq l < k\)”, tacitly needs \(\Omega_{l+1}(n) \neq \emptyset\), which his standing assumption provides.

Proof. Let \(B_\varepsilon \subseteq \mathfrak o(n)\) be a ball on which \(\exp\) is a diffeomorphism onto a neighbourhood of \(I\) in \(O(n)\), invariant under \(A \mapsto -A\) and orthogonal conjugation. Let \(J \in \Omega_k(n)\) and \(A \in \mathfrak o(n)\).

Assertion 1. If \(AJ = -JA\), then \(J\exp A\) is a complex structure; for \(A \in B_\varepsilon\) the converse holds. Indeed \((J\exp A)^2 = J^2(J^{-1}\exp(A)J)\exp A = -\exp(J^{-1}AJ)\exp(A)\), which is \(-I\) iff \(\exp(J^{-1}AJ) = \exp(-A)\); this holds if \(J^{-1}AJ = -A\), and for \(A \in B_\varepsilon\) only then.

Assertion 2. If \(AJ_\alpha = J_\alpha A\), then \(J\exp A\) anti-commutes with \(J_\alpha\); for \(A \in B_\varepsilon\) the converse holds. Indeed \(J_\alpha J\exp A = -J\exp(J_\alpha AJ_\alpha^{-1})J_\alpha\), which is \(-(J\exp A)J_\alpha\) iff \(\exp(J_\alpha AJ_\alpha^{-1}) = \exp A\).

  1. So \(\Omega_k(n) \cap J\exp(B_\varepsilon) = J\exp(B_\varepsilon \cap \mathcal T_J)\); as \(A \mapsto J\exp A\) is a chart of \(O(n)\), \(\Omega_k(n)\) is near \(J\) an open piece of the linear subspace \(\mathcal T_J\) in this chart (components may have different dimensions). The \(O(n)\)-geodesic \(t \mapsto J\exp(tA)\), \(A \in \mathcal T_J\), stays in \(\Omega_k(n)\) for all \(t\) by the “if” halves, so \(\Omega_k(n)\) is totally geodesic by Lemma 2.2(a): this is Milnor’s “clearly implies”.

  2. The reflection of \(O(n)\) in \(J\) is \(I_J(S) = JS^{-1}J\) (Lemma 21.1), and for \(J' \in \Omega_k(n)\), \(I_J(J') = -JJ'J\) is orthogonal, squares to \(JJ'J^2J'J = J^2 = -I\) and anti-commutes with each \(J_\alpha\). So \(I_J\) is an isometry of \(\Omega_k(n)\) (Lemma 2.2(c)) fixing \(J\) with derivative \(-1\), reversing the geodesics through \(J\); \(\Omega_k(n)\) is compact, so each component is a symmetric space.

  3. Distances in \(\Omega_k(n)\) are \(\geq\) distances in \(O(n)\), and \(\rho_O(J_k, -J_k) = \rho_O(I, -I) = \pi\sqrt n\). For \(J' \in \Omega_{k+1}(n)\) let \(A = J_k^{-1}J' = -J_kJ'\): then \(A^2 = -J_k^2J'^2 = -I\), \(A\) anti-commutes with \(J_k\) and commutes with each \(J_\alpha\), \(\alpha < k\), so \(A \in \mathcal T_{J_k}\) is a complex structure and \(J_k\exp(\pi tA) = \gamma_{J'}(t)\) (Lemma 1.1). This \(O(n)\)-geodesic lies in \(\Omega_k(n)\) (Assertions 1, 2) and has length \(\pi\sqrt n\), so it is a minimal path, hence a minimal geodesic, of \(\Omega_k(n)\) (Corollary 10.7), and the distance in \(\Omega_k(n)\) is \(\pi\sqrt n\). Conversely, a minimal geodesic \(\gamma\) of \(\Omega_k(n)\) from \(J_k\) to \(-J_k\) is an \(O(n)\)-geodesic of length \(\pi\sqrt n\), so \(J_k^{-1}\gamma\) is minimal from \(I\) to \(-I\): \(\gamma(t) = J_k\exp(\pi tA)\) with \(A\) a complex structure (Lemma 24.1). As \(\gamma(t) \in \Omega_k(n)\) for small \(t\), the “only if” halves give \(AJ_k = -J_kA\), \(AJ_\alpha = J_\alpha A\), and then \(J' = J_kA\) is in \(\Omega_{k+1}(n)\) (\(J'^2 = -J_k^2A^2 = -I\), \(J_kJ' = -A = -J'J_k\), and \(J'\) anti-commutes with \(J_\alpha\) because \(J_k\) does and \(A\) commutes with it), with \(\gamma = \gamma_{J'}\). The homeomorphism follows as in Lemma 24.1. \(\square\)

Remark (Milnor p. 138). The point \(J'\) corresponding to a minimal geodesic is its midpoint \(\gamma_{J'}(1/2)\). All of \(\Omega_k(n)\) lies on the sphere \(|J|^2 = n\) in \(M_n(\mathbb R)\), and \(\langle J', J_k\rangle = -\operatorname{tr}(J'J_k) = 0\) since \(J'J_k\) is skew: the minimal geodesics are great semicircles from the “pole” \(J_k\) to \(-J_k\) through the “equator” \(\Omega_{k+1}(n)\), as in the picture of §22 for antipodal points of \(S^{n+1}\).

3. Stabilization and the statement of the periodicity theorem (Milnor pp. 138, 142)

To pass to the limit we need structures on a block that is added again and again. Let \(\sigma = \bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)\), \(\tau = \operatorname{diag}(1,-1)\), \(\kappa = \bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)\); any two anti-commute, \(\sigma^2 = -I\), \(\tau^2 = \kappa^2 = I\). On \(\mathbb R^{16} = (\mathbb R^2)^{\otimes 4}\) (Kronecker products) put \[\begin{aligned} J'_1 &= 1\otimes 1\otimes\sigma\otimes\tau, & J'_2 &= 1\otimes\sigma\otimes\tau\otimes\tau, & J'_3 &= \sigma\otimes 1\otimes\kappa\otimes\tau, & J'_4 &= \sigma\otimes\tau\otimes\tau\otimes\tau,\\ J'_5 &= \sigma\otimes\kappa\otimes\tau\otimes\tau, & J'_6 &= \tau\otimes\sigma\otimes\kappa\otimes\tau, & J'_7 &= \kappa\otimes\sigma\otimes\kappa\otimes\tau, & J'_8 &= 1\otimes 1\otimes 1\otimes\sigma. \end{aligned}\] Products are computed slot by slot, so two such words anti-commute iff they carry different non-identity letters in an odd number of slots, and a word with one \(\sigma\) is skew with square \(-I\); checking the \(28\) pairs shows that \(J'_1, \dots, J'_8\) are anti-commuting complex structures.

For \(n = 16r\) let \(J_\alpha = J'_\alpha \oplus \cdots \oplus J'_\alpha\) (\(r\) copies) on \(\mathbb R^{16r} = (\mathbb R^{16})^r\). From now on \(\Omega_k(16r)\) is defined with these \(J_1, \dots, J_{k-1}\), with base point \(J_k\). The map \(J \mapsto J \oplus J'_k\) (for \(k = 0\), \(T \mapsto T \oplus I_{16}\)) embeds \(\Omega_k(16r)\) in \(\Omega_k(16r + 16)\), carrying \(J_k\) to \(J_k\).

Definition (Milnor p. 138). \(\Omega_k = \bigcup_r\Omega_k(16r)\) with the colimit topology. The space \(O = \Omega_0\) is the infinite orthogonal group. (Milnor uses all \(n\); the multiples of \(16\) are cofinal.)

The maps \(\varphi_r : \Omega_{k+1}(16r) \to \Omega(\Omega_k(16r); J_k, -J_k)\), \(\varphi_r(J') = \gamma_{J'}\), of Lemma 24.4(iii) are compatible with the embeddings: \[\varphi_{r+1}(J' \oplus J'_{k+1}) = \varphi_r(J') \oplus \delta_k, \qquad \delta_k(t) = \cos(\pi t)\,J'_k + \sin(\pi t)\,J'_{k+1},\] where on path spaces the embedding is \(\omega \mapsto \omega \oplus \delta_k\). This is what Milnor calls “not difficult to see”: the inclusions pass to a limit map \(\Omega_{k+1} \to \Omega\Omega_k\). By the lemma on compact sets in a colimit (Chapter 14, proof of Corollary 23.6), \(\pi_i\Omega_k = \operatorname{colim}_r\pi_i\Omega_k(16r)\), and similarly for the spaces of continuous paths from \(J_k\) to \(-J_k\), which we denote \(\Omega\Omega_k\).

Theorem 24.5. (checked by machine: V15.43, restated) For \(0 \leq k \leq 7\) the limit map \(\varphi : \Omega_{k+1} \to \Omega\Omega_k\) induces a bijection of path components and isomorphisms of all homotopy groups. Consequently, with base points \(J_k\), \[\pi_hO \cong \pi_{h-1}\Omega_1 \cong \pi_{h-2}\Omega_2 \cong \cdots \cong \pi_1\Omega_{h-1} \cong \pi_0\Omega_h \qquad (1 \leq h \leq 8),\] the last bijection being one of sets.

The consequence holds because the paths from \(J_k\) to \(-J_k\) form a space homotopy equivalent to the loops at \(J_k\), compatibly (up to homotopy) with the embeddings, so \(\pi_j\Omega\Omega_k \cong \pi_{j+1}\Omega_k\) (Chapter 14, proof of Theorem 23.3). Milnor states Theorem 24.5 for all \(k \geq 0\), but his proof needs Lemma 24.8 for \(k + 1\) structures, which he gives only for \(k + 1 \leq 8\); \(k \leq 7\) is all that periodicity needs. Milnor’s conclusion is a homotopy equivalence, which needs the two facts quoted at the end of §6; his chain of isomorphisms stops at \(\pi_1\Omega_{h-1}\), and the last bijection is added here. The proof is in §6.

4. The eight spaces (Milnor pp. 138–142)

Given \(J_1, \dots, J_7\), define \[\theta_3 = J_1J_2J_3, \qquad \theta_5 = J_1J_4J_5, \qquad \theta_6 = J_2J_4J_6, \qquad \theta_7 = J_1J_6J_7.\] By Lemma 2.1 these are symmetric orthogonal involutions; any two commute (their index sets meet in one element), and \(J_\alpha\) commutes with \(\theta_{abc}\) iff \(\alpha \in \{a, b, c\}\). Solving for the last factor, \(J_3 = -J_1J_2\theta_3\), \(J_5 = J_4J_1\theta_5\), \(J_6 = J_4J_2\theta_6\), \(J_7 = J_6J_1\theta_7\). The table records which \(J_\alpha\) commute (c) or anti-commute (a) with which \(\theta\):

\(\theta_3\) \(\theta_5\) \(\theta_6\) \(\theta_7\)
\(J_1\) c c a c
\(J_2\) c a c a
\(J_3\) c a a a
\(J_4\) a c c a
\(J_5\) a c a a
\(J_6\) a a c c
\(J_7\) a a a c
\(J_8\) a a a a

Lemma 24.6 rests on two observations.

Lemma 4.1 (odd steps). Let \(J_1, \dots, J_{k-1}\) be fixed and \(a < b < k\). Then \(J \mapsto E = \{v : J_aJ_bJv = v\}\) is a bijection from \(\Omega_k(n)\) onto the set of subspaces \(E\) with \(J_aE = E\), \(J_bE = E\) and \(J_cE = E^\perp\) for all \(c < k\), \(c \notin \{a, b\}\). The inverse is \(J = J_bJ_a(2P_E - I)\), \(P_E\) the orthogonal projection, so the bijection is a homeomorphism when subspaces are topologized by their projections.

Proof. For \(J \in \Omega_k(n)\), \(\theta = J_aJ_bJ\) is a symmetric involution commuting with \(J_a, J_b\) and anti-commuting with the other \(J_c\) (Lemma 2.1), so \(\theta = 2P_E - I\) with \(E\) as stated. Conversely, \(\theta = 2P_E - I\) commutes with \(J_a, J_b\) and, since \(J_cE = E^\perp\) forces \(J_cE^\perp = E\), anti-commutes with \(J_c\); then \(J = J_bJ_a\theta\) is orthogonal, \(J^2 = (J_bJ_a)^2\theta^2 = -I\), and \(J\) anti-commutes with \(J_a, J_b\) (as \(J_bJ_a\) does) and with \(J_c\) (as \(\theta\) does). Finally \(\theta = J_aJ_bJ\) iff \(J = J_bJ_a\theta\). \(\square\)

Lemma 4.2 (even steps). For \(k \geq 2\), \(J \mapsto Q = J_{k-1}J\) is a bijection from \(\Omega_k(n)\) onto the set of \(Q \in O(n)\) with \(Q^2 = -I\) that commute with \(J_1, \dots, J_{k-2}\) and anti-commute with \(J_{k-1}\); the inverse is \(Q \mapsto -J_{k-1}Q\).

Proof. Lemma 2.1 gives the properties of \(Q\). Conversely, for \(J = -J_{k-1}Q\): \(J^2 = J_{k-1}QJ_{k-1}Q = -J_{k-1}^2Q^2 = -I\); for \(c \leq k-2\), \(J_cJ = J_{k-1}J_cQ = J_{k-1}QJ_c = -JJ_c\); and \(J_{k-1}J = Q = -JJ_{k-1}\). \(\square\)

The bijections of Lemmas 4.1 and 4.2, and those built from them in Lemma 24.6 below, are restrictions of affine maps between spaces of matrices (subspaces enter through their projections, and an isometry \(T\) has \(T^{-1} = T^{\mathsf T}\)), with inverses of the same kind; so they are diffeomorphisms between the submanifolds involved, as Milnor states.

\(\Omega_2\) (Milnor pp. 138–139). With \(i = J_1\), \(\mathbb R^n = \mathbb C^{n/2}\), and \(J \in \Omega_2(n)\) is a conjugate-linear complex structure; \(J_1, J, J_1J\) satisfy the relations of the quaternion units, a “quaternionic structure”. For \(4 \mid n\), \(\Omega_2(n) \cong U(n/2)/Sp(n/4)\), with \(Sp(n/4)\) the isometries commuting with \(J_1, J_2\): \(U(n/2)\) acts by conjugation, transitively by Lemma 24.8 below (\(k = 2\)), with stabilizer \(Sp(n/4)\) at \(J_2\).

From now on \(n = 16r\), with the structures of §3. In \(\mathbb R^{16}\) the sixteen joint eigenspaces of \(\theta_3, \theta_5, \theta_6, \theta_7\) are lines (this follows from §5: \(\mathbb R^{16}\) is a minimal \((J'_1, \dots, J'_8)\)-space, and the proof of Lemma 24.8 shows that all sixteen are non-zero), so in \(\mathbb R^{16r}\) they all have dimension \(r\).

Lemma 4.3 (the pieces). (a) Once \(J_1, \dots, J_4\) are fixed, \(\mathbb R^{16r} = V_1 \oplus J_4V_1\), \(V_1 = \{\theta_3 = 1\}\). (b) Once \(J_1, \dots, J_5\) are fixed, with \(W = V_1 \cap \{\theta_5 = 1\}\), \(\mathbb R^{16r} = W \oplus J_2W \oplus J_4W \oplus J_4J_2W\) and \(V_1 = W \oplus J_2W\). (c) Once \(J_1, \dots, J_6\) are fixed, with \(X = W \cap \{\theta_6 = 1\}\), \(\mathbb R^{16r} = \bigoplus_{S \subseteq \{1,2,4\}}J_SX\) and \(W = X \oplus J_1X\). All sums are orthogonal, the summands being the joint eigenspaces of the \(\theta\)’s involved.

Proof. Commuting symmetric involutions split \(\mathbb R^{16r}\) orthogonally into joint eigenspaces; by the table, among \(\theta_3, \theta_5, \theta_6\), \(J_4\) reverses the sign of \(\theta_3\) only, \(J_2\) of \(\theta_5\) only, \(J_1\) of \(\theta_6\) only, and so permutes the joint eigenspaces accordingly. \(\square\)

Lemma 24.6-(3). (checked by machine: V15.11, in a narrower form) \(J_3 \mapsto V_1 = \{\theta_3 = 1\}\) identifies \(\Omega_3(16r)\) with the set of all quaternionic subspaces of \(\mathbb H^{4r}\) (subspaces invariant under \(J_1\) and \(J_2\)). On \(V_1\), \(J_3 = -J_1J_2\); on \(V_2 = V_1^\perp\), \(J_3 = J_1J_2\).

Proof. Lemma 4.1 with \((a, b) = (1, 2)\) and no further \(c\); \(J_3 = J_2J_1(2P - I)\). \(\square\)

\(\Omega_3(16r)\) has components \(G_j(\mathbb H^{4r})\) of varying dimension \(4j(4r - j)\). Milnor restricts to the largest, \(j = 2r\): \(\dim_{\mathbb H}V_1 = \dim_{\mathbb H}V_2 = 2r\), as for our \(J_3\).

Lemma 24.6-(4). \(J_4 \mapsto T = J_3J_4|V_1\) identifies \(\Omega_4(16r)\) with the set of quaternionic isometries \(T : V_1 \to V_2\), the inverse being \(J_4|V_1 = J_3^{-1}T\), \(J_4|V_2 = -T^{-1}J_3\). Thus \(\Omega_4(16r) \cong Sp(2r)\).

Proof. By Lemma 4.2, \(J_4 \leftrightarrow Q = J_3J_4\) with \(Q^2 = -I\), \(Q\) commuting with \(J_1, J_2\) and anti-commuting with \(J_3\), hence with \(\theta_3\). So \(Q\) maps \(V_1\) to \(V_2\) and back, \(T = Q|V_1\) is an isometry commuting with \(J_1, J_2\), and \(Q|V_2 = -T^{-1}\). Conversely, for such a \(T\), \(Q = T \oplus (-T^{-1})\) satisfies \(Q^2 = -I\), commutes with \(J_1, J_2\) (so with \(J_1J_2\)), and anti-commutes with \(\theta_3\), hence with \(J_3 = -J_1J_2\theta_3\). Then \(J_4 = -J_3Q\), which is \(J_3^{-1}T\) on \(V_1\) and \(J_3T^{-1} = -T^{-1}J_3\) on \(V_2\) (\(T\) intertwines \(J_3|V_1 = -J_1J_2\) with \(-J_3|V_2\)). Choosing a base point \(T_0\), \(T \mapsto T_0^{-1}T\) identifies the set with the group of quaternionic isometries of \(V_1 \cong \mathbb H^{2r}\). \(\square\)

Lemma 24.6-(5). (checked by machine: V15.11, in a narrower form) \(J_5 \mapsto W = V_1 \cap \{\theta_5 = 1\}\) identifies \(\Omega_5(16r)\) with the set of subspaces \(W \subseteq V_1\) such that (1) \(J_1W = W\) and (2) \(V_1 = W \oplus J_2W\), orthogonally.

Proof. Lemma 4.1 with \((a,b) = (1,4)\): \(\Omega_5 \leftrightarrow E\) with \(J_1E = J_4E = E\), \(J_2E = J_3E = E^\perp\). Given \(E\): \(\theta_5\) commutes with \(\theta_3\), so \(E = (E \cap V_1) \oplus (E \cap V_2)\) with \(E \cap V_2 = J_4W\); \(J_1W = W\); and \(J_2\), preserving \(V_1\), maps \(W\) onto \(E^\perp \cap V_1\). Conversely, given \(W\), put \(E = W \oplus J_4W\): then \(J_1E = J_4E = E\), \(J_2E = J_2W \oplus J_4J_2W = E^\perp\) by Lemma 4.3(a), and \(J_3E = J_1J_2\theta_3E = E^\perp\). \(\square\)

Remark. \(\Omega_5(16r) \cong Sp(2r)/U(2r)\), where \(U(2r)\) is the group of quaternionic automorphisms of \(V_1\) preserving a fixed \(W\). Indeed \(Sp(V_1)\) acts transitively on the set of such \(W\): a unitary isomorphism \(U : W \to W'\) (for \(i = J_1\)) extends to \(V_1\) by \(J_2w \mapsto J_2Uw\), and this extension commutes with \(J_1\) and \(J_2\); the stabilizer of \(W\) restricts isomorphically to the unitary group of \(W\).

Lemma 24.6-(6). (checked by machine: V15.11, in a narrower form) \(J_6 \mapsto X = W \cap \{\theta_6 = 1\}\) identifies \(\Omega_6(16r)\) with the set of real subspaces \(X \subseteq W\) such that \(W = X \oplus J_1X\), orthogonally.

Proof. Lemma 4.1 with \((a,b) = (2,4)\): \(\Omega_6 \leftrightarrow E\) with \(J_2E = J_4E = E\), \(J_1E = J_3E = J_5E = E^\perp\). Given \(E\): \(\theta_6\) commutes with \(\theta_3, \theta_5\), so \(E\) splits along the four pieces of Lemma 4.3(b), and as \(J_2, J_4\) preserve \(E\), \(E = X \oplus J_2X \oplus J_4X \oplus J_4J_2X\); \(J_1\) maps \(X\) onto \(E^\perp \cap W\). Conversely, given \(X\), define \(E\) by this formula: \(J_2, J_4\) permute its summands; \(J_1E\) is the same sum built on \(J_1X = W \ominus X\), which is \(E^\perp\); and since \(\theta_3, \theta_5\) are \(\pm 1\) on each piece, \(J_3E = J_1J_2E = E^\perp\), \(J_5E = J_4J_1E = E^\perp\). \(\square\)

Remark. \(\Omega_6(16r) \cong U(2r)/O(2r)\): the unitary group of \((W, J_1)\) acts transitively on such \(X\) (a real isometry \(X \to X'\) extends complex-linearly), with stabilizer \(O(X)\).

Lemma 24.6-(7). (checked by machine: V15.11, in a narrower form) \(J_7 \mapsto X_1 = X \cap \{\theta_7 = 1\}\) identifies \(\Omega_7(16r)\) with the set of all subspaces of \(X \cong \mathbb R^{2r}\).

Proof. Lemma 4.1 with \((a,b) = (1,6)\): \(\Omega_7 \leftrightarrow E\) with \(J_1E = J_6E = E\) and \(J_cE = E^\perp\) for \(c = 2, \dots, 5\). Given \(E\): \(\theta_7\) commutes with \(\theta_3, \theta_5, \theta_6\), so \(E\) splits along the eight pieces \(J_SX\); as \(J_1\) preserves \(E\) while \(J_2, J_4\) exchange \(E\) and \(E^\perp\), \[E = \bigoplus_{S \subseteq \{1,2,4\}}J_SX_{(S)}, \qquad X_{(S)} = X_1 \text{ if } |S \cap \{2,4\}| \text{ is even}, \quad X_{(S)} = X_2 = X \ominus X_1 \text{ otherwise}. \tag{4.1}\] Conversely, for any \(X_1 \subseteq X\) define \(E\) by (4.1): \(J_1E = E\), \(J_2E = J_4E = E^\perp\), \(J_6E = J_4J_2\theta_6E = E\), \(J_3E = J_1J_2\theta_3E = E^\perp\), \(J_5E = J_4J_1\theta_5E = E^\perp\). \(\square\)

Again the components \(G_j(\mathbb R^{2r})\) vary in dimension, and Milnor restricts to \(\dim X_1 = \dim X_2 = r\), as for our \(J_7\). Assertion (Milnor p. 141): the largest component of \(\Omega_7(16r)\) is diffeomorphic to the Grassmann manifold of \(r\)-dimensional subspaces of \(\mathbb R^{2r}\).

Lemma 24.6-(8). (checked by machine: V15.42, restated) \(J_8 \mapsto T = J_7J_8|X_1\) identifies \(\Omega_8(16r)\) with the set of isometries \(T : X_1 \to X_2\). Thus \(\Omega_8(16r) \cong O(r)\).

Proof. By Lemma 4.2, \(J_8 \leftrightarrow Q = J_7J_8\), \(Q^2 = -I\), commuting with \(J_1, \dots, J_6\) and anti-commuting with \(J_7\). Then \(Q\) commutes with \(\theta_3, \theta_5, \theta_6\) and with \(J_1, J_2, J_4\), so it preserves \(X\) and is determined by \(Q_X = Q|X\) through \(Q(J_Sx) = J_SQ_Xx\); and it anti-commutes with \(\theta_7\), so \(Q_X\) exchanges \(X_1\) and \(X_2\), with \(Q_X|X_2 = -T^{-1}\). Conversely, given \(T\), put \(Q_X = T \oplus (-T^{-1})\) and \(Q = J_SQ_XJ_S^{-1}\) on \(J_SX\). Then \(Q^2 = -I\); \(Q\) commutes with \(J_1, J_2, J_4\) (as \(J_\alpha J_S = \pm J_{S \triangle \{\alpha\}}\)) and with \(\theta_3, \theta_5, \theta_6\) (scalars on each piece), hence with \(J_3, J_5, J_6\); and it anti-commutes with \(\theta_7\) (on \(J_SX\), \(\theta_7 = (-1)^{|S \cap \{2,4\}|}J_S\theta_7J_S^{-1}\), and \(Q_X\) anti-commutes with \(\theta_7|X\)), hence with \(J_7 = J_6J_1\theta_7\). \(\square\)

Passing to the limit. Under \(J \mapsto J \oplus J'_8\) the spaces \(X_1, X_2\) of \(\mathbb R^{16r+16}\) are \(X_1 \oplus X'_1\), \(X_2 \oplus X'_2\) (lines \(X'_1, X'_2 \subseteq \mathbb R^{16}\)), and \(T \mapsto T \oplus T'_0\) with \(T'_0 = J'_7J'_8|X'_1\). With the base point \(T_0 = J_7J_8|X_1\) and \(T \mapsto T_0^{-1}T\), this is \(O(r) \to O(r+1)\), \(T \mapsto T \oplus 1\). Hence \(\Omega_8\) is homeomorphic to \(O\), compatibly with base points. Likewise \(\Omega_4(16r) \cong Sp(2r)\) is compatible with \(Sp(2r) \to Sp(2r+2)\), and \(Sp = \Omega_4\) is the infinite symplectic group.

Remark (Milnor’s footnote, p. 142). For \(k > 8\), with \(J_9, \dots, J_{k-1}\) also fixed, \(J \mapsto J_8J|X_1\) identifies \(\Omega_k(16r)\) with \(\Omega_{k-8}(r)\), defined on \(X_1 \cong \mathbb R^r\) with the fixed structures \(J_8J_\alpha|X_1\), \(9 \leq \alpha < k\). Indeed \(J_8J\) commutes with \(J_1, \dots, J_7\), hence preserves \(X_1\), and is a complex structure anti-commuting with each \(J_8J_\alpha\) (Lemma 2.1). Conversely, \(\mathbb R^{16r} = \bigoplus_{S \subseteq \{1,2,4,8\}}J_SX_1\) (the flips of \(J_1, J_2, J_4, J_8\) on \(\theta_3, \theta_5, \theta_6, \theta_7\) form a basis of \((\mathbb Z/2)^4\)), and an operator \(C\) on \(X_1\) extends uniquely to \(\hat C\) commuting with \(J_1, \dots, J_7\) and anti-commuting with \(J_8\): \(\hat C(J_Sx) = \pm J_SCx\), with \(-\) iff \(8 \in S\); then \(J = -J_8\hat C\). The same decomposition shows that a space \(V\) with \(k + 8\) anti-commuting structures has \(\dim V = 16\dim X_1(V)\), with \(V\) minimal iff \(X_1(V)\) is; and \(k\) structures \(C_\beta\) on \(X\) give \(k + 8\) on \(\mathbb R^{16} \otimes X\), namely \(J'_\alpha \otimes 1\) and \(\omega'_8 \otimes C_\beta\), where \(\omega'_8 = J'_1\cdots J'_8\) is a symmetric involution anti-commuting with each \(J'_\alpha\). Hence \(m_{k+8} = 16m_k\).

Theorem 24.7 (Bott). (checked by machine: V15.45, in a narrower form) \(\pi_iO \cong \pi_{i+8}O\) for \(i \geq 0\). With the facts quoted at the end of §6, \(O\) has the homotopy type of its eighth loop space \(\Omega^8O\), \(O \simeq \Omega^4Sp\) and \(Sp \simeq \Omega^4O\).

Proof. Theorem 24.5, applied eight times, and \(\Omega_8 \cong O\): \(\pi_{i+8}O \cong \pi_{i+7}\Omega_1 \cong \cdots \cong \pi_i\Omega_8 \cong \pi_iO\). Similarly \(\Omega_4 \simeq \Omega^4\Omega_0\) and \(\Omega_8 \simeq \Omega^4\Omega_4\). \(\square\)

The table (Milnor p. 142, “left to the reader”). By Theorem 24.5, \(\pi_hO \cong \pi_0\Omega_h\) as sets for \(1 \leq h \leq 8\), and \(\pi_0\Omega_h\) is visible from Lemma 24.6, using the connectedness of \(U(n)\), \(Sp(n)\), \(SO(n)\) and of the Grassmannians:
