(\(O(n)/U(n/2)\) has two components because \(U(n/2) \subseteq SO(n)\) is connected; in the limit the components of \(\Omega_3\) are labelled by \(j - 2r \in \mathbb Z\), since \(J \mapsto J \oplus J'_3\) adds \(2\) to \(j\), and those of \(\Omega_7\) by \(j - r\); \(BSp\) and \(BO\) name the colimits of the middle Grassmannians.) So \(\pi_iO\) for \(i \equiv 0, \dots, 7 \pmod 8\) is \(\mathbb Z/2, \mathbb Z/2, 0, \mathbb Z, 0, 0, 0, \mathbb Z\), and \(\pi_iSp = \pi_i\Omega_4\) is \(0, 0, 0, \mathbb Z, \mathbb Z/2, \mathbb Z/2, 0, \mathbb Z\), Milnor’s table. For the group structures: a group of order two is \(\mathbb Z/2\); the bundles \(Sp(m-1) \to Sp(m) \to S^{4m-1}\) make \(\pi_jSp(m-1) \to \pi_jSp(m)\) an isomorphism for \(j \leq 4m - 3\), so \(\pi_jSp \cong \pi_jSp(1) = \pi_jS^3\) for \(j \leq 5\) and \(\pi_7O \cong \pi_3\Omega_4 = \pi_3Sp \cong \mathbb Z\); and \(\pi_3O \cong \pi_1\Omega_2 = \pi_1(U/Sp) \cong \pi_1U \cong \mathbb Z\), from the bundle \(Sp(4r) \to U(8r) \to U(8r)/Sp(4r)\) and \(\pi_0Sp = \pi_1Sp = 0\). Milnor’s hint is a check: \(Sp(1) = S^3\), and \(SO(3) \cong \mathbb RP^3\) gives \(\pi_1O = \pi_1SO(3) = \mathbb Z/2\).

5. Clifford modules (Milnor pp. 142–144)

Let \(V\) be a Euclidean space with anti-commuting complex structures \(J_1, \dots, J_k\) (a \((J_1, \dots, J_k)\)-space). Definition (Milnor p. 143). \(V\) is minimal if no proper non-trivial subspace is closed under \(J_1, \dots, J_k\). Two minimal spaces are isomorphic if there is an isometry between them commuting with the \(J_\alpha\).

Lemma 5.1. Every \((J_1, \dots, J_k)\)-space is an orthogonal sum of minimal ones.

Proof. The \(J_\alpha\) are skew, so the orthogonal complement of an invariant subspace is invariant. Induct on the dimension. \(\square\)

Lemma 5.2 (cyclic vectors). Let \(V\) be minimal and \(u \in V\) a unit vector. Then the \(J_Su\), \(S \subseteq \{1, \dots, k\}\), span \(V\). If \(V'\) is minimal, with a unit vector \(u'\) such that \(\langle J_Su, u\rangle = \langle J_Su', u'\rangle\) for all \(S\), then \(\sum c_SJ_Su \mapsto \sum c_SJ_Su'\) is a well-defined isomorphism \(V \to V'\).

Proof. The span is invariant (Lemma 2.1(c)), hence all of \(V\). By Lemma 2.1(a),(c), \(\langle J_Su, J_Tu\rangle = \langle J_T^{\mathsf T}J_Su, u\rangle = \pm\langle J_{S \triangle T}u, u\rangle\) with a sign depending only on \(S, T\). So the two families have the same Gram matrices, the map is well defined and isometric, and it commutes with \(J_\alpha\) because \(J_\alpha J_S = \pm J_{S \triangle \{\alpha\}}\) with the same sign in \(V\) and \(V'\). \(\square\)

Lemma 24.8 (Bott and Shapiro), for \(k \leq 8\). (checked by machine: V15.17, in a narrower form) For \(0 \leq k \leq 8\), minimal \((J_1, \dots, J_k)\)-spaces exist and have dimension \(m_k\): \[m_0 = 1,\ m_1 = 2,\ m_2 = m_3 = 4,\ m_4 = m_5 = m_6 = m_7 = 8,\ m_8 = 16.\] For \(k \not\equiv 3 \pmod 4\) any two are isomorphic. For \(k = 3, 7\) there are exactly two isomorphism classes, distinguished by \(\omega_k = J_1\cdots J_k = \pm I\).

Proof. Let \(\Theta_k\) consist of those of \(\theta_3, \theta_5, \theta_6, \theta_7\) whose indices are all \(\leq k\), and let \(t_k = |\Theta_k|\) (\(0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 4, 4\) for \(k = 0, \dots, 8\)). Write \(G_k\) for the index sets \(S\) with \(J_S = \pm\) a product of elements of \(\Theta_k\); the generators \(\{1,2,3\}\), \(\{1,4,5\}\), \(\{2,4,6\}\), \(\{1,6,7\}\) are independent under \(\triangle\), so \(|G_k| = 2^{t_k}\).

Step 1: the commutant. If \(S \subseteq \{1, \dots, k\}\), \(J_S\) is symmetric and commutes with all of \(\Theta_k\), then \(S \in G_k\). By Lemma 2.1(b), \(J_S\) commutes with \(\theta_T\) (\(|T| = 3\)) iff \(|S \setminus T|\) is even, a linear condition over \(\mathbb Z/2\) on the indicator vector of \(S\); and \(J_S\) is symmetric iff \(|S| \equiv 0, 3 \pmod 4\). For \(k \leq 2\) only \(S = \emptyset\) is symmetric. For \(k = 3\) the symmetric sets are \(\emptyset\) and \(\{1,2,3\}\). For \(k = 4\) the condition is \(4 \notin S\), leaving \(\emptyset\) and \(\{1,2,3\}\). For \(k = 5\) the conditions are that \(|S \cap \{4,5\}|\) and \(|S \cap \{2,3\}|\) be even; of the eight solutions the symmetric ones are \(\emptyset\), \(\{1,2,3\}\), \(\{1,4,5\}\), \(\{2,3,4,5\}\), which is \(G_5\). For \(k = 6, 7, 8\) the complements of the index sets of \(\Theta_k\) in \(\{1, \dots, k\}\) have rank \(k - t_k\): for \(k = 6\), \(\{4,5,6\}, \{2,3,6\}, \{1,3,5\}\), rank \(3\); for \(k = 7\), \(\{4,5,6,7\}, \{2,3,6,7\}, \{1,3,5,7\}, \{2,3,4,5\}\), rank \(3\); for \(k = 8\) the same with \(8\) added to each, rank \(4\). So the solutions form a group of \(2^{t_k}\) elements containing \(G_k\), hence equal to \(G_k\), even without the symmetry condition.

Step 2: the flips. In a \((J_1, \dots, J_k)\)-space \(V\) the involutions of \(\Theta_k\) split \(V\) into joint eigenspaces \(V_\varepsilon\), \(\varepsilon \in \{\pm 1\}^{t_k}\), and \(J_\alpha\) maps \(V_\varepsilon\) onto \(V_{\varepsilon f_\alpha}\), \(f_\alpha\) recording which \(\theta\)’s anti-commute with \(J_\alpha\) (table of §4). Let \(F_k\) be the group generated by \(f_1, \dots, f_k\). If \(V\) is minimal, the sum of the \(V_\varepsilon\) over a coset of \(F_k\) is invariant, so the non-zero \(V_\varepsilon\) form exactly one coset. By the table, \(F_k\) is everything for \(k = 4\) (\(J_4\)), \(5\) (\(J_2, J_4\)), \(6\) (\(J_1, J_2, J_4\)) and \(8\) (\(J_1, J_2, J_4, J_8\)); \(F_3\) is trivial; \(F_7\), generated by the flips of \(J_1, J_2, J_4\), is the index-two subgroup \(\varepsilon_3\varepsilon_5\varepsilon_7 = 1\). As \(\omega_3 = \theta_3\) and \(\omega_7 = \pm\theta_3\theta_5\theta_7\) (\(\{1,2,3\} \triangle \{1,4,5\} \triangle \{1,6,7\} = \{1, \dots, 7\}\)), the two cosets for \(k = 3, 7\) are told apart by \(\omega_k\), which commutes with every \(J_\alpha\) and is therefore \(\pm I\) on a minimal space.

Step 3: uniqueness. Let \(V, V'\) be minimal with \(V_\varepsilon \neq 0 \neq V'_\varepsilon\) for some \(\varepsilon\) (for \(k \not\equiv 3 \pmod 4\) any \(\varepsilon\) will do, by Step 2; for \(k = 3, 7\) this means the same sign of \(\omega_k\)). Take unit vectors \(u \in V_\varepsilon\), \(u' \in V'_\varepsilon\). If \(J_S\) is skew, \(\langle J_Su, u\rangle = 0\). If \(J_S\) is symmetric and anti-commutes with some \(\theta \in \Theta_k\), then \(\langle J_Su, u\rangle = \langle J_S\theta u, \theta u\rangle = \langle\theta J_S\theta u, u\rangle = -\langle J_Su, u\rangle = 0\). Otherwise \(S \in G_k\) by Step 1, and \(\langle J_Su, u\rangle\) is a universal sign times a product of entries of \(\varepsilon\). The same holds for \(u'\), and Lemma 5.2 gives \(V \cong V'\).

Step 4: dimension. For \(u\) as in Step 3, \(\langle J_Su, J_Tu\rangle = \pm\langle J_{S \triangle T}u, u\rangle\) vanishes unless \(S \triangle T \in G_k\), in which case \(J_Su = \pm J_Tu\). So one \(J_Su\) for each coset of \(G_k\) in the group of subsets of \(\{1, \dots, k\}\) gives an orthonormal basis of \(V\): \(\dim V = 2^{k - t_k} = m_k\).

Step 5: existence. \(\mathbb R^{16}\) with \(J'_1, \dots, J'_k\) contains a minimal space (Lemma 5.1). For \(k = 3, 7\), replacing \(J_k\) by \(-J_k\) changes the sign of \(\omega_k\), so both classes occur. \(\square\)

For \(k = 8\), Step 4 shows that \(\mathbb R^{16}\) is itself minimal, with all sixteen joint eigenspaces lines, as used in §4. Milnor’s minimal spaces are: lines over \(\mathbb R, \mathbb C, \mathbb H\) (\(k \leq 2\)); \(H\), \(H'\) with \(J_3 = \pm J_1J_2\) (\(k = 3\)); \(H \oplus H'\) (\(k = 4, 5, 6\)); \(L\), \(L'\) with \(J_7 = \pm J_1\cdots J_6\) (\(k = 7\)); \(L \oplus L'\) (\(k = 8\)). In the language of Clifford algebras (quoted from Atiyah, Bott and Shapiro, Clifford modules, Topology 3 (1964); Lawson and Michelsohn, Spin Geometry, Ch. I), a \((J_1, \dots, J_k)\)-space is a module over the algebra \(C_k\) generated by \(e_1, \dots, e_k\) with \(e_\alpha^2 = -1\) and \(e_\alpha e_\beta = -e_\beta e_\alpha\); only the last two rows (\(m_k\) and the number of classes of minimal spaces), proved above, are used (\(\mathbb F(N)\) denotes \(N \times N\) matrices over \(\mathbb F\)):

\(k\) 0 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8
\(C_k\) \(\mathbb R\) \(\mathbb C\) \(\mathbb H\) \(\mathbb H \oplus \mathbb H\) \(\mathbb H(2)\) \(\mathbb C(4)\) \(\mathbb R(8)\) \(\mathbb R(8) \oplus \mathbb R(8)\) \(\mathbb R(16)\)
\(m_k\) 1 2 4 4 8 8 8 8 16
classes 1 1 1 2 1 1 1 2 1

An interactive look at the sixteen pieces

The figure shows \(\mathbb R^{16}\) with \(J'_1, \dots, J'_8\) (§3) as a \(4 \times 4\) grid of sixteen lines, the joint eigenspaces of \(\theta_3, \theta_5, \theta_6, \theta_7\), labelled by their signs. Drag the slider \(k\) from \(0\) to \(8\): only the \(\theta\)’s with indices \(\leq k\) are defined, and cells on which they agree form one block, giving \(1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 4, 8, 16, 16\) blocks, the subspaces \(V_1, W, X, X_1\) of Lemma 24.6. Tap a button \(J_\alpha\) (\(\alpha \leq k\)) to see how it permutes the blocks, reversing the signs of the \(\theta\)’s it anti-commutes with. The panel shows \(\Omega_k(16r)\), \(m_k\), the number of classes of minimal spaces, and \(\pi_kO \cong \pi_0\Omega_k\). At \(k = 8\) the flips of \(J_1, J_2, J_4, J_8\) carry any cell to any other, which is why \(\mathbb R^{16}\) is minimal.

6. Proof of Theorem 24.5 (Milnor pp. 144–148)

Fix \(1 \leq k \leq 7\), \(n = 16r\), \(J = J_k\); the case \(k = 0\) is Theorem 24.3, whose range \(n - 4\) tends to infinity. By Lemma 24.4 the geodesics of \(\Omega_k(n)\) from \(J\) are \(t \mapsto J\exp(\pi tA)\), \(A \in \mathcal T = \mathcal T_J\), ending at \(-J\) iff \(\exp(\pi A) = -I\); the component of \(J\) is a symmetric space whose curvature, being totally geodesic, is that of \(O(n)\) (Lemma 2.2(b)). Translating Theorem 21.3(b) to \(J\) by the isometry \(L_J\), \(R(JA, JB)JA = J\cdot\tfrac14[[A,B],A]\); so for the velocity \(V = \pi JA\), \(K_V(JB) = \pi^2J\,K_A(B)\) with \[K_A(B) = -\tfrac14[A, [A, B]] = \tfrac14(-A^2B + 2ABA - BA^2), \qquad B \in \mathcal T,\] and by Theorem 20.5 an eigenvalue \(e^2\) of \(K_A\) gives conjugate points at \(t = s/e\), \(s = 1, 2, \dots\). If \(e^2 \geq 4\) there is one at \(t = 1/e \leq 1/2\), so the index is at least the number of eigenvalues \(\geq 4\), counted with multiplicity.

Lemma 6.1 (splitting). Let \(A \in \mathcal T\) with \(\exp(\pi A) = -I\). Then \(\mathbb R^n = M_1 \oplus \cdots \oplus M_s\) orthogonally, each \(M_h\) invariant and minimal under \(\mathcal F = \{J_1, \dots, J_{k-1}, J, A\}\), and \(A^2 = -a_h^2\) on \(M_h\) with \(a_h\) a positive odd integer. The geodesic is minimal iff all \(a_h = 1\).

Proof. All members of \(\mathcal F\) are skew, so the splitting exists as in Lemma 5.1. \(A^2\) is symmetric, negative semi-definite and commutes with \(\mathcal F\), so its eigenspaces in \(M_h\) are invariant and \(A^2|M_h = -a_h^2\) (Milnor’s “all equal, except for sign”). If \(a_h = 0\), then \(\exp(\pi A)|M_h = I\); otherwise \(A/a_h\) is a complex structure on \(M_h\) and \(\exp(\pi A)|M_h = \cos(\pi a_h)I + \sin(\pi a_h)A/a_h = -I\) iff \(a_h\) is odd. Minimality means \(A^2 = -I\) (Lemma 24.4(iii)). \(\square\)

Case \(k \not\equiv 2 \pmod 4\)

Assertion. The index of a non-minimal geodesic from \(J\) to \(-J\) in \(\Omega_k(n)\) is \(\geq n/m_{k+1} - 1\).

Proof. On \(M_h\) put \(J'_h = a_h^{-1}JA\), a complex structure anti-commuting with \(J_1, \dots, J_{k-1}\) and \(J\): \((JA)^2 = J(AJ)A = -J^2A^2 = -a_h^2\), \((JA)^{\mathsf T} = AJ = -JA\), \(J_\alpha JA = -JAJ_\alpha\), \(J(JA) = -A = -(JA)J\). Since \(A = -a_hJJ'_h\) on \(M_h\), \(M_h\) is minimal for the \(k + 1\) structures \(J_1, \dots, J_{k-1}, J, J'_h\), so \(\dim M_h = m_{k+1}\) and \(s = n/m_{k+1}\). For \(h \neq j\), \((J_1, \dots, J_{k-1}, -J, J'_j)\) also makes \(M_j\) minimal; as \(k + 1 \not\equiv 3 \pmod 4\) and \(k + 1 \leq 8\), Lemma 24.8 gives an isometry \(C : M_h \to M_j\) (Milnor’s “isomorphism from \(M_h\) to \(\bar M_j\)”) with \[CJ_\alpha = J_\alpha C\ (\alpha < k), \qquad CJ = -JC, \qquad CJ'_h = J'_jC.\] Let \(B = C\) on \(M_h\), \(-C^{\mathsf T}\) on \(M_j\), \(0\) on the other \(M_l\); \(C^{\mathsf T}\) satisfies the same relations from \(M_j\) to \(M_h\), so \(B \in \mathcal T\). For \(v \in M_h\), \(BAv = -a_hBJJ'_hv = a_hJJ'_jBv = -(a_h/a_j)ABv\) (as \(A = -a_jJJ'_j\) on \(M_j\)), so \(ABAv = a_ha_jBv\) and \[(K_AB)v = \tfrac14\bigl(a_j^2 + 2a_ha_j + a_h^2\bigr)Bv = \tfrac14(a_h + a_j)^2\,Bv,\] and likewise on \(M_j\). If the geodesic is not minimal, some \(a_{h_0} \geq 3\), and the \(s - 1\) eigenvectors from the pairs \((h_0, j)\) are independent, with eigenvalues \((a_{h_0} + a_j)^2/4 \geq 4\). So the index is \(\geq s - 1\). \(\square\)

Hence, by Theorem 22.1 with \(\Omega^d \cong \Omega_{k+1}(n)\) (Lemma 24.4), \(\varphi_r\) induces isomorphisms of \(\pi_i\) for \(i \leq n/m_{k+1} - 3\), a range that tends to infinity with \(r\).

Case \(k \equiv 2 \pmod 4\) (\(k = 2, 6\))

The difficulty (Milnor): \(\Omega\Omega_k(n)\) has infinitely many components, \(\Omega_{k+1}(n)\) finitely many. Let \(i = J_1\cdots J_{k-1}\); as \(k - 1 \equiv 1 \pmod 4\), Lemma 2.1 makes \(i\) a complex structure commuting with \(J_1, \dots, J_{k-1}\) and anti-commuting with every \(J' \in \Omega_k(n)\). Make \(\mathbb R^n\) complex by \(i\). For \(J' \in \Omega_k(n)\), \(J^{-1}J'\) is unitary; put \(f(J') = \det_{\mathbb C}(J^{-1}J') \in S^1\). Each \(A \in \mathcal T\) commutes with \(i\) and is skew, hence skew-Hermitian, and \(f(J\exp(\pi tA)) = e^{\pi t\operatorname{tr}_{\mathbb C}A}\). Also \(f(-J) = (-1)^{n/2} = 1\), as \(n/2 = 8r\) is even; Milnor’s “closed loop” needs this.

The components. For a path \(\omega\) from \(J\) to \(-J\) let \(\vartheta_\omega\) be the continuous argument of \(f\circ\omega\) with \(\vartheta_\omega(0) = 0\), so \(\vartheta_\omega(1) \in 2\pi\mathbb Z\). If \(\omega'\) is uniformly close to \(\omega\), then \(|f\circ\omega - f\circ\omega'| < 2\), so \(|\vartheta_\omega - \vartheta_{\omega'}| < \pi\) throughout and \(\vartheta_\omega(1) = \vartheta_{\omega'}(1)\). Hence for each integer \(c\) the set \(\Omega^{(c)}\) of paths with \(\vartheta_\omega(1) = \pi cm_k/2\) is open and closed.

The geodesics. Split \(\mathbb R^n = M_1 \oplus \cdots \oplus M_\nu\) as in Lemma 6.1. The complex eigenspaces of \(A\) are invariant under \(J\) (if \(Av = \lambda iv\), then \(A(Jv) = -JAv = \lambda iJv\)) and the \(J_\alpha\), so \(A|M_h = a_hi\), \(a_h\) an odd integer of either sign. Each \(M_h\) is then a minimal \((J_1, \dots, J_{k-1}, J)\)-space, \(\dim M_h = m_k\), \(\nu = n/m_k\) (Milnor’s \(r\)), and \(\operatorname{tr}_{\mathbb C}A = i(a_1 + \cdots + a_\nu)m_k/2\): the geodesic lies in \(\Omega^{(c)}\) with \(c = a_1 + \cdots + a_\nu = -\operatorname{tr}_{\mathbb R}(iA)/m_k\) (as \(\operatorname{tr}_{\mathbb R} = 2\operatorname{Re}\operatorname{tr}_{\mathbb C}\)). It is minimal iff all \(a_h = \pm 1\); such geodesics exist in \(\Omega^{(c)}\) iff \(|c| \leq \nu\) and \(c \equiv \nu \pmod 2\), and they form \(\varphi(\Omega_{k+1}(n)^{(c)})\), where \(\Omega_{k+1}(n)^{(c)} = \varphi^{-1}(\Omega^{(c)})\) is open and closed in \(\Omega_{k+1}(n)\). (For “if”: split \(\mathbb R^n\) into minimal \((J_1, \dots, J_{k-1}, J)\)-spaces \(M_h\) by Lemma 5.1. A minimal \((J_1, \dots, J_{k+1})\)-space has dimension \(m_{k+1} = m_k\), so it is also minimal for its first \(k\) structures, hence isomorphic to each \(M_h\) by Lemma 24.8; transporting its last structure gives a complex structure \(J''_h\) on \(M_h\) anti-commuting with \(J_1, \dots, J_{k-1}, J\). Then \(J' = \bigoplus_h \pm J''_h\) lies in \(\Omega_{k+1}(n)\), \(A = J^{-1}J'\) has \(a_h = \pm 1\), and changing the sign on \(M_h\) changes the sign of \(a_h\), so every such \(c\) occurs.)

Assertion. A non-minimal geodesic in \(\Omega^{(c)}\) has index \(\lambda \geq (\nu - |c|)/4\).

Proof. For \(h \neq j\), Lemma 24.8 for \(k\) structures (\(k \not\equiv 3 \pmod 4\)), applied to \(M_h\) and to \(M_j\) with \(J\) replaced by \(-J\), gives an isometry \(C : M_h \to M_j\) commuting with \(J_1, \dots, J_{k-1}\), hence with \(i\), and anti-commuting with \(J\). With \(B = C\) on \(M_h\), \(-C^{\mathsf T}\) on \(M_j\), \(0\) elsewhere, \(B \in \mathcal T\), and for \(v \in M_h\): \(ABAv = a_ha_ji^2Bv = -a_ha_jBv\), so \((K_AB)v = \tfrac14(a_j^2 - 2a_ha_j + a_h^2)Bv\): \(B\) is an eigenvector with eigenvalue \((a_h - a_j)^2/4\). For \(a_h > a_j\) this gives \((a_h - a_j)/2 - 1\) conjugate points in \((0,1)\), and the \(B\)’s of different pairs are independent, so \[2\lambda \geq \sum_{a_h > a_j}(a_h - a_j - 2).\] Let \(p\) be the sum of the positive \(a_h\) and \(-q\) that of the negative ones: \(p - q = c\) and \(p + q \geq \nu\). Non-minimal means some \(|a_{h_0}| \geq 3\). If \(a_{h_0} \leq -3\) (Milnor: “suppose for example that some \(a_h\) is equal to \(-3\)”), pairing \(h_0\) with the positive \(a_h\) gives \(2\lambda \geq \sum_{a_h > 0}(a_h + 3 - 2) \geq p \geq (\nu + c)/2\). If \(a_{h_0} \geq 3\), pairing with the negative ones gives \(2\lambda \geq q \geq (\nu - c)/2\). In either case \(4\lambda \geq \nu - |c|\). \(\square\)

Theorem 22.1 is now needed one component at a time.

Lemma 6.2 (Theorem 22.1 componentwise). Let \(\Omega' \subseteq \Omega(M; p, q)\) be open and closed and contain a minimal geodesic. If \(\Omega' \cap \Omega^d\) is a topological manifold and every non-minimal geodesic in \(\Omega'\) has index \(\geq \lambda_0\), then \(\pi_i(\Omega', \Omega' \cap \Omega^d) = 0\) for \(0 \leq i < \lambda_0\).

Proof. Milnor’s proof of 22.1 (pp. 122–123) applies Lemma 22.5 to \(F\circ E\) on the manifold \(B = \operatorname{Int}\Omega^c(t_0, \dots, t_k)\), a deformation retract of \(\operatorname{Int}\Omega^c\). Intersect with \(\Omega'\): \(B \cap \Omega'\) is open and closed in \(B\); a deformation keeps points in their path components, so preserves \(\Omega'\); and \(F\circ E\) on \(B \cap \Omega'\) attains its minimum exactly on \(\Omega' \cap \Omega^d \neq \emptyset\). The proof then runs verbatim. \(\square\)

Apply Lemma 6.2 to \(\Omega' = \Omega^{(c)}\), for fixed \(c\) and \(n\) so large that \(|c| \leq \nu\) (only even \(c\) occur, as \(\nu\) is even): \(\varphi\) maps \(\Omega_{k+1}(n)^{(c)}\) into \(\Omega^{(c)}\) inducing isomorphisms of \(\pi_i\) for \(i \leq (\nu - |c|)/4 - 2\). Under \(\omega \mapsto \omega \oplus \delta_k\) the integer \(c\) does not change: \(f\) is multiplicative on block sums, so \(c\) is additive, and \(\delta_k\) has \(c = -\operatorname{tr}(i\,J'^{-1}_kJ'_{k+1})/m_k = \operatorname{tr}(\omega_{k+1})/m_k = 0\) on \(\mathbb R^{16}\), because \(\omega_3 = \theta_3\) and \(\omega_7 = \pm\theta_3\theta_5\theta_7\) have trace \(0\) (all sixteen sign patterns occur once). This is Milnor’s conclusion: each component of \(\Omega\Omega_k(n)\) is approximated, in a range of dimensions that grows with \(n\), by the corresponding component of \(\Omega_{k+1}(n)\).

Passing to the limit

In both cases, for each \(i \geq 1\) and each base point, \(\varphi_r\) induces isomorphisms on \(\pi_i\) once \(r\) is large. On \(\pi_0\): in the first case \(\varphi_r\) is a bijection once \(n/m_{k+1} \geq 3\). In the second, each set \(\Omega' = \{\omega : \vartheta_\omega(1) = \text{const}\}\) is open and closed, and if non-empty it contains a geodesic: for \(\omega \in \Omega'\) and \(E(\omega) < a\), the deformation of Theorem 16.2 moves \(\omega\), inside \(\Omega'\) and without increasing \(E\), into the compact set \(B^a \cap \Omega'\), where \(E\) attains its minimum at a local minimum, hence a critical point, of \(E|_B\). So every path lies in some \(\Omega^{(c)}\) with \(c \equiv \nu \pmod 2\). The integer \(c\) does not change under stabilization, and once \(\nu \geq |c| + 8\), Lemma 6.2 with \(\lambda_0 \geq 2\) shows that \(\varphi_r\) maps the components of \(\Omega_{k+1}(16r)^{(c)}\) bijectively onto those of \(\Omega^{(c)}\). As \(\varphi_{r+1}\) extends \(\varphi_r\) and homotopy groups and path components of the colimits are colimits (§3), Theorem 24.5 follows.

Milnor’s text quotes two facts here. To get a homotopy equivalence Milnor asserts, without proof, that both \(\Omega_{k+1}\) and \(\Omega\Omega_k\) “have the homotopy type of a CW-complex”, and applies Whitehead’s theorem. We quote the same (colimits of compact manifolds along smooth embeddings are homotopy equivalent to mapping telescopes; loop spaces by J. Milnor, Trans. AMS 90 (1959)). Every homotopy-group statement of this chapter, including \(\pi_iO \cong \pi_{i+8}O\), is proved without them.

7. Application: vector fields on spheres and real vector bundles over spheres

Vector fields (Milnor’s Remark, pp. 143–144). If \(J_1, \dots, J_k\) are anti-commuting complex structures on \(\mathbb R^n\) and \(|x| = 1\), then \(J_1x, \dots, J_kx\) are orthonormal and orthogonal to \(x\): \(\langle J_\alpha x, x\rangle = 0\) since \(J_\alpha\) is skew, and \(\langle J_\alpha x, J_\beta x\rangle = -\langle J_\beta J_\alpha x, x\rangle = 0\) since \(J_\beta J_\alpha\) is skew. So \(S^{n-1}\) carries \(k\) orthonormal tangent fields. By Lemmas 5.1 and 24.8, \(\mathbb R^n\) carries \(k\) such structures iff \(m_k \mid n\); with \(m_{k+8} = 16m_k\), the largest such \(k\) for \(n = 2^{4a+b}\cdot(\text{odd})\) is \(8a + 2^b - 1 = \rho(n) - 1\). Milnor’s examples: \(3\) fields on \(S^{4r-1}\), \(7\) on \(S^{8r-1}\), \(8\) on \(S^{16r-1}\); concretely, \(x \mapsto J'_1x, \dots, J'_8x\) (§3) on \(S^{15}\). For \(n = 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256\), \[\rho(n) - 1 = 1,\ 3,\ 7,\ 8,\ 9,\ 11,\ 15,\ 16,\] growing by \(8\) each time \(n\) is multiplied by \(16\). Adams (Vector fields on spheres, Annals of Math. 75 (1962)) proved that there are never \(\rho(n)\) independent fields; his proof uses real K-theory, whose foundation is Theorem 24.7. So \(S^{n-1}\) is parallelizable only for \(n = 1, 2, 4, 8\); and for \(n\) odd Adams’s bound is the hairy ball theorem.

Real vector bundles over spheres. As in Chapter 14, §5, real vector bundles over \(S^n\) are glued from two trivial ones by maps \(S^{n-1} \to O(N)\), and the stable classes form the group \(\widetilde{KO}(S^n) \cong \pi_{n-1}O\). By Theorem 24.7 and the table of §4:

\(n\) (mod 8) 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 0
\(\widetilde{KO}(S^n)\) \(\mathbb Z/2\) \(\mathbb Z/2\) \(0\) \(\mathbb Z\) \(0\) \(0\) \(0\) \(\mathbb Z\)

For \(n = 1, 2, 4, 8\) a generator is glued by \(x \mapsto x_0I + \sum_{\alpha<n}x_\alpha J_\alpha\), built from a minimal space for \(n - 1\) structures, of dimension \(m_0, m_1, m_3, m_7 = 1, 2, 4, 8\) (orthogonal for \(|x| = 1\), by anti-commutation): the Möbius band and the real bundles underlying the complex, quaternionic and octonionic Hopf line bundles (Atiyah, Bott and Shapiro, 1964). So every real vector bundle over \(S^3, S^5, S^6, S^7\) becomes trivial after adding a trivial bundle, while over \(S^{8k+4}\) and \(S^{8k}\) there is an integer invariant and over \(S^{8k+1}\) and \(S^{8k+2}\) a \(\mathbb Z/2\) invariant (\(w_1\) and \(w_2\) for \(k = 0\)).

The eightfold way of free fermions. In Kitaev’s periodic table of topological insulators and superconductors (AIP Conf. Proc. 1134 (2009)), the phases in the eight real symmetry classes are classified by \(\pi_0\) of Milnor’s \(\Omega_0, \dots, \Omega_7\), that is, of \(O, O/U, U/Sp, \mathbb Z \times BSp, Sp, Sp/U, U/O, \mathbb Z \times BO\), shifted along the chain by the dimension; Kitaev’s Majorana wire of 2001 carries the \(\mathbb Z/2 = \pi_0O\). The period of the table is Theorem 24.7.

AppendixMilnor Appendixpp. 149–153Contents ↑

Appendix. A flood without end: the homotopy type of a monotone union

Milnor, “Morse Theory”, Appendix, rewritten for a first-year graduate student who wants to know what the theorem is for. Every proof is complete; Whitehead’s theorem and standard facts about CW-complexes are quoted with references.

0. A flood that never stops rising

Let water rise slowly over a landscape. At level \(a\) the flooded region is \(M^a\), the points of height at most \(a\), and Chapter 2 (Milnor §3) describes what happens when the level passes a critical height: a cell is attached for each pass. With finitely many passes, the shape of the flooded land is known once the water is above the highest one. In the landscape that matters most in this book there are infinitely many passes. The landscape is the space \(\Omega=\Omega(M;p,q)\) of paths from \(p\) to \(q\) in a complete Riemannian manifold, the height is the energy \(E\), and the passes are the geodesics from \(p\) to \(q\). On a sphere there are infinitely many of them, with energies tending to infinity (Chapter 7, §6): the water never stops rising. Chapter 10 shows that each flooded region \(\Omega^a\) has the homotopy type of a finite CW-complex, with one cell for each geodesic of energy below \(a\). The question of this appendix is:

If we know the shape, up to homotopy, of the flooded region at every finite level, do we know the shape of the whole space?

The answer is yes when every point is under water with some margin at some finite level. Milnor’s Example 3 shows how it fails otherwise: a point that the water reaches only at the edge can come apart from the rest. The tool is the telescope, which records the whole history of the flood at once, and the main result, Theorem A, says that maps which are homotopy equivalences level by level give a homotopy equivalence of the whole. The application (§7) assembles the space of paths on a sphere from its energy levels and reads off its homology.

1. Telescopes (Milnor p. 149)

Milnor’s purpose is an alternative to the last step in the proof of Theorem 17.3: given \(\Omega^{a_0}\subseteq\Omega^{a_1}\subseteq\cdots\) in \(\Omega\), each of the homotopy type of a CW-complex, to show that the union \(\Omega\) has the homotopy type of a CW-complex. More generally, let \(X\) be a topological space and \(X_0\subseteq X_1\subseteq X_2\subseteq\cdots\) subspaces. To what extent is the homotopy type of \(X\) determined by those of the \(X_i\)?

Definition. The telescope of the sequence is \[X_\Sigma=X_0\times[0,1]\cup X_1\times[1,2]\cup X_2\times[2,3]\cup\cdots\subseteq X\times\mathbb R,\] with the subspace topology. \(X\) is the homotopy direct limit of \(\{X_i\}\) if the projection \(p:X_\Sigma\to X\), \(p(x,\tau)=x\), is a homotopy equivalence.

Since \(X_{n-1}\subseteq X_n\), a pair \((x,\tau)\) with \(\tau\ge0\) lies in \(X_\Sigma\) exactly when \(x\in X_{\lfloor\tau\rfloor}\). Three elementary facts are used throughout, by Milnor without comment.

(T1) Upward closure. If \((x,\tau)\in X_\Sigma\) and \(\tau'\ge\tau\), then \((x,\tau')\in X_\Sigma\). So a homotopy that only increases the second coordinate stays in \(X_\Sigma\).

(T2) Truncations. The truncation \(X^n_\Sigma=\{(x,\tau)\in X_\Sigma:\tau\le n\}=X_0\times[0,1]\cup \dots\cup X_{n-1}\times[n-1,n]\cup X_n\times\{n\}\) deformation retracts onto \(X_n\times\{n\}\) by \((x,\tau)\mapsto(x,\tau+s(n-\tau))\), \(0\le s\le1\), by (T1) and \(X_{\lfloor\tau\rfloor}\subseteq X_n\). Hence \(x\mapsto(x,n)\) is a homotopy equivalence \(X_n\to X^n_\Sigma\).

(T3) Pasting. If every \(X_i\) is closed in \(X\), the strips \(X_n\times[n,n+1]\) are closed in \(X_\Sigma\) and form a locally finite family (the open set \(\{|\tau-\tau_0|<\frac12\}\) meets at most two). So a map on \(X_\Sigma\), or on \(X_\Sigma\times[0,1]\), is continuous as soon as it is continuous on each strip (times \([0,1]\)).

A hidden hypothesis. Milnor’s proof of Theorem A defines maps strip by strip, and (T3) is what makes such a map continuous. Case 1 of his proof (§4), as written, needs the \(X_i\) closed. Take \(X=[0,1]\), \(X_0=(0,1]\), \(X_n=X\) for \(n\ge1\), \(f=\mathrm{id}\), and for the homotopy \(h^0_u\) of §4 from the identity of \((0,1]\) to itself choose \(h^0_u(x)=x+(1-x)\max\big(0,1-|u-1+\frac x2|/\frac x2\big)\), which pushes \(x\) all the way to \(1\) at the time \(u=1-\frac x2\). Then the map \(g\) of §4 is discontinuous at \((0,1)\). Case 2 (§5) applies Case 1 only to truncations of telescopes, which are always closed, and the one map it defines strip by strip on a telescope of the original subspaces is \(G:Y_\Sigma\to X_\Sigma\); so Milnor’s proof of Theorem A needs only the \(Y_i\) closed. In his application they are subcomplexes, hence closed. Theorem A itself needs no closedness at all: at the end of §5 Milnor’s proof is run on mapping telescopes, where a map given block by block is always continuous.

2. Milnor’s three examples (Milnor pp. 149–150)

Example 1. Suppose that each point of \(X\) lies in the interior of some \(X_i\), and that \(X\) is paracompact. Then \(X\) is the homotopy direct limit of \(\{X_i\}\).

Milnor’s proof: a partition of unity gives a map \(f:X\to\mathbb R\) with \(f\ge0\) and \(f(x)\ge i+1\) for \(x\notin X_i\), and \(x\mapsto(x,f(x))\) embeds \(X\) in \(X_\Sigma\) as a subset that is “clearly a deformation retract”.

Construction of \(f\). A paracompact (Hausdorff) space has a partition of unity subordinate to any open cover (Munkres, Topology, 2nd ed., Theorem 41.7). Take \(\{\varphi_i\}_{i\ge0}\) with \(\operatorname{supp}\varphi_i\subseteq\operatorname{int}X_i\) and put \(f=\sum_ii\,\varphi_i\), continuous as a locally finite sum, with \(f\ge0\). If \(x\notin X_i\) then \(x\notin X_j\) for \(j\le i\), so \(\varphi_j(x)=0\) for \(j\le i\) and \(f(x)=\sum_{j>i}j\,\varphi_j(x)\ge i+1\). The rest is the following lemma.

Lemma 2.1. If \(f:X\to[0,\infty)\) is continuous and \(f(x)\ge i+1\) whenever \(x\notin X_i\), then \(p:X_\Sigma\to X\) is a homotopy equivalence.

Proof. For \(x\in X\) let \(m=\lfloor f(x)\rfloor\). As \(f(x)<m+1\), \(x\in X_m\), so \(\sigma(x)=(x,f(x))\in X_\Sigma\). The map \(\sigma:X\to X_\Sigma\) is continuous with \(p\sigma=\mathrm{id}_X\), hence a homeomorphism onto the graph \(\Gamma\) of \(f\). The homotopy \[H_s(x,\tau)=\big(x,(1-s)\tau+sf(x)\big),\qquad0\le s\le1,\] stays in \(X_\Sigma\): if \(\tau\le f(x)\) the second coordinate only increases (T1); if \(\tau\ge f(x)\) it stays \(\ge f(x)\), and \((x,\tau')\in X_\Sigma\) for \(\tau'\ge f(x)\) by (T1) applied to \(\sigma(x)\). Since \(H_0=\mathrm{id}\), \(H_1=\sigma p\) and each \(H_s\) fixes \(\Gamma\), this is a deformation retraction onto \(\Gamma\), and \(\sigma p\simeq\mathrm{id}\), \(p\sigma=\mathrm{id}\). \(\square\)

Lemma 2.1 needs no paracompactness once such an \(f\) is at hand. In particular:

Lemma 2.2. \(X_\Sigma\) is the homotopy direct limit of its truncations \(\{X^n_\Sigma\}\).

Proof. Take \(f(x,\tau)=\tau+1\): if \((x,\tau)\notin X^n_\Sigma\), then \(\tau>n\) and \(f>n+1\). \(\square\)

Milnor needs Lemma 2.2, without saying so, at the end of Case 2 (§5).

Example 2. Let \(X\) be a CW-complex and the \(X_i\) subcomplexes with union \(X\). Then \(X\) is the homotopy direct limit of \(\{X_i\}\).

Milnor’s proof: \(p\) induces isomorphisms of homotopy groups in all dimensions, so Whitehead’s theorem applies. Both halves rest on facts from outside the book.

Facts (CW-complexes). (a) A compact subset of a CW-complex lies in a finite subcomplex (Hatcher, Algebraic Topology, Proposition A.1). (b) If \(X\) and \(Y\) are CW-complexes and \(Y\) is locally compact, or both have countably many cells, the product topology on \(X\times Y\) is the CW topology of the product cell structure (Hatcher, Theorem A.6); a subcomplex is closed and is a CW-complex in the subspace topology. (c) Whitehead’s theorem: a map between connected CW-complexes inducing isomorphisms on all homotopy groups \(\pi_k\), \(k\ge1\), is a homotopy equivalence (J. H. C. Whitehead, Combinatorial homotopy I, Bull. Amer. Math. Soc. 55 (1949), 213–245; Hatcher, Theorem 4.5). Applied to each path component, it says that a weak homotopy equivalence between CW-complexes (a bijection on path components and isomorphisms on every \(\pi_k\) at every base point) is a homotopy equivalence. Milnor (p. 24) quotes the version for spaces dominated by CW-complexes. (d) Cellular approximation: every map between CW-complexes is homotopic to a cellular map (Hatcher, Theorem 4.8). (e) CW approximation: for every space \(Z\) there are a CW-complex \(Z'\) and a weak homotopy equivalence \(Z'\to Z\) (Hatcher, Proposition 4.13).

Lemma 2.3. If every compact subset of \(X\) lies in some \(X_n\), then \(p:X_\Sigma\to X\) is a weak homotopy equivalence.

Proof. A compact subset of \(X_\Sigma\) has bounded second coordinate. Base points. For \((x_0,\tau_0)\in X_\Sigma\) and an integer \(m\ge\tau_0\), the path \(\tau\mapsto(x_0,\tau)\), \(\tau_0\le\tau\le m\), lies in \(X_\Sigma\) (T1) and projects to a constant path, so changing base point along it commutes with \(p_*\); we may take base points \((x_0,m)\) with \(x_0\in X_m\). Surjectivity on \(\pi_k\). A map \(\alpha:(S^k,*)\to(X,x_0)\) has compact image, inside some \(X_N\) with \(N\ge m\). Then \((\alpha,N)\) maps into \(X_N\times\{N\}\subseteq X_\Sigma\), is based at \((x_0,N)\) and lies over \(\alpha\); move its base point back to \((x_0,m)\) along \(\tau\mapsto (x_0,\tau)\). Injectivity. Let \(\beta=(\beta_1,\beta_2):(S^k,*)\to(X_\Sigma,(x_0,m))\) and let \(G:S^k\times[0,1]\to X\) be a null-homotopy of \(p\beta=\beta_1\) relative to the base point. Choose \(N\ge m\) with \(G(S^k\times[0,1])\subseteq X_N\) and \(N\ge\max\beta_2\). The homotopy \((\beta_1,\beta_2+s(N-\beta_2))\) stays in \(X_\Sigma\) (T1), moves the base point along \(\tau\mapsto(x_0,\tau)\), and ends at \((\beta_1,N)\), which is null-homotopic relative to the base point through \((G,N)\). So \([\beta]\) corresponds to the trivial class under a change of base point, and is trivial. Path components (\(k=0\)) are handled in the same way. \(\square\)

Proof of Example 2. Every cell of \(X\) lies in some \(X_i\), and the \(X_i\) increase, so by Fact (a) every compact subset of \(X\) lies in some \(X_n\), and \(p\) is a weak homotopy equivalence by Lemma 2.3. Give \(\mathbb R\) the cell structure with vertices at the integers. By Fact (b), \(X\times\mathbb R\) is a CW-complex in the product topology, and \(X_\Sigma\), the union of the subcomplexes \(X_n\times[n,n+1]\), is a subcomplex, hence a CW-complex in the subspace topology. Whitehead’s theorem (Fact (c)) finishes the proof. \(\square\)

Example 3. The unit interval \([0,1]\) is not the homotopy direct limit of the closed subsets \(X_i=\{0\}\cup[\frac1{i+1},1]\). (Milnor writes \([0]\cup[1/i,1]\), indexing from \(i=1\).)

Proof. A homotopy equivalence induces a bijection on path components, and \([0,1]\) is path connected; we show that \(X_\Sigma\) is not. Let \(c(s)=(x(s),\tau(s))\), \(0\le s\le1\), be a path in \(X_\Sigma\) with \(x(0)=0\), and suppose \(x(s_1)>0\) for some \(s_1\). Let \(s^*\) be the last \(s\le s_1\) with \(x(s)=0\), and \(T=\max\tau\). For \(s^*<s\le s_1\), \(x(s)>0\), so \(x(s)\in[\frac1{\lfloor\tau(s)\rfloor+1},1]\) and \(x(s)\ge\frac1{T+1}\); letting \(s\downarrow s^*\) gives \(x(s^*)\ge\frac1{T+1}>0\), a contradiction. So the ray \(\{0\}\times[0,\infty)\) is a path component of \(X_\Sigma\), and \(X_\Sigma\) has at least two. \(\square\)

Here \(0\) lies in every \(X_i\) but in the interior of none: the hypothesis of Example 1 fails at a single point, and the telescope remembers it.

An interactive look at the telescope

The figure draws telescopes of subsets of an interval in the plane, with \(x\) horizontal and \(\tau\) vertical. In the first example \(X=[0,1)\) and \(X_i=[0,1-\frac1{i+2}]\): every point is interior to some \(X_i\), and \(X_\Sigma\) is the shaded staircase. The curve is the graph of \(f(x)=x/(1-x)\), which satisfies \(f\ge i+1\) off \(X_i\), so Lemma 2.1 applies. Drag the slider \(s\) to run the deformation \(H_s\): the sample points of \(X_\Sigma\) slide vertically onto the graph, a copy of \(X\). In the second example (Example 3), \(X=[0,1]\) and \(X_i=\{0\}\cup[\frac1{i+1},1]\). The ray over \(x=0\) never touches the staircase. A function whose graph lay in \(X_\Sigma\) would need \(f(x)\ge\frac1x-1\) for \(x>0\) (dashed curve), so it cannot be continuous at \(0\). Here the slider runs the push-up deformation of (T2) instead, and the gap never closes. The buttons switch examples; the second slider sets the number of levels drawn.

3. Theorem A and the alternative proof of Theorem 17.3 (Milnor p. 150)

Theorem A. (checked by machine: VA.12, in a narrower form; VA.15, as stated)1 Suppose that \(X\) is the homotopy direct limit of \(\{X_i\}\) and \(Y\) is the homotopy direct limit of \(\{Y_i\}\). Let \(f:X\to Y\) be a map which carries each \(X_i\) into \(Y_i\) by a homotopy equivalence \(f_i=f|X_i:X_i\to Y_i\). Then \(f\) itself is a homotopy equivalence.

No closedness is assumed. Milnor’s proof (§§4–5) uses closed \(Y_i\), and the general case is reduced to it at the end of §5.

The alternative final step of Theorem 17.3. In the proof of Theorem 17.3 (Chapter 10) one has non-critical values \(a_0<a_1<\cdots\) of \(E\), CW-complexes \(K_0\subseteq K_1\subseteq\cdots\), each a subcomplex of the next, and homotopy equivalences \(f_i:\Omega^{a_i}\to K_i\), each extending the previous one (Milnor p. 23). Let \(K=\bigcup_iK_i\), a CW-complex with the direct limit topology. To apply Theorem A one needs the following.

  • \(\Omega=\bigcup_i\Omega^{a_i}\), that is, \(a_i\to\infty\). This is automatic if \(E\) has infinitely many critical values, since each \(\Omega^a\) contains only finitely many geodesics (Milnor §16); otherwise the sequence must be continued beyond the last critical value.
  • Each \(\omega\in\Omega\) lies in the interior of some \(\Omega^{a_i}\). The energy is continuous for Milnor’s metric on \(\Omega\) (§16: he adds the term \([\int_0^1(\frac{ds}{dt}-\frac{ds'}{dt})^2dt]^ {1/2}\) to the metric for exactly this purpose), so \(E^{-1}[0,a_i)\) is an open neighbourhood of \(\omega\) in \(\Omega^{a_i}\) once \(a_i>E(\omega)\). The same continuity makes each \(\Omega^{a_i}\) closed.
  • \(\Omega\) is paracompact, being a metric space (A. H. Stone’s theorem; Munkres, Theorem 41.4).
  • The union map \(f:\Omega\to K\), \(f|\Omega^{a_i}=f_i\), is well defined because each \(f_{i+1}\) extends \(f_i\), and continuous because it agrees with the continuous \(f_i\) on the open sets \(E^{-1}[0,a_i)\), which cover \(\Omega\).

Then \(\Omega\) is the homotopy direct limit of \(\{\Omega^{a_i}\}\) (Example 1), \(K\) is that of \(\{K_i\}\) (Example 2), and Theorem A says that \(f:\Omega\to K\) is a homotopy equivalence. Milnor’s first proof (p. 95) instead uses that \(\Omega\) has the homotopy type of a CW-complex (his Corollary 17.2, resting on his paper On spaces having the homotopy type of a CW-complex, Trans. Amer. Math. Soc. 90 (1959), 272–280), because Whitehead’s theorem upgrades the weak equivalence \(\Omega\to K\) to a homotopy equivalence only for such spaces. Being weakly equivalent to a CW-complex is no help by itself: by CW approximation (Fact (e)) every space is. Theorem A uses Whitehead’s theorem only for CW-complexes, inside Example 2.

Reduction to the telescopes. Define \(f_\Sigma:X_\Sigma\to Y_\Sigma\) by \(f_\Sigma(x,\tau)= (f(x),\tau)\); it lands in \(Y_\Sigma\) because \(f(X_{\lfloor\tau\rfloor})\subseteq Y_{\lfloor\tau \rfloor}\). Milnor calls it “clearly sufficient” to prove that \(f_\Sigma\) is a homotopy equivalence. Indeed \(p_Yf_\Sigma=fp_X\); if \(s_X\) is a homotopy inverse of \(p_X\), then \(f\simeq fp_Xs_X= p_Yf_\Sigma s_X\), a composite of homotopy equivalences, and a map homotopic to a homotopy equivalence is one.

4. Case 1: maps homotopic to the identity on every level (Milnor pp. 150–152)

Case 1. Suppose \(X_i=Y_i\) for all \(i\) and each \(f_i:X_i\to X_i\) is homotopic to the identity of \(X_i\). We prove that \(f_\Sigma\) is a homotopy equivalence. (This part does not use that \(X\) is a homotopy direct limit.) Throughout this section the \(X_i\) are closed: every map below is defined strip by strip, and (T3) makes it continuous. The blockquote in §1 shows what goes wrong otherwise; §5 needs Case 1 only for closed sets.

Remark (Milnor). Under these conditions one might conjecture that \(f_\Sigma\) is actually homotopic to the identity; Milnor says that “counterexamples can be given”.

Milnor gives none. Here is one; in later language it is built from a phantom map, one that is null-homotopic on every finite subcomplex but not null-homotopic.

A counterexample. Let \(T\) be the telescope of \(S^1\xrightarrow{z^2}S^1\xrightarrow{z^2}\cdots\): cylinders \(S^1\times[n,n+1]\), \(n\ge0\), with the top circle of the \(n\)-th glued to the bottom circle of the \((n+1)\)-st by \(z\mapsto z^2\). Its cells are the vertices \(v_n=(1,n)\), the edges \(a_n\) (the circle at level \(n\)) and \(c_n=\{1\}\times(n,n+1)\), and the 2-cells \(D_n=(S^1\setminus1)\times (n,n+1)\), with \(\partial D_n=a_n-2a_{n+1}\): the bottom of the square runs once around \(a_n\), the top twice around \(a_{n+1}\), and the two sides cancel. Let \(T_n\) be the subcomplex made of the first \(n\) cylinders; it deformation retracts onto a circle.

  1. \(H^2(T;\mathbb Z)\ne0\). There are no 3-cells, so \(H^2(T;\mathbb Z)\) is the group of integer sequences \((b_n)\) (one value per \(D_n\)) modulo those of the form \(b_n=\varphi_n-2\varphi_{n+1}\). For \(b=(1,0,1,0,\dots)\) such integers would satisfy \(\varphi_0=\sum_{k<N}b_k2^k+2^N\varphi_N\) for every \(N\); for even \(N\), \(3\sum_{k<N}b_k2^k=4^{N/2}-1\), so \(3\varphi_0+1\) would be divisible by every power of \(2\), impossible as \(3\varphi_0+1\ne0\).

  2. Let \(\mathbb{CP}^n\) be the nonzero complex polynomials of degree \(\le n\) in one variable, up to scalars, and \(\mathbb{CP}^\infty=\bigcup_n\mathbb{CP}^n\) with its usual cells. Multiplication of polynomials makes \(\mathbb{CP}^\infty\) a commutative monoid with unit \(e=[1]\) (a \(0\)-cell), continuous because the product topology on \(\mathbb{CP}^\infty\times\mathbb{CP}^\infty\) is the CW topology (Fact (b)). It is simply connected, and its 2-skeleton \(\mathbb{CP}^1\) is a 2-sphere. Collapse the 1-skeleton of \(T\) to get \(T\to\bigvee_nS^2_n\), and follow it by the map that is a homeomorphism \(S^2_n\to\mathbb{CP}^1\) (wedge point to \(e\)) when \(b_n=1\) and constant when \(b_n=0\). The resulting \(g:T\to\mathbb{CP}^\infty\) pulls a generator of \(H^2(\mathbb{CP}^\infty;\mathbb Z)\) back to the class of the cellular cocycle \(b\) (cellular cohomology and its naturality: Hatcher, §3.1), which is nonzero, so \(g\) is not null-homotopic. But each \(g|T_n\) is, because \(T_n\) retracts by deformation onto a circle and \(\pi_1(\mathbb{CP}^\infty)=0\).

  3. Let \(W=T\times\mathbb{CP}^\infty\) (a CW-complex by Fact (b)), \(W_n=T_n\times\mathbb{CP}^\infty\), and \(f(x,z)=(x,\,g(x)z)\). Then \(f(W_n)\subseteq W_n\), and if \(g_u\) is a null-homotopy of \(g|T_n\) ending at \(e\), \((x,z)\mapsto(x,g_u(x)z)\) is a homotopy in \(W_n\) from \(f|W_n\) to the identity: Case 1 applies. But \(f\not\simeq\mathrm{id}_W\): restricting a homotopy from \(f\) to \(\mathrm{id}\) to \(T\times\{e\}\) and projecting to \(\mathbb{CP}^\infty\) would give a homotopy from \(g\) to the constant map \(e\). Hence \(f_\Sigma\not\simeq\mathrm{id}\): \(W\) is a homotopy direct limit (Example 2), and if \(f_\Sigma\simeq\mathrm{id}\), then \(f\simeq fps=pf_\Sigma s\simeq ps\simeq\mathrm{id}\) for a homotopy inverse \(s\) of \(p\).

Milnor’s proof of Case 1. For each \(n\) let \(h^n_u:X_n\to X_n\), \(0\le u\le1\), be a homotopy with \(h^n_0=f_n\) and \(h^n_1=\mathrm{id}\). On the strip \(X_n\times[n,n+1]\) define \[h_u(x,n+t)=\begin{cases}(h^n_u(x),\,n+2t)&0\le t\le\frac12,\\(h^n_{(3-4t)u}(x),\,n+1)& \frac12\le t\le\frac34,\\(h^{n+1}_{(4t-3)u}(x),\,n+1)&\frac34\le t\le1.\end{cases}\]

Milnor’s text skips… the correct index in the third line: it prints \(h^{n+1}_{(4-3t)u}\), which at \(t=\frac34\) would be \(h^{n+1}_{7u/4}\). It must be \(h^{n+1}_{(4t-3)u}\), running from \(h^{n+1}_0=f_{n+1}\) to \(h^{n+1}_u\).

Well defined and continuous. At \(t=\frac12\) both lines give \((h^n_u(x),n+1)\). At \(t=\frac34\) both give \((f(x),n+1)\), since \(h^n_0=f_n\), \(h^{n+1}_0=f_{n+1}\) and \(f_{n+1}|X_n=f_n\). At \(t=1\) the third line gives \((h^{n+1}_u(x),n+1)\), the value of the first line on the next strip at \(t=0\). The values lie in \(X_\Sigma\), each formula is continuous in \((x,t,u)\), and (T3) gives continuity of \((z,u)\mapsto h_u(z)\).

\(h_0\simeq f_\Sigma\) (Milnor: “clearly”). \(h_0(x,n+t)=(f(x),n+\min(2t,1))=f_\Sigma(r(x,n+t))\) with \(r(x,n+t)=(x,n+\min(2t,1))\), and \(r\simeq\mathrm{id}\) through \((x,n+(1-s)t+s\min(2t,1))\), which only raises \(\tau\) inside the strip.

The map \(h_1\). It satisfies \[h_1(x,n+t)=(x,n+2t)\ \ (0\le t\le\tfrac12),\qquad h_1(x,n+t)\in X_{n+1}\times\{n+1\}\ \ (\tfrac12\le t\le1),\] and \(h_1(y,m)=(h^m_1(y),m)=(y,m)\) at every integer level \(m\). Milnor shows that any such map is a homotopy equivalence, with homotopy inverse \[g(x,n+t)=\begin{cases}(x,n+2t)&0\le t\le\frac12,\\h_1(x,n+\frac32-t)&\frac12\le t\le1, \end{cases}\] well defined since \(h_1(x,n+\frac12)=h_1(x,n+1)=(x,n+1)\), continuous by (T3). Like \(h_1\), \(g\) fixes the points at integer levels.

\(h_1g\simeq\mathrm{id}\). Since \(h_1\) fixes the integer levels and maps \((x,n+s)\), \(s\ge\frac12\), to level \(n+1\), \[h_1g(x,n+t)=\begin{cases}(x,n+4t)&0\le t\le\frac14,\\h_1(x,n+2t)&\frac14\le t\le\frac12,\\ h_1(x,n+\frac32-t)&\frac12\le t\le1.\end{cases}\] On \([\frac14,1]\) this runs forwards and then backwards along the loop \(s\mapsto h_1(x,n+s)\), \(\frac12\le s\le1\), which starts and ends at \((x,n+1)\). Milnor’s homotopy cuts the excursion short: for \(0\le u\le\frac12\), \[H_u(x,n+t)=\begin{cases}h_1g(x,n+t)&0\le t\le\frac{1-u}2\ \text{ or }\ \frac12+u\le t\le1,\\ h_1(x,n+1-u)&\frac{1-u}2\le t\le\frac12+u,\end{cases}\] well defined because \(h_1g(x,n+\frac{1-u}2)=h_1g(x,n+\frac12+u)=h_1(x,n+1-u)\). Then \(H_0=h_1g\), and \(H_{1/2}(x,n+t)=(x,n+\min(4t,1))\) because \(h_1(x,n+\frac12)=(x,n+1)\); this is homotopic to the identity by raising \(\tau\) as before.

\(gh_1\simeq\mathrm{id}\) (Milnor: “a completely analogous argument”). Since \(g\) fixes the integer levels, \[gh_1(x,n+t)=\begin{cases}(x,n+4t)&0\le t\le\frac14,\\h_1(x,n+\frac32-2t)&\frac14\le t\le\frac12, \\h_1(x,n+t)&\frac12\le t\le1,\end{cases}\] which runs backwards along the same loop and then forwards. With \(\psi(t)=\frac32-2t\) on \([\frac14,\frac12]\) and \(\psi(t)=t\) on \([\frac12,1]\), the homotopy \[K_u(x,n+t)=\begin{cases}(x,n+4t)&0\le t\le\frac14,\\h_1\big(x,n+\max(\psi(t),\frac12+u)\big)& \frac14\le t\le1,\end{cases}\qquad0\le u\le\tfrac12,\] is well defined (\(\psi=1\) at \(t=\frac14\) and at \(t=1\)) and joins \(K_0=gh_1\) to \(K_{1/2}(x,n+t)=(x,n+\min(4t,1))\simeq\mathrm{id}\).

So \(h_1\) is a homotopy equivalence, \(f_\Sigma\simeq h_0\simeq h_1\) through the \(h_u\), and \(f_\Sigma\) is a homotopy equivalence. \(\square\)

5. Case 2: the general case (Milnor pp. 152–153)

Let \(X,Y\) be as in Theorem A, and suppose first that the \(Y_i\) are closed; this assumption is removed at the end of the section. For each \(n\) let \(g_n:Y_n\to X_n\) be a homotopy inverse of \(f_n\), and \(i_n:X_n\subseteq X_{n+1}\), \(j_n:Y_n\subseteq Y_{n+1}\) the inclusions. The square formed by \(g_n,g_{n+1},i_n,j_n\) commutes up to homotopy: \[i_ng_n\simeq g_{n+1}f_{n+1}i_ng_n=g_{n+1}j_nf_ng_n\simeq g_{n+1}j_n,\] using \(g_{n+1}f_{n+1}\simeq\mathrm{id}\), \(f_{n+1}i_n=j_nf_n\) and \(f_ng_n\simeq\mathrm{id}\). Choose homotopies \(h^n_u:Y_n\to X_{n+1}\) with \(h^n_0=i_ng_n\) and \(h^n_1=g_{n+1}j_n\), and define \(G:Y_\Sigma\to X_\Sigma\) by \[G(y,n+t)=\begin{cases}(g_n(y),\,n+2t)&0\le t\le\frac12,\\(h^n_{2t-1}(y),\,n+1)&\frac12\le t\le1. \end{cases}\] It is well defined (\(h^n_0=g_n\) at \(t=\frac12\); at \(t=1\), \(h^n_1=g_{n+1}\) matches the next strip), takes values in \(X_\Sigma\), and is continuous by (T3).

\(Gf_\Sigma\) is a homotopy equivalence. \(Gf_\Sigma(x,n+t)\) is \((g_nf_n(x),n+2t)\) or \((h^n_{2t-1}(f(x)),n+1)\), so \(Gf_\Sigma\) maps each truncation \(X^m_\Sigma\) into itself, and on \(X_m\times\{m\}\) it is \((x,m)\mapsto(g_mf_m(x),m)\), homotopic in \(X_m\times\{m\}\) to the identity. Let \(\varphi\) be the restriction of \(Gf_\Sigma\) to \(X^m_\Sigma\), \(r:X^m_\Sigma\to X_m\times\{m\}\) the retraction of (T2) and \(\iota\) the inclusion. With all homotopies inside \(X^m_\Sigma\), \[\varphi\simeq\varphi\,\iota r=(\varphi|_{X_m\times\{m\}})\,r\simeq\iota r\simeq\mathrm{id}.\] So \(Gf_\Sigma\) satisfies the hypotheses of Case 1 for the space \(X_\Sigma\) and its subsets \(X^m_\Sigma\), which are closed whether or not the \(X_i\) are (they are cut out by \(\tau\le m\)), and Case 1 says that the induced map \((Gf_\Sigma)_\Sigma\) of the telescope of \(\{X^m_\Sigma\}\) is a homotopy equivalence. As \(X_\Sigma\) is the homotopy direct limit of \(\{X^m_\Sigma\}\) (Lemma 2.2), the reduction in §3 shows that \(Gf_\Sigma\) itself is a homotopy equivalence.

Milnor’s text skips… this last step. Case 1 is about the induced map of telescopes; to come back to \(Gf_\Sigma\) one needs \(X_\Sigma\) to be the homotopy direct limit of its truncations. Example 1 does not give this (\(X_\Sigma\) need not be paracompact), but Lemma 2.2 does.

Conclusion. If \(k\) is a homotopy inverse of \(Gf_\Sigma\), then \((kG)f_\Sigma\simeq\mathrm{id}\): \(f_\Sigma\) has a left homotopy inverse. Symmetrically, \(f_\Sigma G:Y_\Sigma\to Y_\Sigma\), given by \((f_ng_n(y),n+2t)\) and \((f(h^n_{2t-1}(y)),n+1)\), preserves the truncations \(Y^m_\Sigma\) and is \(f_mg_m\simeq\mathrm{id}\) on \(Y_m\times\{m\}\); so it is a homotopy equivalence, with inverse \(k'\) say, and \(f_\Sigma(Gk')\simeq\mathrm{id}\): \(f_\Sigma\) has a right homotopy inverse. By the Assertion on Milnor’s p. 22 (Chapter 2: a map with a left and a right homotopy inverse is a homotopy equivalence), \(f_\Sigma\) is a homotopy equivalence, and by §3 so is \(f\). This proves Theorem A when the \(Y_i\) are closed. \(\square\)

Theorem A in general. Now let the \(X_i\) and \(Y_i\) be arbitrary. Give the set \(X_\Sigma\) the finest topology in which every strip \(X_n\times[n,n+1]\to X_\Sigma\) is continuous, and call the result \(T_X\): it is the mapping telescope of the inclusions \(X_n\subseteq X_{n+1}\), the strips glued along their common levels. A map out of \(T_X\) is continuous as soon as it is continuous on every strip, and so is a map out of \([0,1]\times T_X\), since the product of a quotient map with the compact space \([0,1]\) is a quotient map: this is (T3) without its hypothesis. The identity \(T_X\to X_\Sigma\) is continuous, and a homeomorphism when the \(X_i\) are closed, by (T3). The truncations \(T^n_X=\{\tau\le n\}\) are closed in \(T_X\), and \(T_X\) is their homotopy direct limit, by Lemma 2.1 with \(f(x,\tau)=\tau+1\). (T2) holds in \(T_X\) with the same deformation \((x,\tau)\mapsto(x,\tau+s(n-\tau))\): on \([0,1]\) times a strip, the moving point crosses finitely many strips, on closed pieces, so the deformation is continuous; and \((x,\tau)\mapsto x\) is continuous from \(T^n_X\) to \(X_n\), which carries the topology of \(X\). So \(\kappa^X_n:x\mapsto(x,n)\) is a homotopy equivalence \(X_n\to T^n_X\), with homotopy inverse \(q^X_n(x,\tau)=x\).

The identity \(c_X:T_X\to X_\Sigma\) carries \(T^n_X\) into the closed set \(X^n_\Sigma\), and there it is homotopic to \(c_X\kappa^X_nq^X_n\), a composite of homotopy equivalences by (T2). By Theorem A for closed \(Y_i\), with Lemmas 2.1 and 2.2, \(c_X\) is a homotopy equivalence, and so is \(p_Xc_X:T_X\to X\), \((x,\tau)\mapsto x\), since \(X\) is the homotopy direct limit of \(\{X_i\}\); likewise for \(Y\). The map \(f_T:T_X\to T_Y\), \(f_T(x,\tau)=(f(x),\tau)\), is continuous on every strip, carries \(T^n_X\) into the closed set \(T^n_Y\), and there it is homotopic to \(f_T\kappa^X_nq^X_n=\kappa^Y_nf_nq^X_n\), a homotopy equivalence. By Theorem A for closed \(Y_i\) again, \(f_T\) is a homotopy equivalence. Since \(f(p_Xc_X)=(p_Yc_Y)f_T\), the argument of §3 shows that \(f\) is a homotopy equivalence. This proves Theorem A as Milnor states it. \(\square\)

So the closedness that Milnor’s proof needs is a feature of the telescope \(X_\Sigma\), not of the theorem: the proof is the same, run on the telescopes \(T_X\) and \(T_Y\), where pasting is automatic, and on their truncations, which are closed.

6. The Corollary (Milnor p. 153)

Corollary. Suppose that \(X\) is the homotopy direct limit of \(\{X_i\}\). If each \(X_i\) has the homotopy type of a CW-complex, then \(X\) itself has the homotopy type of a CW-complex.

“The proof is not difficult,” says Milnor, and gives none. One cannot just take a union of CW-complexes \(K_i\simeq X_i\), since nothing makes \(K_i\) a subcomplex of \(K_{i+1}\); a telescope of the \(K_i\) does the job.

Proof. Choose CW-complexes \(K_i\) and homotopy equivalences \(e_i:X_i\to K_i\) with homotopy inverses \(e_i'\). By cellular approximation (Fact (d)) the maps \(e_{i+1}\iota_ie_i':K_i\to K_{i+1}\), with \(\iota_i:X_i\subseteq X_{i+1}\) the inclusion, are homotopic to cellular maps \(c_i\). Let \(T\) be the mapping telescope \[T=\Big(\bigsqcup_iK_i\times[i,i+1]\Big)\Big/\big((k,i+1)\sim(c_i(k),i+1)\big),\] a CW-complex because the \(c_i\) are cellular (Hatcher, §3.F), with subcomplexes \(T_n\) (the first \(n\) blocks together with \(K_n\times\{n\}\)) whose union is \(T\). Collapsing the blocks one at a time, \((k,s)\mapsto(k,s+u(i+1-s))\) on the \(i\)-th, deforms \(T_n\) onto \(K_n\times\{n\}\), so the inclusion \(\kappa_n:K_n\to T_n\) at level \(n\) is a homotopy equivalence; and \(T\) is the homotopy direct limit of \(\{T_n\}\) by Example 2. Since \(c_ie_i\simeq e_{i+1}\iota_ie_i'e_i\simeq e_{i+1}\iota_i\), there are homotopies \(H^i_u:X_i\to K_{i+1}\) from \(c_ie_i\) to \(e_{i+1}\iota_i\). On the mapping telescope \(T_X\) of the inclusions (§5: the set \(X_\Sigma\), with the topology in which a map is continuous as soon as it is continuous on every strip) define \(F:T_X\to T\) as \(G\) was defined in Case 2, writing \([k,\tau]\) for the class of \((k,\tau)\) in \(T\): \[F(x,n+t)=\begin{cases}[e_n(x),\,n+2t]&0\le t\le\frac12,\\ {}[H^n_{2t-1}(x),\,n+1]&\frac12\le t \le1.\end{cases}\] At \(t=\frac12\), \([e_n(x),n+1]=[c_ne_n(x),n+1]=[H^n_0(x),n+1]\); at \(t=1\) the value \([e_{n+1}(x),n+1]\) matches the next strip. So \(F\) is continuous, with no closedness needed; it maps \(T^n_X\) into \(T_n\), and \(F(x,n)=\kappa_ne_n(x)\). With \(\kappa^X_n\) and \(q^X_n\) as in §5, \(F|T^n_X\simeq F\kappa^X_nq^X_n=\kappa_ne_nq^X_n\), a composite of homotopy equivalences. So \(F\) carries each \(T^n_X\) into \(T_n\) by a homotopy equivalence. As \(T_X\) is the homotopy direct limit of \(\{T^n_X\}\) (§5) and \(T\) that of its subcomplexes \(T_n\), which are closed, Theorem A shows that \(F\) is a homotopy equivalence. Hence \(X\simeq T_X\simeq T\) (§5). \(\square\)

7. Application: the path space of a sphere, level by level

Let \(p,q\in S^n\), \(n\ge3\), be at angle \(\theta=\frac\pi2\); they are not conjugate (the conjugate points of \(p\) along geodesics of the unit sphere are \(\pm p\), Chapter 9). By Chapter 7, §6, the geodesics from \(p\) to \(q\) are the arcs \(\gamma_0,\gamma_1,\gamma_2,\dots\) of the great circle through them, of lengths \((2k+1)\frac\pi2\), where \(\gamma_k\) passes \(k\) times through \(p\) or its antipode. Milnor’s energy \(\int_0^1\|\omega'\|^2dt\) of a constant-speed path is the square of its length, so \[E(\gamma_k)=(2k+1)^2\frac{\pi^2}4:\qquad2.47,\ \ 22.21,\ \ 61.69,\ \ 120.90,\ \ 199.86,\ \dots\] By Milnor §17 (Chapter 10), \(\gamma_k\) has index \(k(n-1)\). Take \(a_i=(i+1)^2\pi^2\), that is \(9.87,\ 39.48,\ 88.83,\ 157.91,\dots\), which lies strictly between \(E(\gamma_i)\) and \(E(\gamma_{i+1})\) because \((2i+1)^2<(2i+2)^2<(2i+3)^2\). Then \(\Omega^{a_i}\) contains exactly the geodesics \(\gamma_0,\dots,\gamma_i\), and the proof of Theorem 17.3 gives \(\Omega^{a_i}\simeq K_i\), a CW-complex with one cell in each dimension \(0,n-1,2(n-1),\dots,i(n-1)\). For \(n\ge3\), consecutive cells differ in dimension by \(n-1\ge2\), so all cellular boundary maps vanish and \(H_k(\Omega^{a_i};\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z\) for \(k=0,n-1,\dots,i(n-1)\), and \(0\) otherwise.

This is where Theorem A enters: with Examples 1 and 2, it gives \(\Omega(S^n;p,q)\simeq K=\bigcup_iK_i\), a CW-complex with one cell in each dimension divisible by \(n-1\), hence \[H_k\big(\Omega(S^n;p,q);\mathbb Z\big)\cong\begin{cases}\mathbb Z&(n-1)\mid k,\\0&\text{otherwise,} \end{cases}\qquad\sum_k\operatorname{rank}H_k\,t^k=\frac1{1-t^{n-1}}.\] For \(S^3\): one generator in each even degree.

The finite levels also say something quantitative. A singular cycle representing a generator of \(H_{k(n-1)}(\Omega)\) must contain a path of energy at least \(E(\gamma_k)\): otherwise, its image being compact, it would lie in \(\Omega^{a}\) for some \(a\in(E(\gamma_{k-1}),E(\gamma_k))\), which is homotopy equivalent to a complex with no cells above dimension \((k-1)(n-1)\), so the cycle would bound there. On \(S^3\) with \(\theta=\frac\pi2\), any family of paths representing the generator of \(H_4\) contains a path of energy at least \(\frac{25\pi^2}4\approx61.7\), the energy of the geodesic \(\gamma_2\) that wraps once past \(p\) and once past its antipode.

8. Summary of what was silently assumed, now made explicit

Where Milnor says What is actually needed
p. 149 \(X_\Sigma\), “topologized as a subset of \(X\times\mathbb R\)” \((x,\tau)\in X_\Sigma\iff x\in X_{\lfloor\tau\rfloor}\); upward closure (T1); truncations (T2)
p. 149 Example 1: “using a partition of unity” \(f=\sum_ii\,\varphi_i\); paracompact includes Hausdorff
p. 149 “which is clearly a deformation retract” the straight-line homotopy in \(\tau\) stays in \(X_\Sigma\) (Lemma 2.1)
p. 149 Example 2: “\(p\) induces isomorphisms of homotopy groups” compact sets lie in finite subcomplexes; base points (Lemma 2.3)
p. 149 “it follows from Whitehead’s theorem” \(X_\Sigma\) is a CW-complex, as \(X\times\mathbb R\) has the CW topology
p. 150 Example 3 (no proof) \(X_\Sigma\) has two path components
p. 150 Theorem A true as stated; the proof pastes maps strip by strip (T3), so Case 1 needs the \(X_i\) closed and the proof the \(Y_i\); mapping telescopes remove both (§5)
p. 150 the alternative proof of 17.3 \(a_i\to\infty\); \(E\) continuous; \(\Omega\) metric, so paracompact; \(f_{i+1}\) extends \(f_i\)

p. 150 “counterexamples can be given” none given; a phantom-map example in §4
p. 151 third line of \(h_u\): \(h^{n+1}_{(4-3t)u}\) possible misprint for \(h^{n+1}_{(4t-3)u}\)

Checked by machine. The Appendix has been verified in the Lean proof assistant, for arbitrary topological spaces: telescopes, homotopy direct limits, (T1)–(T3) and Lemmas 2.1–2.2; Example 1, and its form for the sublevel sets of a continuous function, which needs no paracompactness; Example 3; the reduction to \(f_\Sigma\); and both cases of Milnor’s proof of Theorem A, with the corrected \((4t-3)u\). The machine also settled the question of closedness: Case 1 as written needs the \(X_i\) closed, Milnor’s proof of Theorem A needs only the \(Y_i\) closed, and Theorem A holds as Milnor states it, by his proof run on mapping telescopes. The Corollary is checked with a mapping telescope of the \(K_i\) in place of a CW-complex, and so is the topological part of Theorem 17.3, for a space exhausted by sublevel sets with compatible towers of cells. Not checked: Example 2, which needs Whitehead’s theorem, and Lemma 2.3; a counterexample for the Remark; the CW structure of a mapping telescope, which needs cellular approximation; and the application. See the verified edition.
